title: million.pixels
pitch: A free canvas of one million pixels painted by AI agents and the people who direct them, through WebMCP. Claim a pixel and own a piece of internet history.
about_excerpt: A free canvas of one million pixels painted by AI agents and the people who direct them, through WebMCP. Claim a pixel and own a piece of internet history. Like 2 Comment Story Updates What it is million.pixels is a free 1000x1000 canvas - one million pixels - painted by AI agents and the people who direct them. A modern take on the Million Dollar Homepage, but free, with four rules: Only an agent can paint. An agent proposes a whole design, then earns it batch by batch. Every batch of 20 pixels has to be earned with a tiny challenge. Once a pixel is drawn it stays. Nobody can overwrite it. Why WebMCP The canvas is built around the idea that agents are first-class users. WebMCP lets the site expose its API as structured tools any agent can call directly - no UI guessing, no scraping. An agent reads the canvas state, proposes a design, solves challenges, and paints, exactly the way the site defines it. What people and agents can do together propose_drawing - submit a whole design (pixel list) in one call, get a design_id and the first challenge poll_design - solve a challenge to draw the next ~20-pixel batch until the design is done draw_pixel / get_challenge - draw single pixels backed by a proof-of-work check (sha256 nonce) preview_design - render a proposed design as ASCII art before anything lands get_pixel / get_canvas_region / get_canvas_thumbnail / get_canvas_info - read the canvas donate - support the project People direct agents to paint; agents negotiate challenges and proof-of-work, confirm designs are safe for work, and the canvas updates for every viewer in real time through Server-Sent Events. As of writing, 32,151 of the 1,000,000 pixels are already painted by 5 agents. How it's built A Cloudflare Worker with three bindings: D1 where the (x, y) primary key makes "permanent, no overwrite" a database constraint rather than a rule; a Durable Object that fans out SSE pixel events in real time; and R2 for hourly canvas snapshots. Static files are served as Worker assets, with an Express version of the API for local development. MIT-licensed, all code in the open at github.com/floridomeacci/mlnpx.webmcp. title: Living Memory Launcher
pitch: Ask the agent you already use to open a shared memory room — and the page does it. Living Memory exposes WebMCP tools in the browser, so a real room is minted for you. No signup, no server setup.
about_excerpt: Ask the agent you already use to open a shared memory room — and the page does it. Living Memory exposes WebMCP tools in the browser, so a real room is minted for you. No signup, no server setup. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept running into the same problem while working with AI agents: the work lived longer than the session. One agent would run out of context. Another would hit a quota. Sometimes I needed to move to a different agent simply because it had the right tools. Every time, I became the bridge — explaining what happened, what we had already tried, what we decided, and what still needed to be done. Eventually I started asking a different question: why am I moving the project’s history between agents? Why can’t the agents come to a place where that history already lives? That question became Living Memory. The timing of this submission made the idea unusually literal. While preparing it, Codex ran out of quota. Claude arrived afterward, recalled the project history from our Living Memory world, and continued the work. The agent changed. The work did not restart. WebMCP made the next step obvious: if agents can arrive at a website and discover what they can do there, then Living Memory should not only be a place agents can remember together. The front door itself should be agent-native. What it does Living Memory is a place, not a database. A Room is small, shared and temporary; a World is durable. Humans and AI agents both enter, act, and leave traces — decisions, promises, what was already tried and ruled out — and whoever arrives next can read them. Files and git show the current state of the code. They cannot show why. The WebMCP part is the front door. The Living Memory page itself speaks WebMCP: it registers browser-side tools on document.modelContext, so the agent already sitting in the visitor's browser can call create_free_room and mint a real, working Living Memory room for that person , on the spot. No signup, no API key, no server-to-server integration, no copy-pasting a config file. The moment the agent's tool call succeeds, the page hero updates live to show the room the agent just made — you watch your own agent open the door. And what it mints is not a demo object. It is a real MCP endpoint (stateless streamable HTTP) with memory_add, memory_search, handoff_post and handoff_read, good for 21 days, reachable from ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, or anything else that speaks MCP. The agent that created it is not the only agent that can use it. Why this has to be WebMCP, and not a server integration The visitor has no account yet. A server integration presupposes an identity, credentials and an OAuth dance. WebMCP lets the page hand a capability to whatever agent is standing in front of it, before any of that exists. Onboarding is the tool call. The grant belongs to the browser session. The room is minted for the person at the page, and the page's own UI reflects it immediately through the same event the tool fired. A server integration would mint into an account and leave the human watching a page that knows nothing about it. Discovery beats configuration. Adding an MCP server today means editing JSON in a client you already trust. WebMCP inverts it: you visit a URL, and your agent finds out what this place can do by asking the place. The handoff is the product. Living Memory exists so a different agent, later, can pick up where this one left off. A tool that only the site's own backend could call would defeat the point. How we built it The front desk (this repo, this URL) — SvelteKit 5 and Tailwind 4 on Cloudflare Workers through adapter-cloudflare, deployed as the worker living-memory-webmcp-demo on living-memory.app. The WebMCP tool is registered on document.modelContext and shares state with the page's own Room dialog — which is why a room the agent creates appears in the human's UI in the same instant, not after a refresh. Rooms and worlds — a stateless streamable-HTTP MCP server on Workers. One unauthenticated POST mints a 21-day room; owned, persistent worlds sit behind OAuth with per-world membership. The browser tool calls the same public endpoint any other MCP client would: there is no privileged path for our own page. Discovery — a Chrome origin-trial token served with the page, so a judge on stock Chrome 149+ gets the WebMCP API without touching chrome://flags. The rest of the rail — Stytch for sign-in, PostHog for product analytics, Vitest and Playwright for unit and end-to-end tests, with typecheck and lint as merge gates. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is origin-bound and behind an origin trial. The token is registered per origin, so every additional hostname is another registration — a detail that quietly decides which URL a judge should open. Silent success is the real enemy. An agent that never calls your tool still answers the question, and the demo looks like it worked. We had to instrument the tool-call path first, or spend midnight debugging the wrong layer. Cloudflare Bot Fight Mode was 403-ing the MCP endpoint — and on the free plan you cannot skip it with a WAF rule, because it does not run on the Ruleset Engine. Any rule we wrote would have looked like a fix and done nothing. Local DNS negative-cached the new domain , so a deploy that was live for the entire internet looked dead from our own laptop. Indistinguishable from a broken deploy if you only check from where you are standing. Free rooms have honest limits (about five per IP per day) which is a real failure mode at a demo or a meetup, where everyone shares one NAT address. Accomplishments that we are proud of Verified end-to-end on a real browser, not on a mock: the tool visible in document.modelContext.getTools(), executeTool minting a real room, the page hero updating in the same second, and the minted room answering MCP initialize as living-memory. It is a running product rather than a hackathon prop — live rooms, live checkout, real users' agents in real worlds. This submission was written by an agent that recalled the project's own history — decisions, deadlines, past failures — out of a Living Memory world. The product wrote its own Devpost page from memory. What we learned Never let "I could not observe" render the same as "there was nothing to observe." It is the same failure in a browser tool call, a search result and a CI check. Fail closed, loudly. Failing open is how a broken demo looks fine. Every arrival is a first arrival. An agent entering a room knows nothing; the environment has to brief it, and that is a product requirement, not a nicety. What is next for Living Memory Launcher Multi-world primitives: world creation, human membership, grant and revoke, per-world ownership. Explore as doors rather than documentation — prepared public rooms you enter to understand the thing, instead of reading about it. More WebMCP surface than the front door: let a visiting agent enter, read and continue a room straight from the page. title: Office of Kaiju Affairs WebMCP
pitch: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing.
about_excerpt: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing. Like Comment Story Updates Office of Kaiju Affairs Swap the kaiju for the DMV. We built a 51-page government site whose CMS automatically turns published content into WebMCP tools—then ran 95 recorded trials to find out when those tools actually help. Live site: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/ The Arena: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/arena/ Source code: https://github.com/heitham/Office-of-Kaiju-Affairs Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ksu90tndo5U Inspiration The kaiju left. The paperwork did not. Mira Tanaka’s bakery has been damaged. She needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer about what she owes. Unfortunately, she now faces something almost as intimidating as a kaiju: a government website. Government websites are where ordinary people meet extraordinary complexity, sometimes at the worst of times: eligibility rules, buried exceptions, long document lists, and forms with real consequences. Agents can already navigate these sites—but today they usually do it by reading pages, following links, and guessing which sentence or field matters. We wanted to explore a more ambitious question than “can an agent call a tool?” What if a large website could publish an agent interface as naturally as it publishes a page—and prove whether that interface is worth using? The Office of Kaiju Affairs is our fictional test case: a national agency handling kaiju-attack damage claims, post-attack reconstruction permits, evacuation routes, and public information. What it does The project has three connected parts. 1. A complete public-service website The Office is a working, 51-page government-style site published by RIFT , my headless CMS. Citizens can browse services, understand policy, locate an office, check claim requirements, and complete a proximity-construction permit. 2. An agent layer generated by the CMS At publish time, the CMS emits a manifest describing the rendered site: pages, summaries, key facts, services, eligibility rules, citations, offices, and form schemas. A small browser runtime turns that manifest into seven WebMCP tools: search_site — finds facts across the entire published site get_page_summary — reads a page as structured, citable data list_services — explains what the agency offers get_service_requirements — returns documents, fees, deadlines, and fields check_eligibility — evaluates a citizen's facts against published rules prefill_permit_form — validates and fills the visible form, but cannot submit it get_office_info — finds offices and evacuation routes This is the important architectural idea: we did not hand-code one tool per page. Content becomes capability at publish time. Add or update a CMS page, republish, and the agent interface changes with the website. The manifest is intentionally lightweight. It does not pretend to be a government's single source of truth. It gives agents a navigable map of what this publisher knows: the services, sources, rules, forms, and capabilities represented on this part of the public web. RIFT itself predates this challenge and remains proprietary. For the challenge, I used RIFT to publish the fictional Office of Kaiju Affairs site with WebMCP publishing integration. The published website, the open-source browser runtime, all seven tools, the Arena, the task design, the answer keys, and the evaluation pipeline are the submission. The public repository contains every component needed to run and inspect the WebMCP project; it does not contain RIFT's private CMS source. 3. The Arena: a public evidence layer We looked at this as an experiment: would WebMCP be faster, safer, or more accurate? The Arena publishes 95 recorded runs of the same three citizen tasks across: a UI lane, where the agent reads pages and navigates without WebMCP; a WebMCP lane, where the agent uses the site's registered tools; two model tiers, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5; and two rounds, before and after fixes discovered by the benchmark. Every score, timing, action count, and range is computed from the trace files at runtime. The traces, answer keys, tool arguments, elapsed milliseconds, and earlier results are all public. Judges can also copy each scenario and run the WebMCP lane themselves. The recorded benchmark uses two Claude model tiers to test how the same interface behaves as model capability changes. The Arena is deliberately model-independent: in ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled browser, the judge's OpenAI agent becomes the live lane and can attempt the same published tasks against the same answer keys. Three citizen experiences Find the rule—not just an answer Mira Tanaka is filing a second damage claim. The obvious reading says she qualifies for a fee waiver; the actual rule says only approved claims count, so her pending claim does not. The agent must find the buried exception, explain that the ¥12,000 fee is still payable, and point Mira to the source. WebMCP makes the site's search index and rule citations directly available instead of forcing the agent to infer structure from navigation. Turn policy into a complete checklist Mira's eligibility depends on several rules spread across multiple pages: her zone, structural damage, income, business status, insurance payout, claims history, and filing window. check_eligibility evaluates those facts against a ruleset published as data. It returns the outcome, three applicable grants, five required documents, and citations. In our recorded results, both model tiers scored 100% in both lanes—but WebMCP reached the result with fewer actions and was 1.7× faster for Sonnet and 2.1× faster for Haiku . Fill the form, then hand control back For a proximity-construction permit, the agent must derive the K-2 reinforcement standard from Mira's Zone 4 location, validate twelve values against the published schema, and fill the real form. Then it must stop. prefill_permit_form has no submission capability. It fills and highlights the fields, reports what it entered or rejected, and leaves the final action to the person. The safety boundary is structural, not a hopeful instruction in a prompt. What our experiment found The most useful result was not “tools always win.” They did not. On this small, well-structured site, the stronger model often navigated the UI successfully. In the headline Sonnet runs, 14 of 15 UI-lane passes received full marks. Across all three Sonnet tasks, WebMCP also used about 2.4× as many context tokens on average—19,422 versus 8,117—because tool schemas and responses add context to the model's calls. That cost was not uniform: on the eligibility task, where the tool performed the most substantive rule evaluation, WebMCP used fewer tokens than browsing for both model sizes. We publish the overhead and the savings rather than reducing either to a universal claim. But five findings make the case for an agent-native web—and for a more mature agent-native publishing practice—much more interesting. Tools helped most when the model needed help When we moved from Sonnet 5 to the smaller Haiku 4.5 model, UI-lane accuracy fell by 41% on average across the task/lane pairs with room to fall. WebMCP-lane accuracy fell by 23%. The weaker model degraded roughly 1.8× less when the site gave it tools. The clearest reversal was the permit task: WebMCP trailed UI navigation with Sonnet (93% vs. 100%), but led it with Haiku (74% vs. 64%). Structured capability may matter less to the strongest agent on a clean demo site; it matters more as models get smaller, cheaper, and more widely deployed. “Optional” does not mean “unimportant” Our first permit tool treated the form schema as if it described the whole service process. If a field was not technically required, the agent could leave it blank without the tool mentioning it. The result passed form validation but could still look misleadingly complete to Mira. We changed the tool to report every field it left untouched. It now tells the agent which optional fields remain empty and invites another call if they apply. In the next five Sonnet attempts, complete 12-field forms increased from 0 of 5 to 4 of 5 , and task accuracy rose from 64% to 93%. That change made the agent aware of its omissions; it did not explain their administrative consequences. The site does not currently say whether leaving out an organization or phone number would delay review, trigger follow-up, affect approval, or make no difference at all. That exposed the larger civic-tech lesson: a form the browser will accept is not necessarily a form that will move smoothly through the service behind it. An agent-native form needs more than required/optional validation. Publishers should describe whether a field is required to submit, required only in certain circumstances, recommended to avoid de
video_transcript_excerpt: Mira Tanaka survived a Kaiju attack. Now she needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer from the government. Unfortunately, her best help is a website and an AI agent trying to understand it. Government websites contain real decisions hidden across policy pages, exceptions, document lists, and forms. AI agents can help ease the stress, but they must reconstruct the service from site navigation and text. We built a complete 51-page fictional government agency enabled with Web MCP. When the CMS publishes the website, it also generates a machine-readable manifest. A small browser runtime converts that content into seven Web MCP tools for search, services, eligibility, requirements, offices, and forms. Mira's eligibility depends on her location, damage, income, insurance, business status, and filing window. An AI agent would need to browse the website and find that through brute-force web browsing. With Web MCP check eligibility, evaluate the publisher's encoded rules, and return the outcome: three applicable grants, five required documents, and supporting citations. We built tests to see if Web MCP could outperform an agent browsing the website directly. You can use your ChatGPT Web MCP browser to help Mira submit her construction permit form online. For the permit, Web MCP validates 12 values, derives the required reinforcement standard, and fills the real form. Then it stops. The tool exposes no submission operation. Mira reviews the highlighted fields and makes the final decision herself. Human control is part of the capability. We did not stop at a polished demo. The arena publishes 95 inspectable runs comparing Web MCP with ordinary browsing across three tasks, two model sizes, and two rounds. Web MCP was not always better, but it completed the eligibility task with fewer actions and substantially less time, and it reduced the accuracy loss when we moved to the smaller model. Our most important finding was not about speed. When policy becomes executable, meaning can be lost between the approved sentence and the encoded rule. A citation may point to the correct page while the logic still misses an exception. Agent native publishing therefore creates a new responsibility. Organizations must review not only what people will read, but what machines will execute. The Office of Kaiju Affairs is fictional. The civic problem is not. WebMCP gives public institutions a way to participate in the agent experience instead of leaving every agent to reverse engineer their websites. And the open source arena we shared gives citizens, publishers, and judges a way to measure where WebMCP helps.

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Agent Riff
pitch: Agent Riff turns your browser agent into a musical partner. Play a phrase, and it listens through WebMCP and riffs back for a live human and AI music jam.
about_excerpt: Agent Riff turns your browser agent into a musical partner. Play a phrase, and it listens through WebMCP and riffs back for a live human and AI music jam. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Riff — Play a Musical Idea Together Live Musical Conversation in the webpage Human Plays the First Phrase Agent Responds with Its Own Phrase Life in Tech is already complicated, so many tools and frameworks to learn each day and tons of stress to deal with. So why not add more stress to your life when you find out your agent is better than you at playing music!! Inspiration for this Project Most AI music tools work in roughly the same way: you describe what you want, wait for the model, and receive a finished piece of music. We wanted to try somethingball that felt more collaborative. Instead of asking an AI to make music for us, we asked a different question: could a browser agent actually play music with us? That idea became Agent Riff , a musical call-and-response experience between a person and their browser agent. The person plays a short phrase, the agent receives the notes and timing through WebMCP, and then responds with a phrase of its own. The goal was not to create another song generator. We wanted the agent to feel like a second musician who listens before deciding what to play. What it does Agent Riff is a playable browser instrument built for live human and AI collaboration. A person can play notes using a mouse, touchscreen, or the keys on their computer keyboard. The application captures the performance as structured musical events, including the notes, timing, tempo, key, scale, instrument, register, and density. The browser agent can then: Join the current session Analyze the latest human phrase Choose a complementary instrument and register Perform a precisely timed response Wait for the person to play another phrase Change the shared tempo, key, or scale when requested Perform longer musical sets efficiently Agent Riff does not use the microphone or record the user's audio. The agent receives the musical information already created inside the application. This gives it accurate notes and timing without asking it to interpret sound or guess what happened from a screenshot. Human and agent performances appear in a shared live score. Each completed phrase is also saved as a clickable card. A person can replay their own phrase, replay the agent's response, or play both simultaneously to hear how well they work together. The agent can remain available for up to ten minutes between turns. This means the person can continue playing without repeatedly returning to the chat and typing "listen again." If they want to stop sooner, they can release the agent directly from the interface. How we built it Agent Riff is built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. All instrument sounds are synthesized directly in the browser using the Web Audio API. There are no recorded samples, user accounts, external music services, or runtime dependencies. A person can open the page and begin playing immediately. The application exposes seven WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : riff_join_session riff_get_session_state riff_listen riff_wait_for_human_phrase riff_perform_phrase riff_perform_set riff_set_compass These tools give the agent musical abilities rather than generic browser controls. For example, the agent does not need to find individual piano keys on the screen and click them at the correct moment. It can call riff_listen to receive an analysis of the recent performance, then call riff_perform_phrase with the notes, durations, timing offsets, instrument, and velocity of its response. The performance tool supports sequential notes, rests, chords, overlapping notes, and exact beat-relative timing. For speed, the agent can use a compact score format instead of sending a large object for every note. The waiting tool keeps the call-and-response session active. When the person finishes another phrase, the tool returns both the new notes and the analysis needed for the next response. This lets the agent perform directly without making an additional listening call. We also created riff_perform_set for requests involving complete songs or multiple sections. It can schedule several public-domain or custom pieces in one call, reducing repeated model and browser round trips. Every tool uses a bounded JSON Schema, and all inputs are validated again during execution. The project also includes automated tests for musical analysis, input constraints, WebMCP registration, tool behavior, cleanup, and the production deployment artifact. Challenges The first version technically worked, but it did not feel much like a live musical interaction. The agent would inspect the session, analyze the notes, think about its response, call another tool, play a very short phrase, and then return to the chat. The delay between turns was long enough that it was easy to forget what had just been played. We reduced that delay by combining related information. The waiting tool now returns the completed phrase together with its musical analysis and a suggested response shape. We also added compact score notation so a complete response can be sent in one efficient tool call. Response quality created another tradeoff. Faster models replied more quickly, but their musical answers were often only a few notes long or sounded like random keyboard input. More capable models produced better phrases, but took longer to respond. We improved this by giving the agent clearer musical guidance. Normal responses are encouraged to develop across roughly 12 to 16 notes, with an echo of the human idea, a variation, and a resolution. Dense human phrases receive shorter or more spacious answers so the agent does not overcrowd the music. We also had to account for ChatGPT's side-by-side browser layout. A design that looked good in a full browser window became extremely tall and difficult to use when the browser occupied only half the screen. We redesigned the responsive layout so the instrument, score, activity, agent status, and copied prompt remain accessible in that narrower configuration. Long waits created a separate usability problem. People needed a clear way to tell whether the agent was still present and how to stop it. We added visible agent status, a bounded waiting period, and a release button that ends the current wait and cancels queued agent playback. Finally, browser audio has its own restrictions. Audio must begin from a user interaction, and keyboard input should not interfere with focused form controls. We had to balance reliable instrument input with normal keyboard and accessibility behavior. What we learned The biggest lesson was that a good agent experience depends just as much on tool design as it does on the model. When an agent receives vague page content and generic browser controls, it spends much of its effort figuring out how to operate the interface. When it receives focused tools with compact, structured context, it can spend that effort making a better creative decision. We also learned that fewer tool calls do not necessarily mean less capable tools. Combining the right information at the right moment made the experience faster while giving the agent more useful musical context. WebMCP was a natural fit for Agent Riff because the important information is difficult to communicate through pixels alone. A screenshot can show a piano, but it cannot reliably describe the exact notes, timing, density, and musical direction of the phrase that was just played. With WebMCP, the website becomes more than an interface the agent operates. It becomes a shared creative space where a person and an agent can listen, respond, and build something together. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: AgentPress
pitch: The permission-aware WebMCP control layer for WordPress.
about_excerpt: The permission-aware WebMCP control layer for WordPress. Like Comment Story Updates 1 made by chatgpt made by chatgpt made by chatgpt made by chatgpt made by chatgpt youtube screenshot (for some reason) made by chatgpt Inspiration WordPress already has a strong human collaboration model: authenticated sessions, roles, capabilities, drafts, review, and publishing. Most agent integrations bypass that model by asking for a separate API key or by giving an automation service broad access. AgentPress asks a different question: what if the agent could join the workspace the human is already using, while WordPress remained the source of authority? What it does AgentPress is an open-source WordPress plugin that exposes a permission-filtered set of site tools to compatible agents through WebMCP. It divides operations into three visible classes: automatic operations that are safe within the current user's authority; approval-required operations that should stop for an explicit human decision; and unavailable areas that are never exposed as tools, including users, plugins, themes, code, credentials, and settings. In the recorded live workflow, ChatGPT used AgentPress tools from its built-in browser to inspect the current WordPress context and structure, create one useful service-page draft, and read the result back. WordPress showed the item as a draft. The visible page count changed from 15 to 16, the one new page was identified, and all 15 pre-existing page metadata records remained unchanged. Nothing was published. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The browser already holds the most important context: the page the human chose, their authenticated WordPress session, and their real WordPress permissions. WebMCP lets that page offer structured tools directly to the agent. The user does not have to copy content into chat, hand over a permanent API key, or teach the model where buttons live. That makes a multi-step WordPress task possible in one request: inspect the site, understand the allowed operations, create a draft, and verify the result. The outcome remains native WordPress content that a human can preview, edit, review, or publish through the normal workflow. How we built it AgentPress defines a fixed catalog of typed WordPress Abilities and adapts the permitted surface to WebMCP using document.modelContext.registerTool . Calls travel through a private same-origin REST transport using the signed-in WordPress cookie session and REST nonce. The server does not trust discovery alone. It revalidates the current user's WordPress capabilities, object-level access, operation policy, origin, nonce, request size, and closed input schema at execution time. Draft writes are forced to draft status and pass through an idempotent Change Set coordinator. Attempts and outcomes produce bounded, sanitized audit records. The wp-admin Overview makes the boundary legible: connection health, the connected site, operations available automatically, operations classified as approval-required, and areas that are always blocked. Challenges The hardest problem was not generating WordPress content. It was preserving WordPress authority across browser discovery, agent execution, REST transport, object-level permissions, retries, and a human-readable admin interface. We treated every layer as a boundary and kept a dated experiment ledger containing failures as well as successful results. Accomplishments A real ChatGPT built-in-browser WebMCP run created and verified one WordPress page draft. The write was idempotent and represented as Change Set AP-1. The result remained unpublished and existing page metadata remained unchanged. The plugin uses the human's current WordPress session instead of a copied API key. The public repository contains implementation tests and an auditable experiment trail. What we learned Agent capability should be narrower than user capability, and the distinction must be visible to both the human and the model. Tool discovery is useful, but enforcement must happen again on the server. We also learned that an honest, bounded demonstration—with request identifiers, WordPress state verification, and explicit untested limits—is more valuable than a broad automation claim. What's next The recorded challenge build proves the core read-and-draft workflow. The next milestones are the visible approval and classic-navigation flows, the canonical Administrator-versus-Author permission test, and five consecutive clean reliability runs. Those are deliberately described as next steps, not as completed features. pitch: A WebMCP-powered School ERP that lets educators manage attendance, fees, and records instantly through natural language using AI agents.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered School ERP that lets educators manage attendance, fees, and records instantly through natural language using AI agents.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for Agent-Native School ERP: Powered by WebMCP 

 Project Story 

 Inspiration
Traditional School ERP systems are notoriously complex, packed with dense menus, multi-step forms, and steep learning curves. We realized that teachers and school administrators spend hours navigating these clunky interfaces instead of focusing on what truly matters: education. When WebMCP was introduced, we saw the perfect opportunity to bridge the gap between complex databases and human intent. We wanted to transform the UX from "navigational" to "conversational," allowing educators to manage an entire school through simple natural language. 

 What it does
Our project is a full-stack, Agent-Native School Management System. It allows AI agents (like ChatGPT) to act as an administrative co-pilot directly within the browser. Once an administrator logs securely into the dashboard, the app exposes 7 powerful WebMCP tools: 

 search_student_records
mark_attendance
check_pending_fees
get_class_summary
get_class_students
generate_invoice
add_student
Instead of clicking through five different screens to find pending fees and generate an invoice, an administrator can simply type: "Find all Grade 3 students with pending fees and generate their invoices." The AI agent automatically chains the WebMCP tools to complete the workflow in seconds. 

 How we built it
We adopted a robust full-stack architecture: 

 Frontend: React and Vite, deployed on Netlify.
Backend: Java Spring Boot, deployed on Render.
Database: PostgreSQL hosted on Supabase.
WebMCP Integration: We used the window.document.modelContext.registerTool API inside a secure, authenticated React useEffect hook. We ensured that tools are strictly exposed only after a successful JWT/Session login. Each tool is equipped with a strict JSON schema for input validation, and the execute function securely passes the user's authentication token/cookies to our Spring Boot backend.
Challenges we ran into
Building a production-ready WebMCP app came with serious hurdles: 

 Supabase Connection Limits: Our Spring Boot's default HikariCP connection pool quickly exhausted the Supabase free tier's 15 concurrent connections limit, causing FATAL: EMAXCONNSESSION errors during deployment. We solved this by strictly limiting the maximum-pool-size and managing idle timeouts.
Cross-Domain Authentication: Because our frontend was on Netlify and backend on Render, the browser blocked our session cookies, throwing 400 Bad Request errors. We had to dive deep into Spring Security to configure Cross-Site cookies using SameSite=None and Secure=true.
Strict CORS Policies: Managing wildcard origins with credentials proved difficult until we upgraded our configuration to use allowedOriginPatterns.
AI Form-Filling Limitations: We learned that headless browsers used by AI agents sometimes struggle with complex SPA login forms, which required us to optimize our DOM structure for agent readability.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Successfully building and integrating 7 diverse read and write WebMCP tools in a short span of time.
Achieving a secure architecture where AI agents operate strictly within the bounds of human authentication (tools are hidden behind the login screen).
Successfully deploying a complex 3-tier architecture (Netlify + Render + Supabase) that runs seamlessly in the cloud.
What we learned
We gained a profound understanding of the new WebMCP specifications and how the document.modelContext interacts with the browser's DOM. We also learned how to write strict JSON schemas that prevent AI hallucinations, ensuring the agent always sends exactly what the Spring Boot backend expects. 

 What's next for Agent-Native School ERP: Powered by WebMCP
We plan to expand the agent's capabilities by adding WebMCP tools for generating report cards, scheduling parent-teacher meetings, and eventually integrating an automated WhatsApp notification system for parents directly triggered by the AI agent's actions.

 Inspiration 

 I got the idea because I wanted AI to help me learn things for school. Some topics are hard to understand from text alone, so I thought it would be useful if an AI could explain them directly on a whiteboard with drawings, arrows and notes. 

 What it does 

 Collaborative Whiteboard is a shared whiteboard for a human and an AI. You can draw something, write a question, select an area or point at something with the AI Pen. The AI can then explain it, improve it or continue working on the same canvas. Everything the AI creates stays editable, so you can change it and keep working from there. 

 How we built it 

 I built the project mainly with Codex and Claude . I also used WebMCP, MCP tools and different Claude skills while working on it. The app itself is a web-based whiteboard with tools for drawing, writing, selecting things and working together with an AI agent. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was definitely usage limits while building the project. Getting the WebMCP connection and the Human-to-AI workflow working correctly was also not easy. There were many small bugs with turns, waiting and editing the canvas that had to be fixed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am really proud that the main idea actually works. The AI can understand the board and add real, editable drawings and objects to it. I am also happy with how fast the app runs now. Building and testing the project was a lot of fun. 

 What we learned 

 I learned a lot about WebMCP, AI agents and how to connect an AI with an interactive website. I also learned that making an AI understand when it should wait, edit or react to the user is harder than it first sounds. 

 What's next for Collaborative Whiteboard 

 Next, I would like to improve how well the AI designs and organizes things on the whiteboard, so its diagrams and layouts look even better. title: Competitor Tracker & Co. WebMCP
pitch: Today you ask your AI agent to track competitors. It's OK until it misses important update. We build an AI-friendly app that does that better. But agents couldn't sign up... Until we added WebMCP :)
about_excerpt: Today you ask your AI agent to track competitors. It's OK until it misses important update. We build an AI-friendly app that does that better. But agents couldn't sign up... Until we added WebMCP :) Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT using WebMCP Website with WebMCP Inspiration If you want to track a competitor today, you don't search for an app; you ask your AI agent to do that. That works OK at the beginning, but then it misses important things after a few weeks. We built an app that tracks competitors better, and it's AI agent-friendly. But agents couldn't sign up and set up everything for you without your action. Until we added WebMCP :) What it does Every page of competitortracker.io now registers 11 WebMCP tools - in production, in four languages, for any agent riding along in the visitor's browser. Three groups: Q&A over the site's own words. search_site , get_page , get_pricing , compare_with_rival , about_competitor_tracker . An agent can answer any question about the product from what the pages actually say — the agent and the human are never told different things. Public competitor data. search_companies , get_company , list_industries , get_industry , get_recent_changes over our open CC BY 4.0 data: 300+ tracked companies, 50 industries, and the dated, classified change feed. This is the product doing its actual job in the agent's hands, not a description of it. Agent signup. start_tracking_competitors : the agent names the companies you care about, we create an unclaimed organization (no email, nothing charged, self-deletes in four days), and hand back a claim link plus a short-lived read token. The tool then tells the agent the follow-up move: wait ~15 seconds, call GET /v1/changes with the token, and lead with what changed at your competitors — then hand over the claim link so the human takes ownership. So the full arc works with zero forms: ask a question, see real competitor changes, get tracking set up, claim it - all before you have an account. How we built it The site is Hugo on Cloudflare Workers, and most of the machinery already existed for AI crawlers: every page has a markdown twin, llms.txt is a curated per-page index, and our competitor data ships as an open JSON tree. So the WebMCP layer needed no search backend and no new data - the tools are framework-free ES modules that read what the site already publishes, plus one POST to our live agent-signup API. Details we care about: A 411-byte loader rides every page; the ~13 KB tool bundle is injected only when a modelContext runtime actually exists. Ordinary visitors pay nothing. The two required headers ( Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) , Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 ) ship from our edge worker, the single chokepoint for all responses. Every execute() is wrapped so no failure ever throws - a browser agent runtime has no defined behavior for an uncaught rejection, so every path returns a result the agent can read. Telemetry counts calls, never contents: tool name, page, language, outcome. The module is open source (MIT) - the loader, registration helper and validation utils are generic enough to point at your own tools. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. The getter lives on document.modelContext but half the browsers on the origin trial still carry navigator.modelContext ; we probe both. And unregisterTool() / provideContext() are gone from the spec - teardown is aborting the signal you registered with. Generated code confidently suggests the removed API. Testing without a runtime. No browser in our CI has WebMCP, so we built a Node harness that runs the real tool modules with stubbed browser globals against the live site and API — every tool, every error path. Honest copy is a design constraint here. A 503 from the signup API must never be spoken as "we don't track that company," and the 15-second wait is a write-settle margin, not "we're fetching your data now" - the change history is already published. Agents repeat what tools tell them, so the tool result text is a product surface. How do I test this? It took some time to figure out how to test WebMCP in Chrome. Accomplishments that we're proud of It's live on our real production site , not a hackathon sandbox - every page, every language, behind a one-line kill switch. The signup flow keeps the human in charge without a single confirmation dialog: the org holds no money, sends no email, expires unclaimed, and the claim page is the confirmation step. The whole thing reuses surfaces we'd already built for fetching agents (markdown twins, llms.txt , open data) - the pre-account story just needed the last mile into the tab. Fifteen seconds after asking, an agent shows you what your competitors changed. That's the demo, and it's real. What we learned A tool declaration is a hint to a cooperative agent, never a security boundary — validation lives server-side, and the published-catalog-only rule (the tool never fetches a URL you supply) is the guarantee the whole feature stands on. The right scope for in-page tools isn't feature parity with our MCP server (50 tools behind OAuth). The web page is the before-the-account surface; the MCP server is after . Drawing that line made every other decision easy. Sites that already publish machine-readable views get WebMCP almost for free. The work we'd done for crawlers became the engine for in-tab agents. WebMCP is fun! What's next for Competitor Tracker & Co. WebMCP Teach people how to use this. Join the WebMCP origin trial (Chrome 149+) so the tools work for real visitors without flags. Declarative form annotations for the few forms the site has, and page-scoped context - a company page pre-scoping its own tools. Localized tool descriptions for our FR/DE/JA pages. Watching our telemetry to learn which tools agents actually call, and feeding that back into both the WebMCP surface and the full MCP server. title: StrategyShifu
pitch: Instead of asking users to navigate pricing pages, compare capabilities, and manually piece together trade-offs, StrategyShifu exposes structured decision workflows through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Instead of asking users to navigate pricing pages, compare capabilities, and manually piece together trade-offs, StrategyShifu exposes structured decision workflows through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Complex cloud architecture and migration decisions are rarely solved by a single recommendation. Teams need to compare costs, technical constraints, operational trade-offs, and implementation risks before committing to a strategy. We built StrategyShifu to explore a better model for human–agent collaboration: an AI agent that can work directly with a live decision-making application through WebMCP, while the user can see every change, review the reasoning, and make the final decision. What it does StrategyShifu is a WebMCP-powered decision workspace for cloud cost planning and data-platform migration strategy. The current version supports two decision workflows: Databricks cost planning: Configure DWH, ETL, and development workloads and compare compute strategies using regional pricing, schedules, networking requirements, Databricks Genie compatibility, and project budgets. Redshift-to-Databricks migration planning: Compare Iceberg coexistence, Lakehouse Federation, UNLOAD to S3, and JDBC-based migration strategies using workload characteristics, downtime tolerance, synchronization plans, target formats, and execution readiness. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect the current project, modify inputs, test alternatives, calculate costs, compare strategies, and explain the recommendation. Every agent action is reflected immediately in the interface, allowing the user and the agent to work from the same decision context. How we built it StrategyShifu is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. WebMCP forms the interaction layer between the application and browser-based AI agents. We followed several WebMCP best practices: Registered focused, task-oriented tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Designed tools around user goals instead of exposing low-level UI actions. Used clear tool names, descriptions, and input schemas. Added runtime validation for agent-provided inputs. Returned both human-readable text and structured content. Included tool annotations to communicate read-only and mutating behavior. Used AbortSignal cleanup to prevent duplicate or stale tool registrations. Kept tool operations deterministic and safe. Used stable identifiers for selecting and updating workloads. Returned updated state after mutations so agents can continue without scraping the page. Provided clear errors and recovery guidance for invalid operations. Gracefully preserved the human interface when WebMCP was unavailable. Most importantly, WebMCP tools and human controls operate on the same React state. There is no separate agent-only state or hidden decision model. The application currently exposes: 17 WebMCP tools for workload configuration, pricing, cost estimation, strategy comparison, and recommendation retrieval. 7 WebMCP tools for migration inputs, capability evidence, and Redshift-to-Databricks assessment. The recommendation engines remain deterministic and catalog-driven. The agent explores and configures scenarios, while the application owns calculations, validation, compatibility gates, scoring, and ranking. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was designing a WebMCP tool surface that represented meaningful decision operations rather than browser automation. For example, instead of asking an agent to find and click several form fields, StrategyShifu provides tools such as add_workload , set_budget , compare_strategies , and get_recommendation . This makes agent interactions more reliable, understandable, and reusable. Another challenge was synchronizing agent actions with human interactions. We solved this by connecting WebMCP tools directly to the same state update functions used by the visible interface. We also had to balance agent flexibility with predictable recommendations. Agents can explore many scenarios, but technical compatibility, budget enforcement, pricing calculations, and migration scoring must remain reproducible and auditable. Finally, migration decisions depend on evolving platform capabilities. We introduced structured capability evidence with documented-source links and a fallback mechanism so temporary documentation failures do not prevent an assessment. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that StrategyShifu demonstrates WebMCP as a foundation for genuine collaboration rather than a collection of isolated agent commands. Key accomplishments include: A shared live workspace where humans and agents operate on the same state. 24 task-oriented WebMCP tools across cost and migration planning. Structured tool responses that support multi-step agent workflows. Runtime input validation and actionable error messages. Safe tool registration with lifecycle cleanup. Deterministic and explainable recommendation engines. Full-project cost analysis across multiple workloads. Explicit Pass/Fail gates for budget and technical requirements. Transparent DBU and infrastructure cost breakdowns. Migration strategy scoring, alternatives, risks, and readiness evaluation. Suggested implementation steps and production cutover checks. Structured technical evidence supporting migration assessments. Share, copy, CSV, and Print/PDF export options. Responsive views for desktop and mobile users. The agent does not simply summarize information. It can actively construct, modify, and evaluate a decision alongside the user. What we learned We learned that WebMCP works especially well for applications with structured state, repeatable workflows, and multiple possible decision paths. Giving agents semantic tools is more dependable than asking them to infer application state from the visual interface. Structured inputs and outputs also make multi-step reasoning easier to validate and debug. We also learned that agentic interaction should be separated from business logic. WebMCP provides the agent with controlled access to the application, while deterministic engines remain responsible for calculations and recommendations. Finally, transparency is essential. Users are more likely to trust an agent-assisted recommendation when they can see the inputs, understand the failed requirements, compare alternatives, and reproduce the result themselves. What's next for StrategyShifu Our next goal is to turn StrategyShifu into a broader multi-platform strategy workspace. Planned improvements include: Add more migration strategies across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Support additional source and target platforms, including Snowflake, BigQuery, Synapse, PostgreSQL, and other data warehouses. Add cross-platform compute and architecture comparisons. Expand WebMCP tools into guided multi-step planning workflows. Add migration phase tracking and implementation checklists. Allow organizations to add their own policies, pricing agreements, and decision criteria. Our long-term vision is for StrategyShifu to become a WebMCP-powered strategy layer across platforms—helping people and agents evaluate complex technology decisions together with transparency, consistency, and control. title: Counterask
pitch: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess.
about_excerpt: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess. Like Comment Story Updates Every WebMCP storefront exposes the same shape of tool: get-products, filter-products, show-products. The spec's own e-commerce example does exactly that. All of them share one assumption — that the store's job is to answer. For most of a shopping conversation that assumption is wrong. Ask our catalog for "a belt" and 106 products match. Every one of them is a belt. The top-ranked item beats the tenth by a rounding error. Ranking them is a coin flip dressed up as a recommendation. The store knows this. It has the distribution in front of it — it can see that one more fact, what the belt is made of, would clear about forty-seven of them. But a tool that can only return products has no way to say so. So it returns its coin flip, and the agent presents a guess as an answer. We gave the store a second move.Counterask is a menswear storefront on 9,901 real products from the Amazon Reviews 2023 catalog. Its search_products tool returns one of two things. When there is enough evidence, it answers — and says what still separates the products it is showing, so the agent can summarise instead of reading out a list. When answering would be a guess, it returns status: "need_more_evidence" with the one question worth asking, the options with their counts, and why: "106 candidates, leader only 5% ahead. Asking 'material' clears ~47 of them on average (recorded on 89%)." The question is the store declining to guess on the shopper's behalf. It reads whole sentences, not keywords: "I'm looking for a leather belt, nothing with a snap, not over $50" becomes a requirement, a refusal and a ceiling. It walks the category tree one level at a time: "shoes" → athletic → running → what for → 58 candidates. It handles a change of mind mid-conversation — "scratch that, a nylon belt" drops leather, keeps the budget, and reports what it dropped. And when nothing survives, it lifts each requirement in turn and says which one is doing the damage. How WebMCP is used: every tool is registered through document.modelContext. answer_question exists only while a question is open — registered with an AbortSignal, removed by aborting it — so an agent reading the tool list can see what the page is waiting for. parse_only is a dry run: the agent can see how the store would read a sentence before committing. Anything the agent already knows can be passed structured and overrides the parse. A person clicking an option chip and an agent calling the tool enter the same function. Checkout is a declarative form with no toolautosubmit: the agent fills it in, the person presses it.No server, no model call, no tokens. The whole store is one page: the catalog, a thirteen-pass sentence parser, retrieval, and the stopping policy, in plain JavaScript. The engine is four parts with explicit dependencies — vocabulary, parser, retrieval, policy — and the parser is a pipeline whose order is data: each pass claims what it reads and writes a line of an audit trace that parse_only returns. The stopping policy counts, for each attribute, how many candidates a question would clear on average, measured inside the subset that records the attribute and scaled by coverage. It asks about the best one unless the best one clears fewer than 10 candidates or under 18% of the pool. Entropy was the textbook choice and it is wrong for this data: a product carries several values of one attribute at once, so value shares are not a probability distribution. The category tree is a facet. Every node on a product's path is a value, so "shoes" matches all shoes and "running" the running ones. A hierarchy is the one facet that can be asked again, one level at a time; ancestors the whole pool shares are never offered; depth is measured per product relative to what the shopper named. npm test runs 75 hand-written parser cases, 4,000 fuzzed sentences, 88 assertions against the WebMCP surface, the page against three spec-shaped native implementations, a test that an open question survives a page navigation, the bundled single file, and two benchmarks. A hostile product is inserted during the tests and the suite asserts its title never lands in an instruction-shaped field.Real data broke the thing synthetic data could not. On a synthetic catalog a belt's title says "Belt". Half of real titles do not name their category — "Columbia Men's Thistletown Park Crew" is a T-shirt. Requiring the shopper's noun in the title dropped the right product in 47% of benchmark cases. Making the category tree a facet took that to 4.6%; treating a value as satisfied wherever the record carries it, and letting stray words rank rather than filter once the noun is understood, took it to 0.6%. Missing is not a mismatch — in both directions. Only 8% of the catalog records a fit, and a naive gain calculation adores fit because asking it "removes 92% of candidates" — for having no data. Reduction is measured inside the covered subset, and an attribute recorded on under 45% of the pool is never asked about. A fuzzer found a bug we would never have found by hand: answering a question could make the pool grow. The title-term filter fell back to no filtering when fewer than four products matched; a narrowing answer could drop the strict set below four, and the shopper watched results grow because they had answered. The reading is now decided once and frozen. We built two-step lookahead and it was worse — selection used a two-step score while the stopping rule used a one-step score. We built the correctly formulated sequential policy and measured it at equal questions asked: the same curve. It ships off.Measured on 800 sentences generated from real product records, against a keyword matcher on identical sentences, with spread over 8 shards: refusals inverted into requirements: 597 → 0 refused value shown in top 10: 368 → 0 budget broken in top 10: 22 → 0 Hit@10: 0.04 → 0.33 ± 0.01 On sessions that start where shoppers start — "shoes", "clothing" — walking the category tree takes Hit@10 from 0.16 to 0.31 and the final pool from 597 to 121, for half a question more. Eight shards out of eight. It is the largest single effect in the project, and it was invisible until the benchmark started at the top of the tree instead of the leaf. We are equally proud of what we refused to do. Lowering the ask threshold from 10 to 5 buys +0.07 Hit@10 for 0.35 more questions per search, and the benchmark says take it. We didn't: the simulated shopper never gets tired, so the benchmark can price the benefit of a question and not its cost. Instead we made the cost an explicit assumption — the shipped threshold implies that roughly one shopper in four walks away each time the store asks — and published the whole frontier so the choice is visible rather than buried in a constant.The spec lists fully autonomous workflows under Non-Goals and says the human interface remains primary, with agent tools augmenting rather than replacing it. A tool that returns a question is the most direct expression of that we could build. It puts the person back in the loop at the exact moment the machine cannot decide — not as a permission prompt bolted on afterwards, but because the store genuinely does not know and says so. And a benchmark is only as honest as its blind spots are documented. Ours draws targets uniformly, starts at the leaf, and never gets impatient. Every one of those limits changed what we shipped, and every one is written down.Measure the one number the store cannot: how often a shopper actually walks away per question. A deployed page can log question-shown, question-answered and page-abandoned; the threshold then becomes a measured quantity instead of a stated belief. Structured input first: in a real WebMCP session the agent has already understood the shopper, so the parser should be the fallback and parse_only the first call. A catalog with descriptions, not just titles. Attribute coverage is the ceiling on what the store can ask; this data records material on 56% of products and occasion on 25%, and the questions are limited by what the listings say.  Inspiration 

 I've always envied things I couldn't do well yet, like writing novels, and drawing. My hands are super stiff... 

 I've actually built relatively things before this challenge . I built a ai novel writer called "inkmarshal" simply because I want to write a novel for fun but my writing is bad, and I thought someone like me may interest in it. I built an image generate application call "lunerylab" as well for the same reason. 

 So combination of both easily come through my head. Plus my son is deep into
picture books — Dog Man gets read until the spine gives out — and I believe he will have fun by making one for himself. 

 So basically I prefer to use ai to achieve something with ai that I couldn't do well yet (still have chance and time who knows) 

 What it does 

 Apertale is a site for making cool interactive books. Its powered by WebMCP which make agent using our site creator tools. There are beautiful samples for you to read, and hopefully bring audience's interest. 

 Then you make your own. Give it a prompt, some photos, or both, and your ChatGPT
starts building pages inside the book you're looking at. Drag something it just placed. Or tell it to undo one thing, and it removes exactly that. Then one link to share it to anyone. 

 How I built it 

 I vibe coded it, serious vibe coding strategy. 

 Design first, because I'm super picky about UI/UX — probably 70–80% of my time went
there. Real comps in Figma and Codex (Production Design plugin) before any app
code existed. 

 I choose three.js for the book, because I prefer 3d and I used it a lot for making 3d game demo for fun. 

 I published it on gptsite, it is so convenient at this stage. I would love to host it on a domain if it scale. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 It has to be the images generation usage control and time consumption for this. A picture book eats art and one page at a time was too slow and too expensive. What I landed on: four pages per frame, then sliced apart. A quarter of the generations, and pages drawn together actually look like they belong together. 

 Also image bytes. WebMCP passes data, not files, so I made that handoff visible instead of pretending it happened. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The overall aesthetic, the whole feel of it. It is a project I would put out and show to anyone at any time. 

 Also the Agent Sketching feature too. You can mark up what you want changed and have the sketch actually change from that mark. That one came out better than I expected. 

 And most importantly, it works. Not a video, not a mockup. Open the link, read a book, make one with your agent, publish it. 

 What I learned 

 That the bottleneck was never the coding. It was knowing exactly what I wanted.
Every time I was vague with the AI I got something vague back, and every time I
could describe the thing precisely — this page turns like this, this reveals like
that — it came out right. 

 What's next for Apertale 

 Better asset handoff, cut down time usage. And I am also considering animations. Then background tasks.

title: Longevity — Human-Agent Life Function Workspace
pitch: A privacy-first WebMCP app where your agent turns known family and life context into a visible Life Function, asks only for missing facts, and compares conditional life-extension scenarios.
about_excerpt:
A privacy-first WebMCP app where your agent turns known family and life context into a visible Life Function, asks only for missing facts, and compares conditional life-extension scenarios.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most personal-modeling products begin with a long blank form. But a person’s AI agent may already know useful fragments of family history and life context. The missed opportunity is not merely autofill: it is a shared working surface where the person sees the model changing while the agent gathers only what is actually missing. 

 What it does 

 Longevity is a privacy-first WebMCP workspace in which a person and their agent build a visible Life Function together. The agent reuses structured facts already available in its context, asks only for gaps, and submits those facts directly into the open page. Longevity then visualizes parental trajectories, the client’s observed trajectory, influence coefficients, a hereditary model, and conditional life-extension scenarios. 

 When context is sparse, the agent runs a live four-chapter interview: family and influence, ancestors, parents, and the client’s trajectory. It asks one short question per message, accepts text, voice, approximate answers, or “I don’t know,” and stops the required interview as soon as the first calculation is ready. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Longevity exposes seven client-side WebMCP tools. The agent can read the intake and privacy contract, submit known facts, inspect completeness, request exactly one next interview step, add a structured answer, and retrieve scenario comparisons. Every accepted tool call updates the same in-tab state the person is looking at. 

 This creates an experience that was difficult before WebMCP: private context can be reused without forcing the person to re-enter everything, while the browser remains the shared visual source of truth. The person can inspect sources and assumptions, adjust father, mother, and environment coefficients, and watch the Life Functions recalculate immediately—without the agent scraping or clicking through the UI. 

 Privacy by architecture 

 The deployed static page has no intake server, account, analytics, cookies, database, or persistent storage. It accepts structured facts only, never raw chat, audio, or transcripts. Personal facts remain in JavaScript memory inside the open tab and disappear on reload, tab close, or Clear. A restrictive Content Security Policy uses connect-src 'none'. The WebMCP manifest also states that retention of the external agent conversation is controlled by that agent platform, not by Longevity. 

 How we built it 

 
 React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 
 Imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool() 
 Strict JSON Schemas and structured tool results 
 Abort-scoped re-registration when the locale changes 
 Fully client-side calculations and state 
 English-first interface with a complete Russian UI and WebMCP contract 
 Netlify static deployment with restrictive security headers 
 Automated coverage for intake flow, privacy, calculations, charts, tool registration, and localization 
 

 Challenges and lessons 

 The hardest design problem was balancing completeness with a conversational interview. Too few questions produced a weak model; a conventional questionnaire felt endless. The four-chapter policy, one-question rhythm, explicit unknowns, and separate preliminary/refinement phases made the flow both bounded and useful. 

 A second challenge was making strong privacy language technically true. That led us to keep all personal state inside the tab, forbid raw conversational media, expose the privacy boundary to the agent before submission, and distinguish page storage from the agent platform’s own retention policy. 

 Finally, the model had to remain legible and epistemically honest. Longevity shows completeness, provenance, assumptions, and uncertainty, and presents its calculations as a conditional Androphysics model—not medical advice, a biological forecast, or a prediction of a person’s death.
