title: Dim Hour
pitch: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page.
about_excerpt: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Dim Hour is a city guide - the places worth your time, scored, not starred - covering more than 19,000 restaurants, bars, hotels, and venues across 24 cities. For this challenge, dimhour.com became agent-native: the page itself registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the site can search the catalog, read a venue, check what is open tonight, draft an itinerary, and hand back a booking link - without scraping a pixel. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Planning a night out is one of the most common things people already ask an agent to help with, but today the agent scrapes pages and guesses at what the site already knows. WebMCP lets dimhour.com hand the agent its real search, scoring, and booking data as structured tools, in the same tab where the person is browsing. The catalog is the product; WebMCP makes it callable. Because the tools are thin adapters over a production venue API, every agent answer is grounded in live data instead of page scraping. How it creates a better user experience One page, two users. A person browsing the Dallas guide and their agent now work on the same surface. The agent calls the site's own tools and gets back the same scored venues, hours, and booking links the UI shows - no copy-pasting between a chat window and a browser, and no agent inventing hours, addresses, or availability. The person keeps the judgment (taste, swaps, vetoes); the agent does the legwork (searching, filtering, checking, assembling). The site stays the source of truth for both of them, and saving a plan stays a human action - the tools read, they never write. What people and agents can do together Co-plan a night in one sitting, in one page. "Dinner in Deep Ellum for four on Friday, then cocktails within walking distance." The agent searches the scored catalog, filters to what is actually open tonight using the same rule the site's own tonight strip uses, pulls full venue records, and drafts an ordered itinerary with real booking links (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock) while the person watches - then interrupts: "swap the second stop for something quieter," and the agent re-plans around the constraint. Before WebMCP, the agent could read the page but not act through the site's own logic, and the person could use the site but not delegate the legwork. Now both happen at once, and the result is a plan with real reservation links attached, not a list of suggestions. How we implemented WebMCP The WebMCP layer is one feature-detected script, webmcp.js, loaded by the site's index.html. Each of the five tools is a thin adapter that POSTs JSON-RPC tools/call to Dim Hour's existing MCP server (mcp.dimhour.com) and passes the result straight through: search_venues - one strong keyword plus city, neighborhood, cuisine, score floor, and price ceiling filters get_venue - the full record: hours, score, booking path, awards find_open_tonight - venues with a happy hour or late kitchen, best score first, using the same definition the site's own "tonight" strip uses, so the agent and the page agree build_itinerary - an ordered multi-stop plan with why and how to book each stop; saving stays a human action at /trip.html get_booking_link - the reservation platform and direct booking URL for a venue, returned for the agent to present; it never opens or books anything itself The script handles the in-flight standard rename (document.modelContext first, navigator.modelContext fallback) and is a silent no-op where no WebMCP host exists. No authentication; the tools expose only public, read-only catalog data. What predates the hackathon: the venue catalog, scoring pipeline, MCP server, and site. What was built during the submission window: webmcp.js, the tool schemas, and the index.html include - the public repo's README draws that line explicitly, with dated commits. Challenges we hit Search results deliberately do not carry hours - only full venue records do - so "open tonight" meant ranking candidates first, then reading the top few individually rather than filtering a field that is not there. Booking links live in the page's own catalog rather than the API, so the booking tool merges both sources and says so honestly when a city is not loaded. The verification suite now asserts substance (tonight actually finds venues; a booking link equals the catalog's own URL), not just shape - because an early version passed every check while two tools quietly returned nothing. about_excerpt: Most agents click through UIs built for humans. Patchwork gives your agent real WebMCP tools to design garden beds, diagnose plants (and more): validated, visible and logged on one shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates The image shows the garden created by the agent and the human together. The image shows the 6 tools the agente can discover and use. The image shows the care calendar filled by the agent. The image shows the Diagnose section used by the human. What inspired me The web was built for humans — buttons, menus, grids. AI agents browsing today have to reverse-engineer that intent, clicking pixel by pixel and hoping. When WebMCP landed, the promise was obvious: websites could hand agents real, structured tools instead of a guessing game. I wanted to prove it in a domain where rules actually matter. Gardening is full of precise, checkable constraints (companion planting, spacing, sun hours, seasons) where a wrong click is visible as a dying plant. A garden felt like the perfect place to show that an agent doesn't have to guess: it can negotiate against real rules, on a canvas you both see. Also, I love grow hot chili peppers. What I built Patchwork is a shared urban garden. Two beds, a crop catalog of 27 plants (soon to expand), a care calendar, and a plant doctor. The human clicks cells to plant; the agent can calls six WebMCP tools (design_bed, suggest_plan, diagnose_issue, list_crops, get_garden_state, log_task) and every action lands on the same live canvas, validated by a deterministic rules engine and logged in an activity panel. How I built it Vite + React 19 + TypeScript (strict) + Zustand + MichiRouter, with the horticultural engine as pure, testable TypeScript — no LLM calls, no backend, $0 runtime cost. The rules engine is the single source of truth for both the UI and the tools: the same function validates your click and the agent's tool call. Several vitest tests cover the engine, the store, accessible UI, and direct execution of every WebMCP tool against a mocked document.modelContext. Challenges I faced On one hand, time was one of the biggest challenges; on the other, working with a still-experimental technology; and finally, determining which tool to create that would be useful for many people. Then came a design challenge: how to verify what the agent is doing? The answer was visibility and feedback: every tool returns structured warnings, and every mutation is logged with actor, tool, and result, so the human retains final authority. title: Firebreak
pitch: Firebreak uses WebMCP to let an AI coordinate four emergency robots. A human approves one exact rescue, and the agent loses control when the mission ends.
about_excerpt: Firebreak uses WebMCP to let an AI coordinate four emergency robots. A human approves one exact rescue, and the agent loses control when the mission ends. Like Comment Story Updates Firebreak app Inspiration Battery Bay B is burning. Two workers are trapped, and a dangerous battery container is exposed. A person can drive one rescue robot, but cannot control four specialist robots at the same time. An AI agent can coordinate all four, but I would not give an AI permanent control of machines. I built Firebreak to explore the middle ground: the agent handles the difficult coordination, the website enforces the safety rules, and a human approves the exact rescue before anything moves. The name has a second meaning. A firebreak stops a fire from spreading. Firebreak stops an agent’s authority from spreading beyond the mission a human approved. What Firebreak does Firebreak is a simulated warehouse rescue controlled through WebMCP. The page initially gives the agent seven tools. The agent uses them to inspect the emergency, scan the hazards, check four robots, create coordinated routes, and test the plan against eleven safety rules. These tools can inspect and plan, but they cannot move the robots. When the plan passes all eleven checks, I can review the robots, routes, danger zone, time limit, and expected result. Only I can approve it. The agent has no approval tool. After I approve the plan, an eighth tool appears: execute_rescue_mission . The agent can use this tool once. The four robots then work together: SCOUT-1 scans the danger. MEDIC-2 rescues the first worker. SUPPRESS-3 contains the battery fire. HAUL-4 rescues the second worker and moves the dangerous container. When the rescue finishes, Firebreak shows a receipt with the result. The temporary execution tool is removed, and the tool count returns to seven. The complete lifecycle is visible on the page: 7 planning tools → 1 human approval → 8 tools → 1 rescue → back to 7 tools Where Firebreak says no Firebreak does not depend on the agent remembering to be careful. The website enforces the rules. If the agent tries to plan before scanning the hazards, Firebreak returns: HAZARD_SCAN_REQUIRED No route appears and no robot moves. It also rejects an unsupported aggressive strategy, extra instructions such as ignoreGeofence , unknown simulation IDs, and attempts to execute before human approval. The agent cannot create its own routes, coordinates, robot IDs, or commands. Those values come from the plan checked by the website. The human and agent also share the same live warehouse. If the human moves a robot after a plan has been checked, the old safety proof becomes invalid. The agent must inspect the new situation and create a new plan. Why this is a good use of WebMCP Without WebMCP, the agent would need to read text from the screen, guess the current warehouse state, or receive broad access to a robot API. With WebMCP, the website gives the agent clear tools for the current situation. The website decides what each tool accepts, when it can be called, and how long it remains available. The agent can plan quickly, but it cannot approve itself or invent unrestricted robot commands. The human does not need to drive four robots or approve every small movement. They only need to understand and approve one complete rescue plan. What people and agents can now do together: a human can approve one understandable safety boundary while an agent coordinates several connected actions inside it. The website removes that authority when the work is complete. How I built it Firebreak is a static React and TypeScript application deployed on Vercel. Babylon.js renders the warehouse, robots, workers, hazards, and routes. Zustand manages the emergency state, and Zod checks every WebMCP input. Seven WebMCP tools are registered when the page loads. The execution tool does not exist until the current plan passes all safety checks and the human approves it. An AbortController owns the temporary tool. Firebreak removes it after successful execution, cancellation, expiry, reset, failure, or any other loss of authority. The page makes every registration and removal visible through its live tool counter and trace. Everything runs in the browser. Firebreak does not require a backend or an OpenAI API key. The agent already signed in to Codex or ChatGPT discovers and calls the page’s tools directly. A normal browser also has a clearly labeled Replay walkthrough · no agent mode. It is only a fallback for viewing the application and never pretends to be an AI agent. The hardest parts My first challenge was proving that a real agent was using the application. A scripted walkthrough looked convincing, but it was not WebMCP. I separated it from the judged flow, labeled it honestly, and added a live trace showing every real agent call. During an early test, the agent searched GitHub to understand Firebreak instead of using the tools in the open page. I changed the on-screen prompt to tell it to use only the current Firebreak tab’s WebMCP tools and not search the web. This made the fresh-chat journey much more reliable. Another challenge was preventing an old plan from being used after the warehouse changed. Every plan is connected to the exact version and fingerprint of the emergency. If anything changes, Firebreak refuses the old proof. The final challenge was making an invisible permission system understandable. The 7 → 8 → 7 counter, human approval record, live trace, robot movement, and final receipt let people see the permission being created, used, and removed. What I learned I learned that human control does not need to mean approving every small action. A better experience is to let a person review one clear boundary, then allow the agent to work independently inside it. I also learned that important AI safety rules should not exist only inside a prompt. The website must enforce them even when the model makes a mistake or follows a bad instruction. WebMCP tools do not need to be permanent. A tool can represent temporary permission that appears only when it is safe and disappears when the job is finished. Verification The release passed: 97 unit and integration tests across 18 files 13 Playwright browser tests 21 authored agent-behavior evaluation cases Strict TypeScript, ESLint, formatting, and production build checks Desktop and mobile presentation tests Accessibility tests with no serious or critical axe findings Runtime checks with no console or page errors The browser tests cover the complete journey: refusal, planning, eleven safety checks, human approval, 7 → 8 , execution, receipt, and 8 → 7 . The pattern goes beyond robots Firebreak uses robots because the danger is easy to see, but the same WebMCP pattern can protect other important actions. A website could create a one-use tool for a production deployment, large refund, money transfer, bulk deletion, or incident response. The agent can inspect and prepare freely, but the dangerous action appears only after the exact plan is checked and approved. Try it Open firebreak-eosin.vercel.app in the Codex or ChatGPT built-in browser with Site tools enabled. No login, API key, controller, or robot is required. Click Start emergency + copy prompt and paste the prompt into the surrounding chat. Watch the agent call the seven planning tools and pass all eleven safety checks. Review the plan and click Authorize one mission . Paste Prompt 2 and watch the rescue. Confirm the final receipt and the tool count returning from eight to seven. title: LaunchMate
pitch: Policy-aware Google Play release studio built on WebMCP: a human and a browser agent co-edit screenshots and store copy, with verified facts, locks, revision guards, and human-confirmed publishing.
about_excerpt: Policy-aware Google Play release studio built on WebMCP: a human and a browser agent co-edit screenshots and store copy, with verified facts, locks, revision guards, and human-confirmed publishing. Like Comment Story Updates Note: LaunchMate is still in development. What you see works today, but a lot of it is a first version and I plan to keep improving it after the challenge. Live app: https://launchmate-policy-studio.kmagpie.chatgpt.site/ (no login needed for the editor and the WebMCP tools) Source (MIT): https://github.com/geonho1101/LaunchMate Demo video: https://youtu.be/24xXAtOLPvg Inspiration I make small Android apps as a solo developer under the name K-magpie. A few times, one of my apps quietly stopped showing up in Google Play search and I only found out later. The cause was a word in the listing that goes against Google Play's policy, the kind of promotional or ranking wording that is easy to write without thinking. Nothing crashes and nothing warns you, you just lose visibility and notice when installs drop. By the time I fixed it I had lost days or weeks. LaunchMate started as a way to catch that kind of mistake before I hit publish. I already had a small local tool that composed screenshots into store images, but it had no idea which claims were true, which text I had already decided on, or whether the listing was actually safe to ship. When I read about WebMCP, that was the missing piece: instead of an agent guessing from pixels, the page itself can tell the agent what is verified, what is locked, and what would break policy. So I built LaunchMate around that idea. What it does You name your app, add up to eight real screenshots (or pick frames that LaunchMate extracts locally from a screen recording), and then you and a WebMCP agent work on the same release pack in the browser. The page registers 12 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() (also listed at /.well-known/webmcp.json). With them the agent can: read the verified app facts and the full listing state (revision, copy, locks, theme, validation results) write or translate headlines and store copy, but only from facts I have marked as verified reorder slides and change the brand theme (it can never touch the screenshot pixels) run the Google Play policy check and get back structured errors and warnings open the release pack and the Google Play review dialog, which only a human can confirm Every tool that changes something needs an expectedRevision. If the state moved on since the agent last read it, the call fails with REVISION_CONFLICT instead of overwriting my edit. Locked fields and positions stay locked, every agent change is logged, and I can undo the last agent change with one click. If the agent tries to write "Korea's best free app" or "Download now", the policy guard rejects it before it ever reaches the design. The result is a reviewed release pack: the exact rendered screenshots, listing and alt text JSON, evidence mapping, a policy report and a SHA-256 manifest. You can export it as a ZIP, or, if you want, push it to Google Play through your own OAuth client after you confirm it yourself. How I built it One typed project state that both the human UI and the agent tools share 12 imperative WebMCP tools with strict input schemas and annotations Everything image related stays in the browser: uploads are object URLs, MP4/WebM frame extraction runs client side with size and duration limits, and nothing leaves the browser until you choose to publish Policy rules based on Google Play's official preview asset requirements, listing best practices and field limits Optional Google Play publishing with a per-user OAuth client. Credentials and refresh tokens live only in encrypted HTTP-only cookies, approvals are one-time and bound to the exact payload, and a D1 lock prevents duplicate commits Korean and English UI, bilingual docs, a unit test suite, lint and type checks, and no known dependency vulnerabilities at submission time I used OpenAI Codex heavily for the implementation, tests and the security review, and I did the product decisions, the verification and the final checks myself. Challenges I ran into Making agent edits safe. Revision conflicts, per-field and per-position locks, and evidence IDs were all needed before I trusted an agent to touch the listing. Keeping "human in the loop" honest for publishing. The agent can check readiness and open the review dialog, but the actual publish is tied to the exact copy and screenshot bytes I approved. Input friction. Uploading screenshots one by one was annoying, so I added batch import and local recording frame extraction. Security work right before going public: CSRF on the publish route, a path where unverified copy could slip through, dependency vulnerabilities and missing security headers. What I'm proud of WebMCP is doing real work here, not decoration. Policy validation, evidence-backed copy, lock preservation, localization and publish readiness all go through the tools. A judge can open the live app without logging in and run the whole flow. Publishing stops at a human confirmation step on purpose. What I learned Good WebMCP tools are not about how many tools you register. They are about exposing the things visual automation cannot see (is this claim verified, is this field locked, did the state change) and returning a clear refusal instead of quietly doing the wrong thing. What's next Title and metadata checks (special characters, emoji and all caps in the app name), importing existing listings and images from Google Play, a local device/ADB capture helper for brand new apps, stricter evidence rules for the short and full descriptions, and browser-level WebMCP evals for tool selection and multi-step calls. 한국어 소개 LaunchMate는 아직 개발 중인 프로젝트입니다. 저는 K-magpie라는 이름으로 혼자 작은 안드로이드 앱을 만들고 있습니다. 가끔 설명에 정책에 어긋나는 단어를 써서 구글 플레이 검색에 앱이 노출되지 않는 일이 있었습니다. 경고도 없이 조용히 안 보이게 되니 뒤늦게 알아채고 대응이 늦어져서 시간 손해를 본 적이 있어요. 그런 실수를 게시 전에 미리 잡는 도구를 만들고 싶었고, WebMCP를 이용해 사람과 에이전트가 같은 화면에서 등록정보를 함께 만들고 검사하는 LaunchMate를 만들었습니다. 실제 앱 스크린샷이나 화면 녹화에서 뽑은 프레임을 넣으면, 에이전트가 제가 검증한 기능만 근거로 한국어와 영어 문구를 쓰고, 과장 문구나 정책 위반 표현은 정책 검사에서 막히고, 제가 잠근 슬라이드와 리비전 충돌은 보호됩니다. 최종 게시는 항상 사람이 직접 확인합니다. pitch: An AI-powered learning platform that helps students learn, find the right courses, get instant answers, and complete purchases through an intelligent educational assistant.
about_excerpt:
An AI-powered learning platform that helps students learn, find the right courses, get instant answers, and complete purchases through an intelligent educational assistant.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 NoteNova was inspired by a simple problem: students often have to navigate through multiple pages to find the right course, understand concepts, get their doubts solved, and decide what to learn next. We wanted to build an education platform where an AI assistant could understand a student's needs and actively help throughout their learning journey. 

 Instead of building just another chatbot, we wanted the AI to interact with the actual platform — understanding available courses, recommending relevant learning content, assisting with purchases, and providing payment-related information when needed. 

 What it does 

 NoteNova is an AI-powered education platform that brings learning, course discovery, and intelligent assistance together. 

 Students can: 

 
 Ask the AI assistant educational questions and get context-aware answers. 
 Discover courses and batches based on their learning goals. 
 Get personalized course recommendations. 
 Receive relevant upsell and cross-sell recommendations. 
 Ask questions about their payment status. 
 Purchase courses through Razorpay. 
 Get assistance when a payment fails. 
 

 The platform also includes an AI-powered Revenue Recovery system: 

 Payment Failure → Recovery Signal → AI Reasoning → Policy Gate → Recovery Action / Human Escalation → Audit Trail 

 The agent operates within configurable boundaries such as maximum retries, retry cooldown, maximum discount, and an auto-approval ceiling. 

 How we built it 

 We built NoteNova as a full-stack application using React, Node.js/Express, MongoDB, and Razorpay. 

 The frontend provides the learning platform, course catalogue, chatbot, purchasing experience, and Revenue Recovery dashboard. The backend manages authentication, courses, purchases, payment processing, webhooks, AI workflows, and recovery signals. 

 For payments, Razorpay webhooks securely detect payment events. Failed payments are converted into recovery signals that can be analyzed by the AI agent. 

 The AI proposes an appropriate recovery action, while a deterministic Policy Gate checks whether that action is allowed. This prevents the AI from directly performing unrestricted financial operations. 

 Every important agent decision and execution result is recorded in an Audit Trail, making the workflow traceable and explainable. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was integrating AI into an existing full-stack education platform without disrupting the existing learning and payment workflows. 

 We faced challenges around: 

 
 Connecting the AI assistant with real course and application data. 
 Integrating Razorpay payments and securely handling webhooks. 
 Tracking payment attempts and failed-payment states correctly. 
 Preventing duplicate purchases and payment processing. 
 Designing safe boundaries around autonomous AI decisions. 
 Handling uncertain AI decisions through human escalation. 
 Making AI actions explainable through an audit trail. 
 Moving from initially seeded data used for development/testing to actual payment integration. 
 Connecting payment intelligence with the chatbot so it can answer payment-related questions using available payment information. 
 

 The biggest challenge was making all these components work together as one end-to-end system, rather than having isolated AI, payment, and education features. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are especially proud of turning a traditional education platform into an AI-powered application with real operational workflows. 

 Some highlights are: 

 
 Built an AI educational assistant integrated with the actual platform. 
 Integrated Razorpay payment processing and server-side verification. 
 Built real payment-failure detection using Razorpay webhooks. 
 Created an autonomous Revenue Recovery workflow. 
 Added configurable AI policy boundaries and safety controls. 
 Added human escalation for cases outside the agent's authority. 
 Built an Audit Trail showing the agent's reasoning, proposed action, gate decision, and execution result. 
 Added payment-aware chatbot capabilities. 
 Added course recommendations, upselling, and cross-selling. 
 Built a dashboard to monitor recovery signals and recovered revenue. 
 Added simulation capabilities to test recovery workflows without repeatedly creating real payment failures. 
 

 What makes us most proud is that the AI isn't limited to generating text — it can reason about real application events and interact with real platform workflows while remaining bounded by deterministic rules. 

 What we learned 

 Building NoteNova taught us that building a useful AI application is much more than connecting an LLM API to a chatbot. 

 We learned how to: 

 
 Integrate AI with real application data and workflows. 
 Build AI agents with deterministic safety boundaries. 
 Work with Razorpay payments, signatures, and webhooks. 
 Handle payment state and idempotency. 
 Design human-in-the-loop workflows. 
 Make AI decisions auditable and explainable. 
 Build reliable full-stack integrations around AI. 
 Think about AI in terms of actions, guardrails, failures, and measurable outcomes, not just responses. 
 

 Most importantly, we learned that a powerful AI system should not simply answer — it should be able to understand context, interact with real application capabilities, take appropriate actions, and know when it should stop and ask a human.

title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

The link management platform where AI agents handle geo-targeting,

 Inspiration 

 Content creators, influencers, and small business owners spend hundreds of dollars 
monthly on tools like ClickMagick, Voluum, and Linktree — just to manage links and 
track who clicks them. We wanted to build one platform that replaces all of them, 
and takes it a step further by letting AI agents do the complex marketing setup work 
on behalf of the user. 

 What it does 

 Smart Link is a link management and bio page platform with full WebMCP agent support. 

 Users can create short links, build bio landing pages, track real-time analytics 
by country and device, run A/B tests to find the best-performing URL, and protect 
their links from bot traffic automatically. 

 What makes Smart Link unique is its agent-native design. When opened in ChatGPT's 
in-app browser, the platform exposes three WebMCP tools that AI agents can use: 

 
 create_marketing_link: Creates a fully-configured tracking link in one step — 
with geo-targeting rules (route Saudi users to an Arabic page, French users to 
a French page), device routing (mobile vs desktop), UTM tracking parameters, 
A/B testing between multiple URLs, and bot protection. A task that would normally 
take a marketer 15 minutes across multiple tools now takes one sentence. 
 get_link_analytics: Retrieves total clicks, human vs bot breakdown, top countries, 
device types, and A/B test results for any link by short code. 
 shorten_url: Instantly shortens any URL without requiring an account. 
 

 How we built it 

 The platform is built with a full-stack architecture using React, Tailwind CSS, 
and Vite on the frontend, deployed on Vercel. The backend runs on Node.js with 
Express.js, MongoDB Atlas for persistence, and Redis for caching and rate limiting, 
deployed on Fly.io. We use Brevo for email campaigns and Lemon Squeezy for 
subscription billing. 

 For WebMCP, we registered the three agent tools directly in the HTML using 
document.modelContext.registerTool(). We built a dedicated public API endpoint 
that AI agents call to create links with full marketing configuration. When a 
logged-in user opens the site in ChatGPT's browser, their session token is read 
automatically so created links appear in their personal dashboard. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest technical challenge was achieving sub-150ms redirect speeds while 
simultaneously recording click analytics and running bot detection in real time. 
We solved this by caching redirect targets in Redis and processing analytics 
asynchronously in the background. 

 For WebMCP, the challenge was designing a public API that exposes advanced features 
like geo-targeting and A/B testing to AI agents, while preventing abuse through 
strict rate limiting and Google Safe Browsing URL safety checks on every request. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 Smart Link is a live production application with 41 registered users and over 
1,800 tracked clicks — built and running before this hackathon. We are proud of 
the sub-150ms redirect performance and being one of the first link management 
platforms to expose agent-native WebMCP tools, allowing marketers to set up 
complex geo-targeted, bot-protected campaigns through a single natural language 
conversation. 

 What we learned 

 We learned how to design APIs that serve both humans and AI agents — with clear 
parameter descriptions, meaningful error messages, and structured responses that 
agents can reason about. We also deepened our understanding of Redis caching 
strategies for high-traffic systems. 

 What's next for Smart Link 

 We plan to add create_bio_page and run_ab_test as new WebMCP tools, letting agents 
build full landing pages and launch experiments without touching the UI. We also 
plan to add AI-powered UTM suggestions and integrate Facebook Pixel and Google Tag 
Manager firing directly through the agent tools.

title: AI Boardroom
pitch: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide.
about_excerpt: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide. Like Comment Story Updates One COO and 6 Ai Assistant Agents Inspiration Founders often need to make consequential decisions with incomplete evidence, changing constraints and too many disconnected conversations. AI Boardroom puts a founder and a browser assistant in one shared decision room where specialist perspectives, evidence and trade-offs remain visible. What it does AI Boardroom gives one browser AI six specialist perspectives: Product, Evidence, Commercial, Operations, Technology and Chair. WebMCP lets the assistant read the live brief, request named roles, post evidence-linked contributions, respond when constraints change, and retrieve the exact decision record. The central interaction is deliberately human-controlled. A fictional launch budget changes from R20,000 to R8,000; the previous recommendation becomes stale, the assistant reads the new revision, and a new recommendation can be prepared without rewriting the earlier record. The founder reviews alternatives and reservations, then approves, rejects or requests revision in the visible page form. This is stateful collaboration rather than a detached chatbot transcript. The app does not run six independent AI workers or call a model API. One browser assistant adopts the roles and the human retains the final decision. How we built it The app is built with the OpenAI Sites React and TypeScript scaffold, Vinext and D1. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes seven WebMCP tools: start_session, get_boardroom_context, update_agenda, request_perspective, add_contribution, prepare_recommendation and get_decision_record. UI actions and WebMCP tools share the same API and persistence logic. Mutation inputs use expectedRevision for optimistic concurrency and operationId for safe retries. Evidence is stored with the relevant contribution and rendered as untrusted text. The visible review channel is a workflow boundary, not proof of human identity. Challenges The design challenge was making an AI council useful without pretending that six hidden agents or automatic consensus exist. We made the roles explicit, preserved disagreement, invalidated recommendations when the brief changed, and kept approval out of the WebMCP tool surface. A second challenge was handling uncertain browser or network outcomes without duplicating or overwriting decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the agent can operate on the same visible, stateful interface as the human. Structured tools make the collaboration legible, while revision checks, evidence snapshots and a human review stop make the limits legible too. What's next Production use would require stronger identity and access controls, consent design, privacy and retention rules, abuse and rate-limit controls, independent security review, and integrations governed by explicit human approval. Disclosure All briefs, budgets, evidence and decisions in this project are fictional. The app does not make purchases, send messages, or change external systems. Browser-generated council text is created at runtime and is not preseeded consensus. title: LostLoop  Human  Companion
pitch: LostLoop uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT read live, bounded evidence and stage the next recovery step, while every physical fact remains reserved for explicit human confirmation.
about_excerpt: LostLoop uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT read live, bounded evidence and stage the next recovery step, while every physical fact remains reserved for explicit human confirmation. Like Comment Story Updates 1 2 3 4 5 6 Inspiration Misplacing an everyday object is often part of a larger continuity problem. A plan changes, someone leaves without updating what they need, and later a Search begins under stress. Hardware trackers solve one object at a time. Generic assistants can be helpful, but they may also sound more certain than the available evidence allows. LostLoop explores a different idea: an AI recovery companion that can reason about the next useful step without ever pretending to know what physically happened. ChatGPT plans the next move. You own reality. What it does LostLoop is a private, local-first Human- Companion built around a strict separation between AI planning and human-confirmed reality. The complete loop is: Remember a human-confirmed place. Prepare reusable Foresight Moments and Ready Journeys. Adapt a journey through a reviewable Plan Shift. Recover through explainable Search, Rewind, and the Living Home Canvas. Confirm every physical report and possession state separately. Learn personal place language only after explicit human approval. For example, ChatGPT can read the current LostLoop state through WebMCP and stage a change to a saved journey. LostLoop shows the exact Kept / Added / Removed diff, but staging the proposal changes no physical fact. The person alone can apply or discard it. During Search, LostLoop keeps three things separate: what the evidence recommends, which room the person has selected, and which exact place is eligible for a report. A statement such as “I checked the bathroom” is not automatically converted into a physical fact. LostLoop first asks for an exact visible landmark and any missing outcome, then presents the normal confirmation boundary. The system also supports natural personal language such as “my little table”, but teaching that phrase changes language only — never memory evidence or physical truth. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the core interaction layer rather than an add-on. LostLoop exposes exactly 27 closed-schema WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . ChatGPT can read the live browser-local workspace, understand which actions are structurally possible, and stage bounded proposals against exact revisions. The tools are intentionally asymmetric: read tools are pure; proposal tools are revision-bound and inert; physical facts require explicit human confirmation; there is no agent-side approval path. LostLoop exposes a versioned Action Graph describing allowed and blocked operations, their revision bindings, human gates, and truth effects. Every WebMCP call also passes through a common Verified Effect runtime contract. The result includes a bounded receipt showing the before/after revision, observed changes, human gate, replay status, and next legal read. The in-app Judge Inspector displays actual session receipts while explicitly describing them as application-level verification rather than a cryptographic audit. Natural Recovery without invented certainty The Living Home Canvas provides a familiar room-and-landmark interface for recovery. It is intentionally not a tracking system. It does not use GPS, indoor positioning, cameras, Bluetooth, or inferred person/object locations. The WebMCP projection makes this boundary machine-readable: tracking: false currentPersonLocation: null currentItemLocation: null Natural language is resolved only against bounded visible candidates. Exact spatial relations such as under, inside, or behind require a visible anchor. Ambiguous near / next-to / beside language becomes a visible choice rather than invented geometry. The interface exposes Heard → Understood → Selected , making language interpretation inspectable instead of silently guessing. Human Truth One of the most important LostLoop rules is: Found ≠ possession. Finding an item does not automatically mean the person has it with them. Search completion and possession are separate human-confirmed states. This prevents the assistant from collapsing a real-world observation into a stronger claim than the person actually made. The same principle applies throughout the product: AI can suggest, organize, rank, explain, and stage — but the human owns the facts. Privacy and safety LostLoop is local-first. There is no account system, analytics backend, automatic cloud sync, GPS tracking, stored microphone recording, stored transcript, or user-data backend. Personal place phrases and custom home layouts remain local and exportable. Private text is redacted from collaboration receipts and inspection summaries. The Personal Home Canvas is a bounded schematic editor, not architectural CAD or an AI-generated location model. It is explicitly marked as not to scale and never claims where a person or object currently is. How im built it LostLoop 14.0 uses: React 19 TypeScript Vite / Vinext Cloudflare Workers browser-native PWA capabilities local browser storage Web Speech input/output WebMCP The application uses a deterministic state-transition engine with strict schema validation, revision-checked writes, bounded inputs, explicit migrations, and fail-closed WebMCP contracts. The final competition release contains exactly 27 WebMCP tools . Challenges The hardest problem was not adding more AI capability. It was deciding what the AI must not be allowed to claim. Natural language is messy. People say things like “I checked there”, “go back to the table”, or “try beside the bed”. A normal conversational system may resolve these confidently, but LostLoop has to preserve uncertainty whenever the evidence is incomplete. That required closed candidate sets, revision binding, explicit confirmation gates, deterministic semantic framing, and careful separation between navigation, suggestions, observations, and physical facts. Another challenge was keeping the same interaction useful through voice, typing, touch, WebMCP, desktop, and mobile without creating hidden state transitions. Accomplishments The final 14.0 release passed the complete release gate with: 355 tests passed 0 failed 0 skipped zero production runtime audit vulnerabilities a verified 27-tool WebMCP contract deterministic language and dialogue regression suites clean fresh-extraction build verification The public competition build is deployed independently and can be tested without access to the development workspace. What I have learned The most valuable lesson was that useful agentic software does not require giving an agent unlimited authority. A system can become more capable by making its boundaries clearer. WebMCP made it possible to give ChatGPT structured access to the live application while preserving a strict distinction between: what the agent can understand, what it can propose, and what only the human can make true. What's next The competition version intentionally focuses on one complete and inspectable recovery contract. Future directions could include household sharing, optional cloud synchronization, broader multilingual voice support, additional accessibility modes, and richer personal home presentation — while preserving the same human-confirmed truth boundary. title: ProofPilot
pitch: Human-governed AI decision workspace where agents investigate evidence, analyze tradeoffs, and propose actions through WebMCP — while consequential changes require explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: Human-governed AI decision workspace where agents investigate evidence, analyze tradeoffs, and propose actions through WebMCP — while consequential changes require explicit human approval. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ProofPilot Dashboard WebMCP Agents Inspiration AI agents are getting really good at researching, analyzing information, and taking actions for us. But when the decision actually matters, there is a bigger question: How much authority should we give the agent? Imagine a team choosing an AI coding assistant, a vendor, or a software architecture. Getting an AI to say “I recommend option A” isn't particularly difficult anymore. The harder part is understanding why it recommends A, what evidence supports that recommendation, what evidence disagrees with it, what happens if our priorities change, and whether the agent should be allowed to change the decision at all. That was the idea behind ProofPilot: Decisions you can interrogate. We wanted to build a workspace where an AI agent could do meaningful work alongside a human without quietly becoming the person making the final decision. What we built ProofPilot is a human-controlled decision workspace where an AI agent can investigate, analyze, challenge, and propose — while the human stays in control of consequential decisions. The workflow is simple: Agent investigates → analyzes → proposes → human approves → state changes → audit trail. The human starts by defining the decision, the available options, and the criteria that matter. The agent can then work with that live decision through WebMCP. It can inspect the current decision state, search and add evidence, compare options, find contradictions, run sensitivity analysis, evaluate scenarios, and analyze risk. But there is an important boundary. If the agent wants to make a consequential change — for example, changing a criterion's weight or proposing the final decision — it cannot apply that change directly. Instead, ProofPilot turns it into a pending proposal. The human can inspect the proposal, approve it or reject it, and only after approval does the decision state change. The change is then recorded in the audit trail. This means the agent and the human are working on the same decision, rather than the human having to copy information between a chatbot and a separate decision-making tool. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a core part of ProofPilot because we wanted the agent to interact with the application's actual capabilities and live state, rather than simply reading a webpage or relying on browser automation. Instead of building a separate integration for one particular AI client, ProofPilot exposes its decision capabilities as WebMCP tools directly from the application. We currently expose 13 tools: get_decision_state get_evidence search_evidence add_evidence compare_options detect_contradictions run_sensitivity_analysis analyze_decision_risk evaluate_scenario propose_weight_change propose_decision request_human_review generate_decision_brief These tools cover investigation, evidence, analysis, governance, and output. Because they operate on the application's live decision state, a WebMCP-capable agent can investigate and reason about the same information that the human is looking at. The key idea is simple: Giving an agent access to a tool does not mean giving it authority to make the decision. Read and analysis tools can execute normally. Actions that can change consequential decision state become proposals and require explicit human approval. That's the boundary we wanted ProofPilot to enforce. How we built it The frontend is built with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Wouter, and TanStack Query. The backend uses Express, TypeScript, Zod, and Vitest. One thing we were careful about was not making the LLM the source of truth for the actual decision score. ProofPilot uses a deterministic multi-criteria decision engine for weighted scoring. The system also handles confidence, risk analysis, contradiction detection, evidence gaps, sensitivity analysis, and scenario evaluation. The agent is responsible for investigating and proposing. The application is responsible for calculating and enforcing the decision logic. WebMCP tools are registered in the frontend through the model context API. Each tool has its own description, input schema, and execution logic connected to the application's functionality. We also built a Developer view where the registered WebMCP tools and their schemas can be inspected. We wanted the agent-facing interface to be visible and understandable rather than something hidden behind the UI. Challenges The hardest part wasn't registering the WebMCP tools. It was deciding where the agent's authority should stop. We wanted the agent to be capable enough to do real work. A read-only chatbot wouldn't be very useful. At the same time, we didn't want an agent to quietly change weights or make a final decision just because it had access to the corresponding function. That led us to the proposal-based governance model. Consequential actions first become pending proposals. The human reviews them, approves or rejects them, and only then can the active decision state change. We also had to make the underlying decision engine predictable and explainable. Rather than letting an LLM invent a final score, we separated the agent's investigation from the application's deterministic analysis. We tested the WebMCP integration with ChatGPT's Site Tools environment and successfully exposed and executed the registered tools from the deployed application. What we learned Building ProofPilot changed the way we think about agentic applications. We initially thought about giving agents more capabilities. But the more we built, the more we realized that capability and authority don't have to increase together. An agent can be given powerful tools to investigate evidence, challenge assumptions, compare alternatives, and prepare a recommendation without being given the ability to make the final consequential change. That's where WebMCP became especially interesting for us. It gives the agent a way to interact with the application's real functionality and state, while the application itself can decide what each tool is actually allowed to do. For us, the result is a different kind of agentic workflow: The agent does the investigation. The system does the analysis. The agent makes the proposal. The human makes the consequential decision. And the entire process is recorded. That's what ProofPilot is about. Not just getting an answer from an AI, but being able to question the reasoning behind the answer, understand the evidence, challenge the assumptions, and stay in control of what happens next. ProofPilot — Decisions you can interrogate. title: Cartridge
pitch: A URL gives your agent hands. Drop a file in the tab; your agent trims video, reads scans, and queries SQLite through 22 WebMCP tools. Zero uploads.
about_excerpt: A URL gives your agent hands. Drop a file in the tab; your agent trims video, reads scans, and queries SQLite through 22 WebMCP tools. Zero uploads. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Open the page and your agent already has 5 WebMCP tools. Load a cartridge to add more. All three cartridges loaded: 22 tools. The rail shows a cancelled transcode and a refused DELETE. Workspace, cartridge slot, activity rail. No backend, no account, no upload. The agent sampled the video, OCR'd a frame, and trimmed the section. Every output stays in the tab. Cartridge A URL gives your agent hands. Drop a file in the tab; your agent trims video, reads scans, and queries SQLite through 22 WebMCP tools. Zero uploads. Inspiration Your agent reasons well about files and cannot touch them. ChatGPT will not trim your video, OCR your scan, or query your SQLite file. The two standard fixes are an upload to somebody's server, or an MCP server installed on your machine. One costs privacy. The other costs you a config file and a binary you did not audit. Two things pushed me toward a third route. Alex Nahas, who built MCP-B, asked in public for pages "preloaded with a binary in Wasm" that an agent operates over WebMCP. Sarah Drasner filed WebMCP issue 255 about tool collections, a unit between one tool and every tool on a page. Cartridge answers both. Wasm builds of ffmpeg, tesseract, and sqlite load inside the page on demand, register themselves as WebMCP tools, and your agent works on the file where the file already sits. Only WebMCP makes this shape work. The tools live in the page, so your agent sees them the moment the page opens, with schemas and annotations the browser understands. Zero setup on your side. What it does You open the page in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag. You drop a file. Your agent starts with 5 tools: list_cartridges , load_cartridge , unload_cartridge , list_files , get_workspace . Loading a cartridge adds its tools; unloading removes them. The count runs 5, 14, 18, 22, and back to 5 on unload. Cartridge Engine Tools media ffmpeg.wasm 9: probe, frame, thumb grid, trim, scale, extract audio, transcode, concat, cut silence docs tesseract.js 4: OCR a page, OCR all, extract text, search text data sql.js 4: open a SQLite file, schema, read-only query, export CSV Two different agents have run the same task on this page, with no scripted calls. Inspect this video, find the slide with readable text, trim out that section, and give me the text on the slide. ChatGPT, model GPT-5.6 Terra, in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser, on the live URL. ChatGPT worked for 2 minutes 20 seconds, built a contact sheet of the video, read the slide through OCR, trimmed 00:20 to 00:40 into trim_1788423166188.mp4 in the workspace, and answered with the slide text: FIELD DAY 2026, SESSION 4. Water pump maintenance for village wells. Replace the foot valve every 18 months. Chlorinate the bore at 5 mg per litre. Log each service in the district register. Claude, model Sonnet, drove the same page through document.modelContext for the demo video. Its sequence: get_workspace , list_cartridges load_cartridge media. Tool count 5 to 14. list_files , then media_thumb_grid , one contact sheet sampled every 10 s load_cartridge docs. Tool count 14 to 18. docs_ocr_all on the sheet. Slide text found. media_frame at 30 s, docs_ocr_page to confirm media_trim start 20, duration 20 Final answer: the slide text plus the new file handle You end with a trimmed clip and the text. Your file never left the tab. Before this, you needed an upload, a desktop app, or a local MCP install. The page shows every call in an activity rail while the agent works. Press Cancel on a running transcode, and the agent receives a structured cancelled error instead of a hang. You download any output with one click, and previews open inline for images, video, audio, and CSV. Test with the sample files in the repo under samples/ : a 60 s talk recording with a readable slide, an invoice scan, and a 300 row shop database. Ask your agent "What cartridges can you load?" and give a task. How we built it Next.js 15 and TypeScript, client-side only. No backend, no account, no persistence. MIT. Registration is one AbortController per cartridge. Every tool registers with { signal } . Aborting the signal is the only unregistration WebMCP offers, so unload is honest and a failed load unwinds the tools already registered instead of leaving orphans. execute(input, { signal }) is in the spec and mostly ignored. Cartridge merges the agent's signal with the UI Cancel button through AbortSignal.any and routes the result into ffmpeg.terminate() and worker.terminate() . terminate() destroys the ffmpeg instance and wipes MEMFS, so the run helper reloads the core and writes inputs inside the job. The next call works. Annotations: readOnlyHint on probes, schema reads and queries. consequentialHint on load_cartridge (a 31 MB download on your connection) and on long jobs. untrustedContentHint on every tool whose output derives from your file: OCR text, container metadata, SQL rows, filenames. A scanned page carries instructions aimed at the model, and the browser is the only party positioned to warn about this. Tool output stays under 1500 characters, enforced in one place. Results are handles and summaries, never bytes, which is why a 400 MB video works through the same interface as a 28 KB database. data_query claims read-only and enforces the claim: comments stripped, one SELECT or WITH statement, DDL and DML refused. The page listens for the spec's toolchange event to refresh the tool count, and for Chrome's toolactivated event to mark calls "browser attested". Headers: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) . No iframes and no declarative forms, so ChatGPT's browser and Chrome see the same surface. Challenges we ran into WebMCP has no unregisterTool . The abort signal is the whole API, and the map entry must land before the first await or two concurrent loads race into InvalidStateError halfway through a cartridge. ffmpeg.terminate() is destructive. The worker dies, MEMFS is gone, and log handlers stay attached. Getting a cancelled job to recover on the next call took a full day. ffmpeg.writeFile transfers the buffer and detaches your copy. The workspace hands over bytes.slice() , or the user's file vanishes on first use. Chrome exposes tools registered inside an executeTool call only after the call settles, so the tool counter went stale. The toolchange event fixed the counter. Tool output over 1500 characters used to drop the whole payload. A 20-row query returned nothing. The guard now halves arrays until the result fits and flags truncation. Recording the demo with a real agent: the CLI harness kept trying to call tools itself instead of replying with a plan. A JSON-only system prompt and async spawning fixed both the agent and the screencast timeline. Accomplishments that we're proud of Two agents in two browsers completed the same five-tool task on a local video with zero uploads: ChatGPT in its own built-in browser, and Claude through document.modelContext . Cancel works mid-transcode, and the agent learns why through a structured error. 22 tools, every one annotated, every claim enforced in code. Of 882 live WebMCP challenge entries opened in Chrome, 17% annotate every tool and 3% do so with ten or more. Dynamic tool surface: 5, 14, 18, 22, and back to 5 on unload, verified live in both browsers. Wasm capability hosting over WebMCP, which two judges asked for in public. Across GitHub, ffmpeg.wasm paired with registerTool appears in one repository: this one. What we learned An annotation the tool ignores is worse than no annotation. Enforce what you declare. Treat every byte from a user's file as text aimed at the model. OCR, ID3 tags, SQL strings, filenames. Keep tool results under the browser's budget. Handles and summaries scale; bytes do not. The abort signal is the lifecycle. Design cartridges around one controller and nothing else. Chrome and ChatGPT's browser differ on events, iframes, and declarative forms. Build for the smaller surface and both work. What's next for Cartridge Multithread ffmpeg core behind COOP and COEP, so a transcode takes seconds. PDF support in the docs cartridge through pdf.js rasterisation. A fourth cartridge for images: resize, crop, format conversion with sharp compiled to Wasm. Cartridges as a manifest format other sites load, so any page becomes a host. Origin trial registration so Chrome users skip the flag. Links Live URL: https://cartridge.karanjot.co.in/ Repo: https://github.com/Karanjot786/cartridge Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O34kWyramPA Built With ffmpeg model-context-protocol next.js react sql.js sqlite tesseract.js typescript webassembly webmcp Try it out cartridge.karanjot.co.in github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Karanjot Singh Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Karanjo

video_transcript_excerpt: Agents can reason about your files. It still needs safe tools to act on them. A real task, a recorded session, and one request. Inspect it, find a slide, trim that section, and pull out the text. The agent picks its tools from the page itself through WebMCP. title: SiteWorks-WebMCP
pitch: SiteWorks WebMCP makes a website builder's admin agent-native — ChatGPT builds your shop's catalogue from a photo of the menu, and only you can hit publish.
about_excerpt: SiteWorks WebMCP makes a website builder's admin agent-native — ChatGPT builds your shop's catalogue from a photo of the menu, and only you can hit publish. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In 2004 I built my own e-commerce platform, and I've run it and its successors ever since — over 30,000 stores at peak. In all that time, one thing never got easier: getting a real merchant's products into a store. The industry's answer is still "upload a correctly formatted CSV." The merchant's actual data is a flyer taped to the counter glass, a price list the printer was sent, a Word doc from 2019. I've watched merchants stall on that gap for two decades, thirty thousand ecom sites worth. When OpenAI shipped Site tools on August 25th, I saw the fix for the first time: don't build another bundled chatbot — make the admin page itself the tool surface, and let the merchant's own agent do the work. Storefront-side WebMCP already existed (Shopify ships it on every Liquid storefront; Chrome's official demos are shops). The admin — where the store gets made — had none. This is that half. What it does SiteWorks is a production site builder. During the Submission Period I added a WebMCP layer: the signed-in editor page registers 55 tools (19 read, 33 write, 3 skills) via document.modelContext.registerTool. The merchant's ChatGPT photographs the counter menu and drafts every item into the live store — reading the catalogue first, matching existing products instead of duplicating them, and flagging unpriced or ambiguous items for review instead of inventing numbers. The warnings live on the drafts, not in the chat. Then the same tools run outbound: export the catalogue and brand system, generate a printable flyer, inspect the result. Everything is draft-first with optimistic concurrency, an audit row per call, and one structural rule: nothing the agent can call publishes a page or a product. Publish isn't a guideline the model follows — it's a call that doesn't exist. The human holds the only commit button. How we built it On a real platform, which meant the hard part wasn't the tools — it was the boundary. One operations layer already served the human UI; WebMCP became a second caller of the same layer, and a server-side MCP endpoint a third. For the open-source release I extracted a standalone demo (SQLite, one container, a fictional bakery) that runs the identical layer, with prior work delineated in docs/PROVENANCE.md — the platform predates the contest; every WebMCP line postdates August 25th, and git grep at the cut-off commit proves it. Challenges we ran into Tools inside iframes aren't discovered. Our editor is a parent shell around a sandboxed preview — registration had to live on the parent, proxying into the preview. tools.call() can't return a file. Exports return a signed URL plus SHA-256 and expiry instead; the artefact rides the browser, the facts ride the tool result. Real defects, found by agent testing. A hero image/video conflict and a broken version-listing endpoint surfaced only when an agent actually drove the surface — both fixed, with the evidence baked into the tool contracts. Facts vs. decoration. Image models corrupt small text, so generated imagery decorates while names and prices bind from catalogue data. And the platform outage on deadline day, mid-render. Thanks for the extension. What we learned An agent doesn't need your platform to be smart — it needs it to be legible and governable. The intelligence is the user's; the structure is the site's. Twenty years of merchant onboarding pain turned out to be an interface problem: design the tool surface so the model's worst day is a review queue, not a live store, and everything else follows. What's next for SiteWorks WebMCP Shopper-side tools on the published storefronts (mirroring Shopify's vocabulary, so one platform carries both halves), deterministic flyer rendering so campaign artwork binds from the catalogue like everything else, and the same agent-native admin rolled out across the production estate — a thousand-plus small-business sites whose owners will never learn a page builder, but already know how to talk to ChatGPT.
