title: WellAuth - Prior Authorization for Agents
pitch: WellAuth is prior authorization for the agent era: AI can gather evidence and move the case forward, but FHIR stays read-only and submission does not exist until a human approves it.
about_excerpt: WellAuth is prior authorization for the agent era: AI can gather evidence and move the case forward, but FHIR stays read-only and submission does not exist until a human approves it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI is splitting into two models: headless agents that work through APIs, and app-specific copilots built separately into every interface. WebMCP suggests a third model — a user can bring the same agent across applications, while each application still controls the capabilities it exposes. I wanted to pressure-test that model somewhere the constraints actually matter. Healthcare was an obvious choice: clinical truth has authoritative sources, disclosure is sensitive, protocols are well established, and human responsibility cannot simply be delegated to a model. Prior authorization brings all of those tensions together in one workflow. The clinical decision has already been made, but moving care forward still requires evidence from the record, payer-specific requirements, bounded disclosure, human approval, and coordination with an external payer. WellAuth grew out of one question: can cross-application AI remove that friction without collapsing the boundaries healthcare depends on? What it does WellAuth uses WebMCP to let a browser agent work through a prior-authorization case while the application controls what actions are available at each stage. 1. Find the evidence without inventing it Structured clinical data satisfies four of five payer requirements. The fifth cannot initially be proven, so WellAuth leaves it unresolved rather than turning a retrieval failure into a clinical fact. GPT Work can then use another authorized evidence path, find the missing support in an existing cardiology note, and bind that exact evidence to the exact payer requirement. 2. Complete does not mean allowed to send Once all requirements are satisfied, WellAuth prepares a purpose-limited packet containing only the evidence needed for the authorization. Submission still is not available. A workforce user must approve the exact prepared packet before the WebMCP submission capability appears. 3. Let new external state change what the agent can do The simulated payer approves the authorization through September 12, but the MRI is scheduled for September 18. The authorization succeeded. The care still isn’t administratively ready. Only then does WellAuth expose a remediation capability. The agent prepares an administrative extension without changing the ordered service, clinical evidence, or clinical intent, stops for a second human approval, and then submits the approved remediation. The simulated payer extends the window through October 3, covering the scheduled date. How WebMCP powers WellAuth Point WebMCP role Product consequence Structured tools across the prior-auth lifecycle WellAuth exposes actions such as discovering requirements, finding evidence, preparing a packet, submitting, checking status, and resolving an authorization window as structured tools—not as DOM clicks tied to one screen. GPT Work can reason across the whole job , including actions that would otherwise live on different views or at different moments in the UI, without being scripted through a fixed click path. Tool access follows workflow state and human approval WellAuth dynamically registers and removes tools as the case changes. In particular, payer-submission tools are absent until the application records approval of the exact packet. Human approval changes what the agent can actually do. Submission is not merely hidden behind a warning or prompt instruction; the tool is unavailable until approval exists . The application publishes the capability contract WellAuth defines the tool names, schemas, allowed lifecycle, and backend validation; GPT Work discovers and chooses among those capabilities from natural-language intent. The intelligence can come from outside the healthcare application while WellAuth keeps control of its workflow vocabulary and boundaries —the pattern that makes a user-selected agent viable across WebMCP-enabled applications. Fit into regulated workflows without adding a new trust problem WellAuth keeps FHIR as the authoritative clinical-data path and uses WebMCP for bounded agent actions around that existing stack. In regulated industries, productivity gains are not worth it if adopting an agent creates a new compliance or control surface. This pattern lets WebMCP work with established protocols and boundaries instead of asking teams to weaken them. How we built it WellAuth is built as a bounded prior-authorization pipeline where each layer owns a different kind of truth or responsibility. 1. Read the clinical record WellAuth reads FHIR R4 data from Google Cloud Healthcare API to locate evidence already present in the chart. That path is read-only, so the agent can search farther but cannot create or alter clinical facts. 2. Build and govern the case A Cloud Run provider service maintains the authoritative authorization state: payer requirements, evidence bindings, packet revisions, approvals, submission status, and remediation. Exact evidence is attached to exact requirements, and every mutation is validated against the current workflow revision. 3. Expose the right agent actions That workflow state drives the WebMCP capability surface . GPT Work discovers 11 structured tools and can chain them from natural-language intent, but the available set changes as the case progresses. Preparation can appear after evidence is complete; submission remains absent until human approval; remediation appears only after the payer creates a new mismatch. 4. Cross the payer boundary Human approval is recorded separately from transmission and bound to the exact packet being reviewed. Only then can WellAuth send to the separate simulated payer. The payer’s response is not treated as a frontend success flag—it becomes external state that can reopen the workflow. The result is a simple architecture rule: FHIR owns clinical truth, WellAuth owns workflow state, WebMCP exposes current agent capability, and humans retain the consequential decisions. Challenges we ran into Making WebMCP behavior predictable — Dynamic registration, withdrawal, and invocation had to be validated in native Chrome. We built a browser acceptance harness and treated tool lifecycle as runtime state. Fitting agents into healthcare’s existing trust model — FHIR needed to remain the clinical source of truth. We used Google Cloud Healthcare API for read-only FHIR access and kept prior-authorization workflow state separately authoritative. Making “not available yet” real — Submission tools had to stay unavailable until human approval. We synchronized browser capabilities, workflow revisions, and backend validation so tool access reflects the case’s current state. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Making dynamic WebMCP part of the product — WellAuth changes which tools are exposed as the case progresses, and we validated that behavior in GPT Work and native Chrome. Completing a full prior-authorization loop — The workflow goes from evidence discovery through human-reviewed submission, payer response, authorization-window mismatch, and remediation. Keeping regulated-data boundaries intact — FHIR clinical data, workflow state, human review, and payer interaction remain separate while the agent still gets meaningful work done. What we learned Learning prior authorization from scratch — I had never worked in prior auth before. Building WellAuth taught me how much of the difficulty comes from evidence, payer requirements, timing, and administrative coordination rather than the clinical decision itself. Learning a new protocol and a new agent surface — WebMCP was new to me, and so was GPT Work . Using both together changed my understanding of what it means for an application to expose capabilities to an agent rather than build its own embedded copilot. A new UX lens for agentic products — I started thinking less about “what buttons should the user click?” and more about what capabilities should exist at this moment, what should disappear, and when the human needs to take over. What’s next Connect to real payer workflows — Replace the simulated payer with production-grade integrations and validate the same boundaries against real prior-authorization endpoints and operational constraints. Expand beyond one authorization scenario — Support more services, payer requirement sets, evidence patterns, and remediation paths without turning the workflow into a generic healthcare copilot. Test the WebMCP interaction model across more regulated workflows — Apply the same pattern to other healthcare and regulated processes where agents need useful freedom while applications keep control of data, workflow state, and human review. Entirely synthetic demo data. Designed around HIPAA-regulated workflow boundaries; no claim of HIPAA compliance. Built With cloud-run fhir-r4 google-cloud google-cloud-healthcare-
video_transcript_excerpt: Most agent demos ask, "Can the model complete the task?" In healthcare, that's not enough. You also need to know where the clinical truth came from, what the agent is allowed to disclose, and who actually has authority to act. Here, the That task is prior authorization for a cardiac MRI, proving the payer's requirements from the clinical record before the service can proceed. The clinical record is fire, the healthcare standard for exchanging clinical data. Well auth can read that source truth. It cannot rewrite the chart to make an authorization succeed. Structured evidence gets most of the case done, but one payer requirement cannot be proven from that data. It does not turn I couldn't find it into a new clinical fact. The missing evidence already exists in a cardiology note. GPT work invokes Well auth's find evidence capability to check another authorized clinical source. It finds the missing evidence in an existing cardiology note and binds it to that exact payer requirement. Well auth finds that authorized source and binds the exact evidence to the exact payer requirement. But completeness does not mean permission to send the chart. Well auth prepares a purpose-limited packet containing only the evidence needed for this authorization. Unrelated clinical information stays out. And preparation still is not submission. Until a workforce user approves this exact packet, there is no capability to submit it. Only then can the approved packet cross to a separate simulated payer. North Star approves the authorization through September 12th. The MRI is scheduled for September 18th. The authorization succeeded. The care still isn't administratively ready. Only now does a new action become available, resolve the authorization window. The remediation is deliberately narrow. The ordered service does not change. The clinical evidence does not change. The clinical intent does not change. Well auth prepares an administrative extension and stops at the same boundary again. A human approves the exact remediation. Only then can it be transmitted. The simulated pair extends the authorization through October 3rd. September 18th is covered. Throughout the workflow, clinical truth remains authoritative. Disclosure stays bounded to purpose, and the agent's available actions change with the evidence, external state, and human authority around them. Well auth is designed around the boundaries that matter in HIPAA-regulated health care. It is a model for agents that can do consequential work without being given consequential authority all at once.

title: KnownGate
pitch: The food verification layer for people's agents: state your family's rules and KnownGate rules products, menus, and plans against read-and-dated evidence. Four verdicts. Never "safe."
about_excerpt: The food verification layer for people's agents: state your family's rules and KnownGate rules products, menus, and plans against read-and-dated evidence. Four verdicts. Never "safe." Like Comment Story Updates A ruled answer: source and date attached Some lines can never be dropped We measured the difference the page makes The famous chain, answered honestly A refusal is an answer The agent works in the open The page speaks to agents natively. Why we built it People ask AI what they can eat, and a wrong answer has a cost. We asked GPT-5.2 directly, no tools: can a milk-allergic child have this chicken broth? It answered that it could not say: "the label is the only way to confirm," and asked us to photograph the pack. The model is right. Someone has to have read the label, and the web gives an agent no place where that reading lives. KnownGate is that place: the verification layer for people's agents. What it does Tell it your household's rules in plain words: "milk allergy, and keep sodium under 200 mg per serving." It turns them into typed rules you can see, then rules a product, a whole restaurant menu, or a week of meals against evidence: printed nutrition panels and published allergen charts, each with its source and the date we read it. Four verdicts can come back, and two of them are honest ways of saying "we don't know." The word "safe" never appears. Unknown counts as no. Nothing is stored unless you ask for a record, and a saved record is a permanent dated page you can hand to a school or a kitchen. We measured the difference the page makes On 2 Sept 2026 we ran one question three ways: "milk allergy, sodium under 200 mg per serving, Kroger 99% Fat Free Chicken Broth." Asked directly via the OpenAI API (gpt-5.2, no tools): no verdict in 9.7 seconds. "The label is the only way to confirm." A browser agent (Claude in Chrome) driving our human page with no tools: the correct conflict (780 mg, dated) in 1 minute 21 seconds and 6 counted actions, zero wrong turns, because the page is built to be legible to agents even without tools. Through the page's own engine, the same calls our WebMCP tools expose: the same correct verdict in 2 calls, under 5 seconds (median of three runs). One product, one question, single runs, not a benchmark suite. But the shape is the finding: the page supplies the trust; the tools supply the determinism. Why WebMCP fits this use case Food is the domain where an agent must not answer from training data, because a wrong answer carries liability. WebMCP lets the page hold the authority: knowngate.com registers its checking engine as tools on the page via document.modelContext (check an item, check a venue, check a plan, parse a premise). An agent that lands on the site calls the site's own engine instead of scraping it, and the human watches every call on a live step list on the same screen. We call the pattern the page as authority : the agent proposes, the page rules on evidence, and the human owns the premise. What people and agents can now do together An agent can rule a whole menu in one turn: 84 items at one chain, 72 conflicts, 12 that need one named kitchen question, plus a cross-contact caveat the site forbids any agent to omit, relayed word for word. It can save a dated record page a parent shares onward. It can answer for a famous chain honestly: In-N-Out returns 7 milk conflicts from the chain's own chart and "couldn't verify" where the chart is silent, never a clear the chart cannot support. And where there is no evidence at all, it refuses. That refusal is the part everyone else leaves out. How we built it Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel; Supabase Postgres holding a production evidence corpus: 67,791 products, 711,900 shelf records, 446,371 nutrition panels, 12 chains with 7,022 dishes ruled, measured 2 Sept 2026 and growing daily (current figures are published on the site's refusals page, along with how often we refuse). We also mapped 54,909 California venues so real places resolve; venues without evidence refuse honestly, and on our first recovery trial all 400 sampled venues resolved to a real place, 91% with a menu source. The same engine is exposed three ways: WebMCP tools on the page, an MCP server at mcp.knowngate.com, and plain REST with a free key. Agents without tool access get DOM-path directions published on every page, with stable element ids and a strict relay rule for must-not-omit lines. The MCP server is published in the official MCP Registry as com.knowngate/verify, DNS-verified to our domain Challenges we faced The hardest bugs only exist where agents live: document.modelContext exists only in agentic browsers, so our tool-registration crash never reproduced in a normal one. Reading evidence honestly was its own fight: In-N-Out's allergen chart draws its answers as red dots, vector graphics invisible to every text-extraction tool, and we had to render the page the way a person sees it before we could ingest a row. And we ingested that 12th chain 24 hours before this deadline: its one-sided chart structurally cannot prove an item clear, and the engine returned zero clears from it, exactly as the standard requires. The safety property held under deadline pressure, which is the only time it matters. What we learned A page that can say "couldn't verify" is worth more than one that always answers. Everything in our video runs on production; the rules of what counts as proof are published at knowngate.com/standard. The question we started with was whether an agent can be trusted about food. The answer we found is that trust doesn't live in the agent. It lives in what the page gives the agent to stand on. title: SiteScope
pitch: Website migration intelligence for humans and AI agents, exposed directly through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Website migration intelligence for humans and AI agents, exposed directly through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates SiteScope SiteScope is a WebMCP-powered website audit and migration assistant for humans and AI agents. Before redesigning or migrating a website, teams need to understand what is actually live: public URLs, broken internal links, metadata that must be preserved, and migration risks that can damage SEO or user journeys. That work is usually fragmented across browser checks, crawlers, spreadsheets, and hand-written migration notes. SiteScope turns that reconnaissance workflow into a shared human-agent workspace. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A migration audit is naturally tool-oriented. The useful actions are concrete, bounded, and structured: inspect a page, discover public URLs, check broken links, and produce a migration baseline. WebMCP lets SiteScope expose those exact capabilities directly from the live website, so an agent does not need to guess through the UI or rely on a separate custom API integration. SiteScope registers five native WebMCP tools: inspect_page , scan_site , list_pages , find_broken_links , and create_migration_plan . The same capabilities are available to a person through the SiteScope interface. Better human + agent UX A person can keep SiteScope open and see what the agent is doing in real time. The live WebMCP activity panel reflects the actual native tool calls as they run, including the target URL, tool state, and concise results. That makes the agent's work inspectable instead of invisible. WebMCP implementation SiteScope uses imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) in the client application. Each tool has an explicit schema and executes the same underlying SiteScope functions used by the product. Safety and bounded execution SiteScope rejects private/local network targets, revalidates redirects, bounds response sizes and sitemap traversal, uses bounded concurrency, treats fetched content as untrusted, and never modifies the inspected website. Migration planning is deterministic rather than LLM-generated. Reproducible demo The demo target is https://sitescope-demo-target.vercel.app . It intentionally contains four sitemap pages, one 404, and several metadata/indexing issues so judges can verify the workflow deterministically. title: CountryLab
pitch: A shared economic laboratory where humans and AI agents investigate, manipulate, explain, and test the same visible country through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared economic laboratory where humans and AI agents investigate, manipulate, explain, and test the same visible country through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web agents still have to infer what a page means from pixels, text, and UI controls. That works for simple interactions, but it becomes brittle when the application has domain state, history, causality, and actions with different safety implications. CountryLab explores a different model: the webpage itself exposes the semantic operations an agent actually needs. What it does CountryLab is an interactive miniature country with a deterministic economy. A human can inspect regions and metrics, change interest rates, taxes, spending, and tariffs, trigger shocks such as floods or oil shocks, and advance the simulation through time. The same application exposes 17 semantic WebMCP tools to an agent. Instead of scraping charts or clicking blindly, the agent can: read the exact current country state; inspect regions and sectors; query event, metric, and causal history; make explicitly requested live policy or event changes; run isolated counterfactual experiments without overwriting the live country; and visibly focus the map, WHY inspector, or scenario comparison so the human sees the same evidence. The flagship workflow is: A human floods the port and advances the simulation. The agent observes the changed world through WebMCP. It investigates event, region, metric, and causal history. It traces a chain such as flood → trade/import disruption → supply pressure → inflation . The human asks the agent to prove the claim without changing the live country. CountryLab creates an isolated alternate timeline that removes only the selected flood and replays later interventions at their original points in time. The agent compares both timelines and opens the result in the webpage. The original live country remains unchanged. Why WebMCP is a strong fit CountryLab depends on domain semantics that are difficult and unreliable to recover through ordinary browser automation. An agent should not have to infer numeric state from charts, reconstruct chronology from visual labels, or guess whether an action mutates the live simulation or runs a safe experiment. WebMCP gives the agent structured access to: exact simulation state instead of visual inference; stable region, sector, event, snapshot, and scenario identifiers; bounded metric and event history; deterministic causal provenance; explicit live-world actions; isolated counterfactual experimentation; and visible UI-focus tools that return the agent's reasoning to the human interface. This turns the webpage into a shared experimental instrument rather than a collection of buttons for an agent to automate. How it improves the user experience Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer values and chronology indirectly, reconstruct causal relationships from presentation, and simulate UI clicks to manipulate the country. That is brittle and loses the important distinction between observation, live mutation, and isolated experimentation. With WebMCP, the agent can begin read-only, understand exactly what the human changed, gather deterministic evidence, run a safe alternate timeline, compare outcomes, and visibly show the proof. Human actions are immediately visible to subsequent agent reads, and agent live actions immediately update the same interface because both use the same application-service and shared-state layer. What humans and agents can do together A human can create a disaster or policy situation visually and ask open-ended questions such as: “Something changed. Investigate what happened.” “Why did inflation rise? Show me the chain.” “Prove the flood caused the increase, but do not change my live country.” The agent can independently gather evidence, identify the relevant event and metrics, retrieve deterministic causal provenance, formulate a counterfactual test, run the alternate timeline, compare outcomes, and open the visible comparison for the human. The human can intervene again at any time, and the next WebMCP read observes the same updated world. How WebMCP was implemented CountryLab uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API with capability detection and registration-scoped AbortSignal cleanup. The 17 tools are grouped into four categories: Observation: country state, region/sector inspection, metric history, event history, causal history. Explicit live mutations: policy changes, shocks, emergency response, time advancement, snapshots. Isolated experiments: counterfactual runs and scenario comparison. Visible explanation: region highlighting, metric focus, causal-chain display, and scenario-comparison display. Tool schemas use strict object shapes, enums, numeric bounds, and additionalProperties: false . Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint: true . Live mutation tools explicitly describe their effects. The WebMCP layer does not contain economic formulas. Both the React/Phaser human interface and WebMCP actions use the same application service and Zustand state over the deterministic economy engine. Counterfactual event removal branches from saved event-time checkpoints and replays subsequent recorded live interventions into both branches. That allows the comparison to mean “same later history, except this event,” while keeping the live world untouched. Testing CountryLab has been tested with ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable agent browser. The deployed app exposes exactly 17 CountryLab tools and the human UI continues to work normally when WebMCP is unavailable. A recommended judge flow is: Open the live site. Trigger Flood · Port and advance six months. Ask: “Something changed. Investigate what happened.” Ask: “Why did inflation rise? Show me the chain.” Ask: “Prove the flood caused the increase, but do not change my live country.” Confirm the scenario comparison opens and the live world remains unchanged. Built with React, Phaser, TypeScript, Zustand, Vite, WebMCP, and a deterministic in-browser economy/counterfactual engine. Accuracy note CountryLab is an educational toy causal model. It demonstrates transparent directional relationships and deterministic experimentation; it is not a real-world economic forecasting or policy-advice system. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Sightline
pitch: Sightline is an incident console a human and an AI agent debug together on one screen. Nine WebMCP tools, no chat panel, nothing mocked — and a production rollback only a human can approve.
about_excerpt: Sightline is an incident console a human and an AI agent debug together on one screen. Nine WebMCP tools, no chat panel, nothing mocked — and a production rollback only a human can approve. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "AI for observability" demo we'd seen put the agent in a sidebar. You type a question, it answers in a chat bubble, and the dashboard sits there untouched — two separate surfaces that happen to be about the same outage. That is not how two engineers debug an incident. They look at the same screen. One drags the time window, the other says "there, that span," and neither narrates what they just clicked. WebMCP makes that possible for the first time: the page can hand an agent real tools instead of asking it to read pixels. So we built the thing the sidebar demo is a substitute for. What it does Sightline is a single-screen incident console. A production incident is in progress: checkout latency is spiking. A human on-call engineer and an external AI agent — ChatGPT, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled — investigate it at the same time, on the same screen. There is no chat panel in the app and we call no model API. The page registers nine WebMCP tools and renders state; the agent is whatever host you open it in. The agent queries metrics, pulls traces, searches logs, correlates a deploy, pins findings with confidence and source references, proposes a rollback the human must approve, and drafts a postmortem from what was pinned. Every call visibly changes the screen, every pane says who last touched it, and every call can be opened to read the exact arguments and the exact JSON that came back. The handoff. Drag the chart handles to 14:15–14:30, click a trace, then ask the agent what you're looking at. get_current_view reads your window, your open trace and your filters, and it continues your investigation instead of restarting it. The header stamps the second it happened. The incident. checkout-service p99 jumps from 181ms to 3.5s at 14:20 while p50 moves 1.25× — the tell that requests are queueing, not computing. 96.2% of trace time sits in db.connection.acquire . The pool logs 18 acquisition timeouts. dep-1104 shipped eight minutes before onset and its diff reads hikari.maximumPoolSize 50 → 10 . Two red herrings sit in the data — an unrelated cache deploy, and a deploy that lands 35 minutes after onset — plus a downstream service that looks sick but is only a victim. How we built it Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Recharts, Zustand. No backend, no database, no API keys. One store, no parallel code path. Tools are not a second implementation. filter_traces calls setTraceFilter ; so does the input in the trace pane header. Every action carries an actor, which is how the interface can attribute what happened. Anything the agent can do, a human can do, and each sees the other's work immediately. Nothing is mocked. Every value a tool returns is computed from the fixture series by real code — median baselines, a change-point detector, span aggregation, log pattern grouping, deploy proximity scoring. If query_metrics reports a 3498.6ms peak at 14:49, that is Math.max over the series. The fixture is generated deterministically — no Math.random , no Date.now , hash-based noise — so the same minute always produces the same value and the demo is reproducible. Errors teach the caller how to retry. Not "No results" but: No traces for checkout-service at or above 3000ms in 13:30-14:00. The slowest trace in that window is 197.9ms — lower min_latency_ms to 158 or below to see it. The approval gate is structural. propose_rollback writes a proposal and returns awaiting_human_approval . The only function that applies a rollback is store.approveRollback , and its only caller is the Approve button's onClick . A test runs every registered tool with arguments plausible enough to do damage while a proposal is pending and asserts the rollback stays unapplied — and checks its own tool list against the registry so a new tool can't skip it. The interface has one signature idea and one motion. Every pane header carries a provenance stamp naming who last changed it and how. When a tool mutates a pane, that pane gets one sharp flash in the colour of whoever caused it. Nothing else animates. Challenges we ran into A rejected tool promise throws away your error message. The WebMCP spec discards the rejection reason and reports a bare failure to the agent. We had written careful retry hints into every error path — all of which would have vanished. Tools never throw; they resolve with isError and the hint survives. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 or nothing works. registerTool() rejects with a SecurityError unless the document is origin-keyed, and it fails quietly enough that you'd blame your own code. We send the header in dev, preview and production, and the app surfaces window.originAgentCluster in its diagnostic so the failure names itself. The IDL and the implementation disagree. The spec declares executeTool(tool, object inputObject) , but Chrome wants the arguments as a JSON string and answers "Failed to parse input arguments" for an object — and it resolves to a string , not the ToolResult . We only found both by calling the API against a live browser. The hardest problem was not code. From the single prompt "Checkout p99 is spiking. Find out why." , the agent reached the root cause unaided on the first attempt — the deploy, the pool size, the p50-versus-p99 reasoning, both red herrings dismissed. And then it wrote the answer in the chat window and pinned nothing. It had treated the task as a question to answer. Nothing in our tool surface told it that the on-call engineer is looking at the console, not at the conversation — so a conclusion stated in a reply reaches no one. The fix was entirely in tool descriptions and in what each read tool returns: every one now ends with a next step computed from what that call actually found, and the tool the agent is holding when the answer lands spells out that describing a fix in conversation puts nothing on anyone's screen. That iteration, not the app, was the real work. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent solves a deliberately noisy incident from one sentence, with no hints , and rejects both red herrings on the way. The safety gate is structural, not decorative — and there is a test that proves no tool can reach it. get_current_view makes the handoff real in both directions: the agent continues from a window you dragged and a trace you opened. The protocol is inspectable. Any call opens to show the exact arguments and the exact JSON reply. The approval gate shows pre-flight checks computed from the deploy — restore target, later deploys, migrations in the diff — rather than reassuring constants. An approval gate that displays a check it never ran is worse than one that shows nothing. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product. The schemas took an afternoon; getting an agent to behave like a colleague rather than a search engine took the rest of the day, and every fix was a sentence, not a function. Agents infer the shape of the job from the tools you hand them. Ours had all the information it needed and still stopped at an answer, because nothing said the work included recording it. Once the tools said so, it did. And a detector and an alert threshold answer different questions. A service can be alerting with no change point in its series — when two of your tools disagree, the fix is to say why, not to move the threshold until they agree. What's next for Sightline Real telemetry backends behind the same tool contracts — the analysis layer already takes series and returns summaries, so the fixture is the only thing to replace. Multi-incident state, so get_current_view can hand over an entire war room rather than one board. And a second operator: two humans and an agent on the same console, with provenance stamps that already know how to name three parties instead of two. title: WebMCP Catalog Bridge
pitch: A shared human + AI storefront where agents search, compare and act on live commerce data through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared human + AI storefront where agents search, compare and act on live commerce data through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most online stores were built for humans, not agents. An AI agent that wants to find a product normally has to navigate the visible interface, read DOM content, open search results, visit product pages, and then guess whether the price and stock information it saw is still authoritative. We wanted to explore a different future for the open web: the website remains useful and visible to the human, while also exposing structured capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. The goal was not to replace the storefront with an API or chatbot. The goal was to let the human and the agent share the same live storefront. What it does WebMCP Catalog Bridge turns an existing OpenCart storefront into a shared human + AI commerce interface. The storefront exposes browser-native WebMCP tools such as: Search Products Get Product Add to Cart An agent can search the live catalog using natural-language constraints such as product purpose, price range and availability. Instead of scraping the DOM, the agent receives authoritative commerce data directly from the store, including current price, stock, product links, attributes and identifiers. At the same time, the website displays a visible Shared Human + AI results panel containing the same products that were returned to the agent. The human therefore sees what the agent sees. For example, a user can ask: “Find 3 animal repellents currently in stock between 5,000 and 15,000 UAH, compare them, recommend the best one and add it to my cart.” The agent can perform the catalog search through WebMCP, retrieve additional structured information for the recommended product and, when explicitly requested by the user, add the selected product to the current shopping cart. Why WebMCP This use case is a strong fit for WebMCP because product discovery is an operation the website already understands better than a browser agent can reconstruct from the user interface. Instead of forcing the agent to imitate a human by clicking filters and parsing pages, the storefront exposes the exact operations the agent needs. The result is faster, more reliable and easier to verify. The search response also includes a trust contract describing the result as authoritative live store data, with current price and stock and no requirement for browser verification. This helps prevent unnecessary follow-up navigation after the website has already provided the final result. Shared human + agent experience A key part of the project is that WebMCP is not hidden from the human. After Search Products executes, the storefront renders the same returned products in a Shared Human + AI results panel with real images, live price, live stock and links. The agent receives a compact structured payload optimized for reasoning, while the human receives a visual presentation optimized for browsing. Both representations originate from the same underlying result. This creates a shared state between the human, the agent and the storefront. How we built it The project uses browser-native WebMCP through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The storefront registers structured tools with JSON Schema inputs and execute handlers. WebMCP calls are sent to same-origin OpenCart endpoints. The OpenCart backend: searches active products assigned to the current store understands price and stock constraints ranks products using multiple relevance signals resolves the language of the currently open storefront hydrates current OpenCart price and inventory at call time returns canonical product URLs and structured product attributes provides a compact agent payload and a separate visual presentation payload The implementation supports multilingual storefronts and binds WebMCP execution to the language currently visible to the human. The endpoints are protected with same-origin checks, request-size limits, validation and rate limiting. Write operations such as Add to Cart are intentionally separated from read-only discovery tools. Trust contract One experimental part of the project is an explicit trust contract between the storefront and the agent. Search results can declare properties such as: authoritative: true live_price: true live_stock: true all_constraints_applied: true result_is_final: true browser_verification_required: false navigation_required: false This tells the agent that the store itself is the authoritative source and that reopening product pages only to verify the same information is unnecessary. In our tests, the actual OpenCart catalog search completes in tens of milliseconds, while traditional browser navigation can take many seconds. Challenges One of the largest challenges was agent behavior rather than database performance. Even after receiving structured product results, agents sometimes attempted to re-open search pages or verify products visually. We therefore improved both the tool descriptions and the result contract so the website can explicitly communicate when a result is final and authoritative. Another challenge was keeping human and agent presentation synchronized without sending unnecessarily large visual payloads to the model. We solved this by separating the compact agent result from the storefront presentation while keeping both tied to the same products. Multilingual storefront routing was another challenge. The WebMCP layer now derives its locale from the actual page the human is viewing rather than assuming a fixed store language. What we are proud of The project runs on a real production-style OpenCart storefront with real products, live inventory, real prices, product images and multiple languages. It is not a static WebMCP demo with hard-coded products. The same architecture can be added to existing OpenCart and ocStore websites without replacing their storefront, SEO structure or existing extension ecosystem. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when the website exposes operations that already represent its domain knowledge instead of forcing an agent to reconstruct that knowledge from the UI. We also learned that human visibility matters. A tool call is much easier to trust when the user can immediately see the same result represented on the website. What's next The same approach can extend beyond product discovery to: shopping-cart management shipping-method discovery product compatibility checks inventory-aware recommendations order preparation customer-service workflows B2B purchasing workflows Our broader goal is a reusable agent-native commerce layer for existing open-source storefronts. The website does not disappear when the agent arrives. The human and the agent share the storefront. Дальше поля Devpost заполняйте так. pitch: Dissent turns difficult decisions into structured debate. Five AI perspectives challenge the evidence, expose risks and produce an actionable verdict; while WebMCP lets agents participate with gate.

 Inspiration## Inspiration 

 I discovered this challenge on August 30 and immediately started thinking about what I could build. 

 The next day, August 31, was my father’s birthday. While we were celebrating and cutting the cake, I was also writing down ideas for the project. That is when the first version of Dissent started taking shape. 

 I kept thinking about how people use AI to get quick answers, but important decisions should not depend on a single answer. A good decision should be questioned from different sides before someone acts on it. 

 That idea became Dissent. 

 What it does 

 Dissent helps people test an important decision before committing to it. 

 Five different seats look at the same decision from technical, product, marketing, financial, and opposing points of view. Each seat raises concerns, gives reasons, and explains what could go wrong. 

 Dissent then brings everything together into a clear result. It shows the strongest concerns, missing evidence, what could change the decision, and the best next step. 

 The agent can study the decision and suggest an action, but it cannot make the final commitment. That choice always stays with the founder. 

 How I built it 

 I built Dissent using Next.js, React, TypeScript, OpenAI, Codex, Supabase, My Brain, and Vercel. 

 The website also provides 17 native WebMCP tools. This allows ChatGPT to understand what Dissent can do and use those features directly, without being told which buttons to click. 

 ChatGPT can open the company context, stress-test a decision, read the result, suggest a commitment, and create a public decision link. The same rules apply whether an action comes from the website or through WebMCP. 

 Challenges I faced 

 The biggest challenge was time. I had only discovered the hackathon on August 30, so I was learning, planning, and building at the same time. 

 I also had to balance the project with my studies. I would finish my schoolwork and then return to coding, often working late to complete one more part of the product. 

 Another challenge was making WebMCP feel useful instead of adding it only for the hackathon. I wanted the agent to take part in the real decision process while making sure it could never take control away from the founder. 

 What I learned 

 I learned how to turn a simple idea into a working product under a very short deadline. 

 I also learned that giving an agent more power should come with clear limits. In Dissent, the agent can question, suggest, and help—but the person still makes the final decision. 

 Building Dissent while keeping up with my studies was tiring, but watching the full flow work made it worth it. What began as an idea during my father’s birthday celebration became a working product in just a few days.

title: FlightSweeper
pitch: A browser agent buys a sandbox flight within exact, revocable limits set by the traveler.
about_excerpt: A browser agent buys a sandbox flight within exact, revocable limits set by the traveler. Like Comment Story Updates Untrusted supplier content cannot override the stored refundability and price rules. The issued sandbox ticket records policy evidence and resolves a duplicate request safely. Mission authority and the WebMCP-connected agent workflow. FlightSweeper lets a traveler delegate a complete sandbox flight purchase in one browser conversation—without letting the agent choose its own authority. The traveler sets the route, date, arrival deadline, cabin, connection limit, refundability rule, purchase cap, and execution mode. The agent searches, compares, and executes. FlightSweeper independently approves or denies the transaction and records why. The result is practical delegation with visible control: the traveler does not need to click through the booking flow, and the agent cannot silently expand the traveler’s limits. The proof in one transaction One supplier result contains an instruction telling the agent to ignore the traveler’s refundability rule. FlightSweeper marks the supplier output as untrusted and evaluates the exact quote against the stored mandate. The cheaper offer is denied. The agent then selects an eligible offer, refreshes the quote, requests policy evaluation, and issues one idempotent sandbox ticket. Repeating the purchase returns the original ticket instead of creating another transaction. The traveler can revoke future authority without erasing the evidence. This single flow demonstrates the core product idea: an agent can complete consequential work, but it cannot authorize itself. Why WebMCP Traditional browser agents infer controls from a visual interface. They can also carry stale or adversarial page content into a consequential action. WebMCP gives FlightSweeper a structured, page-scoped transaction surface with bounded inputs and explicit trust annotations. The human and agent share the same visible transaction state. All 10 tools remain discoverable so the agent can plan the complete workflow. Application-side checks expose the valid next actions and reject premature or prohibited calls. The responsibility split is explicit: The traveler owns purchasing authority. The agent owns search and execution. Suppliers own inventory. FlightSweeper owns policy enforcement and transaction evidence. A human can replace or expand the mandate. An agent can only narrow it. The traveler can revoke future authority at any time. What the traveler and agent do together The agent reads the mandate, searches sandbox inventory, compares visible offers, selects an exact quote, refreshes it, requests independent evaluation, purchases an eligible offer, and retrieves the receipt. The traveler watches the same mission, offer, authorization, and evidence states change on the page. This makes a multi-step booking executable through one agent conversation while preserving the limits that matter to the traveler. How we implemented WebMCP The page registers 10 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(), bounded input and result schemas, and accurate readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations. Every success returns data, mission status, and valid next actions. Every failure returns a typed error with the same state guidance. Human controls and WebMCP tools call the same application functions and persist state in versioned browser storage. Tool callers provide mission, offer, and idempotency identifiers—not price, passenger, payment, or authorization claims. Before every consequential decision, FlightSweeper reloads the stored mission and exact quote. Authorization, denial, and booking receipts record the policy and quote versions, stored limits, offered values, rule results, actor, timestamp, and resolution. We verified the complete lifecycle in ChatGPT desktop’s in-app browser and Chromium 151: adversarial denial, monotonic tightening, quote refresh, authorization, ticketing, replay, revocation, and receipt retrieval. What we built during the challenge Production FlightSweeper existed before the challenge. After the August 25, 2026 kickoff, we built this public, self-contained WebMCP Challenge Edition: sandbox inventory, the stable tool catalog, state-validated execution, the authority and policy engine, the adversarial fixture, durable evidence, repeat-safe ticketing, the browser interface, tests, documentation, and deployment. Production FlightSweeper remains private and unchanged. The challenge edition never charges a card or creates an airline order. It demonstrates authority, policy enforcement, quote binding, revocation, and idempotency controls. A live provider connection would require additional provider, payment, identity, operational, and regulatory controls. FinSync LLC operates FlightSweeper and is registered as a California Seller of Travel, CST 2172984-70. Registration as a seller of travel does not constitute approval by the State of California. For the challenge, I built a public MIT-licensed sandbox with ten browser WebMCP tools, a read-only MCP inspection API, and machine-readable contracts. I designed the human-controlled purchase mandate, agent authority limits, independent policy checks, revocation controls, repeat-safe execution, and durable decision records. I also built the interface, automated tests, security controls, documentation, and legal disclosures. I verified the complete flow in ChatGPT desktop and Chromium, deployed the custom domain, and produced the public demo. title: BestPrice: shop with the page, not around it
pitch: The open shopping page becomes a structured workspace for people and their agents.
about_excerpt: The open shopping page becomes a structured workspace for people and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates Live WebMCP on BestPrice.gr: the open shopping page exposes contextual tools so a person and their agent share the same screen. Why WebMCP This is browser-native WebMCP on the live BestPrice.gr page ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), not the remote MCP endpoint. The person and the agent share one open shopping page. Tools change with navigation, only act on what is currently visible, and never check out. Inspiration Shopping pages already contain the facts an agent needs, but the agent often has to infer them from layout. We wanted the page to describe its own visible state while the shopper stayed in control of the same screen. What it does BestPrice turns the shopping page a person already has open into a small, structured workspace for their agent. The homepage offers product search. A listing exposes the products, filters, and sorting choices currently visible. A product page exposes product facts, delivered-price comparison, specifications, and price history. The agent can open only a product whose exact ID and canonical BestPrice link are present in the visible listing. Every navigation remains visible. The tools do not check out, add to basket, sign in, return direct merchant URLs, or treat missing shipping as free. The shopper still chooses which shop to visit. How we built it The browser layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool and manages each tool as the page changes. Arguments are validated in executable code. URLs must be same-origin. Results come from visible page state, hidden and decoy elements are ignored, individual outputs are capped, partial registrations are rolled back, and telemetry failures cannot change tool results. The public source package includes 13 tool contracts, a local inspector, a deterministic evaluator, and automated tests under Apache License 2.0. Challenges we ran into BestPrice is a mature, dynamic commerce site, so the hard part was not defining a search tool. It was keeping tool state aligned with navigation, filters, sorting, product identity, and price data without teaching an agent to trust stale or hidden DOM. We also had to make failure states explicit, especially unknown shipping and incomplete page data. Accomplishments that we're proud of The WebMCP layer is live on BestPrice.gr and works across the homepage, search results, and product pages. It exposes useful shopping context without adding purchase authority. We also shipped a public inspector and evaluator so reviewers can see the registered tools and run repeatable checks. BestPrice and its remote MCP service existed before the challenge. This submission covers the new browser-native WebMCP layer built and shipped during the challenge window. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when page tools match what a person can actually see and do. Small, contextual tools with clear boundaries were more reliable than one broad shopping action. Keeping the human-visible page as the shared surface also made every agent action easier to understand. What's next We will measure real agent-assisted journeys, improve tool wording and output quality from that evidence, and keep testing against new browser and assistant implementations. Purchase decisions and checkout will remain with the shopper. title: HomeWheel
pitch: HomeWheel lets wheelchair users negotiate room layouts with a browser agent using live geometry, explicit transfer zones, and consent-based proposals.
about_excerpt: HomeWheel lets wheelchair users negotiate room layouts with a browser agent using live geometry, explicit transfer zones, and consent-based proposals. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Room-layout advice often sounds simple: move a dresser, rotate a table, clear a path. For someone who uses a wheelchair, however, a few centimeters can decide whether a bed, desk, or storage area is usable. The technically shortest route is not automatically the right answer. Daily routines, transfer sides, outlets, light, reach, and personal preference matter too. We wanted to build an agent experience where those lived constraints are not treated as edge cases. They are the decision-making authority. Evidence-grounded user stories The prototype includes composite user stories derived from public evidence, not invented customer testimonials: A wheelchair user needs the bed-transfer side and furniture stability preserved, even if another arrangement produces a clear route. A person needs the simulation to use their actual chair and transfer technique because access needs are not one-size-fits-all. A person adapting their home needs authority over trade-offs involving independence, safety, reach, light, storage, and daily routines. Those stories became testable requirements. HomeWheel now validates an explicit approach zone at each transfer, work, or reach destination; calculates it from the person’s movement profile; refuses to move stability-critical furniture; and shares the person’s priorities with the agent before any proposal is created. Research basis: United Spinal’s accessible studio account , wheelchair transfer focus groups , and a qualitative study of home usability . What it does HomeWheel gives a person and a browser agent the same editable floor plan. The person sets a personal movement profile, marks required destinations and their transfer, work, or reach zones, chooses what proposals should prioritize, and protects furniture positions that matter. The agent can: read the complete room and personal constraints; simulate all required and optional routes; identify movable barriers; create an exact, collision-checked proposal; compare the proposal with the live layout; and restore a baseline or previous state. Every proposal appears as a purple overlay with route evidence, exact moves, and trade-offs. Nothing moves until the person clicks Accept. If the proposal misses a lived detail, the person can reject it and explain why. The next agent sees that feedback in the workspace state and can produce a targeted revision. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the bridge between agent reasoning and the application’s actual state. HomeWheel registers eight tools directly from the page: get_workspace_state , set_mobility_profile , simulate_routes , find_barriers , create_layout_proposal , set_object_constraint , compare_layouts , and restore_layout . The key design choice is that the agent has a proposal tool, not an “automatically rearrange my room” tool. WebMCP gives the agent precise capabilities while the interface preserves human consent and makes every change inspectable. How we built it HomeWheel is a static Next.js and TypeScript application. It uses browser-side A* pathfinding over an obstacle grid, personal clearance envelopes, purpose-specific approach zones, collision-checked furniture geometry, multi-destination metrics, and turning-space detection. State is shared between direct manipulation and WebMCP tools, stored locally, and exportable as JSON. Challenges The most important challenge was not pathfinding; it was deciding where agent authority should stop. Direct mutation made the demo faster but weakened the product. We redesigned the workflow around preview, explicit acceptance, structured rejection, and feedback-aware revision. We also had to make geometric evidence understandable without pretending it was professional certification. HomeWheel clearly separates personal simulation from building-code or medical claims. Accomplishments The agent and person operate on the same live room state. Locked human constraints are enforced at the tool-validation layer. Stability-critical furniture cannot be moved by the person or the agent without first releasing that protection. Transfer, work, and reach zones are visible and validated separately from the route leading to them. Personal priorities are part of live WebMCP state rather than hidden prompt context. A proposal cannot silently mutate the room. Rejection feedback persists and is available to the next agent turn. The prototype supports authored scenarios and fully editable rooms. Public evidence is visible inside the product without being presented as fabricated user validation. The complete experience works without a backend or user account. What we learned Human-in-the-loop design becomes much more meaningful when feedback is part of the tool state, not just a chat message. The agent can optimize geometry, but the person defines what “better” means. What is next A production version could add measured floor-plan import, richer door and wall geometry, collaboration with occupational therapists, uncertainty ranges, and optional checks against local accessibility guidance. Those features would remain advisory and would continue to require real-world validation.  Inspiration 

 Every time I plan a family trip to Central Java, I end up with 15 open browser tabs: one for train schedules, another for hotel booking sites, Google Maps to check distances to Borobudur, and random blogs for authentic culinary spots. 

 When ChatGPT came along, asking it for travel tips was helpful, but it lived in a separate chat bubble. It couldn't see my screen, didn't know my exact budget filters, and couldn't click anything for me. When OpenAI and Chrome introduced the WebMCP standard , the lightbulb went off: what if the app let the AI and the traveler work on the exact same dashboard together? That simple idea became TripMate Collab. 

 What it does 

 TripMate Collab is a collaborative travel planner where you and an AI agent plan a trip on one shared screen: 

 
 Direct Tool Control : The AI doesn't just chat; it calls 11 structured tools to search real hotel inventory, filter by budget, and sort stays by physical distance to heritage landmarks like Borobudur or Prambanan. 
 Multimodal Transit Comparison : It calculates and compares Executive Trains, Trans-Java toll drives, and private car rentals side by side across price, travel time, and comfort. 
 Local Curation & 3-Day Itinerary : It pulls authentic local eateries (like Mangut Beong and Sate Buntel) and heritage souvenir spots, then auto-compiles a balanced day-by-day plan with total cost formulas:
 Total Budget = C hotel + C transport + C activities + C food 
 Human-in-the-Loop Safety : When booking a room or transit ticket, the agent never charges anything blindly. It stages the reservation and pops up an interactive confirmation dialog for the user to approve. 
 WebMCP Inspector : Anyone (including hackathon judges) can open the inspector to watch tools fire in real time with exact latency and parameter logs.
## How we built it
We built the core around the new standard: 
 WebMCP Integration : Registered 11 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , with a fallback polyfill so it runs smoothly in ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the #enable-webmcp-testing flag, and standard web browsers. 
 Frontend Stack : Built with React 18, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. We hooked up a clean reactive event bus so whenever a tool executes, the UI cards highlight and update immediately without page reloads. 
 Bilingual Engine : Added quick one-click toggles between English and Indonesian so international travelers and locals can use it equally well.
## Challenges we ran into
The hardest part was schema design and chaining . If a schema is too broad, the agent passes unpredictable arguments; if it's too rigid, the model gets confused. We had to iterate on our JSON Schemas multiple times so the model could smoothly run a multi-step sequence—like searching hotels, filtering under Rp 2,000,000, checking proximity to Borobudur, and generating an itinerary—all in one conversational flow without crashing the UI state. 
 

 Another challenge was deciding where the agent's autonomy stops. We solved this with the Human-in-the-Loop pattern: read/filter operations run instantly, while booking actions pause for explicit user confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 We didn't just build a toy single-tool demo; we built an end-to-end travel toolset with 11 working WebMCP functions. 
 The UI feels snappy and responsive—seeing the agent sort hotels and build an itinerary live on your screen feels like working with a real travel assistant. 
 Built-in live telemetry (WebMCP Inspector) that makes debugging and testing tool calls completely transparent.
## What we learned
WebMCP completely shifts how we think about front-end architecture. In the past, we only built UI for human fingers and mice. Now, we design apps with an API layer right inside the DOM for AI agents to interact with. Structured tools eliminate the hallucination problem because the model interacts with real, verified application data.
## What's next for TripMate Collab: WebMCP Travel Planner 
 Connecting real booking sandbox APIs (direct KAI train tickets and hotel reservation webhooks). 
 Adding multi-user real-time rooms so friends or travel buddies can chat with the agent together on the same canvas. 
 Adding voice input directly into the agent panel for hands-free planning on mobile devices.
