title: Solaris — agent-native solar sizing lab
pitch: A home solar sizing lab where the agent doesn't fill in your form it searches. One WebMCP tool call evaluates 2,000 configurations in 40ms, in the browser, against the same state your sliders write to
about_excerpt: A home solar sizing lab where the agent doesn't fill in your form it searches. One WebMCP tool call evaluates 2,000 configurations in 40ms, in the browser, against the same state your sliders write to Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it## Inspiration I looked through the WebMCP demos that already exist — hotel booking, sports storefronts, restaurant reservations, movie tickets — and noticed they mostly share the same shape: The agent searches, filters, fills, and submits. It does what a person could already do, only faster. I wanted to build the other thing: a web app where the agent has a capability the interface fundamentally cannot offer. Sizing a home solar system turned out to be the perfect problem. A solar system is a three-way trade-off between panels, battery, and inverter. The best configuration depends on how all three interact, along with electricity usage and tariffs. There are thousands of sensible combinations. A person moving sliders can explore one configuration at a time. An agent can search the entire design space. That difference is the project. What Solaris Does Solaris is a browser-based solar and battery simulator that lets humans explore systems manually — while giving AI agents the ability to search the design space computationally. You can use Solaris normally: Adjust solar panels Adjust battery capacity Adjust inverter size Change daily energy consumption Run simulations See annual generation, grid dependence, cost, and payback But you can also ask for an outcome instead of a configuration: "I use about 14 kWh a day, mostly evenings. Find me the cheapest setup over ten years that keeps me at least 80% off the grid." The agent can call grid_search . Instead of moving sliders one by one, it evaluates roughly 2,000 possible configurations in about 40 milliseconds , ranks them against the requested objective and constraints, and returns the best trade-offs. Solaris then visualizes the search: Every configuration the agent evaluated The trade-off frontier The best options at different budgets The selected configuration The agent can then apply the winning configuration, and the sliders visibly move on screen. Why This Is WebMCP The most important part of Solaris is that grid_search has no meaningful UI equivalent. A slider can represent one value. A button can trigger one operation. But grid_search takes: Parameter ranges An optimization objective Constraints A requested result size …and evaluates thousands of possible combinations. There is no sensible "Search 2,000 configurations" button for a human to use interactively. The agent isn't simply operating the existing interface. It has gained a new computational capability through the web page. That is what I wanted to explore with WebMCP. The browser is the computational environment Solaris runs entirely in the browser. There is no backend, no external simulation service, and no separate MCP server holding the model state. The simulator and the WebMCP tools operate on the same client-side state. So if a human changes the battery slider halfway through an agent conversation, the agent can call get_state and immediately see the new configuration. The browser supplies the model and compute. The agent supplies the search strategy. WebMCP connects the two. What Humans and Agents Can Do Together Solaris enables interactions that are difficult to express through a traditional UI. 1. Ask for outcomes instead of settings Instead of figuring out which slider values to use, a person can describe the result they want. "Keep me at least 80% off-grid while minimizing my 10-year cost." The agent searches the design space and shows the resulting trade-offs. 2. Explore the agent's reasoning space Solaris doesn't only return the winner. It visualizes the configurations the agent explored, allowing the human to see the shape of the optimization problem and the alternatives that were rejected. The result becomes something the human can inspect rather than a black-box recommendation. 3. Human changes become agent context A user can manually change the system after an agent recommendation and ask: "Was that a good idea?" The agent reads the current browser state and can compare it against the previous configuration. 4. Expensive computation requires human approval Searches over more than 200 configurations trigger an approval dialog that tells the user how much computation will be performed. The user can approve or decline the operation. A refusal is returned to the agent as structured tool output, allowing it to respond intelligently rather than treating the action as an error. How I Built It Solaris is a self-contained HTML application with no backend, build step, or external dependencies. The simulation model is deterministic JavaScript. It models: Hourly solar generation across 8,760 hours A daylight generation profile Monthly peak-sun-hour scaling Inverter clipping Battery charging and round-trip efficiency Battery discharge Grid imports Energy exports Annual costs and payback There are two simulation fidelities. simulateFull runs all 8,760 hours and powers the detailed UI. simulateFast uses twelve representative days scaled to a year and powers parameter sweeps. The two agree within 0.1% on annual generation. WebMCP Tools Solaris exposes nine tools through document.modelContext : get_model_spec get_state set_params run sweep grid_search pin_run compare_runs explain_state The most important is grid_search . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "grid_search", description: "Search several parameters together and return the best configurations found.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { ranges: { type: "object" }, objective: { type: "string", enum: [ "min_annual_cost", "min_payback", "min_total_cost_10yr", "max_self_sufficiency" ] }, constraints: { type: "object" }, topN: { type: "integer" } }, required: ["ranges"] }, execute: async (input) => { // Build grid → request approval when necessary // → evaluate → rank → return compact results } }); Every tool call is wrapped with telemetry before registration, allowing the interface to display the tool name, arguments, duration, and number of simulations performed. Large searches run in chunks with a progress indicator so the browser remains responsive. Results are also returned compactly — top configurations plus aggregates rather than thousands of raw rows. Challenges Getting the economics right My first cost assumptions made the optimization landscape almost useless. The default configuration already achieved roughly 99% self-sufficiency, meaning grid_search could evaluate thousands of configurations only to discover that the starting point was already nearly optimal. I brute-forced the search space, found the optimum sitting on a slider boundary, and retuned the tariffs and component costs. The optimum moved into the interior of the search space. That made the optimization meaningful. Teaching the agent when to use each tool My first tool descriptions simply explained what each function did. That produced timid behavior. The agent would sometimes use a one-parameter sweep when the user's question required a joint search. The solution wasn't more code. It was better tool descriptions. I explicitly described when each tool should be preferred , and made it clear that grid_search exists specifically for questions that cannot be answered efficiently by manipulating individual controls. That changed the agent's behavior dramatically. Approval without approval fatigue Putting a confirmation dialog in front of every operation would train users to blindly click through it. Instead, Solaris only requires approval once a search exceeds 200 configurations. The dialog shows the number of configurations and the estimated computation rather than presenting a vague "Are you sure?" What I Learned The most interesting discovery came from the agent itself. The cheapest configuration deliberately undersized the inverter, producing a DC:AC ratio of around 1.6 . It accepted some midday clipping because the clipped energy would only export at ₹1.50, while additional inverter capacity cost ₹7,000 per kW. I didn't explicitly encode that conclusion. It emerged from the search. That was the moment the idea clicked for me: The interesting result wasn't sitting in the UI waiting to be clicked. And it wasn't something I had manually programmed the agent to say. It emerged from giving the agent the ability to explore a space that would be impractical for a human to explore manually. What's Next Solaris is one example of a broader pattern. Many useful problems aren't about finding a single value. They're about exploring a frontier . The same architecture could apply to: Financial scenario planning Staffing and queue optimization Logistics Engineering tolerances Resource allocation Energy systems Capacity planning Wherever a browser can hold a model, WebMCP can potentially give an agent the ability to describe

title: VELLAR
pitch: The marketplace writes the tools. Every paid API becomes a callable WebMCP tool automatically, no code, no registration, just a real payment. Built on Stellar ecosystem.
about_excerpt: The marketplace writes the tools. Every paid API becomes a callable WebMCP tool automatically, no code, no registration, just a real payment. Built on Stellar ecosystem. Like Comment Story Updates Explorer for viewing settled transactions Developer Docs Landing Page WebMCP hackathon submission Ui Inspiration AI agents can browse the web but they cannot pay for things. We have been building the infrastructure to change that for months. Vellar is the agent-payments stack for Stellar, a passkey smart wallet with on-chain spending policies, an open-source x402 facilitator that verifies and settles payments including policy-governed smart accounts other facilitators reject, a trust-ranked Bazaar that catalogs payable APIs from real settlement data, a VS Code extension that lets any developer gate an API endpoint for payment in under a minute, and an explorer that indexes every settlement on-chain. When the WebMCP Challenge launched, we had one question: what happens when you put a browser-native agent interface on top of a live, running payment infrastructure that already has real endpoints, real settlements, and real USDC moving through it? What it does Vellar x402 is a live API marketplace for AI agents, powered by the full Vellar stack. Open the page in a WebMCP-enabled browser and the agent sees a set of callable tools, not because a developer wrote them, but because real sellers deployed real endpoints, received real on-chain USDC payments through the Vellar Facilitator, and earned their way into the Vellar Bazaar catalog. Nobody wrote call_uuid . The marketplace did. The page queries the live Bazaar at load time, filters for endpoints with real settlement history and verified trust scores, and dynamically registers a WebMCP tool for each one. As sellers list new endpoints and earn trust through real payments, new tools appear automatically without a single line of code changing. The tool list is a live query result, not a specification frozen at build time. Three core tools handle the agent workflow: search_vellar_bazaar searches the live Bazaar catalog for payable endpoints with prices and trust status. pay_and_call provisions a throwaway Stellar wallet, acquires USDC, signs a real x402 payment, and returns the response with an on-chain tx hash. check_vellar_earnings shows a seller's real settlement history from the Vellar Explorer. Every additional tool is generated live from the Bazaar. When an agent calls call_uuid , a real Stellar transaction settles. The tx hash is verifiable on Stellar Expert. How we built it This submission is the WebMCP layer on top of months of infrastructure. The Vellar Facilitator is an open-source x402 verify/settle service live at https://facilitator.vellar.xyz . It includes a 50-account channel pool proven at 50 true-simultaneous settlements with zero sequence failures, a Bazaar discovery layer that auto-catalogs endpoints from real payment data, and a trust layer that ranks results by settlement count and on-chain contract verification. The Vellar Wallet is a passkey smart wallet on Stellar with programmable on-chain spending policies. An agent gets a scoped session key with a spending limit enforced by a policy contract. Go over budget and the chain refuses before any money moves. The Vellar VS Code Extension is live on the VS Code Marketplace (VellarWallet.vellar-x402). Any developer can open an Express, Fastify, or Next.js route file, run one command, and have a working x402 payment gate injected with the Bazaar discovery extension included. Their endpoint self-lists in the Bazaar on first payment. The WebMCP layer is built in Next.js on Render, using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill for broad browser compatibility and @x402/core plus @x402/stellar for the payment flow. All payment logic runs server-side so throwaway keypairs never touch the browser. Every external call is proxied through our own API routes to eliminate CORS failures in browser tool execution. Challenges we ran into Sequence number contention at scale. Stellar serializes transactions per source account. Under concurrent load, multiple settlements racing on one account produce txBadSeq failures. We built and load-tested a 50-account channel pool, 50 simultaneous payments, zero sequence failures, p95 under 12 seconds, before this hackathon started. That infrastructure is what makes pay_and_call reliable under real agent usage. Dynamic tool generation edge cases. Catalog URLs become tool names. Path templates like /inspect/:address, localhost entries, and naming collisions all needed filtering before a single registerTool call was made. A tool guaranteed to fail on every invocation is worse than no tool. CORS at the WebMCP boundary. Browser-based tool execute functions cannot call cross-origin APIs without CORS headers. Every external call is proxied through Next.js API routes so tools never fail silently in a browser context. Proving it is real. The easiest thing to fake in a hackathon demo is an on-chain payment. We did not fake it. Every tool call that involves a payment produces a tx hash verifiable on Stellar Expert. Accomplishments that we're proud of The marketplace writes the tools, not the developer. That sentence sounds simple. Behind it is a live payment facilitator handling concurrent settlements, a trust-scored discovery catalog built from real on-chain data, a passkey smart wallet with programmable spending policies, a VS Code extension that onboards sellers in under a minute, and now a WebMCP layer that turns all of it into callable agent tools automatically. Any developer who deploys an x402-gated endpoint using the Vellar VS Code extension and receives one real payment is automatically callable by every agent using this page. Zero integration work. Zero registration form. The payment is the registration. Every tx hash in this submission is real. Every settlement in the earnings table represents a real throwaway wallet that funded itself, acquired USDC on the Stellar testnet DEX, and paid a real endpoint autonomously. Nothing mocked. No simulated responses. What we learned Building the WebMCP layer took days. Building the infrastructure that makes it meaningful took months. The hardest problems were not in the browser API. They were in the payment rails, sequence number contention under concurrent Stellar settlements, the difference between a txBadSeq and a TRY_AGAIN_LATER, why a fee-bump transaction separates fee payment from sequence number management, what it actually takes to prove 50 concurrent settlements with zero failures. We learned that "the agent pays for it" is a sentence that sounds simple and takes an entire stack to make true. What's next for VELLAR Vellar is about to launch on Stellar mainnet. Real USDC, real agents, real commerce, no intermediary, no API key, no account, just a payment and a response. The Vellar Wallet already supports passkey smart accounts with on-chain spending policies. An agent with a Vellar session key and a spending limit enforced by a policy contract can use this WebMCP page to discover and pay for APIs autonomously, within a budget its owner set, revocable at any time, with every payment verifiable on-chain. The tool list on this page grows itself. Every endpoint that transitions from unverified to proven-unconfirmed to verified in the Bazaar becomes a new callable WebMCP tool automatically. As Vellar goes to mainnet and the Bazaar fills with real production endpoints, the marketplace that writes the tools gets bigger, richer, and more valuable to every agent that uses it. We built the marketplace. We are about to open it for real.  Inspiration 

 This is my first hackathon, and I'm probably way over my head, but I wanted to jump in and use it as a learning experience. I wanted to put something together that was practical for a small business who could use a WebMCP enabled browser/agent to work through tasks easily. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave me an opportunity to learn more about WebMCP. At first, I thought it might be gimicky, but after building this partial app, I definitely see the value. 

 Most of my coding experience has been in HTML and data analytics. Working with Codex has given me a way to sort of turn back the clock and work on the type of project I've always wanted to try. 

 Lastly. I'm close to retirement. I've always been technically inclined, but not formally educated in development. What Codex has done for me, which may sound silly, is it makes me feel young. I enjoy building, and taking part in this hackathon pushed me out of my comfort zone. Even though the project is simple, I'm proud of it. 

 What it does 

 FieldProof helps contractors keep job photos, completed work, and daily notes together. When a project is ready to wrap up, a browser agent can check the records, find missing information, and prepare updates for the contractor to review. The contractor decides which updates to save. After a successful recheck, FieldProof opens a handoff packet that can be printed or saved as a PDF for the client. 

 How I built it 

 I built FieldProof with Codex using React, TypeScript, and Vite. Project records and photos stay in the browser through IndexedDB and Dexie. Render hosts the app. 

 The FieldProof concept and some initial coding existed before the challenge. For the hackathon, I added WebMCP tools and built the review process around them. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One challenge was making the agent’s work easy to see. Initially changes made by the agent were buried in a side panel. I had to change layout so someone watching could understand what the agent found and what needed a decision. 

 Another challenge was testing whether an agent was actually using WebMCP. I tested with a separate agent session and checked which tools it called. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I’m proud that that I competed and completed my first hackathon! I know the reality is that this isn't a complex tool, it doesn't have wiz-bang features or amazing motion graphics. I'm not building a rocket, or some major SaaS product. However, it's mine. It's the type of thing I like to build, and it make a process easier for people. 

 What I learned 

 I learned how much the interface matters. A tool can work correctly and still leave someone wondering what happened. People need to see the result and understand what to do next. 

 What's next for FieldProof 

 My next step is to continue building the rest of the app, get feedback from contractors and see whether FieldProof fits how they actually keep job records. I want to improve the wording, make photo capture easier on a phone, and refine the handoff packet based on what clients need.

title: Intent Relay
pitch: Teach a workflow once, then translate the intent across WebMCP-enabled websites — without replaying clicks.
about_excerpt: Teach a workflow once, then translate the intent across WebMCP-enabled websites — without replaying clicks. Like Comment Story Updates Intent mapped to Orbit’s WebMCP capabilities: 5 preserved, 2 adapted, 1 not transferable, 1 sent to Human Queue. A provenance-backed Intent Contract proposed from the demonstration, with every rule reviewed and approved by the human. Orbit’s draft is prepared, but publication stays human-only: the agent can prepare; only the human can publish. What it is Most WebMCP demos ask what an agent can do on one site. Intent Relay asks what happens to human intent across sites. Intent Relay does not replay clicks. It translates human intent across the web: a human demonstrates a workflow once on a WebMCP-enabled site, reviews what that demonstration means , and carries the approved intent to a structurally different site. How it works The Workbench orchestrates two embedded demonstration providers built for this prototype — Gather (source) and Orbit (destination). They are separate HTTPS origins that structure the same job differently, on purpose. Demonstrate. You set up an event in Gather the way you always would. Gather exposes semantic state through WebMCP, and the trace records what each choice means — not where you clicked. Verify. From that demonstration, the agent side proposes an Intent Contract : rules with provenance, each citing the recorded actions that justify it. Nothing counts until you approve it — rule by rule. Transfer. Intent Relay discovers the capabilities Orbit exposes through WebMCP and maps your approved intent against them. The canonical demo result: 5 preserved — transfer unchanged 2 adapted — a 24-hour reminder becomes "1 day", because that's how Orbit counts 1 not transferable — Orbit has no equivalent, so it is excluded visibly, never silently 1 needs your decision — genuinely ambiguous Human Queue. The ambiguous one stops here: the demonstration used a native waitlist; Orbit doesn't have one. The agent doesn't guess — you decide, and only then does it prepare Orbit's draft. The Human Queue is a feature, not a failure state. Publish. Publication is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP tool. The prepared draft waits for a human. The agent can prepare; only the human can publish. Why WebMCP matters here Traditional browser automation can repeat actions on one interface, but it is brittle the moment two sites expose different structures and concepts. Intent Relay depends on what WebMCP makes possible: websites publishing machine-readable capabilities instead of an agent scraping DOM structure or replaying screen coordinates. Real browser-discovered tools via document.modelContext across three origins (Workbench, Gather, Orbit) Cross-origin semantic capability discovery — Orbit declares what it accepts, and mapping decisions are driven by those declarations Deployed to production through the Chrome Origin Trial — the demo runs in normal Chrome without WebMCPTesting flags Explicit human boundaries: contract approval, ambiguity decisions, and publication are human-only Challenges we ran into Cross-origin discovered tool objects. Real DiscoveredTool objects carry cross-origin WindowProxy references that cannot safely live in React state — the implementation separates sanitized display metadata from the raw browser handles used for invocation. Representing semantic mismatch without guessing. Every approved rule must land in exactly one explicit status (preserved / adapted / not transferable / needs decision) — "almost matches" is a first-class outcome, not an error path. Origin Trial across three origins. Three distinct HTTPS origins each needed correct Origin Trial configuration to run flag-free in production. What we learned WebMCP solves capability exposure — semantic equivalence between sites still needs reasoning and explicit boundaries. The most interesting case is not when two sites match perfectly, but when they almost match: that is exactly where human judgment matters most, and where an agent that refuses to guess is more useful than one that automates blindly. How it's built React + TypeScript + Vite in npm workspaces (three apps plus shared packages for contract types, validation and mapping logic), WebMCP via document.modelContext , three HTTPS origins on Cloudflare Pages behind the Chrome Origin Trial, 241 unit tests and a Playwright end-to-end suite, plus runtime validation in real Chrome. What's next (future work) More WebMCP-enabled providers; richer Intent Contract schemas; portable workflows across marketplaces, productivity and travel tools; shared semantic vocabularies; deeper provenance and policy handling. None of this exists yet — the prototype intentionally proves the transfer model on two deliberately different providers. title: Rehearse
pitch: A browser agent rehearses spatial repairs, but only a person can approve the exact patch.
about_excerpt: A browser agent rehearses spatial repairs, but only a person can approve the exact patch. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Temporary clinics and other short-lived spaces are often planned under time pressure. A layout can look plausible while still hiding a blocked route, narrow pinch point, inaccessible destination, or obstruction. Rehearse turns that fragile planning moment into a controlled collaboration between a person and a browser agent. What it does Rehearse deliberately starts with an unsafe temporary-clinic layout. A WebMCP-capable browser discovers five typed tools that let an agent read the current layout, run five deterministic spatial checks, stage a visible repair as ghost geometry, apply only the exact proposal a person approved in the interface, and verify the committed result with a SHA-256 receipt. The central demo is a failure-and-recovery sequence. After the agent stages a repair, the person locks reception. That increments the layout revision and makes the proposal stale. Rehearse rejects the old patch without moving anything. The agent must re-read state, produce a new lock-aware plan, and wait for approval again. This is a planning rehearsal, not regulatory accessibility certification. How we built it The React and TypeScript interface and the WebMCP tools call one shared command layer. The deterministic route engine uses bounded-grid A* with stable tie-breaking. Repair search excludes locked objects and returns compact structured results suitable for an agent. A proposal is bound to both its base revision and a SHA-256 hash. Human approval is UI-only: there is no tool that lets an autonomous agent approve its own patch. Apply succeeds only when the current visible proposal, approved hash, and base revision all still match. It commits atomically, reruns every check, and emits a verification receipt. The app has no API key, model call, database, or server requirement. It is deployed as a public HTTPS site on Netlify and the complete source is MIT licensed. WebMCP tools get_layout_state reads revision, geometry, locks, findings, proposal, and receipt state. run_route_audit runs the deterministic route and spatial audit. stage_layout_patch stages a visible lock-aware repair without mutating committed geometry. apply_layout_patch applies only the exact current proposal already approved by a person. verify_layout reruns checks against the committed revision. Challenges we ran into The difficult part was preserving a trustworthy boundary between agent autonomy and human control. We had to make stale work impossible to replay, keep manual and WebMCP actions behaviorally identical, compact tool results without hiding important state, and show proposed geometry clearly enough for a person to judge it before approval. The production flow passed in Chrome 151 through the native WebMCP surface, including discovery, invocation, stale rejection, lock-aware replanning, exact-hash approval, atomic apply, and verification. Accomplishments Five native typed WebMCP tools operating real shared application state. Visible ghost patches instead of invisible agent mutation. Revision-bound, hash-bound approval with replay and stale-work rejection. Deterministic lock-aware replanning and atomic apply. Eight automated tests, 93.71% statement coverage, 89% branch coverage, and Lighthouse accessibility 100. A public production deployment, reproducible testing guide, agent eval catalogue, and MIT-licensed source. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a site exposes domain operations that are difficult to reproduce safely through generic DOM actuation. Structured tools make spatial state, constraints, and failure reasons legible to an agent. But capability alone is not enough: consequential mutations still need an explicit human checkpoint, freshness guarantees, and a verification artifact. What's next The current build focuses deeply on one temporary-clinic scenario. Next steps would add floor-plan import, persistent projects, shared review sessions, richer constraint libraries, and organization-specific policy packs while keeping the same propose → inspect → approve → apply → verify control model. title: GoPic for Agents
pitch: Turn a real-world sign into the right place. GoPic uses visual evidence, location context, and WebMCP tools so agents can identify and ground real-world businesses from storefront photos.
about_excerpt: Turn a real-world sign into the right place. GoPic uses visual evidence, location context, and WebMCP tools so agents can identify and ground real-world businesses from storefront photos. Like Comment Story Updates GoPic turns a storefront photo into structured OCR, place candidates, and a grounded result for WebMCP agents. What it does Inspiration Travelers constantly see useful information in the physical world — storefronts, restaurant signs, shop names, addresses — but turning that visual clue into the correct place on the web is still surprisingly awkward. OCR can read text, but reading text is not the same as identifying the right real-world place. Businesses can share the same name, signs can use unfamiliar scripts, and users may not know what to type into search. GoPic already explored this problem as a mobile visual-search product. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to take the next step: expose that visual sign-to-place workflow directly to AI agents. What it does GoPic for Agents lets a human provide a storefront or sign photo and an optional location hint. GoPic then: analyzes the visible sign text, combines the visual evidence with location context, returns structured place candidates, identifies the strongest grounded result when the evidence is sufficient. The same workflow is exposed to compatible agents through three WebMCP tools: gopic_get_sign_context gopic_analyze_sign gopic_get_place_candidates This allows an agent to discover and invoke GoPic's capabilities directly from the webpage instead of guessing how to interact with the UI. How I built it The challenge website is a lightweight HTML, CSS, and JavaScript experience designed for both humans and WebMCP-enabled agents. WebMCP tools are registered using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The analysis flow is: Human photo → WebMCP tool → Supabase Edge Function → visual analysis → structured OCR and place candidates → grounded result The backend runs as a Supabase Edge Function. API credentials are stored only as server-side secrets and are never exposed to the browser or committed to the public repository. The public demo endpoint also includes origin checks, image type and size validation, and rate limiting. Challenges I ran into One challenge was separating simple OCR from actual place grounding. A sign may contain a business name, branch information, an address, phone number, and descriptive text, and not all of it should be treated as a place name. Another challenge was making the same workflow useful to both humans and agents. The page needed to remain understandable as a normal website while also exposing structured actions that an agent can discover and execute. I also spent time tightening the public demo architecture so that API credentials were not exposed and the live implementation matched the public source repository. What I learned WebMCP changes the role of a website. Instead of being only a visual interface that an agent has to interpret, the page can explicitly describe the actions it offers and the structured data those actions return. That makes it possible to combine human intent — "this is the sign I care about" — with an agent's ability to act quickly on the web. What's next The larger vision for GoPic is to make real-world visual information directly actionable. A traveler should be able to point at a sign, menu, storefront, product label, or other physical-world clue and let an agent understand what it is, identify the relevant real-world entity, and continue the task on the web. For this challenge, the focus is intentionally narrow: See the sign. Find the real place. title: ShipReel
pitch: Your AI agent edits video inside the browser tab. Say "cut this to 60 seconds" and it does — trimming dead air, syncing footage to what you actually said. Nothing ever uploads.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent edits video inside the browser tab. Say "cut this to 60 seconds" and it does — trimming dead air, syncing footage to what you actually said. Nothing ever uploads. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ShipReel Inspiration Every demo video starts the same way: a raw voiceover, a few screen recordings, and forty minutes of dragging clip edges around. The work isn't really creative. It's finding the twenty-three places where I paused, trimming each one, then hunting for the moment I said “here is the terminal” so I can put the terminal footage there. That is exactly the kind of tedious, constraint-satisfying work an agent should do. But most AI video editors solve it by moving your footage to a server. For a screen recording of an unreleased product, that can be a non-starter. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. The agent doesn't need your files — it needs your editor. What it does ShipReel is a video studio that an agent can drive through WebMCP while I stay in control. I can set a target runtime and give the agent a goal such as: “Cut this down to 60 seconds and put the terminal recording where I talk about the terminal.” The agent can inspect the timeline, detect dead air, search the transcript, place relevant footage, trim clips, add zooms, and optimize the edit until it fits the runtime budget. In a test run, a single optimize_duration call took the bundled 108.7-second edit to the 60-second target . Every action appears in an Agent Activity panel in plain English: “Removed 26.4s of dead air” “Dropped 4 lines of narration — 20.3s” “Found "Here is the terminal" in the narration at 17.4s” “Placed the terminal recording at 17.4s” The underlying WebMCP tool name and arguments remain visible underneath as evidence. My own manual edits appear in the same activity feed, so a drag I make by hand and a cut made by the agent become one shared history. The footage doesn't have to be the bundled kind. Dropping a screen recording onto the timeline adds it to the project — nothing uploads, and it takes exactly the same path as the bundled clips, so every tool treats it identically. The clip id comes from the filename, so login-flow.mov lets me say, “put the login flow clip at 45 seconds.” The agent sees the imported footage on its next get_project_state , the same way it sees a manual edit. Why this had to be WebMCP, not a backend MCP server Most agent integrations can use a remote MCP server. This one is different. The media is held in page memory. HTMLVideoElement decodes video, Canvas composites the preview, the Web Audio graph handles audio, and encoding uses MediaRecorder — all inside the tab. There is no remote media service that needs to own the edit. A backend MCP server would not naturally have access to the live timeline state, decoded audio, or the rendered frame the user is looking at. The clearest example is preview_at . preview_at does not change the edit. It moves the user's playhead so the agent can show the human exactly what it is referring to. Over a backend-only protocol, that tool has little meaning. With WebMCP, the agent can operate on the same live interface the human is watching. During testing inside ChatGPT's built-in browser, the agent independently called preview_at at 17.4 seconds to show the clip it had placed. I had not explicitly asked it to preview that timestamp. That was the point where the premise stopped being an architectural argument and became a visible demonstration. The agent is a guest in the editor, not the other way round. How I built it ShipReel is built with React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind and Vite. The editing engine is written from scratch without a video-editing library. Ripple delete across tracks remove_ranges accepts an array of time spans and closes all the gaps in one operation, keeping narration and footage aligned. Instead of making the agent issue a separate request for every silent section, it can remove a whole set of ranges in a single tool call. Silence detection find_silences analyzes the decoded audio with windowed RMS and derives a threshold from the recording itself. The bundled voiceover contains 28.3 seconds of detected dead air . Runtime optimization optimize_duration is the high-level tool. It first reclaims low-cost time such as silence, then escalates to progressively more expensive edits such as filler removal and whole-sentence removal until the edit fits the requested runtime. It protects the opening sentence from becoming a candidate because saving a few seconds is not worth destroying the hook. When multiple lines could close the remaining gap, the optimizer prefers the shortest sufficient line, avoiding unnecessary loss of narration. Real-time in-tab export The export path drives the same player/compositor used for preview and captures its canvas and audio graph with MediaRecorder . The render clock runs in a Worker instead of relying on requestAnimationFrame , so rendering is not tied directly to the visible frame loop. Fourteen WebMCP tools Fourteen tools are available across two states. At boot — 7 tools: get_project_state search_transcript find_silences optimize_duration remove_ranges place_clip preview_at After footage is present — 7 additional tools: trim_clip move_clip set_clip_speed add_zoom remove_clip get_export_status export_video The clip-editing tools register only when there is footage on the video track, so the agent is not offered actions that are meaningless in the current state. Tool descriptions are designed around one job per tool, non-overlapping responsibilities, bounded outputs, and recovery-oriented error messages. Human + agent collaboration ShipReel is not designed around replacing the human editor. The agent handles repetitive operations and constraint satisfaction. The human can still inspect the result, move clips, change timing, or intervene at any point. For example: “Preview the terminal section.” The agent can call: preview_at(17.4) I see the exact part of the edit it is referring to, decide whether the placement is good, and continue directing the work. That makes the browser itself the shared workspace between human and agent. Challenges Making “hit a target runtime” an agent problem instead of a guessing game The first version reclaimed whatever time it could and then stopped, returning candidate sentences for me to choose between. That worked, but it did not solve the actual problem. The rewrite turned runtime optimization into an iterative constraint problem: reclaim silence reclaim low-cost filler remove whole sentences only when necessary stop immediately when the target is satisfied A subtle selection detail mattered. When multiple lines could close the remaining gap, the optimizer chooses the shortest sufficient line instead of deleting more content than necessary. That turned a 60-second target from a rough approximation into a controlled optimization process. A silence-detection bug I only found by writing evals find_silences originally truncated its returned list at a response cap while still reporting the full count. That meant an agent could remove only the ranges it received and incorrectly believe the job was complete. I changed the tool to make truncation explicit and to instruct the agent to call again for the remaining ranges. The fix came from an agent-level evaluation, not from a traditional unit test. Layout that only broke where it mattered The preview frame used an aspect-ratio box with a max-height , which behaved correctly at desktop widths but failed inside the narrower layout used by ChatGPT's browser pane. I found it in a responsive audit at 900×800 — and then realised ChatGPT's browser pane renders below that same breakpoint, so it would have hit exactly there. The content-sized grid row allowed the preview to grow beyond its intended slot and paint over the timeline. What I learned Write evals for the tool surface, not just the code I built a 17-task evaluation suite that drives real Chrome with WebMCP enabled and executes the same sequences a competent agent would perform. The suite caught real bugs that ordinary unit tests did not expose. It also runs against the production deployment, so I can validate the same behavior that a judge will see. The seventeenth task covers bring-your-own-media end to end: a screen recording goes through the real file input, the agent is told about it, the footage is placed by name, and the resulting canvas is verified to remain untainted — an important check because imported media can otherwise silently break browser export. Tool design is product design The most useful WebMCP decision was adding the high-level optimize_duration tool. Without it, an agent has to manually orchestrate silence detection, transcript search, filler removal and sentence selection across many calls. With it, the agent can express the user's goal directly while still using the lower-level tools for the rest of the editor. Show the reasoning, not the log Raw tool calls prove th

title: Swarm | Spaces Where Humans and Agents Work Together
pitch: OS and Decision Graphs for model agnostic agentic AI work. Build complex systems using Swarm Spaces as building blocks, collaborate and fully manage with other Humans and Agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: OS and Decision Graphs for model agnostic agentic AI work. Build complex systems using Swarm Spaces as building blocks, collaborate and fully manage with other Humans and Agents via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tools (54 available) Initiating prompt pasted into demo showing Swarm UI in browser Human approval required before agent can execute task Separate agent from the ChatGPT hosted in Swarm Cloud begins executing the task ChatGPT uses WebMCP to return the results back into the thread and from here, collaborative work can continue Result is published in the Swarm UI as an artifact Inspiration For this challenge I wanted to explore a more consequential use of WebMCP: using a website as a secure gateway from one conversation into persistent work performed by other agents, without removing humans from important decisions. Real world work spans shared evidence, specialist agents, asynchronous execution, organizational permissions, and decisions that must remain accountable to a person. Swarm already organizes this work in persistent Spaces. The WebMCP Challenge gave me the perfect opportunity to make each Space directly understandable and operable by ChatGPT through a bounded, typed interface instead of DOM scraping/browser automation (or strictly API/regular MCP). What it does My demo takes place in a visually simple Supplier Launch Decision Space. The Space contains two supplier evidence Artifacts, a Decision Graph, an unresolved recycled material compliance claim, a connected Supplier Verification Agent (cloud hosted GPT5.6 Terra through Swarm), and a human approval policy. From one ChatGPT conversation, the user gives a single goal. ChatGPT then uses the tools exposed by the active Swarm page to: Read the Space metadata, Decision Graph, participants, and existing Artifacts. Identify the unresolved compliance claim and the exact evidence already available. Request a verification Run from Supplier Verification Agent. Post a durable status message containing the delegated agent and Run ID. Stop at a human approval gate before any agent execution begins. Observe the same Run transition into execution after the person approves it in Swarm. Read the completed Run, Markdown Artifact, action traces, evaluation state, evidence IDs, and approval timestamps. The connected cloud hosted agent verifies only what the existing Space evidence supports. In the recorded run, one supplier's recycled aluminum declaration is supported while the second supplier's evidence remains insufficient. The resulting Artifact preserves those distinctions and states that no supplier launch may be approved or promoted without a separate human decision. The Run and Artifact remain in the Space after the initiating ChatGPT conversation ends. Another authorized person or agent can inspect the same Space from anywhere in the world and pickup the work from there. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a browser agent would have to inspect rendered text, infer which controls represent domain actions, and hope that UI changes do not break its workflow. It would also be difficult to communicate which actions the signed-in user is actually permitted to perform. With WebMCP, the page exposes a Space specific catalog of typed operations. ChatGPT works with concepts such as Runs, Artifacts, approval requests, evaluations, participants, and Decision Graph nodes rather than guessing at buttons or scraping layout. This produces a better experience in four ways: Less friction: one goal can initiate a structured multi-step workflow without repeatedly re-entering context. More reliability: calls target stable domain operations rather than visual coordinates or page structure. Durable collaboration: delegated work, provenance, and results survive outside the original conversation. Visible human control: the browser agent can request and observe an approval gate, but it cannot approve or deny on the person's behalf. This means WebMCP becomes the entry point through which one conversational agent can coordinate persistent execution by other agents inside a controllable workspace. Human authority is a system rule For the gated request, ChatGPT calls swarm_request_agent with: { "required_approval_actions": ["approve.launch"] } Swarm atomically creates the human message, blocked Run, and approval request. The Run is not claimable while the gate is pending. Approving queues that same Run for an authorized runtime; denying cancels it. Approval and denial are deliberately absent from the browser agent's WebMCP tool catalog, so prompt wording cannot bypass the policy. The final read only step compares the recorded approval and execution timestamps. It also distinguishes approval to perform verification from the separate authority to approve a supplier launch. A completed agent task is evidence for a decision, not the decision itself. How I built it The browser adapter is written in TypeScript and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The signed-in Swarm page obtains a bounded catalog filtered for the current user and Space. Tool inputs and outputs use explicit schemas, and mutations require stable idempotency keys. Each invocation returns through same origin Swarm API routes. The server remains authoritative for authentication, tenant isolation, Commands, Permits, approval policy, evidence access, response limits, and audit records. The browser receives neither provider credentials nor a general purpose HTTP or SQL tool. Long running work is reconciled through a bounded read only Space revision wait. When the revision changes, ChatGPT uses typed read tools to retrieve the exact Run, Artifact, approval request, trace, or evaluation that changed. This keeps asynchronous execution observable without granting additional authority. The broader Swarm application uses React and Next.js for the product interface, Go services, PostgreSQL, and Google Cloud Run. The public challenge repository contains the reviewed WebMCP browser adapter, public contracts, tests, build instructions, export provenance, and an Apache 2.0 license. It intentionally excludes credentials, provider implementation, and private deployment configuration. Challenges I faced The hardest part for me was preserving one coherent state across ChatGPT, the human facing thread, an approval record, a queued Run, a cloud runtime, and a durable Artifact. I had to make asynchronous state visually and semantically consistent. The approval card must remain linked to the exact Run; the same Run must transition live after approval; and every later read must select that Run rather than a similarly named historical result. I also had to separate observation from authority. A model needs enough context to identify a pending decision and explain it, but that does not mean it should receive the capability to resolve the decision. Enforcing that boundary in server side permissions, rather than relying on prompt instructions, was essential. Finally, I needed a public repository that demonstrates real production integration without exposing private infrastructure or secrets. So I created a reviewed, one way source snapshot with reproducible hashes and tests while keeping the hosted service as an explicit external dependency. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it describes domain intent and policy, not when it merely recreates clicks as tools. Stable IDs, typed contracts, idempotency, provenance, and explicit approval states make agent behaviour easier for both machines and people to understand. I also learned that human in the loop cannot be a sentence added to a prompt. It must be represented by durable state that prevents execution until the right person acts. Once that is true, the interface can clearly show what is waiting, what was approved, what executed, and what authority still remains with a human. What I added for the WebMCP Challenge Swarm existed before the challenge period, although it had no WebMCP capability. The challenge specific work is the WebMCP browser integration and the end to end experience around it: the document.modelContext.registerTool adapter, Permit filtered Space catalog, safe invocation contracts, approval aware agent requests, read only asynchronous reconciliation, public source export, tests, documentation, and the deterministic Supplier Launch Decision demo. What's next The demo uses one ChatGPT orchestrator and one cloud hosted verification agent so the flow is easy to follow. The same model can support larger Spaces in which people and multiple specialist agents contribute research, execution, review, and decisions over time. This means you can have Spaces with multiple humans, dozens of connected agents all working collaboratively. The even bigger scale comes from when you give agents permissions across multiple spaces, allowing for cross space connections and this turns Swarm into a global network layer for humans and agents. Built With chatgpt go google-cloud gpt5.6 javascript

 Inspiration 

 Online shopping can be really time-consuming, especially if you are trying to get, for example, a pair of second-hand sneakers. With Bargainer, you can just tell you ai agent that you want to buy sneakers and sit back and watch as it shows you all available options, negotiates the price, and gets you a final deal that you have to improve. It saves time and effort. It's online shopping done the modern way. 

 What it does 

 AI agents negotiate and reach a deal on both the buyer and seller side that needs to be approved (or is auto-approved, if enabled). Makes use of WebMCP tools to provide all the information to the agents. 

 How we built it 

 It is built as a React and TypeScript SPA. It is client-side with no backend. It is deployed on Netlify. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is a newer technology, so a lot of my work came from trial and error, as I didn't know much about it beforehand either. React StrictMode's double-mounting broke tool registration until I rebuilt it around AbortController cleanup (the spec has no unregisterTool). Tool errors are opaque to agents, so I return structured {ok: false, message} responses instead of throwing. And the human gate needed a 60-second approval token so the tool can tell the agent "waiting on the human" instead of silently blocking. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I had very little time to make this project, as I found out about it much later. But 9 registered and running WebMCP tools in such a short time feels like a win. 

 What we learned 

 This is my first ever hackathon. I gave it my best and hope to win, but even if I don't, it was a very valuable learning experience for me. I learnt about WebMCP and how its tools can be used effectively. I learnt to plan, code, test, and debug a project with a time crunch. 

 What's next for Bargainer 

 I will build a lightweight backend that will allow real buyer agents to join from other devices instead of simulated ones.

 Inspiration 

 Cross-border trade across Africa under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) holds immense potential, yet micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) lose millions daily due to complex Harmonized System (HS) tariff codes, varying MFN vs. AfCFTA preferential rates, hidden border clearance fees, and tedious manual customs declarations. 

 So I built SwiftClear to transform African cross-border logistics into an agent-native experience. I exposed web tools directly via the new WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard enabling browser AI agents to autonomously look up tariff rules, compute duty savings, and prepopulate customs manifests for traders in seconds. 

 What it does 

 SwiftClear is an agent-native AfCFTA trade compliance and customs declaration workspace. Key features include: 

 AI Trade Analysis : Instant HS tariff classification, rule-of-origin verification, and duty breakdown powered by Google Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite. 

 WebMCP Tool Suite : Exposes structured client-side tools directly onto navigator.modelContext so external AI web agents (or in-page agents) can query trade rules and drive the application UI. 

 AfCFTA Preferential Tariff Calculator : Calculates baseline MFN duty vs. AfCFTA preferential rates, VAT, security fees, escort fees, and net USD savings across key African transport corridors (e.g., Kano to Accra, Mombasa to Kampala). 

 Live WebMCP Inspector & Terminal : Provides a real-time event stream of WebMCP tool registration, execution requests, parameters, and dynamic DOM updates. 

 How I built it/WebMCP Architecture 

 SwiftClear is built using a modern, resilient tech stack: 

 WebMCP Standard : Implemented client-side tool registration on navigator.modelContext with a robust fallback polyfill (src/utils/webmcpPolyfill.ts) supporting event dispatching for tool execution. 

 Registered WebMCP Tools :
1) lookup_hs_code : Resolves product descriptions to 6-digit HS codes, duty rates, and AfCFTA eligibility using Gemini 3.1 Flash.
2) calculate_duties : Calculates exact duty fees, VAT, port handling, escort fees, and total clearance costs based on declared consignment value and quantity.
3) populate_customs_manifest : Injects parsed manifest state directly into the frontend reactive DOM. 

 AI Backend : Express server (server.ts) and Vercel serverless endpoint (api/gemini/analyze-trade.ts) using @google/genai with gemini-3.1-flash-lite, structured JSON schema enforcement (responseMimeType: "application/json"), and offline trade fallback models. 

 Frontend : React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Framer Motion, and Lucide Icons. 

 Challenges and Accomplishments 

 WebMCP Browser Compatibility : Chrome's native WebMCP flag (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing) exposes a native navigator.modelContext object. I designed a dual-layer registration architecture that seamlessly interfaces with both native browser environments and standalone WebMCP bridges without breaking page state. 

 Structured AI Responses : Enforcing strict JSON schema validation with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to guarantee reliable numeric duty rates and standardized HS codes for seamless tool execution. 

 Trade Fallback Engine : Built a robust offline AfCFTA tariff matrix ensuring the application remains 100% operational even during network or credential unavailability. 

 What's next for Swiftclear 

 Expanded Corridor Coverage : Expand tariff data across all 54 AfCFTA signatory nations. 

 Real-time Customs API Sync : Integrate direct webhooks with national customs systems (e.g., Ghana Single Window, Nigeria Trade Portal). 

 Multi-Lingual Agent Support : Enable French, Swahili, Arabic, and Portuguese agent interactions for cross-regional trade facilitation.

title: Con-Sche — a construction schedule an agent can operate
pitch: An agent reads the float on a live construction schedule and moves the work — through WebMCP, without the schedule ever leaving the browser.
about_excerpt: An agent reads the float on a live construction schedule and moves the work — through WebMCP, without the schedule ever leaving the browser. Like Comment Story Updates Con-Sche — Construction schedules that agents can actually operate Live app: https://hackathon-con-sche.pages.dev/ Repository: https://github.com/tatelog/Hackathon-Con-sche (AGPL-3.0) Open the link and a real schedule is already loaded. No sign-up, no sample to pick, nothing to configure — the WebMCP tools are registered and ready to call. What it is Con-Sche is a browser-based editor for ADM network schedules — the arrow-diagram form of critical path scheduling that construction sites in Japan still run on. A single project holds hundreds of activities linked by dependencies. Move one activity and the effect ripples through the whole network. It runs entirely in the browser. Schedule data is stored locally in IndexedDB (via Dexie.js) and is never sent to a server. With WebMCP, an agent sitting next to the user can read that schedule and change it — without the data ever leaving the page. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 1. The data cannot leave the browser. A construction schedule is one of the most sensitive documents a contractor owns. It exposes delivery dates, subcontractor assignments, and — by implication — cost structure. Firms will not upload it to a third-party server so that an assistant can read it. A conventional MCP server would require exactly that: ship the data out, process it remotely, ship the result back. WebMCP removes the requirement. The tools run inside the page, against state already in the user's browser. Nothing is transmitted. The privacy constraint that blocks AI adoption in this industry simply does not apply. 2. The computation is already local. Con-Sche calculates CPM (ES/EF/LS/LF, total float, free float, critical path) on the client. When an agent shifts an activity, the recalculation happens immediately, in the same process. The agent asks a question and gets an answer grounded in a real solver — not an approximation, and not a round trip. 3. The data model was already structured for this. This is the part we want to be clear about: Con-Sche was not retrofitted with an API wrapper. It was built as a local-first application with an explicit activity/event graph, because that is the correct way to model an ADM schedule. When WebMCP arrived, exposing that graph took seven tool definitions — not a rewrite. An app designed to keep its own state coherent turns out to be an app an agent can operate. How it creates a better user experience Network schedules are read by specialists. To move one activity in a GUI you must know which arrow to grab, how far it may travel, and what it will drag with it. Total float — the number of days an activity can slip without delaying the project — is computed but not obvious. Most site staff never see it. With an agent in the loop, that knowledge becomes conversational: "How many days can I delay the 3F concrete pour?" "What work is scheduled for today?" "Push the steel erection back three days and tell me what it hits." The agent reads float, checks the allowed range, applies the change, and reports the new project duration. The user does not need to know the vocabulary of CPM to benefit from it. Every change an agent makes goes through the same undo stack as a human edit. The user stays in control of their own document. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before: interpreting a network schedule was tacit knowledge held by experienced schedulers. "The drywall is running late — can we absorb it?" was answered by a person who could hold the network in their head, or by nobody. Now: the question is answered against the actual graph, in the browser, in one turn. In the demo the agent looks up the drywall activity, reads its total float — zero, it sits on the critical path — and says plainly that any delay there moves the completion date. Told the work will take four more days, it updates the duration; CPM recalculates and the project goes from 97 days to 101. One undo puts it back, because the agent writes through the same history stack a person does. Concretely, an agent working with Con-Sche can: Summarise an entire schedule including full CPM results ( get_schedule ) Report how far one activity can move in each direction, and what it would affect ( get_activity ) Change a duration and return the recalculated project duration, so a delay reported on site becomes a new completion date in one turn ( update_activity_duration ) Shift an activity within its allowed range ( shift_activity ) Detect circular dependencies and orphaned event nodes ( validate_schedule ) Answer "what work is happening today?" ( get_activities_on_date ) Find activities by name, zone, or floor ( find_activities ) This is not a chatbot describing a picture of a schedule. It is an agent holding the same object the user is holding. How we implemented WebMCP Registration is feature-detected and non-invasive: export function registerConScheTools(): void { if (typeof document === 'undefined') return const modelContext = document.modelContext if (!modelContext || typeof modelContext.registerTool !== 'function') return for (const tool of ALL_TOOLS) { try { void modelContext.registerTool(withTelemetry(tool)) } catch (e) { console.warn(`[webmcp] tool registration failed: ${tool.name}`, e) } } } On a browser without WebMCP, nothing happens and ordinary users see no change. A failure to register one tool cannot take down the others or the app itself. Design decisions worth naming: Tools read and write the in-page schedule store only. They operate on the Zustand store backed by local IndexedDB. No schedule content is sent anywhere. This is enforced by the shape of the code, not by policy. Mutating tools are undoable. update_activity_duration writes through the same history stack as a manual edit, so a single undo reverses what the agent did. The demo ends on exactly that. Tools return structured, bounded results. get_activity reports the legal shift range and the affected chain, so the agent can reason before acting rather than guessing and retrying. Telemetry records the tool name only. A separate Cloudflare Worker + D1 logs who called which tool and when — never schedule data. This is the metering layer for future paid tiers, and it was built so that usage can be billed without the operator ever seeing a customer's schedule. Stack: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Konva.js (canvas rendering), Zustand (state), Dexie.js (IndexedDB), Tailwind CSS. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages, with Cloudflare Workers + D1 behind the telemetry endpoint. Prior work vs. work during the Hackathon Con-Sche existed before this Hackathon and is a shipped product. Per the rules, here is the split. Before the Submission Period (as of 2026-08-07): The Con-Sche ADM editor, CPM solver, and local-first storage model (IndexedDB) All seven WebMCP tools ( src/webmcp/ ), committed 2026-08-07 The usage-telemetry endpoint ( workers/api/src/webmcpEvent.ts ) During the Submission Period (2026-08-25 – 2026-09-03): Relicensed to AGPL-3.0 so the source is genuinely open Split this open build out of the hosted product into its own repository, and removed the landing page, the sign-up gate, the usage telemetry and the commercial pathways. The scheduling engine and the WebMCP layer are untouched Translated the entire interface to English — roughly 900 strings, down to the messages the tools themselves return to an agent Added a real sample schedule that loads on first visit: an 18-storey office building in fit-out, with exterior, interior, services and site works running in parallel, a genuine critical path, and activities that carry float. Judges and agents start on something worth asking questions about instead of a blank canvas Submission materials and demonstration video We are entering an existing application rather than a new one. What we are putting forward is not "we added WebMCP in ten days" but "we had spent months building an app whose state an agent could safely operate, and WebMCP was the interface it had been waiting for." What we learned The most useful realisation was not a technical one. It was that WebMCP changes who has to supply the AI. Construction firms in Japan are not short of AI. Their staff already have an assistant open. What has been missing is a way for the software they work in to be operated by the assistant they already have and already trust. Until now the answer was for every vendor to embed a model in their own product, and carry the cost, the support burden and the privacy problem that comes with it. WebMCP lets us stop doing that. We publish the tools; the customer brings the agent. For a small vendor selling into a conservative industry, that is a different economic proposition entirely — and it is why we think WebMCP matters specifically for construction software, not just generally. title: OpenAssist Daily Workspace
pitch: One visible workspace where people and agents safely organize daily work together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: One visible workspace where people and agents safely organize daily work together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates OpenAssist turns scattered work into one visible, voice-enabled WebMCP workspace. OpenAssist brings email, tasks, and calendar into one calm WebMCP workspace. A clear multi-account inbox keeps urgent mail visible while treating external content as untrusted. A Shopify catalog gives the agent structured product search with visual results. Every change pauses at an exact preview before anything is applied. The approved cart update is executed once, read back, and visibly verified. The activity view separates agent reads from user-approved changes for a complete audit trail. The movable voice agent uses the same WebMCP tools while the workspace stays visible. Inspiration My work is spread across several accounts, inboxes, task lists, calendars, notes, ideas, and projects. I wanted one calm place that could organize my day, remember useful context, and let agents help without hiding what they are doing. What it does OpenAssist Daily Workspace brings email, tasks, calendar, notes, memory, accounts, and activity into one clear workspace. The public judge workspace uses safe synthetic data. In normal use, the OpenAssist ChatGPT app connects Gmail, Tasks, Calendar, Drive, and other Google services, bringing a user's information into this same workspace. Through WebMCP, an agent can search, focus, organize, and act on that information while the user sees the result. Changes remain behind clear approvals. The Shopify example uses the same WebMCP approach. The agent can search the connected catalog, show product images and details, and prepare a cart action for approval. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess how a page works or use a separate system the user cannot see. OpenAssist exposes clear tools for the actions available on the page, so the person and agent share the same context. Reads happen immediately. Changes first show an exact preview. The user approves the action, OpenAssist runs it once, verifies the result, and records it in Activity. Email, attachments, and website content are treated as untrusted and cannot approve actions. How I built it The ChatGPT Site uses document.modelContext.registerTool and a shared registry for tool schemas, safety rules, demo behavior, and private Workspace mappings. The site is hosted on ChatGPT Sites. Cloudflare Workers and D1 provide isolated demo storage. The private workspace connects to OpenAssist Workspace and Composio-managed Google services without copying private Google content into the demo database. The voice agent runs in an isolated Cloudflare Container using Codex and my ChatGPT subscription for the demonstration. It calls the same WebMCP tools as the browser, so every result, preview, approval, and completed action remains visible in the workspace. Challenges The biggest technical challenge was streaming Codex voice from an isolated Cloudflare Container into the live site while keeping the browser, voice session, and WebMCP tool results in sync. A spoken request had to reach Codex, call the correct site tool, update the visible workspace, show any required approval, and return a spoken response without losing context. I also had to keep judge data separate from private data and prevent email or other outside content from becoming instructions. Accomplishments OpenAssist gives the agent useful tools while keeping every important action visible. The same interface works for personal daily planning and for demonstrating safe actions across connected services. What I learned An agent-friendly website needs more than automation. People and agents need a shared view, clear limits, and visible proof of what changed. What's next I want OpenAssist to become a practical second brain that organizes projects and research, remembers useful context, plans active work, and helps people safely assign prepared work to agents. title: Apptome
pitch: Zero-configuration, secure interoperability across web apps—entirely in your browser, powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Zero-configuration, secure interoperability across web apps—entirely in your browser, powered by WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 The open web is incredibly powerful, but deeply siloed. Today, if you want your CRM to talk to your invoicing tool, you have to rely on third-party automation servers, manage complex webhooks, and hand over highly sensitive, long-lived API keys. I was inspired by the WebMCP draft specification because it flips this model upside down. I wanted to explore a future where integration happens securely on the client side —where humans and AI agents can collaborate directly in the browser to move data between apps safely, transparently, and without ever exposing a backend API key. 

 What it does 

 Apptome (via the Connectome Hub) is a zero-configuration, secure interoperability layer for the we. It automatically discovers WebMCP capabilities exposed by your open we apps and unifies them into a personal graph. 

 When you want to execute a workflow—like taking a client from your CRM and generating a bill in your Invoicing app—you initiate it in our sidebar. Our Cloudflare Workers AI agent kicks in to semantically map the data from the source app to the destination app's required JSON schema on the fly. Finally, it presents you with the exact payload for human-in-the-loop confirmation. The agent does the heavy lifting, but the human remains in total control. 

 How I built it 

 Our architecture is split into three main layers: 

 
 The Spoke Apps: I built sample single-page applications that natively expose their local functionality using document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 The Bridge: A lightIight client-side script that monitors toolchange events and securely relays the available WebMCP capabilities to our central Hub via WebSockets. 
 The Hub & AI Mapper: Deployed entirely on Cloudflare Workers , the Hub maintains the user's persistent tool graph. I use Cloudflare Workers AI ( @cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast ) to perform the semantic mapping between differing tool schemas. The user interface is a secure, cross-origin iframe (the "Surface") injected over the host app. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Browser security is notoriously unforgiving! Because I am committed to maintaining the web's Same-Origin Policy (SOP) without bypassing it, managing cross-origin iframes, strict Content-Security-Policies (CSP), and secure weSocket transports was a massive challenge. I also ran into real-world anti-tracking hurdles (like Brave browser's Shields aggressively blocking our Cloudflare Turnstile human-verification checks) which forced us to deeply understand third-party iframe behaviors. Finally, tuning the LLM to output deterministic, strictly-typed JSON schemas without hallucinating required careful prompt engineering. 

 Accomplishments 

 It is gratifying to have demonstrated true N-to-N interoperability entirely on the client side. The "magic" moment of watching the AI seamlessly map fields from one app's schema to another app's schema—without requiring the user to manually drag-and-drop fields—is something I're very proud of. Furthermore, I built a highly secure architecture that enforces human consent for every action, proving that AI agents can be both immensely powerful and completely safe. 

 What I learned 

 I gained a deep understanding of the WebMCP draft specification and the paradigms of client-side tool discovery. I also leveled up our skills in edge computing with Cloudflare Workers, handling WebSockets at the edge, and seamlessly integrating serverless AI models into real-time we applications. Most importantly, I learned that the future of agentic we workflows depends on strict, transparent security boundaries. 

 What's next for Apptome 

 Our immediate next step is expanding our prototype from "stub" apps to real-world SaaS products. I plan to build a browser extension that can act as the WebMCP bridge, bringing Apptome's capabilities to legacy we apps that don't yet support WebMCP natively. I also want to explore integrating local, on-device SLMs (Small Language Models) so the semantic mapping can happen entirely locally for ultimate privacy.
