title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: IdentityMap Witness
pitch: Catch identity-mapping mistakes before they go live. A WebMCP agent proves every broken rule with the fewest test users, then rechecks every edit while a human keeps control.
about_excerpt: Catch identity-mapping mistakes before they go live. A WebMCP agent proves every broken rule with the fewest test users, then rechecks every edit while a human keeps control. Like Comment Story Updates A human reviews three pending safety rules before confirming them. The minimal witness: three synthetic users, four violation rows, every broken rule exposed. A relevant page edit immediately marks the previous evidence STALE. Fresh checks produce a revision-bound GREEN review packet. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Identity-mapping rules often exist only as an unsaved draft in an administrator's browser. The failures that matter tend to appear at the edges: a case-sensitive check puts a contractor in the employees group, a missing manager becomes an empty string, or stale directory data overrides HR. At that point, the page is the only place that knows the current draft, its revision, its fields, and its rules. WebMCP lets the page expose that information through five structured, least-privilege tools. The agent can work with the page's actual semantics instead of guessing from labels or DOM layout, even though the draft has not reached a server. How it creates a better user experience The administrator continues editing the draft in the normal page. The agent reads that exact draft and its revision, then stages three safety rules. Those rules stay pending until the administrator reviews their cards and clicks Confirm all . Once confirmed, the agent finds the smallest set of synthetic users that exposes every violation. For each result, the page shows which source value won, which value lost, and why. The agent can preview a redacted fix, but the administrator makes the edit. An edit immediately marks any dependent evidence STALE . The agent must test the new revision before it can prepare a GREEN review packet. There is no Save or Apply tool; applying the mapping remains a normal page control outside WebMCP. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before The administrator and agent can reason about a draft that exists only in the browser, using evidence that expires when its basis changes. Expressions, source priority, and confirmed rules can each invalidate an earlier result. Every evidence record therefore carries its revision and dependencies. When it becomes stale, the page strikes through the old rows and blocks the old packet. The agent handles the exhaustive search for edge cases across the synthetic population. The administrator confirms the rules and makes the actual edit. That division prevents proof from an older draft from being presented as proof of the current one. How we implemented WebMCP The top-level document registers five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) in app.js . They read the session and draft, stage rules, find a minimal counterexample set, preview a patch, and prepare the review packet. Strict schemas reject malformed input and extra fields. Failed calls leave the committed draft unchanged. Responses have size limits and redact CANARY_ fixture strings. We initially tried to wait for human approval inside one long-running tool call. In our ChatGPT in-app-browser testing, pending calls ended after roughly 22 seconds. The implemented flow therefore stages the rule cards and returns. After the administrator responds, the agent reads the new state on its next turn. The suite has 310 passing tests. On Chrome 152, we also run fresh-session registration checks and a 12-round trace that combines real DOM edits with WebMCP calls. Inspiration Identity teams merge records from Active Directory, an HR system, and an identity provider such as Okta before the resulting profiles determine access. The merge rules may still be an unsaved browser draft while the administrator works on them. Small mistakes can have large effects. A case-sensitive condition may classify a contractor as an employee. A missing manager may turn into an empty string instead of null . Stale directory data may take precedence over HR. These problems are easy to overlook without the right edge cases. An AI agent can help search for those cases, but unrestricted UI control introduces a different set of risks. The agent may guess what a field means, use evidence from an older draft, or act before a person has reviewed the result. What it does Two boundaries are important up front. Unsaved-draft preview already exists as a first-party product pattern. A different page-local agent with access to the same state and rules could also run this engine. IdentityMap Witness contributes a page-authored safety contract and an evidence lifecycle that causes old proof to expire. IdentityMap Witness reviews an identity-mapping draft before it is saved. A witness is the smallest set of synthetic users required to expose every safety rule that the current draft violates. The workflow is: The agent reads the exact unsaved draft and its revision. It stages three safety rules. They remain pending until a person reviews the cards and clicks Confirm all . The agent finds the fewest synthetic users that demonstrate every violation. The result explains which source value won, which lost, and why. The agent previews a redacted fix, and the person performs the actual edit in the page. The edit marks dependent evidence STALE . The new revision must be tested before the agent can prepare a GREEN review packet. The agent never receives a Save or Apply tool. Apply mapping (manual page control) remains outside the WebMCP surface and is not used in the demo. Why WebMCP The page is the source of truth for the live draft. It owns the fields and rules, tracks the revision, and decides which operations are allowed. WebMCP exposes that knowledge through five structured, least-privilege tools instead of making the agent infer it from labels or DOM structure. The tools return redacted evidence tied to a particular revision and reject calls made against old state. This allows the administrator and agent to work with data that has not reached a server while confirmation and editing remain visibly under human control. A general browser agent could inspect the interface. The difference here is that the page itself defines the contract, which makes the workflow reviewable and prevents stale conclusions from being silently reused. How we built it The application uses vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, and Node 21+. Five document.modelContext tools read the session, stage rules, find a minimal counterexample set, preview a patch, and prepare the review packet. The browser, test suite, and evaluation all use the same deterministic engine. Tool inputs use strict schemas, so extra or malformed fields are rejected. A failed call does not change the committed draft. Responses are size-limited and redact CANARY_ fixture strings. Before-and-after diffs are minimized for firstName , lastName , email , displayName , and managerId . This is a synthetic tripwire, not a general-purpose PII detector. Evidence records include the revision and dependencies used to determine whether they remain valid. There are 310 passing tests. Chrome 152 runs three fresh-session registration checks and a 12-round trace with real DOM edits and WebMCP calls. A hand-audited oracle verifies that the first search returns {P2, P3, P4} . This is one of two audited minimal sets of size three, and its four violation rows cover all four seeded defect classes. Challenges we ran into The central problem was that a correct result could become unsafe after the draft changed. An edit to an expression, source priority, or confirmed rule may invalidate earlier reasoning. Evidence is therefore tied to those exact dependencies; relevant edits strike through the old rows and prevent the old packet from being used. Human approval could not remain pending inside one tool call. In our own ChatGPT in-app-browser test on 2026-08-29, pending calls ended after roughly 22 seconds. That observation is not part of the repository's automated evidence. The current tool stages the cards and returns, the administrator confirms them, and the agent reads the updated state on its next turn. We also turned stale buttons, malformed inputs, hostile text, and empty source values into executable failure cases. What's next The demo currently uses eight synthetic personas, tab-local state, and an exhaustive search sized for this fixture. It is not connected to a real identity provider or a save operation. Unsaved-draft preview is not new on its own, and another page-local agent could run the same engine. The contribution here is the page-authored safety contract and the lifecycle that expires old proof. The Browser-Use and Full-CDP comparison arms have been designed but not run, so we make no comparative claim. Next, we would connect a real provider behind the same redaction boundary, test larger datasets with consent, persist review history, and add signed audit rece

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: client-weave
pitch: ClientWeave: An agent-native workspace where buyers and AI scope services, calculate seller-governed pricing, and book consultations—with humans retaining final control.
about_excerpt: ClientWeave: An agent-native workspace where buyers and AI scope services, calculate seller-governed pricing, and book consultations—with humans retaining final control. Like Comment Story Updates buyer goal service discovery service details shared scope guided scope validation deterministic pricing consultation availability agent-capabilities human confirmation confirmed booking Inspiration Buying professional services is rarely a simple checkout flow. Buyers often begin with an incomplete goal, refine requirements through conversation, wait for a quote, and then schedule a consultation. AI agents can accelerate this process, but consequential actions—such as submitting a lead or booking time—should remain under direct human control. That tension inspired ClientWeave : an agent-native professional-services CPQ workspace where buyers and browser agents collaborate on the same scope, while the seller controls pricing and the buyer retains the final say. What it does ClientWeave creates a shared, attributed workspace for service discovery, scoping, pricing, and consultation booking. A browser agent can: Discover services relevant to the buyer’s goal Create and update a structured scope Calculate deterministic, seller-governed pricing Find available consultation times Finalize a confirmed lead or booking Every scope change records whether it came from the buyer or the agent, making the process transparent and auditable. The key safety boundary is intentionally simple: an agent cannot confirm an action on the buyer’s behalf. Before a lead is submitted or a consultation is booked, the buyer must directly confirm the exact current summary in the interface. If the scope or quote changes afterward, that confirmation becomes stale and finalization is rejected. How we built it ClientWeave is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, Zod, and TanStack Query . The application exposes six browser-native WebMCP tools: discover_services create_scope update_scope price_scope find_consultation_slots finalize_confirmed_scope These tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() with a compatibility fallback for older browsers. They use the same authenticated and audited HTTP boundaries as the regular user interface, so agent interactions do not bypass the application’s validation or security model. The codebase separates deterministic domain rules from framework and infrastructure concerns. Pricing uses canonical inputs, versioned rules, integer minor units, and per-line rounding to ensure that the same scope always produces a reproducible quote. Public scope links use restricted, expiring capabilities rather than owner-level access. We also added structured validation, origin checks, secure cookies, content security policies, rate limiting, redacted observability, audit events, and retention workflows. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was designing collaboration without silently transferring authority from the person to the agent. Hiding a confirmation button from an agent was not enough; the server also needed to verify that a human directly confirmed the exact scope, quote, and intended action currently being finalized. Another challenge was keeping state consistent across the visual interface, WebMCP tools, pricing engine, and database. An agent could update a scope while the buyer was reviewing it, so we needed freshness checks and clear invalidation rules to prevent stale quotes or confirmations from being used. Designing safe public access was also demanding. Buyers should be able to participate without creating an account, but a private scope link must grant access to only one scope and must never provide workspace-owner privileges. Finally, we wanted the agent experience to be reliable without depending on brittle DOM scraping. Creating narrow, well-described WebMCP tools—and ensuring they behaved exactly like the human-facing workflows—required careful contract and integration testing. What we learned We learned that agent-native software works best when agents receive structured capabilities rather than instructions to imitate clicks. WebMCP made the available actions explicit, typed, and easier to audit. We also learned that human oversight should be enforced as a system invariant, not presented as a warning message. Direct confirmation, confirmation freshness, limited capabilities, and server-side authorization all work together to preserve meaningful human control. Most importantly, attribution changes the quality of collaboration. When every change clearly shows whether it came from a person or an agent, users can review the process instead of merely trusting the final result. What’s next Next, we want to expand ClientWeave with richer seller-defined pricing rules, reusable scope templates, additional scheduling integrations, and collaborative comments. We also plan to explore approval policies for larger deals while preserving the same core principle: agents can help move work forward, but people remain responsible for consequential decisions. title: Mandate
pitch: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents are locked out of nearly every high consequence system on earth. Not because they lack the capability, a model can read a payment queue and spot a duplicate or a sanctions hit faster than a person can, but because none of these systems has a way to grant an agent partial authority: enough to be useful, bounded enough to be safe, revocable the instant a human changes their mind. Today the choice is binary. Either the agent gets your credentials and can do everything you can do, or it gets nothing. Every bank, hospital, and factory picks nothing, and rationally so. WebMCP changes where that decision can live. Because tools are defined by the page itself, not by the model or its vendor, the site gets to decide what an agent may do, under what conditions, and for how long. Mandate is what that looks like on a bank's payment operations desk, where getting it wrong moves real money. What it does Mandate is a bank payment operations desk with an AI agent connected through WebMCP. The agent can investigate freely: read the queue, check a beneficiary, ask a partner screening bureau to recheck a sanctions match, but it cannot release a single payment on its own authority. To act, it has to negotiate. It calls propose_mandate , asking for what it needs, for example "up to 5,000 euros a payment, 50,000 total, SEPA only, verified beneficiaries only, for the next thirty minutes." That request shows up on the desk as a card a person can edit before agreeing: tighten the ceiling, shorten the clock, or refuse outright. The moment they grant it, the page re-registers its tool surface and a tool that did not exist a second earlier now does ( release_under_mandate , revoke_mandate ). The moment they revoke it, those tools vanish from the agent's list mid session. Three things fall out of that same property: A refusal is a conversation, not a 403. When the agent tries to release a payment it has no authority for, it gets back a plain English reason ("Segregation of duties: an agent cannot authorise a payment on its own authority") plus the two tools that would actually work, so it reroutes itself. The human sits inside the tool call, not notified after it. request_authorization returns a promise the page only resolves when a person clicks, so the agent is genuinely blocked and comes back with the real human answer. Nothing leaves the tab. All desk state is client side, so a bank could put real positions behind this and the agent would operate on data that never reaches a third party. What people and agents can do together that they could not before Until now an agent on a desk like this had two settings, and both are useless. Read only, in which case a person still makes every keystroke and the agent is a search box. Or the agent holds a human's credentials, in which case it can do everything that human can do and no bank will ever connect it. There was no way to express "you may do this much, for this long, and I can stop you." Three things happen on this desk that had nowhere to live before: An agent asks for authority in its own words, and a person edits the request before granting it. The agent proposes 5,000 euros a payment. Priya makes it 2,500 and grants that instead. The agent is told in its return value that its request was tightened, and works to the smaller number, leaving behind a 3,960 euro payment it would have been allowed to clear under its own proposal. Neither side had to anticipate the other in advance, which is what makes it a negotiation rather than a settings page. Two organisations settle one case without either handing over its data. The desk cannot see the bureau's watchlist. The bureau never sees the desk's payments. The agent asks the desk, the desk brokers the call across origins, and the answer comes back attributed to the bureau with an audit entry on both sides. That used to be a server to server integration with a contract behind it. Here it is one tool published to one named origin, and it works between two independent deployments. Authority ends mid conversation. A person clicks revoke and the tool the agent was about to reach for is gone from getTools() before its next call. Not a rejected request, and not a permission checked inside a handler: the capability itself stops existing while the session is still open. How it creates a better user experience For the person at the desk, the change is that they stop approving things one at a time and start setting a boundary once. Fifteen payments before a cut off used to be fifteen decisions. It becomes one decision about scope, after which the agent clears everything inside that scope and brings back everything outside it with the reason attached: above the ceiling you set, beneficiary not verified, sanctions match, wrong currency for that rail. Nothing is agreed to by accident either, because the ceiling, the budget, the rails, the beneficiary rule and the clock are all on screen and all editable before anyone clicks grant. For the agent, the change is that a refusal stops being a dead end. Every control answers in the shape a colleague would use: what is blocked, why, and what would work instead. So it reroutes itself instead of retrying the same call or inventing a workaround. And the desk keeps a permanent panel showing what the browser is actually holding, read live from getTools() rather than described in prose. Grant a mandate and the count moves from 18 to 20 on screen, in the same frame as the click. Revoke it and it drops back. Being able to see exactly what an agent may do at this moment is the thing you most want to know when you let one near your money, and it is normally the thing you cannot see at all. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This only works because WebMCP puts tool definitions in the page, computed from live state, instead of behind a static, server hosted tool list. A conventional MCP server hands a fixed set of tools to a client it cannot see. Mandate's tool surface is rebuilt and re-registered against an AbortSignal every time authority changes, so the mandate is real rather than cosmetic: tools do not exist until authority does, and they stop existing the instant it is withdrawn. That loop, an agent asking for authority, a human shaping it, and the tool surface itself changing as a result, is not possible outside a page hosted model. How we built it No backend, no database, no AI model of our own, no build step, and zero runtime dependencies. The visiting agent (Chrome with the WebMCP flag, or ChatGPT's in-app browser) brings the model; the page brings the tools and the governance. Twenty tools across five tiers, plus one published from a separate origin: Read tools with readOnlyHint: true (free rein: search payments, explain a hold, get exposure, pull the audit trail) Prepare tools that move no money (draft, amend, attach evidence) Consequential tools that block on a person ( request_authorization , release_payment , a declarative ask_the_desk form) Governance tools where the agent negotiates its own limits ( propose_mandate , get_mandate , undo_last_agent_action ) Mandate only tools that exist purely while authority is in force ( release_under_mandate , revoke_mandate ) The cross origin piece is Sentinel Screening Bureau, a genuinely separate deployment holding the sanctions watchlist. It never hands the list over. It publishes exactly one tool, scoped to origins it names: await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: 'recheck_beneficiary_screening', description: 'Re-run sanctions screening for one beneficiary.', inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }, { exposedTo: ['https://mandate-webmcp.vercel.app'] }); The desk embeds that origin with allow="tools" , discovers what it publishes with getTools({ fromOrigins }) , and brokers the call under its own governance, so the agent asks the desk and the desk answers with the bureau's decision plus an audit entry. Two organisations cooperating on one decision, neither handing over its data or its authority. The controls behind all of this (segregation of duties, four eyes approval, per role limits, sanctions screening, rail eligibility, duplicate detection, mandate scope) live in a pure, DOM free control engine covered by 34 tests that run on CI. Challenges we ran into Two spec behaviours we only found by testing against real Chrome, not by reading the explainer: executeTool takes a JSON string as its argument, not an object as the explainer shows, and it returns a JSON string too, which the explainer does not mention at all, so we had to handle both raw and serialised result shapes. We also learned the hard way that getTools({ fromOrigins }) is additive, not a filter: it returns your own tools plus the named origin's, so matching a partner's tool by name alone would have let a

title: Forge Ai
pitch: A workspace built for two users: humans and AI agents. Humans set intent; agents use WebMCP to plan, create, modify, and organize real workspace data under human control.
about_excerpt:
A workspace built for two users: humans and AI agents. Humans set intent; agents use WebMCP to plan, create, modify, and organize real workspace data under human control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI web experiences stop at conversation: the agent tells you what to do, while you still have to operate the application yourself. We wanted to explore a different model—what if a website could expose its real capabilities directly to an agent? 

 That idea became Forge , a workspace designed from the beginning for both humans and AI agents. 

 What it does 

 Forge lets a person describe a goal in natural language, such as creating a realistic two-week product launch plan. 

 The agent can inspect the workspace, create and organize tasks, build milestones, modify existing work, and propose changes through WebMCP tools . 

 Humans stay in control: they can review agent-proposed changes, approve or reject them, and undo important actions. 

 Instead of an AI that only generates suggestions, Forge lets the agent actually work with the application's structured state. 

 How we built it 

 We built Forge as a web application with a visual project workspace, an integrated agent panel, structured project data, an activity log, and a human approval workflow. 

 The core of the project is WebMCP. Forge exposes real application capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including project, task, planning, workspace, approval, and undo operations. 

 The UI and agent use the same underlying application state, so an agent action immediately becomes a visible change in the workspace. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making WebMCP more than a technical demo. The tools had to perform real application operations and work together as a coherent workflow. 

 We also had to design a clear boundary between agent autonomy and human control, especially for changes that modify or remove existing work. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 We built a complete human-agent workflow instead of a chatbot wrapper. 

 A user can give Forge a goal, the agent can use multiple WebMCP tools to work on the project, the application can show exactly what the agent did, and the human can review, approve, reject, or undo changes. 

 We are especially proud that WebMCP is part of the product's interaction model rather than an add-on feature. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that making a web application agent-friendly requires more than adding AI. The application's capabilities need clear structured interfaces, predictable inputs and outputs, good state management, and strong human feedback loops. 

 WebMCP gave us a way to think about the website itself as something an agent can understand and operate. 

 What's next for Forge AI 

 We want Forge to evolve from a project workspace into a broader agent-native environment where humans and agents can collaboratively create, organize, and execute complex work across different types of web applications.

title: Guild
pitch: The multiplayer visual workspace where humans and local AI teammates plan, design, and build software together on one shared canvas.
about_excerpt: The multiplayer visual workspace where humans and local AI teammates plan, design, and build software together on one shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Building software with AI still feels surprisingly fragmented. A product brief may live in a document, architecture in a diagram, tasks in an issue tracker, designs in another tool, and implementation evidence inside pull requests. AI assistants usually operate in separate chat windows with incomplete context. Humans spend time copying information between tools, resolving conflicting output, and figuring out what changed. We asked a simple question: What if humans and AI teammates could build a software project together inside the same visible workspace? That idea became Guild . Guild is inspired by the flexibility of Whimsical, the multiplayer presence of Figma, the structured execution of Linear, and the capabilities of modern coding agents. The difference is that AI is not hidden behind a chat sidebar. AI Workers appear as actual project collaborators with defined roles, owned workspace regions, live progress, visible results, and accountable changes. WebMCP was essential to this vision. Traditional browser agents have to interpret pages from pixels, DOM elements, and button labels. That approach is fragile and gives the agent very little understanding of the product’s actual domain. With WebMCP, Guild can expose structured operations such as: Search the project canvas Read semantic relationships Create or update project artifacts Launch a team of AI Workers Monitor active Jobs Add precisely anchored feedback Publish immutable design revisions Record implementation evidence Stop, retry, or undo work Guild is therefore not merely a web application that an agent can operate. It is a shared collaboration environment intentionally designed for people and agents to use together. What it does Guild is a multiplayer visual workspace where humans and locally running AI Workers build the same software project on one shared infinite canvas . Instead of separating product thinking, architecture, design, implementation planning, feedback, and AI execution across disconnected applications, Guild keeps everything in one persistent project context. One shared infinite canvas Every Guild project has one multiplayer canvas with three creation modes. Diagram mode Diagram mode supports: Product requirements Brainstorming User journeys User flows System architecture Database architecture API relationships AI and agent architecture Decisions and impact maps Task mode Task mode supports: Engineering tasks Implementation plans Bugs Reviews Testing Launch checklists Project status Task cards can contain Markdown descriptions, checklists, status, priority, labels, assignees, links, and semantic relationships. Wireframe mode Wireframe mode supports: Product screens Web and mobile interfaces Interface states User flows Low-fidelity prototypes Design annotations These modes share the same canvas rather than creating separate diagram, task, and design applications. Fifteen neutral canvas object types Guild uses a small set of flexible visual primitives: Shape Sticky note Text Mind-map node Table Icon Image Link Section Annotation Drawing Task Stack Wireframe frame Wireframe component Semantic metadata gives these objects their project meaning. A shape can represent a service, database, API, requirement, decision, or AI system without requiring a separate renderer for every software concept. Objects can be connected with relationships including: contains informs requires implements represents supports depends_on calls reads_from writes_to emits triggers verified_by affects blocks supersedes This produces a visual software-project graph rather than a collection of unrelated cards. Multiplayer collaboration Multiple people can work in the same workspace in real time. Guild synchronizes: Cursor position Canvas viewport Current selection Editing state Comments Canvas changes Worker progress Runner availability Project activity Every human, WebMCP, and Worker action is attributed in the activity history. AI Workers with real responsibilities An AI teammate in Guild is called a Worker . Each Worker is configured through a Role Profile containing: Name and handle Project responsibility Instructions Local execution engine Owned canvas section Visual identity Available capabilities For example, a Guild team could include: Product Lead Product Designer Systems Architect Research Engineer Backend Engineer Frontend Engineer Security and Evaluation Lead A user can save these Role Profiles as a team and launch them together with one project brief. Team Runs and Jobs When the user selects Run Team , Guild deterministically creates one Job for each selected Role Profile. Every Job receives: The same high-level brief Role-specific instructions Full bounded read context An owned section An atomically reserved canvas region Optional dependencies A short-lived assignment capability Workers can understand the broader project, but they can modify only the objects and regions assigned to them. Guild does not use a hidden planning model to decide which Workers should run. The user-selected team and its configuration determine the Job fan-out. Visible parallel work Workers do not disappear into background chat sessions. Guild shows: Which Worker is active Whether it uses Codex or Claude Code What it is currently doing Which canvas section it owns Which object it is working on Whether its Job is queued, running, blocked, failed, or completed What artifacts and comments it produced If no compatible local Runner is available, the Job remains durably queued and the interface truthfully displays Waiting for Runner . Canvas-native feedback and revision Humans can annotate work directly on the Guild canvas or inside a hosted design preview. Feedback may be attached to: An entire workspace A section A specific canvas object A precise point on a design A selected rectangle on a design An immutable screen revision Annotations remain drafts until the user opens Review & Send . Guild groups the feedback by the responsible Worker and creates at most one revision Job per target Worker. Every exact anchor is preserved, including the design revision, route, viewport, scroll position, point, or rectangle. Immutable design revisions Design Workers can publish hosted previews as immutable revisions. Guild stores: Design-set identity Deployment identity Preview origin Screen names and routes Desktop and mobile viewports Related canvas objects Capture status Revision history Human approval decisions Users can inspect a design inside Guild, compare revisions side by side or with a slider, request changes, and approve a specific immutable revision. Implementation evidence External implementation work can be reported back into Guild as bounded evidence: Repository Branch Commit Pull request Changed files Checks Preview deployment Related canvas objects Provenance Guild carefully distinguishes a reported claim from independently verified information. A reachable link may be labeled Link verified , but Guild does not falsely claim that it executed a test or inspected a commit when it did not. Reversible execution Human actions, WebMCP calls, and Worker changes pass through the same command service. Each accepted operation creates an attributable Change Set . Team Runs can be undone with conflict awareness, preserving unrelated human edits made afterward. Jobs can also be stopped or retried. Stale Worker attempts are fenced so they cannot continue writing after cancellation or reassignment. Guild's 25 WebMCP tools Guild exposes 25 structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . These tools operate on the real application state. They are not mocked endpoints or a separate agent-only database. Each tool has: A clear natural-language description A structured input schema Runtime validation Authentication and workspace authorization Abort support Audited execution Machine-readable results The same domain rules used by the human interface Workspace discovery and understanding 1. list_workspaces Lists the Guild workspaces available to the signed-in user. This gives the browser agent an explicit starting point instead of forcing it to infer workspace names from navigation elements. 2. get_workspace_context Reads bounded live project context, including: Workspace metadata Canvas objects Semantic relationships Role Profiles Saved teams Team Runs Runner state Placement guidance Color guidance The response is intentionally bounded so an agent can understand the project without loading an unbounded canvas. 3. search_canvas Searches visible content and semantic metadata inside one workspace. An agent can find requirements, designs, decisions, implementation tasks, evidence, services, risks, or any other project artifact. I can turn on annotation mode, select the exact component, and and attach a change request to it, and then I can send it to them. The same annotation flow works on design components as well. Here, I want a specific area and I ask the Claude agent to design as per my request. Once I have added the comments and when I'm finished, Guild groups the comments with the responsible agent. I can add one overall note and send revision packets to each of the agent to make the required agent required changes as I want. The follow-up then starts in the local agents I'm already signed into. Codex updates the architecture and the revised result appears inside the scene in the canvas region. The Claude agent has returned the revised design with clear hierarchy, stronger contrast, and the visual direction I requested. Now, I can compare both versions, approve the results, or continue refining it as I want. So, in a nutshell, every agent result is interactive. I can select scenes or evidence, ask the responsible agent to make some change, and receive the answer in the same component. It is a two-way conversation. I can question the result, request changes, verify the sources, and see the agent update the canvas in real time. Now, finally, Guild brings the canvas, agent orchestration, live progress, contextual feedback, versions, approval history, and undo in one workspace. The agents can work in parallel while the project stays visible and the final decision stays with me. So, this is Guild and I hope you like it.

title: Wadi: design and customize a Konkan house with your AI agent
pitch: Structurally sound homes for families who couldn't afford an architect: an agent codes a Konkan home into a 3D model contractors build from, and owners customize it by chatting with a WebMCP agent.
about_excerpt: Structurally sound homes for families who couldn't afford an architect: an agent codes a Konkan home into a 3D model contractors build from, and owners customize it by chatting with a WebMCP agent. Like 7 Comment 7 Story Updates 2 Opening screen of Wadi showing pre-designed models that the user can choose and modify using the AI agent A fully loaded model that is generated from the design language code that was written by an architect with the help of a coding agent The design language code editor that a trained architect can create or modify directly or with a coding agent A graph of the rooms and connections between them that forms part of the structural constraints that ground the AI agents A detailed diagram of a hip roof construction that is automatically generated Floor plans are also automatically generated Elevation views are generated automatically as well Bill of materials for all of the construction (WIP) Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Inspiration In the Konkan (coastal region of the state of Maharashtra in India), many families build their homes with government housing grants. The grant covers construction, but not an architect, so the design falls to the local contractor and mason, who lay out the house room by room from experience. The owner rarely sees what their home will look like until it is standing. Wadi is built for exactly this gap. It is a parametric home designer that produces a full 3D model, dimensioned floor plans, elevations, and a roof, from designs that already follow the standard local materials and construction of the region: the laterite walls, Mangalore tiled hip roof, the raised plinth, the verandah on pillars. A homeowner can walk through their house in 3D before a single brick is laid. A contractor can start from a standard layout or sketch their own, and then refine it, without being a trained architect. That last part is where agents come in, and Wadi uses them for two different people. An architect (or a coding agent acting as one) designs a full house from scratch through Wadi's offline MCP server, authoring the complete model in Wadi's own design language, checked against structural rules at every step. Then the family customizes that design in their own browser through WebMCP. A 3D design tool is hostile to an agent: the scene lives in a <canvas> invisible to the accessibility tree, so the agent is left guessing at buttons. WebMCP fixes that. The site exposes structured design tools the agent calls directly, so a homeowner or contractor can start from a finished local design and just describe changes in plain language, "add a pooja room off the hall, widen the verandah, put the staircase here", while the agent makes real, sound edits and the family watches the model update. What it does Wadi separates the two people who touch a design, over one model and one design language. An architect designs the full house from scratch through Wadi's offline MCP server. Running inside a coding agent (Claude Code, or any MCP client), the architect authors the complete model in Wadi's .wdl design language, adding floors, rooms, a roof, and a staircase, checking each version against the structural rules and previewing the plans, elevations, and roof, all without the app. The family then customizes that design in the browser , through WebMCP and a hosted online MCP server, with nothing to install. The homeowner or contractor opens the app, picks the local design closest to what they want, and talks to an in-browser agent (ChatGPT's built-in browser, or Chrome). The agent reads the design, edits it, resize a room, add a bathroom, change the plot, and applies it, and the person watches the 3D model, floor plans, and roof re-flow live. Because a design is a parametric model, changing one number re-flows the whole house. Both go through the same store the person edits by hand, so agent edits and human edits are the same kind of change, on one live model with one undo history: you can talk a house into shape and then hand-tune it. A live co-editing relay even lets a remote agent edit the model a family is watching, in real time. How we built it The core is a Zod HouseConfig schema, a parametric resolver, and a geometry expander. Any number in the model can be a formula over named variables, points, and guide lines, so the whole house re-flows when one value changes. A generated guide, for example, resolves lazily by index: $$\text{module}.x_i = o_x + i \cdot s_x$$ Every mutation runs through a Zustand store that re-resolves the parametric model, so the 2D and 3D renderers always read resolved numbers. The edit surface is Wadi's .wdl design language , a small language for a whole house (floors, rooms, walls, roofs, variables, formulas), compiled through the real pipeline. Making the DSL the single edit surface was the key decision: an agent reads the current house with get_wdl , edits the text, and applies it with set_wdl , which compiles it, loads it into the same store the UI uses, and returns a structural check. So the agent is not a second app driving Wadi from outside, it is another hand on the same model. Because the person customizing is not an architect , that same set_wdl runs a structural constraint linter on every edit, a growing set of rules that keep a spoken change buildable: a plinth on the lowest floor, a roof on the highest, the roof covering the whole top floor, pillars under any cantilever, upper-floor walls aligned over the walls below, plus checks on slabs, floor heights, openings, room overlaps, and passable connections. Each returns a plain-language warning the agent must resolve, so a change from someone with no design training still lands a real, buildable house. Two MCP surfaces sit on this core. The offline MCP server gives an architect the from-scratch design tools inside their own coding agent ( wadi_check , wadi_preview , wadi_reference , wadi_examples ); it predates the hackathon. During the hackathon we built the end-user side: a hosted online MCP server (a Cloudflare Container at mcp.wadi.house ) so a family's agent (Antigravity, a ChatGPT connector, Gemini) reaches the tools by URL with nothing installed, and the WebMCP layer , which registers the editing tools in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool ( get_wdl , set_wdl , check , list_homes , choose_home , capture_view , undo / redo ) so an in-browser agent drives the live model. A Durable-Object relay bridges the two, letting a remote agent co-edit the very model a user is watching. Because the 3D canvas is invisible to an agent, capture_view renders the current model to an image so the agent can see what it changed. Wadi deploys as a static site (Cloudflare Pages), a Tauri desktop app, and the hosted MCP server; the WebMCP tools register in any WebMCP-capable browser, so ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome both drive the live model. Challenges we ran into One shared model, not two apps. Getting agent and human edits to converge on a single live, parametric model (and one undo history) drove the whole tool design. Keeping a non-architect's edits buildable. Shared walls, doors on connections, the grid, formula-driven re-flow, and a growing set of structural rules all had to be surfaced to the agent, not hidden behind the UI, so that a spoken request from someone with no design training still produces a real, code-respecting layout. The invisible canvas. An agent cannot see WebGL, so we added a capture tool that hands back a rendered view. Getting the tools discovered. WebMCP tools have to be registered synchronously at page load , in the top-level document, or an agent's tool detector, which checks once as the page loads, finds nothing and shows no tools, even though the app registered them a moment later. A rendering gotcha. A WebGL canvas composites above normal HTML regardless of z-index, so an overlay menu kept hiding behind the 3D scene until we moved it into the browser top layer with the Popover API. Ambiguous coordinates and units. Center vs outer wall conventions and the units-per-foot scale had to be pinned down so the agent's numbers land where the contractor expects. Accomplishments that we're proud of Agent and human on one model. Every editing tool goes through the same store mutations as the UI, so the agent's edits and the person's edits are the same kind of change, with shared validation, live re-rendering, and one undo history. title: Cove Fertility — Find Surrogates, Egg Donors & Sperm Donors
pitch: A fertility platform where AI can read a user's journey, find authorized matches, and prepare introductions—while humans retain every consequential decision.
about_excerpt: A fertility platform where AI can read a user's journey, find authorized matches, and prepare introductions—while humans retain every consequential decision. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Home Page Surrogate Profiles Dashboard for Intended Parents Intended Parent Forms Logo Guided Journey Inspiration Fertility and surrogacy journeys are emotionally important, operationally complex, and fragmented across portals, messages, files, calendars, and coordinators. People repeatedly ask: What happens next? Who can I trust? Which profiles fit my path? Cove is designed as a fertility journey operating system: one calm workspace for intended parents, surrogates, egg donors, sperm donors, and qualified human reviewers. For the WebMCP Challenge, we asked a more ambitious question: what if an AI agent could work with Cove's live interface through page-defined tools, understand a signed-in user's current context, and help them move forward without taking away human control? What it does Cove exposes purpose-built WebMCP tools from the pages where the work happens. On the intended-parent dashboard, the agent can call cove_get_parent_journey to read the user's application status, selected family-building paths, candidate-access status, current stage, and recommended next action. A companion tool can bring the guided next-step timeline into view so the user and agent stay grounded in the same screen. In the authorized candidate directory, the agent can: call cove_find_candidate_profiles to filter and rank profiles by candidate type and state; call cove_open_candidate_profile to open a selected profile and return only the details available to that parent; and call cove_prepare_introduction to prepare an introduction note without submitting it. Every tool updates the same interface the person sees. The agent does not create a parallel experience: filters change, results appear, profiles open, and the introduction review dialog is prepared directly in Cove. The final introduction remains a human decision. The tool explicitly returns submitted: false , and the intended parent must review and choose whether to continue. How we built it Cove is a React and TypeScript application deployed on Cloudflare. Supabase provides authentication, PostgreSQL data, storage, and row-level access controls for role-scoped platform data. We created a small WebMCP registration layer around document.modelContext.registerTool . Each page registers only the tools that make sense in its current context and uses an AbortController to cleanly remove them when the React view unmounts. Inputs use explicit JSON schemas and application-level validation. Candidate searches constrain type, validate two-letter state codes, and cap result counts. Tool annotations distinguish read-only operations from operations that change the visible page. The tool output is intentionally narrow: it returns first names, fit explanations, availability, and access-appropriate summaries—not private contact information. Most importantly, WebMCP is connected to the product's real state and interaction model. The candidate search tool uses the same loaded profile set, filters, sorting, access rules, and UI components as a person using Cove manually. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering tools—it was choosing the correct boundary between assistance and authority. A fertility platform contains consequential decisions and sensitive information. A broadly capable agent would be the wrong design. We instead made every tool role-aware, schema-constrained, and scoped to the page. Search can organize authorized choices; it cannot reveal hidden fields. An agent can prepare an introduction; it cannot submit one. We also had to keep agent actions visible. A successful tool call should never leave the user wondering what changed, so Cove scrolls to the relevant section, updates filters and status copy, and opens the same review surfaces a person would use. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP tools are embedded in a functioning multi-role fertility platform rather than a standalone demo. Agent results and the human-facing interface remain synchronized. Authorization and data minimization are part of the tool design. The most consequential action in the demo ends at a clear review boundary. The experience reduces navigation and repetitive coordination while preserving informed human decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a site publishes small, domain-specific capabilities instead of asking an agent to infer intent from pixels and DOM structure. The tool schema becomes a product contract: it says what an agent may do, what it may return, and where a human must remain responsible. We also learned that good agentic UX is visible UX. Users should see the filters, profiles, explanations, and prepared actions—not just receive a hidden background response. What's next for Cove Next we plan to extend the same model to Journey Rooms, match-meeting scheduling, document and medical-record status, and contextual support. Routine questions and reversible actions can be automated; eligibility, matching, consent, and other high-stakes decisions will continue to belong to qualified people. The long-term goal is simple: help each user understand what is happening, what they need to do, and when a human is needed —without making them chase updates across disconnected systems. title: WebMCP Forge
pitch: Turn existing portfolios into agent-ready WebMCP sites with one script—scan, map, install, verify, and even use WebMCP itself to build WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn existing portfolios into agent-ready WebMCP sites with one script—scan, map, install, verify, and even use WebMCP itself to build WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Forge scans an existing portfolio, maps its content, lets owners choose agent capabilities, and generates one install snippet. Five-step flow: paste a portfolio URL, scan the site, choose agent capabilities, install one snippet, then verify the live runtime. WebMCP Forge itself exposes WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can scan a portfolio, change capabilities, and generate the integration. ChatGPT discovers WebMCP Forge's 8 Site Tools and uses the builder through WebMCP to update the portfolio URL live. One ChatGPT request reads the current permissions, changes multiple capabilities through WebMCP tools, then verifies the updated state. WebMCP Forge doesn't merely generate WebMCP. The Forge builder itself is an agent-operable WebMCP application. Inspiration WebMCP immediately stood out to me because it changes an important assumption about the web. Most websites are designed entirely for people. An AI agent that wants to use one usually has to interpret the page, find the right controls, and interact with the interface almost like a person would. WebMCP gives a website a much cleaner option: it can explicitly describe the useful things an agent is allowed to do. While experimenting with that idea, I realized there was still a practical problem. Adding WebMCP to an existing website is straightforward for a developer who understands the site's code, but it is a much bigger ask for someone who built a portfolio in Framer, Wix, Webflow, or another site builder. A designer should not have to learn document.modelContext , JSON Schema, CSS selectors, or tool-calling conventions just to make a portfolio usable by an agent. That became the idea behind WebMCP Forge : Point it at an existing portfolio, let it understand the site, choose what agents should be able to do, install one snippet, and verify that the integration is actually live. I chose portfolios as the first use case because they are a good example of a website that contains useful structured information but is still primarily built for human browsing. Projects, experience, skills, education, contact information, and navigation all map naturally to useful agent capabilities. What it does WebMCP Forge provides a guided five-step workflow for turning an existing portfolio into a WebMCP-enabled site. 1. Point it at your portfolio The user enters the URL of an existing portfolio. WebMCP Forge fetches the site and analyzes its structure rather than asking the user to describe how the site was built. 2. Review what was found The scanner identifies useful portfolio content such as: projects skills work experience education navigation profile information contact information The interface shows a simple summary of what was detected so the owner can verify that the site was understood correctly. 3. Choose what agents can do The site owner decides which capabilities should be available to an agent. For example: learn about me browse my projects inspect a specific project search my projects show my skills read my experience read my education share my published contact information navigate my portfolio focus a particular project on the page The normal interface deliberately avoids exposing WebMCP implementation details. A portfolio owner chooses capabilities in plain language while WebMCP Forge handles the underlying tool definitions. 4. Install one snippet WebMCP Forge generates a small script tag that can be added to the website once. The runtime loads the site's published WebMCP configuration and registers the appropriate tools in supported browsers. The owner does not need to regenerate the integration every time a project or skill changes. The runtime reads the current live site rather than maintaining a separate copy of the portfolio content. 5. Verify the real installation I did not want the product to stop at "here is some generated code." WebMCP Forge can check the actual deployed website and report whether: the runtime is installed the configuration loaded correctly content mappings are still valid WebMCP is available in the current browser tools were registered projects, skills, experience, and education can still be found on the live site This gives the owner a concrete answer to a much more useful question: Is my website actually agent-ready? Why WebMCP fits this use case A portfolio already has two audiences. The first is a person who wants to look around the site normally. The second can now be an agent trying to answer a question such as: Which of this person's projects demonstrate backend development? Without WebMCP, the agent has to derive that information from the visual website or page structure. With WebMCP, the portfolio can expose a small set of intentional capabilities such as: list_projects get_project search_projects get_skills get_experience The portfolio remains the same website for a human visitor, while an agent gets a structured interface designed specifically for the task. Some tools can also affect what the human sees. For example, focus_project can bring a requested project into view instead of only returning text to the agent. That is the part of WebMCP I found most interesting: the agent and the person can work with the same live interface rather than having separate copies of the application. Use WebMCP to build WebMCP One feature I particularly wanted to include was making WebMCP Forge itself WebMCP-enabled . A compatible agent does not have to operate the builder by guessing where its buttons and switches are. The builder exposes its own tools for actions such as: setting a portfolio URL starting a scan reading the scan result reviewing available capabilities enabling or disabling a capability generating the installation checking verification status That means a user can work with an agent to configure WebMCP for another website. For example, the user could say: Scan my portfolio. Then: Do not expose my contact information. Then: Generate the integration. The corresponding WebMCP Forge interface changes as those tool calls occur. So WebMCP is both what the product generates and part of the interface used to generate it . How we built it WebMCP Forge is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. The backend performs a bounded scan of a public portfolio rather than crawling the entire web. The scanning pipeline has two stages. Deterministic site analysis The first stage uses normal parsing and extraction to inspect things such as: page metadata headings navigation links repeated DOM structures semantic HTML internal routes contact links likely project collections platform fingerprints This gives the application a compact representation of the site before any model is involved. Semantic interpretation Some portfolio layouts are obvious to a person but difficult to identify from markup alone. For those cases, Google Gemini is used to interpret the extracted structure and map it onto WebMCP Forge's known portfolio concepts. The model does not generate arbitrary JavaScript for the user's website. Instead, WebMCP Forge owns a fixed capability catalogue and validates the structured result before using it. The application also has model fallback and retry handling so a scan is not tied to one model being available. Runtime The script installed on a portfolio is framework-independent browser JavaScript. It can: load the site's published configuration inspect the current page understand the active route read current portfolio content register allowed tools through WebMCP expose diagnostics for verification Normal portfolio visitors do not trigger a Gemini request when an agent calls one of these WebMCP tools. The portfolio itself remains the source of truth. Challenges we ran into Portfolio websites are not standardized The largest practical challenge was that two websites can present the same information with completely different markup. One portfolio may have a clear /projects page and semantic <article> elements, while another may be a single dynamically rendered page with generated class names. I did not want the system to depend entirely on model-generated guesses, so the scanner combines deterministic extraction with semantic interpretation. Avoiding stale portfolio data An early architectural temptation was to scan the website, copy its projects into WebMCP Forge, and have the generated tools return that stored data. That would have made the demo easier, but it would also mean the WebMCP representation became outdated as soon as the owner changed the portfolio. Instead, the configuration stores information about how to find the content , while the runtime reads the live site. If the owner adds another project using the same structure, the WebMCP tools can see it without creating a new integration. Making installation verifiable Generating a script is not the

title: WebMCP Angular KIT tool
pitch: Enterprise Angular 22 toolkit for W3C WebMCP — uniting browser AI agents with 3D WebGL CAD, reactive BI analytics, and a dynamic SubAgents SDK.
about_excerpt: Enterprise Angular 22 toolkit for W3C WebMCP — uniting browser AI agents with 3D WebGL CAD, reactive BI analytics, and a dynamic SubAgents SDK. Like Comment Story Updates Most AI browser agents today are essentially screen-scrapers: they take screenshots, guess button coordinates, or try to parse messy DOM trees. That approach is slow, breaks the moment a CSS class changes, and fails completely when interacting with a canvas element or stateful WebGL scenes. When the W3C published the WebMCP draft, we saw a much cleaner path: expose typed, client-side functions directly from the browser runtime to the model. Instead of treating the web app like a static document an external bot has to inspect from the outside, the user and the agent can mutate the exact same application state in real time, whether that means extruding a 3D CAD mesh at 60 FPS or running financial risk analytics without backend roundtrips. The showcase is built with Angular 22, Three.js, and Bun, organized into four primary layers: First, Angular 22 signals and directives. Rather than wrapping tools in heavy abstractions, we built directives like webmcpTool that bind directly to reactive signals. When a user adjusts an input or the agent calls a tool, state updates synchronously with zero change-detection penalty. Second, the Three.js spatial engine and push-pull extrusion. We built a SceneActionBus to decouple asynchronous tool promises from the Three.js render loop. The agent can draw planar 2D profiles and extrude solid 3D geometry along the face normal vector, while camera movements interpolate across spherical coordinates for smooth transitions. The agent can also call a screenshot tool to pull the raw WebGL drawing buffer and visually verify its own modifications. Third, in-browser memory with IndexedDB and BM25. Rather than standing up an external vector database, we built an episodic memory store on IndexedDB paired with a pure TypeScript BM25 search implementation. Relevance scoring runs standard Robertson-Spärck Jones IDF directly on the client using tuned parameters (k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75), allowing the agent to retrieve user preferences and historical actions in sub-millisecond lookups completely offline. Fourth, a dynamic SubAgents SDK and multi-domain business intelligence. Injecting dozens of tool schemas into every prompt quickly blew through token budgets. We created an SDK that dynamically filters tools per domain, allowing the main agent to delegate tasks to specialized workers (such as analytics or 3D specialists). These workers run isolated multi-turn loops, compute normalized anomaly risk scores across metrics, and return concise execution receipts signed with a client-side SHA-256 hash. We tackled several technical hurdles along the way. Calling Three.js mutations straight out of asynchronous HTTP promises caused frame drops, so we created a queue in SceneActionBus that holds incoming tool commands and executes them strictly on animation frame ticks. Exposing every tool simultaneously caused models to hallucinate arguments or hit context caps; scoping tools dynamically by route and delegating to subagents cut token usage by roughly 85%. Additionally, server-side rendering under Node and Bun crashed whenever code referenced browser globals like window, navigator, or IndexedDB. We resolved this by building an in-memory emulator (WebMcpEmulator) that activates during SSR and in browsers lacking native WebMCP support, eliminating hydration mismatches. Through this process, we achieved 511 unit and integration tests passing on Bun in under 1.5 seconds. The project demonstrated that agent autonomy does not require a heavy backend or remote vector database; native browser primitives like IndexedDB, WebGL, and Signals are remarkably capable when wired directly to function calling. Furthermore, Angular's dependency injection model fits WebMCP tool registration naturally by treating tools as standard injectable providers. Moving forward, our next steps include publishing the webmcp-angular library as an open-source npm package, adding WebXR support to let agents interact with 3D scenes in headsets like Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest, and compiling OpenCASCADE geometry routines to WebAssembly for true solid modeling directly in the browser.
