 ChatGPT calls find_ai_tools via WebMCP. The result lands in the chat and on the page at the same time. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 cleverkitools.com started with a simple question: how far can a non-developer (me) get building a real product with ChatGPT alone? The answer became a curated catalog of 100 vetted AI tools for small and medium-sized businesses, with a KMU score, checked prices and honest caveats for every tool. When WebMCP (and the challenge) appeared, the next question was obvious. What if agents could use that catalog the same way people do? 

 What it does 

 Clever AI Tool Scout is a recommendation interface on top of the catalog. A person / human describes a business task, optionally adds a monthly budget in EUR, and gets up to three fitting tools with a reason, a caution and a link to the full review. An AI agent can do exactly the same through one WebMCP tool, find_ai_tools , with the same two inputs. People and agents share one recommendation engine. 

 Live: cleverkitools.com/webmcp-challenge 

 Why WebMCP is suited for this use case 

 A tool catalog is a structured question with a structured answer. Without WebMCP an agent has to scrape a hundred German profile pages, guess prices and infer categories. With WebMCP the site says exactly what it can do: give me a task and a budget, I return ranked tools, prices in EUR, cautions and profile URLs. The agent gets a deterministic contract instead of a DOM to navigate, and the site owner keeps control over how recommendations are made.
In addition, I just wanted to try WebMCP 🙂 

 How it improves the user experience (or AGENT exprience?). 

 
 For people: the same form, same results, nothing changes. No direct improvement. 
 For agents: one straight call instead of dozens of page loads. No open API neccessary. No running MCP server neccessary. 
 

 The Agent Flight Recorder shows every human and agent request of the session as a four-step trace (request received, intent matched, budget evaluated, result returned). Query text stays in the browser. I used it for debugging. 

 What people and agents can accomplish together that was not possible before 

 An agent can now answer "which AI tool should my small business use for X within Y euros" from a curated, price-checked source instead of from training data. It can hand the person a page that already shows the shortlist. The person can refine the task in the form, and the agent can pick that up again. 

 On the other hand, to be honest, well, it's more a tech demo atm and not a super use case, I must admit. I'm sure better use cases will follow. 

 How we built it (we = ChatGPT Codex and me) 

 
 One tool, find_ai_tools , registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Input schema: task (string, required) and max_monthly_budget (number, EUR, optional). 
 The execute handler runs the same recommend() engine as the HTML form, renders the cards into the page and returns structured JSON. 
 The handler respects the AbortSignal passed by the browser. 
 Search core: 13 intents with German and English terms, category weights, tool boosts and a relevance floor. Prices are normalized to EUR from a known regular entry price (checked 21 Aug 2026). 
 Catalog: 100 current tools, 15 new entries, 19 archived tools with replacements, loaded as static data. Everything runs in the browser, no server round-trip. 
 Progressive by design: without document.modelContext the page is a normal form, and the status panel says so. 
 Built with ChatGPT and Codex, deployed on cleverkitools.com. 
 

 What the agent receives: 
 {
 "request": { "task": "…", "max_monthly_budget": 30 },
 "visible_results_updated": true,
 "selection_status": "matched | fallback | archive_redirect | over_budget",
 "matched_intents": ["Video, audio & music"],
 "minimum_monthly_budget_eur": 12.9,
 "recommendations": [
 {
 "name": "OpusClip",
 "profile_url": "https://cleverkitools.com/ki-tools/opusclip/",
 "category": "Social Media & Ads",
 "why_fitting": "…",
 "caution": "…",
 "status": "current",
 "kmu_score": 86,
 "price": "Freemium · ab 15 USD/Monat (ca. 13,13 EUR/Monat)"
 }
 ],
 "archive_match": { "name": "Copy.ai", "status": "archived", "replacement": { "name": "Genspark" } }
}
 
 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is only available in ChatGPT's in-app browser and in Chrome with the flag enabled, so the page had to work as a normal form everywhere else and report its WebMCP state without pretending. The second challenge was keeping one engine for both audiences: the agent needs structured fields, the person needs readable cards, and both had to come from the same call. 

 What's next 

 Not 100% sure yet. Looking for your and other user's feedback.

title: BuildAI Command
pitch: BuildAI Command is a governed AI-agent dashboard where a human and ChatGPT can both run, monitor, & approve the same agent actions through the same page.
about_excerpt:
BuildAI Command is a governed AI-agent dashboard where a human and ChatGPT can both run, monitor, & approve the same agent actions through the same page. 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 BuildAI is our platform for running AI agents under real governance not just chat wrapped around a model, but agents with memory, tools, policy, and human approval built in. When we saw the WebMCP Challenge, the fit was obvious: our whole product thesis is that AI shouldn't act alone on anything risky. WebMCP let us test that thesis in the browser itself could ChatGPT operate our platform the same way a human does, approvals and all, without a custom integration? 

 What it does 

 BuildAI Command is a governed agent dashboard with three panels: 

 
 Agents — see your AI workers and run them on a task 
 Activity — watch runs progress in real time 
 Approvals — approve or reject sensitive actions before they execute (e.g. sending an email) 
 

 The same actions are exposed as WebMCP tools on the page, so an AI agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser can list agents, start a run, check status, and approve a step using the exact same governed path a human would. Say "run the support agent and approve the email if it looks right," and the agent and the platform work together on one screen. 

 How we built it 

 We kept scope deliberately narrow: one screen, one demo flow, our existing BuildAI backend doing the real work. The frontend is a thin client that calls our existing agents/runs/approvals API, with document.modelContext.registerTool() wiring each panel action run, status check, approve/reject into a WebMCP tool an agent can call directly. No new backend, no new auth model: we exposed what already existed, deliberately, as agent-callable tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge wasn't the API integration. it was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do without asking. We didn't want WebMCP to become a backdoor around our own approval gate, so every sensitive action still routes through the same approvals queue whether a human or an agent triggered it. Getting that consistent one governance path, two callers took more design thought than the tool registration itself. Testing reliably in ChatGPT's in-app browser vs. Chrome's WebMCP flag also meant double-checking tool behavior in both environments before we trusted the demo. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is at its best when it exposes real actions with real consequences, not just read-only lookups. Building governance into the tool layer itself rather than trusting the agent to behave is what made this feel like a genuine agent-native product decision rather than a tech demo.

title: Web2MCP
pitch: Web2MCP watches the requests a site makes as you browse, learns their shape, and injects them into the page as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call.
about_excerpt: Web2MCP watches the requests a site makes as you browse, learns their shape, and injects them into the page as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call. Like Comment Story Updates chrome extension agent use case Inspiration WebMCP is a beautiful idea — websites exposing their functionality to AI agents as callable tools. But it has a chicken-and-egg problem: it only works if the website adds it. Almost no site has, and most never will. Meanwhile, every one of those sites is already making perfectly good API calls in your browser, right now, as you use it. So we asked: what if the agent didn't need the site's cooperation at all? What if you could just browse a site normally, and have its APIs turn into agent-callable tools automatically — learned from the traffic the site already produces? What it does Web2MCP is a browser extension that records the API calls a website makes while you browse and injects them as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call. Records every JSON API a page calls — its own backend and third-party APIs — while filtering out static assets and trackers. Aggregates requests into endpoint templates (/users/123 → /users/{id}), inferring JSON Schemas and required fields from what it observes. Injects each endpoint as a WebMCP tool via document.modelContext. Calls replay from the page's own context, so cookies and captured auth headers just work. Pools by website, so subdomains and pages share one tool set; shows a live tool count on the toolbar badge; lists tools in a popup (including the site's own first-party WebMCP tools); and lets you disable injection per site. No config, no schemas to write, no per-endpoint wiring. How we built it WXT + TypeScript + React for a Manifest V3 extension. A MAIN-world content script patches window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest to observe traffic and to register/replay tools; an ISOLATED-world bridge relays messages to a background service worker that does all aggregation, schema inference, and local storage. Injection uses the browser's native WebMCP registerTool API; replay uses the saved native fetch so tool calls never re-trigger recording. The "brain" — URL templating, schema inference, tool naming, aggregation, filtering — is pure, dependency-free modules covered by vitest (60+ tests). A landing page and privacy policy shipped on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges we ran into We tested on real sites, and the real world fought back — which turned out to be the most valuable part. Anti-automation is everywhere. We hit three distinct walls: Linear injects auth in a service worker below the page's fetch (invisible to us → 401); X and GitHub use one-time nonces (x-client-transaction-id, x-fetch-nonce) that expire after a single use (→ 422); Xiaohongshu signs the request body client-side (x-s), so changing any argument breaks the signature (→ 406). We had to map — and honestly document — exactly where record-and-replay can and can't work. Agents under-supply parameters. An LLM calling a search tool would omit sortBy or invent a sessionId, getting empty results. The fix: surface the real recorded request body as an example and merge the agent's fields over it, filling in what it left out. The little things: a signal destructuring crash that broke every tool call, extension-context invalidation after reloads, JSON responses truncated mid-object, and getting WebMCP itself enabled in a custom Chromium browser (via a Finch/variations study). Accomplishments that we're proud of It's genuinely zero-config. Browse a site and its tools appear — with a badge counting them and a popup listing them. It works end-to-end on real sites. We watched an agent successfully call a live government job-search API and read GitHub data through tools Web2MCP recorded — cross-domain, authenticated, no keys. It's honest. We built the "Works great / Can't replay" boundary into the product and the site instead of overselling. It's smart about the data it already has — auto-filling session tokens and merging partial request bodies from real recordings so agents stop failing on missing fields. Users stay in control — per-site disable, one-click clear, everything stored locally and nothing leaves the device. What we learned The real boundary of record-and-replay: it works whenever the request's content isn't itself part of authentication — cookie-authed apps, static tokens, read endpoints, your own products. It can't beat mechanisms designed to stop exactly this (SW-injected auth, one-time tokens, body signatures). Knowing that boundary precisely is more useful than pretending it doesn't exist. Agents need examples, not just schemas. A JSON Schema tells a model the shape; a real recorded request tells it what actually works. Honesty is a feature. Being upfront about limits made the product more trustworthy, not less. What's next for Web2MCP Chrome Web Store release and broader reach as WebMCP ships in stable browsers. Smarter body handling — deep merge, and richer per-parameter examples. First-party passthrough — surface and manage a site's own WebMCP tools alongside recorded ones. An adapter path for hardened sites — optionally invoke the site's own signing/request code (or fall back to driving the real UI) for signature- and nonce-protected APIs. Sharing & sync — export a site's recorded tool set so a team can reuse it. title: PowerForge.Web - Verified WebMCP for Static Sites
pitch: Turn generated documentation sites into verified, agent-native applications without adding an application server.
about_excerpt: Turn generated documentation sites into verified, agent-native applications without adding an application server. Like Comment Story Updates OfficeIMO exposes the read-only search_site Website Tool. PowerForge.Web generates and verifies the complete WebMCP contract. Codex invokes search_site and leaves matching results visible. One opt-in engine capability serves seven independent documentation sites. Inspiration Documentation search is usually designed for people clicking through a page. An agent must either imitate that interface, scrape the rendered HTML, or bypass the site's intended search experience entirely. Those paths are harder to validate and leave the person with little visibility into what the agent actually did. WebMCP provides a cleaner contract: the page can expose a small, typed capability that works inside the current document. We wanted that capability to be reusable across generated static sites rather than implemented as custom JavaScript for one showcase page. What it does On a participating site's search route, PowerForge.Web registers a read-only search_site Website Tool. The tool accepts a bounded query and result limit, searches the site's generated JSON index, and returns structured results containing titles, descriptions, collections, tags, languages, and URLs. The same invocation also updates the visible search page. The agent receives structured data while the person sees the corresponding query and result cards, can inspect the choices, refine the search, and open a result normally. Browsers without WebMCP continue to use the ordinary search page. The live judging target is OfficeIMO: Live application: https://officeimo.com/search/ Demo video: https://youtu.be/xIPtNwYBO58 Public source: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule Why WebMCP is a strong fit Search is a good first agent journey because it benefits from structure without requiring broad authority. WebMCP removes UI guessing, gives the agent an explicit schema, and keeps the action bound to the page the person is already viewing. The tool is read-only, the query is bounded, and the result remains visible. The improvement is not only faster retrieval. The person and agent now share one observable state: the agent can perform the structured search, and the person can immediately review the same results in the website's normal interface. How we built it PowerForge.Web is a .NET static-site engine. A site opts in through the engine's typed agent-readiness configuration and declares a route-scoped WebMCP tool. During generation, the engine: Builds the site's normal search route and JSON search index. Emits a same-origin WebMCP runtime. Registers search_site through the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API. Connects the tool to the visible search UI through a reusable adapter. Verifies the rendered route, executable script ordering, same-origin index and runtime, asset integrity, schema, and declared tool metadata. Advertises WebMCP readiness only when the complete generated artifact passes those checks. The runtime supports cancellation, bounded input, cached index loading, explicit cache invalidation, and theme-owned ranking through an adapter. The current shared implementation intentionally supports a read-only site-search journey; future write or product-specific actions will require separate authority and product contracts. What people and agents can do together Before this addition, a person could search the documentation, but an agent had no explicit contract for using that experience. It had to infer controls or search elsewhere. Now the person can open the OfficeIMO search page and ask Codex to find Word-to-PDF resources using the page's Website Tool. Codex invokes search_site , receives three structured matches, and leaves the OfficeIMO results visible. The person can verify the query, inspect the result cards, and continue browsing from the same page. Challenges we ran into Generated static sites create a different reliability problem from server-backed tools: configuration may look correct while the deployed page is missing its route, index, script, or fingerprinted asset. We therefore treated rendered output as the contract and added both local and remote readiness checks. We also needed to keep structured agent results synchronized with the theme's human-facing search behavior. PowerForge.Web provides a fallback search surface and an adapter that lets richer themes own ranking and rendering without replacing the shared WebMCP runtime. Accomplishments One reusable implementation in the PowerForge.Web engine rather than seven unrelated site scripts. A live, read-only Website Tool recognized and invoked by the ChatGPT/Codex integrated browser. Fail-closed verification of the actual generated and deployed artifact. Visible synchronization between the structured tool call and human search page. Opt-in deployment across seven independent Evotec documentation sites: evotec.xyz, evotec.pl, OfficeIMO, HtmlForgeX, IntelligenceX, CodeGlyphX, and TestimoX. Normal search behavior remains available in browsers without WebMCP. Work completed during the challenge PowerForge.Web existed before the challenge. The WebMCP capability was added as a meaningful extension during the challenge period on September 2-3, 2026. PR #860, Add verified WebMCP site search support: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/pull/860 PR #865, Define safe WebMCP portfolio rollout: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/pull/865 Registration runtime: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/blob/main/PowerForge.Web/Assets/WebMcp/site-search.v1.js Implementation and operating documentation: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/blob/main/Docs/PowerForge.Web.AgentReadiness.md The dated pull requests and commit histories distinguish this WebMCP work from the pre-existing engine and websites. What we learned Adding registerTool is the small part. A reusable implementation also needs truthful discovery, bounded inputs, same-origin resources, script-order guarantees, browser fallback behavior, visible state synchronization, and validation of the final deployed files. Treating those pieces as one contract made the feature safe enough to enable across multiple sites. What's next The next phase is to add richer read-only journeys where a site has a real domain-specific task, such as navigating API surfaces or comparing documented capabilities. Write tools will remain opt-in and will be designed per product rather than enabled across the portfolio by default. Testing instructions Open https://officeimo.com/search/ in ChatGPT's integrated browser. Open the address-bar Site tools menu and confirm that search_site is available as one read tool with no write tools. Attach Browser to a Codex request. Ask: "Use the current OfficeIMO page's search_site Website Tool to find three resources about converting Word documents to PDF. Use only the Website Tool exposed by the page and leave the matching results visible." Confirm that Codex returns structured links and the OfficeIMO search page displays the corresponding query and result cards. No account or credentials are required. Built with WebMCP imperative API PowerForge.Web .NET and C# JavaScript Static HTML and JSON search indexes ChatGPT/Codex integrated browser Repository and license The implementation is available in the public EvotecIT/PSPublishModule repository under the MIT license: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule Built With c# javascript openai static Try it out officeimo.com github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Przemysław Kłys Like Share this project: Updates Przemysław Kłys started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:40 PM EDT

 Inspiration 

 Online shopping involves many steps: searching for products, applying filters, checking specifications, comparing options, finding offers, adding items to a cart, and finally deciding whether to purchase. 

 We asked ourselves: 

 
 * What if an AI agent could actually work with a shopping website instead of simply telling the user what to buy? And can the work become easier for the users as, complex [part will be handled by the AI agent, and the approval part will be under the Humans. * 
 

 Traditional websites are primarily designed for human interaction. An AI agent may be able to read information or navigate the interface, but it does not have a reliable, structured way to use the website's capabilities. 

 This inspired us to build AgentCart , a WebMCP-powered marketplace where humans and AI agents can shop together. 

 Our goal was to explore what happens when a website is designed not only for humans, but also as an active tool interface for AI agents. 

 

 What it does 

 AgentCart allows a user to give an AI agent a natural-language shopping goal. 

 For example: 

 
 "Find me the best laptop for programming under ₹70,000. Prioritize performance and battery life." 
 

 The agent can then: 

 
 Search available products 
 Filter them according to the user's requirements 
 Inspect product specifications 
 Compare the strongest candidates 
 Find the best available offer 
 Add the selected product to the cart 
 Calculate the final price 
 Request human approval before completing the purchase 
 

 AgentCart currently exposes eight WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_products 
 filter_products 
 get_product_details 
 compare_products 
 find_best_offer 
 add_to_cart 
 calculate_cart_total 
 request_purchase_approval 
 

 The WebMCP integration is implemented using: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool() 

 A key part of AgentCart is human-in-the-loop control . The agent can research, compare, optimize, and prepare a purchase, but it cannot complete the simulated purchase without explicit human approval. 

 No real payment or transaction takes place. 

 

 How we built it 

 AgentCart was built using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand . 

 We created a structured electronics product catalog containing product information such as price, brand, category, rating, stock, specifications, features, and offers. 

 The WebMCP integration is implemented in the frontend using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a defined name, description, input schema, and execution function. 

 We designed the tools around the actual shopping workflow rather than exposing only a single generic AI action. 

 The application also includes an Agent Activity panel that makes the agent's workflow visible to the user, for example: 

 search_products → filter_products → compare_products → find_best_offer → add_to_cart → request_purchase_approval 

 We used Git and GitHub for source control and deployed the application using Vercel . 

 The final purchase flow is simulated so that the complete human + agent interaction can be demonstrated safely. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was making WebMCP tool registration reliable. 

 Because the application can initialize more than once, we needed to prevent duplicate tool registrations. We implemented registration safeguards and checks for already-registered tools. 

 Another challenge was making the agent workflow respond differently to different natural-language requests. We did not want every prompt to produce the same demonstration. 

 We therefore implemented dynamic handling for: 

 
 Product categories 
 Budget limits 
 Ratings 
 Battery requirements 
 Cheapest-product requests 
 Comparison requests 
 Offers 
 Purchase and approval workflows 
 

 We also had to carefully separate agent autonomy from human control . The agent can perform research and prepare a cart, but the final consequential action requires explicit human approval. 

 Finally, we focused on making the WebMCP functionality understandable through the user interface instead of hiding the interaction behind the scenes. The Agent Activity panel helps users see what the agent is doing. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that AgentCart goes beyond simply demonstrating that WebMCP tools can be registered. 

 We built a complete shopping workflow around multiple meaningful WebMCP tools, connecting product discovery, filtering, comparison, offer optimization, cart preparation, and human approval. 

 We are especially proud of the human + agent collaboration model . The agent handles the repetitive research and optimization work while the human remains responsible for the final purchase decision. 

 We also built the project as a working, deployed web application rather than only a technical proof of concept. 

 Most importantly, we created an experience where the WebMCP implementation directly changes what the website can do with an AI agent. 

 

 What we learned 

 Building AgentCart taught us that making a website agent-ready is very different from simply adding an AI chatbot. 

 We learned how WebMCP can allow websites to expose structured capabilities that AI agents can use directly. 

 We also learned that tool design matters. Clear tool names, descriptions, input schemas, and appropriate read-only or state-changing behavior are important for reliable agent interaction. 

 Another important lesson was the importance of human-in-the-loop design . Giving an agent the ability to research and prepare actions does not mean it should automatically perform every consequential action and the important action like the approval and payment processing should be taken by Human only. 

 We also learned how frontend state management, WebMCP tool execution, dynamic workflows, and user-facing activity visualization can be combined into one agent-ready web experience. 

 

 What's next for AgentCart 

 AgentCart currently focuses on demonstrating the core WebMCP-powered shopping experience with electronics. 

 The next step would be expanding the marketplace with more product categories and richer real-world data. 

 We would also like to explore more advanced agent capabilities such as personalized preferences, multi-item shopping goals, budget optimization, shipping comparisons, and more sophisticated approval controls. 

 Beyond shopping, the same WebMCP interaction pattern could be applied to other multi-step web experiences such as travel planning, restaurant reservations, service marketplaces, and productivity applications. 

 Our broader vision is a web where websites are not only pages that humans read and click, but active environments that AI agents can work with while humans remain in control. 

 

 Final Thought 

 Before WebMCP, an AI agent could tell you what to buy. 

 With WebMCP, the web can actually work with the agent. 

 AgentCart is our exploration of what that future could look like.

title: WebMCP Demo — a live map for thinking with your own agent
pitch: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan.
about_excerpt: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan. Like Comment Story Updates The live map: your own ChatGPT asks questions, clears "don't know" marks, and turns branches into checkable tasks — via 6 WebMCP tools. What it does Most WebMCP demos let an agent operate a site's transactional surface — fill a form, add to cart. This project inverts that: the page is a blank thinking canvas, and the tools it publishes are generative . You put down one thing you want to figure out ("I want to buy my first home"), and your own ChatGPT — with your context and memory — thinks with you on the map: It starts by asking questions as nodes , not by dumping a plan. You answer by growing branches yourself ; every edit you make on the canvas is delivered to the agent on its next tool call. Mark anything with "Don't know" and your confusion literally becomes the agenda — the agent clears those marks first, with concrete first steps. Steps become checkable task nodes , a Plan view folds the map into goal / premises / next tasks, and checking a task off in either place updates both. The page runs no AI of its own . It publishes six WebMCP tools; the visitor brings the intelligence. Thoughtful use of WebMCP The interesting problems turned out to be protocol-level, and we solved them in ways any WebMCP app can reuse: Read-before-write, enforced server-side. read_map returns a state token; every write requires it. A stale or missing token gets a 409 whose error text steers the agent back to read_map . The guard doubles as optimistic locking between the human and the agent. Human actions as first-class input. Everything the human does on the canvas (add, edit, move, delete, mark, check) is queued and delivered inside the next tool result — with a consuming read reserved for the agent and a non-consuming variant ( ?deliver=0 ) for the page's own refreshes, so the UI can never starve the agent of events. Granularity enforced by schema, not prose. add_nodes accepts at most 3 nodes per call (schema + server both), because a map that fills up in one shot stops feeling like a conversation. A capability split that matches the relationship. Agents can add, annotate, resolve, remove, and bulk-arrange — but the layout engine owns placement, and destructive actions on human-placed nodes are steered to require conversation first. Robust registration in the real world. Tools register before app mount, tolerate late injection of navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext (ChatGPT's browser and Chrome differ), and the footer shows live tool status for devtools-less in-app browsers. Why it matters "I know what I want, but not the way there" is a universal state — buying a home, relocating, incorporating, a first tax return. Chat alone answers and scrolls away; to-do apps assume you already know the steps. A shared, persistent map that your own agent can touch bridges the two: the conversation leaves a structure, and the structure becomes a plan you can execute and check off. Because the page hosts no model and pays no inference cost, this pattern is adoptable by any site: publish tools, let visitors bring their agents. How we built it Go + Postgres single-origin service (API, SSE live updates, static React/TypeScript SPA) on Render. The canvas is Miro-like: pan/zoom, drag, click-to-grow, right-click menu. A height-aware tidy-tree layout engine keeps the map clean after every structural change, verified against real DOM rects. WebMCP tool descriptions live in one file — they were the main behavior-tuning surface, iterated against the real ChatGPT desktop browser. What's next Multiple maps as a shelf, session-to-session continuity ("continue from where the fog cleared last week"), and the same canvas working with other WebMCP-capable agents out of the box. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Taste Gate
pitch: An explainable WebMCP preview gate where agents plan queues and people choose what to reveal.
about_excerpt: An explainable WebMCP preview gate where agents plan queues and people choose what to reveal. Like Comment Story Updates Four narrow WebMCP tools expose previews and proposals — never full post content. The agent proposes an order; the person independently selects and reveals stories. Judge's 45-second path Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask for a preview-only two-card queue. Inspect the four discovered Site tools and the visible proposed queue. Select cards yourself and press Reveal my selected stories . The agent can propose and explain; only the person can choose a reveal. Inspiration Project .taste already proves that a social card can begin as a compact, deterministic 16-byte preview packet. Taste Gate asks a different question: when an agent and a person share the same live page, can the agent help plan attention without silently deciding what the person must open? What it does Taste Gate exposes a preview-only view of a live feed through WebMCP. The agent can inspect media shape, text geometry, engagement heat, visual seed, and existing interaction flags; it can then explain and write a proposed queue. The user sees that proposal in the same page but must select cards and press Reveal my selected stories themselves. The gate filters muted or blocked cards before they reach the agent-facing preview list. It does not infer author identity, topic, timestamp, or full text from a packet. How I built it I reused the existing zero-dependency TypeScript .taste decoder and built a small static JavaScript app around it. The top-level page conditionally registers four WebMCP site tools: get_gate_state list_previews explain_preview set_proposed_queue The normal UI remains fully usable without WebMCP. Full sample content is fetched only when the user uses the ordinary Reveal action. The app labels this honestly as a coordination contract for the demo, not server-enforced privacy. The demo video voiceover is generated with macOS text-to-speech (Samantha). Challenges I ran into The hard part was defining a useful agent boundary without inventing meaning that the 16-byte protocol does not contain. A packet gives layout, media, coarse heat, and social-state signals; it does not justify a claim about a post's topic, author, or relevance. The tools therefore return field-level reasons and explicit non-inferences instead of a hidden recommendation score. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A shared-page agent workflow that stays inspectable by the person using it. Four narrow tools, including a state-changing proposal tool that cannot reveal content or alter the human selection. Tests that reject gated, unknown, and repeated cards and verify that the agent-facing list contains no author, topic, timestamp, or full text. A normal UI fallback and a live ChatGPT desktop-browser check that discovers all four tools. What I learned WebMCP becomes most compelling when it exposes application state that a person can see and review immediately. Narrow, verifiable operations are more useful than a broad agent action that obscures how a decision was made. What's next for Taste Gate Replace the demo content source with an application-controlled hydration endpoint, retain the same packet-only agent contract, and evaluate whether users find proposed queues more understandable than automatic ranking. title: MapsMCP
pitch: Maps that agents can understand
about_excerpt:
Maps that agents can understand
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 MapsMCP, maps that agents can understand, not just click 

 The problem 

 Maps are made for people. We look at the screen, drag it about, zoom in, spot a place, and change direction without really thinking about it. 

 AI agents have a rougher time. Playwright, Selenium, and Appium can click, drag, and scroll, but a map is not a normal webpage. It is a moving visual surface made from tiles, canvas layers, marker clusters, labels, animations, and changing camera positions. 

 The main issue, well, the awkward bit, is that a gesture has no stable meaning. Dragging 280 pixels may move one street at one zoom level and half a city at another. Screen size changes the result. Slow-loading tiles can change it again. An agent may complete the gesture and still have no reliable answer to “Where is the map now?” or “Which places can the person actually see?” 

 That is a poor foundation for ride hailing, food delivery, travel, field work, or emergency response. 

 What I built 

 MapsMCP is a WebMCP-powered interactive map prototype. 

 It keeps a normal human map experience, built with Leaflet and real OpenStreetMap tiles. People can pan, zoom, search places, inspect routes, and select destinations in the usual way. 

 A compatible browser agent gets structured WebMCP tools for the same map. It can inspect the current viewport, move the camera by metres, set an exact location and zoom level, find nearby places, measure distance, plan routes, and add visible shared pins. 

 The map is central London for the demo. The core idea works in any city. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 WebMCP lets a website register structured browser-native tools for an AI agent. Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution function. 

 Maps are especially well suited to this because the map engine already knows the important information. It knows the camera centre, zoom, visible bounds, selected place, distances, pins, and routes. That semantic state is usually hidden behind the visual interface. 

 MapsMCP exposes the useful parts safely and clearly. 

 Instead of an agent attempting to drag right and hoping for the best, it can call pan_map with a compass direction and a distance in metres. Instead of guessing what is visible after a gesture, it can call get_map_viewport and receive the geographic bounds, zoom level, and visible structured places. 

 WebMCP turns a map from a picture an agent pokes at into a workspace it can understand. 

 Better experience for people and agents 

 For a person, MapsMCP still behaves like a map. There is no strange agent-only screen. They can explore normally, see every map movement, inspect the result, and alter the plan. 

 For an agent, the interaction becomes deterministic. It gets stable place IDs and geographic results, rather than an uncertain screenshot after a drag. 

 Together, people and agents can work from the same state. A person might pan across a city to explore. ChatGPT can then inspect that exact viewport, find suitable places nearby, fit destinations into view, plan a route, and leave a shared meeting pin. 

 That handoff is difficult with visual browser automation alone. It can be done with a bespoke private integration, perhaps, but WebMCP makes the capability explicit, discoverable, and browser-mediated. 

 A realistic demo scenario 

 Imagine a traveller visiting London for the first time. 

 They are standing near Tower Bridge, a famous bridge over the River Thames. They want to walk to Borough Market, a nearby food market, and leave a meeting point for a friend. 

 They ask ChatGPT: 
 I am near Tower Bridge, a major London landmark. Find Borough Market, measure
the walking distance, fit both places into the map view, plan a walking route,
and drop a visible pin at Borough Market called “Meet here”.
 
 ChatGPT discovers the MapsMCP WebMCP tools. It finds the locations by stable IDs, measures the distance, moves the visible map, draws the walking route, and drops the shared pin. 

 The traveller sees it all happen. They can keep the plan, drag the map somewhere else, or change their mind. 

 Supported WebMCP tools 

 
 
 Tool 
 What it does 
 
 
 
 get_map_state 
 Reads the full shared map state, including viewport, selected place, route, staged ride, and pins. 
 
 
 get_map_viewport 
 Returns exact camera centre, zoom, geographic bounds, and visible places. 
 
 
 get_places_in_view 
 Lists structured places inside the current visible map area. 
 
 
 search_places 
 Searches the London place catalogue and returns stable place IDs. 
 
 
 get_place_details 
 Returns a place’s details and nearby suggestions without scraping a tooltip. 
 
 
 find_nearby_places 
 Finds places around a known location within a real-world radius. 
 
 
 measure_distance 
 Measures straight-line geographic distance between two places. 
 
 
 pan_map 
 Moves the visible map by compass direction and metres. 
 
 
 set_map_viewport 
 Sets exact latitude, longitude, and zoom. 
 
 
 zoom_map 
 Zooms by a known number of map levels. 
 
 
 fit_places 
 Frames one or more place IDs in the visible map. 
 
 
 focus_place 
 Flies to and selects a place in the human interface. 
 
 
 plan_route 
 Previews car, cycle, or walking routes. 
 
 
 clear_route 
 Removes the visible route preview and staged ride. 
 
 
 drop_pin 
 Places a named visible pin at exact coordinates. 
 
 
 list_pins 
 Lists shared pins currently on the map. 
 
 
 remove_pin 
 Removes a shared pin through its stable ID. 
 
 
 prepare_ride 
 Stages a simulated ride quote. A person still confirms it. 
 
 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 MapsMCP uses WebMCP’s imperative API: 
 await document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_places",
 description: "Search MapsMCP's structured London place catalogue.",
 inputSchema: {
 type: "object",
 properties: {
 query: { type: "string" },
 category: { type: "string" },
 },
 additionalProperties: false,
 },
 execute: async ({ query, category }) => {
 return searchPlaces(query, category);
 },
});
 
 The app registers 18 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with a compatibility fallback for older navigator.modelContext browser implementations. 

 Every tool calls the same React state actions used by the human interface. If an agent pans the map, the person sees the map pan. If it drops a pin, the pin appears on the real map. Registration is owned by an AbortController , so tools are removed cleanly when the page lifecycle ends. 

 What is real, and what is intentionally simulated 

 The map uses real OpenStreetMap tiles and visible attribution. 

 The London locations, route estimates, and ride quotes are deterministic demo data. MapsMCP does not claim live traffic, real restaurant availability, or actual ride booking. That keeps the demo dependable and makes the WebMCP interaction the focus. 

 Why it matters 

 MapsMCP is a small prototype for a much bigger idea. 

 A person should not have to explain a map to an agent through clicks and screenshots. An agent should not have to guess what a map gesture did. 

 WebMCP gives the map a shared language. The person stays in control. The agent stops guessing.

title: Career switch WebMCP
pitch: An interactive skill tree canvas integrated with native WebMCP API to help career switchers visualize learning roadmaps in real time.
about_excerpt:
An interactive skill tree canvas integrated with native WebMCP API to help career switchers visualize learning roadmaps in real time.

 Inspiration 
 The main inspiration making this project is nowadays job market situation. To be more precise, AI dramatically influenced how employers look to the job market. And many jobs became less demanding leading people to loose their jobs. And of course they are pushed to change their job, what they do and learn completely another sphere. But the process of changing the job, learning new things becoming more and more confusing as there are more technologies, instruments are being used day-by-day. That's why people try to use AI to get help in what to learn. But standard generative AI chat bots that provides the pathway, information in plain text format can not be as visual as people can need and thats why they keep being in confuse. But this project - my WebMCP solves this problem.
 
 What it does 
 The name itself is Career Switch MCP, however there is a big future behind it. Its only related to career only for now, in the future, I am planning to make it broader - giving AI agents hands to visualize what they are trying to explain - anything. So,... the application provides an interactive, visual skill tree canvas powered by the WebMCP protocol. Instead of reading plain text guides, users can interact with dynamic skill nodes. Browser-based AI agents directly invoke registered WebMCP tools (`build_skill_tree` and `highlight_skill_gaps`) to render customized roadmaps and instantly highlight missing skills or prerequisites in red.
 
 How we built it 

 Frontend Framework: * Next.js and React for rendering the core web application.
 Canvas Visualization: * React Flow to display interactive nodes, edges, and animated connections. 

 
 AI Integration:** Native WebMCP API ( document.modelContext ) to expose web-level tools directly to AI agents. 
 Styling & UI:** Tailwind CSS for modern design and clean devtools inspector layouts. 
 Deployment:** Hosted live on Vercel.
## Challenges we ran into
Implementing smooth integration with the newly introduced WebMCP browser protocols. 
 Dynamically mapping unstructured AI context calls into organized graph node structures in React Flow without causing state conflicts. 
 Synchronizing visual highlight states (skill gaps) seamlessly between WebMCP tool execution logs and the UI.
## Accomplishments that we're proud of
Successfully building a fully working prototype that bridges browser-native AI agents with visual UI canvases. 
 Creating an intuitive user experience that transforms confusing text into an actionable visual roadmap.

title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. video_title: Estro: The AI Photo Editor That Explains Itself
video_transcript_excerpt: Photo editors expect you to know exactly what saturation, tint, and exposure curves mean. Most people do not. Estro completely changes this dynamic. It is a powerful photo editor that runs entirely in your browser and actually explains itself. You open a project and tell the agent exactly what you want to achieve. Here we ask it to make a cold street photo look like a golden hour shot. We also tell it to explain every control it touches. You just talk to it like a normal person. The agent immediately gets to work. It moves the sliders for you. Every single edit drops a visible card right on the screen. The card names the specific control, shows the exact numerical value, and explains what the term means in plain English. If you do not like a specific adjustment, you just undo that single card without losing your other work. You always keep total control of the image. You do not always want the agent to do the heavy lifting. Sometimes you just want to learn where things are. Here we ask the agent to simply point out the contrast slider without making any changes to the photo. The agent immediately highlights the exact slider in the right panel. It gives you the clear location and the current value. You then drag it yourself. This is how you actually learn the interface and become a better editor. You can also ask it to perform an audit of the image. We ask if any of our recent changes ruined the fine details in the photo. The agent reads the live histogram and tells you exactly what is happening with your pixels. You click the split view to see the final result in comparison. 56 tools, one unified command system, and zero servers. Everything happens locally on your machine. Your photos always stay yours.

Turn every product search into a confident purchase and completed sale.

 Mobile-First AI Guidance A responsive bottom sheet keeps the AI assistant and product catalog accessible at the same time. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Product search is usually where an online purchase begins—and often where it breaks down. 

 A customer may know their vehicle but not the battery size, capacity, polarity, or specifications they need. A traditional search bar expects the right keywords and returns a list of products. If the customer still has questions, they must switch to chat or call support and explain everything again. 

 Small and medium-sized businesses face the same problem across many industries, but building intelligent search, conversational guidance, and human support as separate systems is expensive. 

 That inspired Search-to-Sale : a platform concept that turns product discovery into a guided sales journey. BateríasPower is our working automotive-battery implementation. 

 What it does 

 The customer starts by describing a vehicle in plain language, for example: 

 
 Toyota Corolla 2018 motor 1.8 
 

 Gemini understands the request, while native WebMCP functions perform structured actions inside the browser. The customer can see the catalog update as the agent: 

 
 Searches for compatible batteries. 
 Explains and compares available options. 
 Selects a product. 
 Prepares an informational quote cart. 
 Keeps the conversation and storefront synchronized. 
 

 When the customer wants human assistance, they can start a bidirectional voice handoff without leaving the website. Text chat remains available during the call. 

 The advisor receives the vehicle, conversation history, selected battery, price, and product image. The customer does not need to start over. 

 Our product thesis is: 

 Search + AI Guidance + Human Expertise = Sale 

 The current demo stops before payment: it prepares an informational cart but does not create orders or charge customers. 

 How we built it 

 We built two connected experiences: 

 
 A customer-facing product catalog and AI assistant. 
 A dedicated workspace for the human advisor. 
 

 The storefront and advisor interface use Next.js, React, and TypeScript . Gemini and Google ADK handle intent and agent orchestration. 

 Instead of asking the model to simulate clicks, we expose deterministic catalog operations as native WebMCP functions . These functions search compatibility, compare batteries, change the selected product, and update the cart. Because they share application state with the storefront, every tool call produces a visible result. 

 For human handoff, we built a standalone workflow using LiveKit . It supports bidirectional audio and text while transferring the relevant conversation and product context to the advisor. 

 The application is deployed on Google Cloud Run , with a locally packaged product catalog so the public challenge demo is self-contained. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not generating a recommendation. It was keeping several states consistent: 

 
 What the customer sees in the catalog. 
 What the AI knows from the conversation. 
 Which product is currently selected. 
 What the human advisor receives during handoff. 
 

 We also had to make the experience work on mobile without letting the chat cover the product catalog. We solved this with a collapsible bottom sheet that keeps both experiences within reach. 

 Voice introduced a different set of challenges: microphone permissions require a secure browser context, and the customer and advisor must join the same LiveKit room with limited tokens and synchronized call state. 

 Finally, the handoff needed to include more than audio. We transferred the vehicle, chat history, selected product, price, and image so the advisor could continue the interaction immediately. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built and deployed a complete working journey: 

 
 Natural-language vehicle search. 
 Native WebMCP actions that update the visible storefront. 
 Product comparison and selection. 
 An informational quote cart. 
 A responsive mobile agent experience. 
 Bidirectional voice and text handoff. 
 Conversation and product-context transfer. 
 A dedicated advisor workspace. 
 A public demo running on Google Cloud Run. 
 

 We are especially proud that the AI does not operate behind the scenes. Customers can see what it changes, maintain control of the interface, and involve a human when needed. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP becomes especially useful when the user remains in the interface and can verify each agent action. 

 Structured browser functions were more predictable than relying on simulated navigation or DOM interpretation. They also allowed the AI conversation and traditional interface to share the same state. 

 We also learned that human handoff is not simply a fallback. It is part of the product experience. A handoff becomes substantially more valuable when the advisor receives the context already collected by the AI. 

 Better search helps customers find products. Search combined with explanation, visible actions, and human expertise helps them make decisions. 

 What's next for Search-to-Sale 

 BateríasPower is our first vertical implementation. The broader goal is to make the same Search-to-Sale model reusable by other SMB ecommerce businesses. 

 Next, we plan to: 

 
 Build a lightweight JavaScript SDK that existing ecommerce websites can install with a single script tag. 
 Connect each website's product catalog and UI actions to Search-to-Sale. 
 Add WebMCP-powered search, conversational guidance, and human handoff without requiring businesses to rebuild their storefront. 
 Connect the informational cart to inventory and checkout APIs. 
 Integrate pricing and availability with ERP systems. 
 Add persistent and authenticated customer sessions. 
 Expand vehicle and product compatibility data. 
 Add production-grade advisor routing and notifications. 
 Measure search completion, handoff, and conversion outcomes. 
 Package integrations for popular ecommerce platforms. 
 

 Our goal is to make Search-to-Sale installable on an existing ecommerce website through a lightweight JavaScript SDK—bringing AI-guided product discovery and human assistance to the storefront businesses already have. 

 Our long-term vision is straightforward: give smaller online businesses the kind of guided sales experience that today is usually available only to large commerce platforms.

about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most.
