title: Navwebmcp
pitch: You already write your way for other to use your platform, don't hide it in your browser, expose it using Navwebmcp cuts agent tool, tokens and latency measured, not estimated without browser.
about_excerpt: You already write your way for other to use your platform, don't hide it in your browser, expose it using Navwebmcp cuts agent tool, tokens and latency measured, not estimated without browser. Like Comment Story Updates GIF GIF GIF GIF NavWebMcp — Devpost Submission This is a young repo that takes the MCP and WEBMCP approach and tries to build a new approach that takes the benefits of both and give answers to their weaknesses. Inspiration Every existing way an agent touches a web app pays the same tax: either the agent orchestrates a sequence of raw API calls itself — search, then create, then verify — reasoning about your domain on every single round-trip, or it drives the page like a human would, reading an accessibility tree and clicking through a UI built for eyes and fingers, not for a model. Both cost tokens and latency that have nothing to do with the actual task, and both grow worse as the surface area of the app grows and it is not deterministic. WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) is a promising browser-native answer to half of that problem — a page can register callable tools for an agent the same way it registers event listeners for a user. But the draft standard stops at "here's how a tool gets registered." It doesn't say how an agent should discover fifty tools without paying for fifty tools' worth of schema on every connection, how to layer permissions on top, or how to collapse a five-call workflow into one. That gap — protocol on top of primitive — is what NavWebMcp exists to fill. This repo is also a deliberate proof point for the AOD/ADD methodology (AI-Oriented Development / AI-Driven Development): intent specs framed up front, implementation delegated to agents, and every claim independently verified before being accepted — including, especially, the benchmark numbers below. What it does AgentBridge is a reference implementation of NavWebMcp , a protocol layered on top of WebMCP that adds progressive tool disclosure, RBAC, and composite operations. Instead of an agent stitching together searchAvailability → createReservation → getReservation , it calls one tool — book({ date, time, partySize, name }) — and gets back a validated result. The multi-step orchestration (precondition checks, the write, post-condition validation, and a compensating rollback on failure) runs invisibly behind that single call. On connect, an agent sees only 8 lightweight navigation/meta tools (~180 tokens total) — explore , search , describe_tool , invoke , load_tools , unload_tools , getContext , getCapabilities . The other 48 business operations across reservations, CRM, front-office, tasks, housekeeping, and finance are discovered on demand and either invoked directly or promoted to native tools — so registry size never inflates the cost of connecting. getContext and getCapabilities , called in parallel right after connecting, tell the agent who the user is and exactly what their role permits before it explores anything, so it can ask the user one consolidated question instead of a drip-feed of prompts. Every operation carries a role list ( customer , support , admin ) checked at every call boundary, and destructive operations carry an enforced confirmation gate. The same 48 operations are exposed identically over two surfaces from one registry: in-page WebMCP (session-cookie auth, for browser-native agents) and MCP Streamable HTTP (bearer-token auth, for external agents connecting with no browser at all ). That second point matters more than it sounds: hostVipGuest , a 7-step chain spanning CRM and front-desk, has no UI in this app whatsoever — there is nothing a click-driven tool could even target — yet it's fully callable over MCP HTTP because the tool was never built to depend on a rendered page. It's designed to work identically whether the connecting client is Claude Code, Claude Desktop, MCP Inspector, ChatGPT, or OpenAI's Codex — the orchestration runs in-process against the same handler code no matter who's calling. We proved it against a working demo: a hospitality platform with 56 operations, three composite tools, three role-scoped demo users, and a live audit log streamed over SSE. How we built it Next.js 15 (App Router, React 19) and TypeScript, with Zod as the single source of truth for both runtime validation and JSON Schema generation on both surfaces. @modelcontextprotocol/sdk plus mcp-handler provide the MCP Streamable HTTP transport; zod-to-json-schema converts the same Zod shapes for in-page WebMCP tool registration. Playwright and Vitest back the test and benchmark harnesses. The core design decision was keeping orchestration surface-agnostic: lib/core/book.ts , seatGuest.ts , and hostVipGuest.ts take a call function as a dependency and know nothing about HTTP, cookies, or bearer tokens. The browser wrapper injects serverCall ( fetch("/api/call") , cookie auth); the MCP operation injects makeDispatch(ctx) (in-process, bearer auth). Same business logic, same validation, same RBAC — the only thing that changes is what's plugged into one function parameter. Adding a new operation means writing one file in lib/operations/ and registering it in one index — it then appears on both surfaces automatically with disclosure, RBAC, and audit logging already wired. Following AOD/ADD, the process itself was: write the intent (what the protocol needed to guarantee) before writing code, delegate implementation to agents against that spec, and independently verify — most concretely, by insisting every number in the README's benchmark tables come from an actual measured run ( scripts/bench.mjs , scripts/speedbase.mjs , n=5, real MCP transport, real headless browser) rather than an estimate. Challenges we ran into Getting progressive disclosure right without breaking usability was the hardest design problem — too little detail at connect time and the agent flails; too much and the token savings evaporate. The explore / search / describe_tool split (navigate by path, discover by pattern, fetch schema only when needed) came out of iterating on that trade-off. Keeping the two surfaces genuinely equivalent — not just superficially similar — meant RBAC, confirmation gates, and audit logging all had to live at the operation-registry level rather than in either surface's adapter, or they'd have silently drifted apart the first time someone touched only one of the two files. Benchmarking honestly was its own challenge: it's easy to produce numbers that flatter the architecture. We insisted on comparing against a real Playwright browser-automation lane, not a hypothetical one, which is also what surfaced the finding that mattered most — hostVipGuest has no Playwright row at all, because there's no UI for it to drive. That's not a benchmark gap, it's a demonstration of the actual capability boundary of UI automation versus tool calls. Versioning also took more thought than expected: a single version number couldn't distinguish "the protocol contract changed" from "this role's tool set changed," so getCapabilities() deliberately returns two separate fields — a hand-bumped protocolVersion and an automatically computed, role-scoped capabilityHash — so agents can tell which kind of change happened and react accordingly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The benchmark numbers are real, not estimated, and they're strong: composite calls cut tokens by 72–87% and latency by 67–88% versus raw multi-call orchestration, on both the MCP HTTP and in-browser WebMCP surfaces, with 5/5 reliability across every lane. The saving compounds with orchestration complexity — a 7-op CRM+front-desk chain collapses to a single call with an 87% latency reduction — and testing the operation layer directly is up to 1,300× faster than driving the same flow through a browser. We're equally proud of the fact that the protocol holds up structurally: one operation registry drives two authentication models, two transports, and two calling conventions with zero duplicated business logic, and RBAC/audit/disclosure behavior is provably identical on both because they're enforced in one shared place, not two. And we shipped the consumer half of the protocol too — skills/navwebmcp-agent/ , a portable agent skill for connecting efficiently, discovering operations, and preferring composite calls — versioned independently of the server implementation, so it isn't tied to this one demo app. What we learned The biggest lesson: token and latency cost in agent tooling is mostly a protocol design problem, not a model problem. The same LLM calling the same underlying operations pays wildly different costs depending on whether it has to orchestrate three calls itself or one — that's architecture, not intelligence. We also learned that "the agent needs a browser" is frequently just false. Once business logic is expressed as composable server-side operations, the browser becomes one optional caller among several rather than a load-bearing dependency — which is what let hostVipGuest exist at

title: Overloaded
pitch: A real-time strategy game that keeps more depth than one player can manage, because your agent playsalongside you through its own interface instead of your screen.
about_excerpt: A real-time strategy game that keeps more depth than one player can manage, because your agent playsalongside you through its own interface instead of your screen. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Strategy games are simplified down to what one player can handle. Options get buried in submenus and whole systems get cut before release, and the limit is never the simulation. It is how much a person can look at while the clock is running. A model does not have that limit, which means the depth can stay in and the game does not have to be flattened to be playable. What it does Overloaded is a Napoleonic real-time strategy game. You raise infantry, cavalry and artillery, group them into named formations, and fight over supply depots against a clock. The whole live match is published as nineteen WebMCP tools, so your agent reads the field and gives orders in the same tick you do, from the same match state, without a screenshot and without taking your pointer. It can also write standing orders — instructions the army carries out on its own, with no model involved. How we built it TypeScript with no game engine. Every unit and building is assembled from primitives in three.js, the terrain is painted to a canvas at load, and every sound is synthesised through the Web Audio API, so nothing is loaded from an asset file. The tools call the same command layer the interface calls: issue is what a right-click runs and add_rule is what the panel's new-order button runs, so both sides drive one match object. Challenges we ran into A tool call takes seconds and the game runs at twenty ticks a second, so an agent that only reacts is always acting on information that has already changed. That is what standing orders are for: the agent writes a rule once, and the game runs it the moment the thing it watches reports. The second problem was discovery. The tools published one flat vocabulary while the interface filtered its dropdowns per formation, so an agent had to infer that a battery cannot charge. It now reports, for every formation and base, exactly which orders it can be given. Accomplishments that we are proud of Two people can command the same battle at once without either waiting for the other. And add_rule is a tool whose effect outlives the call it was made in — once written, the order runs with nothing in the loop. What we learned An agent surface is not just the list of things it can do. It is what the page tells the agent about what is possible right now, for this object. A capability that is technically available but not reported is one the agent will never use. What is next More arms and terrain, and a shared match where each side is commanded by a different person and their agent. title: Countersign
pitch: Working Together Under Writer and Agents. AI reads your live underwriting case, catches what you'd miss — fraud patterns, over-insurance, non-disclosure. Proposes. Waits. Nothing binds without you.
about_excerpt: Working Together Under Writer and Agents. AI reads your live underwriting case, catches what you'd miss — fraud patterns, over-insurance, non-disclosure. Proposes. Waits. Nothing binds without you. Like Comment Story Updates Agent can take action on behalf of Underwriters proposing exclusion clauses Inspiration I am working in insurance industry for 20 years and is one of the slowest moving industry when it comes to tech . Underwriting is still done the way it was 20 years ago: an underwriter alone in a tab, manually cross-referencing claims history, other policies, and disclosure forms that live in different systems. The risk factors that matter most — a second policy on the same address, a claim filed right before renewal, a "no prior claims" answer that doesn't match the file — aren't hard to catch, they're just easy to miss when you're moving fast through a queue of files. We wanted to see if WebMCP could let an AI agent sit inside that same case file, alongside the underwriter, and catch what a tired reviewer on their tenth file of the day might not. Not an agent that decides. One that notices, and says so. What it does Countersign is a shared underwriting workspace. The underwriter reviews a live policy application — applicant details, requested sum insured, policy terms. An AI agent, connected through WebMCP tools registered directly on the page, can read the same case data (claim history, other active policies) and propose changes: a risk flag, a premium loading, a change to the excess or an exclusion — each with a plain-language reason citing the specific data behind it. Every proposal lands in a queue, clearly attributed to the agent, and does nothing to the actual policy until the underwriter accepts or rejects it. Nothing binds without a human. Every action — human or agent — is timestamped in an activity log, so the final policy comes with a defensible trail of who decided what, and why. Working together. Underwriter and agent. AI reads your live underwriting case, catches what you'd miss — fraud patterns, over-insurance, non-disclosure. Proposes. Waits. Nothing binds without you. How we built it The app is a single-page React + Vite frontend, no backend — WebMCP tools run entirely client-side against in-memory state. We registered five tools via navigator.modelContext.registerTool : Two read-only tools — check_claim_history and check_other_policies — that return structured data plus computed signals like aggregate exposure across policies Three propose-only write tools — propose_risk_flag , propose_loading , propose_field_adjustment — that never mutate the policy record directly; they push into a pending-proposals queue that only a human accept/reject action can resolve We modeled the mock case data around real underwriting fraud patterns rather than generic risk scores: claims frequency thresholds, sum-insured-vs-declared-value mismatches, and same-address aggregate exposure across multiple insurers. We tested tool discovery and invocation in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, then verified the full flow again through ChatGPT's desktop browser Site Tools before finalizing. Challenges we ran into Getting the human-in-the-loop boundary right took more iteration than the tools themselves — it was tempting to let "safe" proposals auto-apply, but any auto-apply path undermines the audit story that makes this credible for a regulated workflow, so we held the line at approval-gated everything. We also hit the classic stale-closure bug with tool execute callbacks holding onto old state snapshots when the active applicant changed, which we fixed by reading current state through a ref instead of a captured value. Getting WebMCP tool descriptions specific enough that the agent reliably called the right tool with the right applicant ID — rather than guessing or hallucinating case data — took several rounds of tightening the schema and description wording. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that the propose-only architecture isn't just a safety feature bolted on — it's the actual product insight: an LLM in a regulated decision workflow shouldn't want authority, it should want to be legible. Every accepted or rejected proposal, plus the reasoning behind it, is captured automatically, which means the audit trail underwriting teams need for compliance falls out of the design instead of being built as an afterthought. We also managed to build tools that reflect how underwriters actually think — loading vs. excess vs. exclusion as distinct levers, aggregate exposure as a first-class concept — rather than a generic "risk score" that wouldn't hold up to anyone with real domain knowledge. What we learned WebMCP's biggest value isn't letting an agent do more — it's letting an agent act inside a shared object both parties can see and trust, instead of narrating actions in a chat window disconnected from the real record. We also learned how much of "trust" in a human-AI collaboration tool comes from what the system refuses to do automatically, not what it can do. On the technical side: closures over live app state are the easiest way to introduce subtle bugs when wiring WebMCP tools into a React app, and it's worth designing state access through refs from the start rather than retrofitting it. What's next for Countersign Near-term, we'd add a referral tier — when proposed changes cross an underwriter's authority limit (e.g. aggregate exposure above a threshold), Countersign would route them to a senior underwriter instead of a simple accept/reject, matching how real underwriting authority limits work. We'd also like to make agent reasoning traceable at the data level — clicking a proposal highlights the exact claim or policy row it's citing, so nothing the agent says is a black box. Longer-term, the same propose-and-approve pattern applies well beyond underwriting — claims adjudication, loan structuring, compliance review — anywhere a human needs to stay the final signature on a decision an AI can help inform but shouldn't make alone. title: Site2WebMCP
pitch: Nobody will hand-write WebMCP per site. Zero site setup.
about_excerpt:
Nobody will hand-write WebMCP per site. Zero site setup.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Nobody will hand-write WebMCP for every website. Zero site setup. 

 WebMCP lets agents use a site as tools instead of clicking through the UI. That only works if someone builds the tools. Every site is different — hand-writing and maintaining that for the whole web is the real bottleneck. We flipped it: the person who needs agent tools shouldn’t wait on every company to ship WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 Site2WebMCP is a Chrome extension (also available as an agent skill) that reads the forms and buttons already on a live page and exposes them as WebMCP tools. An agent can then run real workflows — search, add to cart, checkout, and so on — without browser control and without the site owner implementing anything. 

 How we built it 

 
 A simple webpage with two demo modes and WebMCP for auto-setup of demo 1 — a playground only. The product generates WebMCP for any external site. 
 Chrome MV3 extension: discover forms and primary actions from the live DOM, plus registerTool where needed. 
 An agent skill that does the same job as the extension — inject into the page, discover DOM actions, register them as WebMCP. 
 

 Challenges 

 Getting from “tools appear” to “an agent actually completes a workflow” was the hard part — especially validating the agent-side path, not just the discovery UI. The runtime still leans on e-commerce-shaped heuristics; proving this beyond that shape is the next fight. Hand-written WebMCP will always be sharper for a given site — this is WebMCP for sites that never shipped it, replaceable when they do. 

 ChatGPT Desktop’s built-in browser is read-only: no extensions, no injected scripts. That blocks dynamically generated WebMCP there. 

 Chrome Web Store review is slow, so the extension isn’t installable from the store yet. 

 What’s next 

 
 Use site JavaScript to find server requests and expose them as tools, with descriptions of what those functions do. 
 Crawl support centres and docs for how to use the site, then turn that into tools and skills. 
 Use llms.txt to extract tools or workflows (chains of tool calls). 
 Use an external or browser-built-in LLM to identify workflows on a site and turn them into tools and skills. 
 Measuring the speed and tokens savings compared to a vanila browser use that does clicks.

title: orqis
pitch: The shelf for specialist AI agents. Browsable by humans, callable by agents — one marketplace where people and their agents discover, invoke, and rate specialist agents together.
about_excerpt: The shelf for specialist AI agents. Browsable by humans, callable by agents — one marketplace where people and their agents discover, invoke, and rate specialist agents together. Like Comment Story Updates list the agents What is orqis orqis is the shelf for specialist AI agents: a marketplace that is browsable by humans and callable by agents . Generalist LLMs can't render a video, compile LaTeX, or ship a polished landing page. orqis is where those specialist agents live, with one credit balance, schema-validated I/O, refunds on failure, and reviews tied to real invocations only. Live URL: https://orqis.xyz Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP A marketplace of agents is, by definition, something both people and agents need to use. Before WebMCP, an agent visiting orqis.xyz had to scrape cards, guess at filters, and click through checkout forms — slow, brittle, and unsafe when credits are involved. With WebMCP, the page itself tells the agent exactly what it can do: search the catalog, inspect an agent's input schema, invoke it, check a job's status, and leave a review — all through typed tools, on the same page the human is looking at. How it creates a better experience Shared context, shared screen. The human browses categories and reads reviews; their agent (in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome) calls search_agents / invoke_agent against the very same page. Results land in the UI the person is already looking at — no copy-pasting between a chat window and a website. Safety by construction. Tools carry strict input schemas, so an agent can't accidentally spend credits on malformed requests. Failed invocations are refunded automatically. Trust that agents can read. Ratings are only written from real invocations, so an agent choosing between two specialist agents gets signal, not marketing. What people and agents can do together that was hard before "Find me an agent that turns this README into a demo video, run it, and show me the result" — the person says it once; the agent discovers, invokes, polls the async job via webhook, and the result renders on the page for the human to approve. Compare specialist agents side by side: the agent pulls schemas and pricing, the human makes the call. Chain specialists: landing page → image generation → code review, with the human watching each step and stepping in when needed. How we implemented WebMCP On page load, orqis registers its tools with navigator.modelContext.registerTool(...) (with a document.modelContext fallback for older builds). Each tool maps 1:1 to an existing orqis REST endpoint, so the tools the browser agent sees are the same ones our @orqis/mcp server exposes to Claude and Cursor — one tool surface, three clients (human UI, in-page agent via WebMCP, and remote agents via MCP). Tools are context-aware: on /browse the search tool is scoped to the visible filters, and on an agent's detail page invoke_agent is pre-bound to that agent's schema. Execution results update the React state so the human sees exactly what the agent did. Built with Next.js, TypeScript, WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext ), MCP ( @orqis/mcp ), REST + webhooks for async jobs. What's next Opening the founding-agent program publicly, richer tool annotations for streaming job progress, and per-tool spend limits the human can set for their agent. title: Inference Chip Index
pitch: A source-linked MLPerf leaderboard that lets people and AI agents compare inference hardware safely in the same visible workspace.
about_excerpt: A source-linked MLPerf leaderboard that lets people and AI agents compare inference hardware safely in the same visible workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inference-hardware comparisons are easy to get wrong. A leaderboard can silently mix workloads, scenarios, accuracy targets, units, or system-level and per-accelerator numbers. Traditional browser automation makes that worse because an agent has to infer meaning from controls and tables. I wanted a safer collaboration model: the website should expose the exact research operations it supports, the agent should act on the same visible interface as the human, and every answer should remain traceable to immutable benchmark evidence. What it does Inference Chip Index turns official MLPerf Inference v6.0 results into workload-specific, source-linked comparisons. Its leaderboard now exposes four imperative WebMCP tools: list_inference_slices discovers valid exact comparison boundaries. configure_inference_leaderboard changes the filters visible to the human. compare_inference_accelerators compares 2–8 accelerator families inside one exact slice and renders the result on the page. clear_inference_comparison removes the shared comparison without resetting the leaderboard. The central safety rule is simple: a tool cannot claim that one chip is universally fastest. Every comparison is constrained to the same release, Closed division, workload, scenario, accuracy target, metric, and unit. Results include immutable GitHub source URLs and SHA-256 hashes. If evidence is missing, the tool returns an explicit missing-evidence reason instead of inventing a number. How I built it The application uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, and Cloudflare Workers through OpenNext. The normalized data is generated deterministically from the pinned MLPerf Inference v6.0 commit 4d3916ac9cf474b679cdfcf492d43a0559418ad1 . During the WebMCP Challenge submission period I added the browser-native collaboration layer with the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Pure validation and comparison logic lives in src/webmcp/leaderboard-tools.ts ; registration and visible state updates live in the leaderboard React component. An AbortController unregisters the tools cleanly when the component unmounts. The WebMCP layer reuses the same checked-in dataset and exact-slice invariants as the site. It does not introduce a parallel ranking implementation, fetch untrusted runtime data, invoke paid endpoints, or expose secrets. Tool input schemas reject unknown fields and validate all slice IDs, vendors, submitters, grouping modes, metric views, and accelerator slugs. Challenge-period work The reproducible data index and Lucid API existed before the event. The WebMCP extension was built specifically during the challenge window. Public commits 7b89ee5 through fd9f65f add the imperative tools, shared-state UI, tests, documentation, security header, MIT license, and production URL documentation. The public deployment includes that extension. Challenges I ran into Converting a dense technical leaderboard into a small, predictable tool surface without duplicating ranking logic. Keeping agent actions visible to the human while preserving manual control of the same React state. Preventing incompatible benchmark dimensions from being compared even when an agent supplies plausible-looking inputs. Explaining absent results as evidence gaps rather than treating them as zero. Preserving immutable provenance in every structured response without overwhelming the visual interface. Accomplishments that I am proud of One agent call can build a three-vendor comparison that immediately appears in the human's browser. Every returned row stays inside an exact benchmark slice and links back to immutable source evidence. The tool surface is read-only with respect to servers and payments, while still making useful visible changes locally. The app contains 145 verified results, 50 submitted systems, 13 normalized accelerators, and 9 exact slices. The implementation passes type checking, 21 automated tests, and a production build. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes domain invariants, not when it merely turns every button into a tool. A good tool contract can make an unsafe action impossible, keep agent and human context synchronized, and communicate uncertainty as structured data. I also learned that browser-native tools can be a better accessibility and audit surface than invisible automation: the human sees the filters change, sees the comparison render, and can verify the same immutable sources the agent used. What's next Add WebMCP tools for methodology explanations and dataset-diff inspection. Let a human pin a baseline row and ask an agent for compatible deltas. Extend the importer to later MLPerf releases while preserving immutable snapshots and tombstones. Add signed dataset manifests so agents can verify provenance independently. Study how WebMCP tool descriptions affect agent selection and user trust in data-heavy workflows. Repeatable demo Open the live leaderboard in a WebMCP-capable browser. Ask: “List the available exact inference comparison slices.” Ask: “For the GPT-OSS 120B Offline slice, compare AMD MI355X, NVIDIA B200, and Intel Arc Pro B60 using official system results.” Observe the comparison appear in the shared page with values, source links, and missing-evidence handling. Ask the agent to clear the comparison or configure another visible slice. Verification npm ci npm run type-check npm test npm run build Verified locally: TypeScript passed, 21 tests passed, and the production build passed. The deployed leaderboard registered all four WebMCP tools, and a live three-vendor comparison returned exact-slice values with immutable sources. title: CapStash WebGPU Verification Lab
pitch: A WebMCP-enabled WebGPU lab where agents can safely run correctness-gated GPU experiments, share state with the human UI, and refuse unsupported performance conclusions.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-enabled WebGPU lab where agents can safely run correctness-gated GPU experiments, share state with the human UI, and refuse unsupported performance conclusions. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Main app + green safety notice Four WebMCP tools visible in Chrome DevTools Completed WG1/WG32 comparison result Inspiration I originally built this project to explore whether CapStash Proof-of-Work could be implemented and verified in the browser with WebGPU. Part of the idea was crypto onboarding: giving people a low-barrier way to inspect how this kind of computation works on their own hardware, run some basic tests, and see the results for themselves without needing to set up a traditional miner. I also liked the idea of eventually making it a little more playful — something where a person could contribute a small amount of browser compute and get something back like a meme, a fortune, or maybe some kind of AI or social interaction. The underlying workload comes from a cryptocurrency Proof-of-Work algorithm, but this project is intentionally a local research and verification tool. There is no live mining . It does not connect to a blockchain network, mining pool, wallet, payout system, RPC service, or block-submission service. Before the WebMCP Challenge, the project had already grown into a fairly complete human-operated WebGPU experiment lab with CPU reference verification, CapStash Core-derived test vectors, profiling, workgroup experiments, and a Guided/Advanced browser UI. Sometime in early August, after manually clicking through my testing suite again, I said to myself, “Why can’t I just make this automated and operable by AI?” At the time, I was bouncing back and forth between ChatGPT, Codex, browser windows, screenshots, and different settings. Because the agent was still interacting with the interface indirectly, I often had to send screenshots or find things manually myself. I was also learning a lot of the underlying technology as I went. When I saw the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, the project seemed like a natural fit for a different question: What happens when an AI agent can operate a technical browser instrument through structured tools instead of scraping the DOM or pretending to click buttons? What it does The browser exposes four WebMCP tools: inspect_compute_environment verify_correctness start_workgroup_comparison get_experiment_status An agent can inspect the available WebGPU environment without starting computation, request bounded correctness verification, start a longer WG1-vs-WG32 experiment, and read structured experiment progress and results. The main workflow asks: Determine whether workgroup size 32 is meaningfully better than workgroup size 1 on this GPU. Verify both configurations first, run a matched comparison, and only recommend a winner if the evidence supports one. Before the longer workload begins, the page requires explicit user approval and clearly describes the local compute workload. After approval, the application automatically: validates WG1 support and compilation, runs its small correctness gate, verifies WG1 against all 294 CapStash Core vectors, performs the same checks for WG32, runs three matched profiling samples for each workgroup size, reports the result through both the human UI and structured WebMCP state. The same existing experiment controller is used by humans and agents. WebMCP does not duplicate the GPU engine or bypass its correctness rules. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent would have to interpret a complicated technical interface, manipulate controls, scrape visible text, and infer whether prerequisites had actually completed. That was one of the things I kept running into while using browser agents myself. They can do a lot by clicking through pages and interpreting what is on screen, but they do not always see an interface the same way a human does. Sometimes they are effectively working from fragments and inferring the rest. With WebMCP, the application can expose the intent and state of the experiment directly in a machine-readable form while still keeping the normal human interface. The agent can request a high-level goal while the application remains responsible for: prerequisite sequencing, correctness gates, experiment concurrency, structured progress, result accounting, safety boundaries, and recommendation policy. An important part of the project is that the agent cannot simply choose whichever performance number looks better. The pre-existing comparison logic includes variability limits and a minimum practical-difference threshold. If the evidence is too noisy or the performance difference is too small, the WebMCP result returns no recommendation. For example, validated runs have correctly returned classifications such as: host-side variability too high for a recommendation effectively tied within observed variability with: recommendationAllowed: false recommendation: null That behavior is intentional. WebMCP makes the instrument agent-operable without weakening its evidence standards. How I built it The application is dependency-free browser JavaScript with: HTML/CSS JavaScript WebGPU WGSL compute shaders a CPU Whirlpool-512 reference implementation deterministic CapStash Core-derived verification vectors WebMCP through document.modelContext static Cloudflare Pages hosting The public challenge repository contains a reconstructed, privacy-sanitized history that preserves the exact pre-challenge baseline and the exact challenge-period changes. The WebMCP work added during the challenge includes: structured WebMCP tool registration, environment inspection, correctness invocation, shared human/agent application state, an asynchronous experiment lifecycle, prerequisite-aware WG1/WG32 orchestration, structured recommendation blockers, consent for longer agent-triggered compute, and WebMCP-specific tests and documentation. The underlying WebGPU hashing, correctness engine, workgroup experiments, profiling, statistics, and human UI all existed before the challenge and are clearly documented as such. Testing and correctness The current project passes: 130 / 130 automated tests 294 / 294 CapStash Core vectors zero CPU/Core mismatches zero WGSL/Core mismatches in validated full runs The final release-hardened workflow was also tested in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. A full approved matched comparison completed: WG1 full verification: 294 / 294 WG32 full verification: 294 / 294 3 valid WG1 samples 3 valid WG32 samples 6 total valid samples 49,152 requested/completed/returned hashes 30 CPU spot checks 0 mismatches 0 pipeline errors 0 device losses 0 deterministic-ordering failures The deployed public site is HTTPS, WebGPU-capable, WebMCP origin-trial enabled, and exposes all four tools in ordinary Chrome. Challenges One thing that surprised me was how quickly the application could actually perform a lot of the work once the WebGPU path was working. I was still learning much of the technology, so seeing the verification and profiling complete as quickly as they did was pretty impressive to me. That also made correctness more important, not less. I added correctness gates fairly early in the project because I did not want speed or interesting benchmark numbers to mean anything unless the output was actually trustworthy. Those gates eventually grew into full CPU/Core/WGSL comparisons and the 294-vector verification used by the final workflow. One lesson I kept coming back to was that when you are building around unfamiliar technology — especially with AI helping — you need strict build rules, safety boundaries, and acceptance criteria. Otherwise it is very easy to get something that looks impressive without really knowing whether it is correct. A more specific WebMCP challenge was handling long-running browser GPU work. Cold WebGPU pipeline compilation could sometimes take more than 20 seconds, which was not a good fit for holding a single WebMCP tool invocation open. The solution was an asynchronous experiment lifecycle: the start tool returns immediately with an experiment ID, while get_experiment_status exposes structured progress and the final result. Another challenge was preserving user control. The longer comparison now enters an awaiting_consent state and starts no GPU work until the user explicitly approves the local workload. A third challenge was provenance. This project existed before the challenge, so I wanted the public submission to make that completely transparent. The repository preserves an exact pre-challenge tree followed by the WebMCP challenge changes and documents the original private source SHAs in PROVENANCE.md . Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am especially proud that the final WebMCP workflow does not bypass the testing system I had already built. The agent uses the same experiment controller and the same correctness gates as the human interface. WG1 and WG32 both have to pass full verification before the comparison is allowed to continue

title: Ombuds
pitch: A form that teaches the agent how to fill it, refuses the answers it cannot accept, corrects the agent when it is wrong, and hands every value to a human before it counts.
about_excerpt: A form that teaches the agent how to fill it, refuses the answers it cannot accept, corrects the agent when it is wrong, and hands every value to a human before it counts. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Ombuds is a work authorization worksheet, rebuilt so that the page is the authority instead of the agent. The worst forms on the web are long conditional government forms. A work authorization application asks you for an eligibility category code, and that one answer silently rewrites which of the next forty questions apply to you. Pick category c(3)(C) and you now owe a CIP code and an employer E-Verify number. Pick c(9) and neither of those exists, and you owe an I-485 receipt number instead. Say you want a Social Security card and both your parents' names become mandatory. None of this is written down anywhere the form can show you. It lives in footnotes and in the head of whoever has filled one out before. Agents are bad at these forms for the same reason people are. An agent reading the screen has no way to know that picking a category changed the rules. A backend MCP server cannot help either, because it has no idea what the person sitting in the browser has already answered. Ombuds moves the rules into the page and hands them to the agent directly. You talk to your agent in plain language about your situation. The page tells the agent exactly which questions apply to you right now, gives it the precise list of values each answer accepts, rejects anything malformed with the actual rule and a valid example so the agent fixes itself, and then holds every single value in a review queue until you personally accept it. Nothing an agent says about your immigration status is true until you agree with it. Three things it deliberately will not do. It will not tick your certification, because only the person filing can attest to their own application, so there is no tool for it at all. It will not give legal consent on your behalf, so the field authorizing disclosure to the Social Security Administration refuses agent writes outright. It will not let you generate your filing packet until every section is valid, your review queue is empty, and you have signed by hand. It is an independent worksheet. It is not affiliated with USCIS, it does not file anything, and everything stays in the browser tab. Inspiration I spent a year doing missionary work in Cambodia and watched people lose months to paperwork written as though the rules were obvious. The rules are never obvious. Putting them in the page, where an agent can be told them directly and a person can still overrule the answer, is a better use of this standard than making a shopping cart marginally faster. How I used WebMCP Eight mechanics. The first five are things WebMCP can do that a backend integration structurally cannot. 1. The tool schemas are generated from live form state. answer-category-questions is one tool with one name. Its schema is assembled from whichever eligibility category you picked. Category c(9) advertises a single field. Category c(3)(C) advertises four completely different ones. Change your category and the tool is unregistered and registered again with an entirely different shape. A server-side tool would have to accept a vague bag of optional strings and hope for the best. This one accepts exactly the four things you actually owe and rejects anything else as FIELD_NOT_APPLICABLE. Every enum is generated the same way from the same lists the HTML renders, so an agent cannot invent a state code or a category code, because the accepted values are sitting in the schema it was handed. 2. One predicate drives both the human UI and the agent's schema. Every conditional field carries a single showWhen function. The renderer uses it to decide whether to draw an input. The WebMCP layer uses the same one to decide whether that field belongs in the tool's schema. The human and the agent are looking at the same form, always, because there is only one description of the form and it cannot drift out of step with itself. 3. Tools appear and disappear so the agent only ever sees a legal move. Sections unlock as their prerequisites become valid, and a section's tool exists only while that section is open. Before Part 1 is valid there is no set-personal-info to call. Answer no to having used other names and add-other-name is not disabled, it is gone. Say your mailing address is where you live and set-physical-address unregisters itself. The agent gets a state machine rather than a flat API, and toolchange tells it when the machine moved. The sidebar shows the live registered set so you can watch tools flash in and out as you answer. 4. Rejections are structured, so the agent corrects itself. The page owns the validation rules, so it can hand back something an agent can act on instead of a red border. Send a bad SEVIS number and you get a machine-readable code, the rule in plain language, where to find the real value on your Form I-20, and a concrete valid example. The agent reads that and fixes its own argument on the next call. Nobody retypes anything. Cross-field conflicts work the same way. Claim category c(3)(C) while declaring H-1B status and you get the specific contradiction with both responsible fields named, because that is the class of error that actually gets real filings bounced back weeks later. 5. Nothing an agent writes is true until a human agrees. State is kept in two layers. Committed values are what the applicant accepted. Pending values are what the agent proposed. Proposals are validated the instant they arrive so the agent gets its feedback immediately without waiting on a human, and they surface in the page as amber diff cards with accept and reject buttons. Only a human click promotes a value. 6. Both halves of the spec, each where it fits. The imperative API carries the conditional sections, because branching logic is exactly what a form cannot express. The category finder at the top of the page is a declarative <form> carrying toolname , tooldescription and toolparamdescription , which a supporting browser turns into a tool with no registerTool call at all, and its submit handler answers the agent through SubmitEvent#respondWith() so the page never navigates away and throws out the conversation. Declarative suits that panel because it is a flat search over a fixed list. One ranked search with synonym expansion backs both paths, so a person typing "spouse of an H-1B worker" and an agent sending the same words get the same answer. Using each API where it fits is the argument the WebMCP explainer itself makes, and building both is what made me believe it. The tag beside the finder reports whether the browser actually synthesized the declarative tool rather than inferring it from a version number, and declarative calls are badged separately in the call log. 7. Tools that cross an origin boundary. The document vault at the bottom of the page is a separate service on its own origin, embedded in an iframe carrying allow="tools" so the permissions policy lets it register tools at all. It registers with exposedTo naming only the form's origin, and the form discovers them with getTools({ fromOrigins: [...] }) and runs them through executeTool . The browser refuses the call unless both halves agree. The point of the split is the trust boundary. The form asks whether a required document exists and when it lapses, and never receives the document. A form that stored your passport scan is a different product with a different risk profile, and only tools that carry an origin can express that difference. The payoff chains both origins: the precheck builds a document checklist here from your eligibility category, then each line is resolved by a tool running over there, coming back as on file, expiring, expired, or missing. My own I-20 line comes back expired, which is the kind of thing you would otherwise learn by mail. Cross-origin exposedTo needs browser support the origin trial does not universally have yet, so the same tools are also reachable over a postMessage bridge with a deliberately identical shape. The calling code does not branch, and the panel reports which transport is actually live rather than claiming the stronger one. Both paths enforce the same origin allowlist, and a probe from a disallowed host origin gets no reply at all. 8. A working answer to an open question in the standard. WebMCP Issue #165 is open on how a tool should prompt the user for explicit authorization mid-execution. No API for it exists yet, so I built one from what the spec already provides, since execute may return a promise and it receives an AbortSignal. request-certification suspends until a person clicks. The page raises the question with the agent's own note attached, cancellation propagates and clears it, and there is no code path by which the agent produces its own approval. An agent may ask for a signature. Only a human can supply one. That replaced an earlier des

Get one format wrong and you find out weeks later by mail. So on the So on the right is every tool this page offers as an agent right now and that's not a fixed list. I answer the first question and two new tools appear. As you keep going you'll see that more that more sections unlock and more tools register with them. An agent is never offered a move this form would refuse. So I So I pick a category here a pending green card and look at the schema this tool advertises to an agent. It asks for one field. So So same tool, same name, nothing reloaded. I switch to STEM work authorization and the schema becomes four completely different fields built out of what this person already answered for the app. So a server can't do that. Now the agent sends a malformed identification number. The page rejects it and hands back the exact rule it broke along with an example that would have passed so the agent has everything it needs. So it re So it reads that, it fixes its own argument and moves on. Nobody had to retype anything. Every Everything that the agent entered is a proposal sitting in a queue and it waits there until a person accepts it. So let me click ac- click accept and it finishes the form. Then one question whether I can file today or not. Answering that takes this form's rules, a filing window off my I-20, a fee and the documents I hold. That That expired document is not from this page at all. It is a vault on a different origin publishing tools to this one form and nothing else. So that the form asks what I hold and never receives it. Now it asked me to sign and its tool call is suspended right this second waiting on a human being. This is still an open question in the specific specification. It can ask for a signature. It cannot sign. Only my click resolves that call and that boundary is deliberate. So I spent a year in Cambodia watching people lose months to paperwork written as though the rules were obvious. They never are. And so this is a form and thing that I built that looks like when it stops pretending.

title: Proofboard
pitch: Evidence-first decision rooms where browser agents structure source-backed research while humans retain approval and final-decision authority.
about_excerpt:
Evidence-first decision rooms where browser agents structure source-backed research while humans retain approval and final-decision authority.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Technology decisions are usually split between chat transcripts, spreadsheets, browser tabs, and memory. Research becomes hard to audit, conflicting claims are easy to miss, and an agent can appear more certain than the evidence allows. Proofboard turns the decision page itself into a durable, inspectable collaboration surface. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Proofboard is a strong fit for WebMCP because the agent must work with the exact state the person is viewing—not a detached copy hidden inside a chat. Native tools let an agent read human-authored constraints, add structured candidates and source-backed claims, and immediately update the same interface. Human edits are visible to the next tool call. 

 What people and agents do together 

 A browser agent can read the room, add candidates, attach validated evidence URLs, and ask Proofboard to surface conflicts and missing fields. It can prepare a shortlist proposal for human review. People can directly edit constraints, inspect every source, exclude or restore candidates, review proposals, and make the final decision. 

 This division of authority is intentional: Proofboard exposes no finalize_decision agent tool. The Make final decision action exists only in the human interface, and the audit trail distinguishes human and AI changes. 

 Better user experience 

 Instead of copying research out of chat, users get one persistent decision room with structured evidence, visible uncertainty, validation errors, provenance, and a human gate. Tool calls update the UI immediately; UI changes are available to subsequent tool reads. The human interface remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 How it was built 

 Proofboard is a React/Vinext application deployed on ChatGPT Sites. The UI and all 16 native WebMCP tools share one immutable reducer and browser-persisted state model. After client mount, the app obtains document.modelContext and registers tools with registerTool(...), typed JSON input schemas, read/write annotations, bounded inputs, URL validation, duplicate rejection, and abort-based unregister lifecycle handling. 

 Read tools cover decision state, constraints, candidates, evidence, conflicts, missing evidence, history, and approval status. Write tools create rooms, constraints, candidates, exclusions, evidence, and shortlist proposals. Applying a shortlist is gated on prior human approval. 

 Verified behavior 

 In Chrome's native WebMCP environment, the public site exposed 16 tools and passed a 5/5 native smoke check. A real natural-language tool run added three candidates to the live UI. A later live state contained four source-backed records, one conflict, and nine missing evidence fields, with AI-attributed history and persisted state visible. 

 The recorded demo does not claim that the pending human-approval step or shortlist application was completed. It shows only the behavior actually captured and verified. 

 Challenges and learning 

 The main challenge was preserving one source of truth across direct human edits, asynchronous agent writes, persistence, and strict validation. WebMCP made the product boundary clearer: agents contribute structured work, while consequential approval and final selection remain visibly human-controlled.

title: Dolly.dev — The UI layer for agent multiplayer
pitch: WebMCP lets an agent work your site invisibly. Dolly is the camera rig that follows the action — connection, live work states, history, and permission - React SDK
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets an agent work your site invisibly. Dolly is the camera rig that follows the action — connection, live work states, history, and permission - React SDK Like Comment Story Updates Keep The Agent Action In Frame WebMCP unlocks multiplayer The Open in ChatGPT button Onboarding, once inside Show the connection Show the work Show what happened Ask for permission Show what’s possible A Simple SDK API Inspiration I've been a product designer for 20+ years, and I've spent a lot of that time lately thinking about the UX of agent and human together in a product. I see this as the next iteration of the web — the way the iPhone forced mobile responsive, agents are going to force something new. Some people think the internet will be distilled down to a chatbox. I don't. But natural language does open up a great UX for just doing the thing without having to know how to do the thing . WebMCP opens the door to co-op multiplayer with your agent — and the agent arrives with all your context: memory, projects, what you're trying to get done. It's becoming a personal operating system. But right now, WebMCP calls tools invisibly. Nothing shows what's happening, whether anything is happening, or what happened. That's fine for headless automation. In multiplayer, the action has to be felt. The UI needs to feel multiplayer. Dolly is my exploration of that idea. What it does Dolly, like the camera rig, follows the action of the agent and keeps it in frame. I built it as an SDK — @dolly/rig — so I can drop it into any project. It covers the full arc of a multiplayer session: Open in ChatGPT button — one click deeplinks the site into the agent, and multiplayer starts: chat on one side, the live app on the other. Onboarding on arrival — the deeplink gets you in the door, but you've landed in an app you've never seen. A first-launch dialog shows what's possible and plants a few ideas to try. Show the connection — a status header that answers the first question: is the agent actually connected? Show the work — a visible lifecycle for every tool call: a full-screen glow while the agent works, a spotlight on the element being changed, progress narrated from inside the call. Show what happened — an auto-logged history of everything the agent did. Magic, with a receipt. Ask for permission — tools can pause mid-execute and wait for a human to click Continue, with an optional countdown for the safe ones and click-only for the destructive ones. Show what's possible — a tools drawer listing everything you and the agent can do together. Keyboard shortcuts, but for the agent. How I built it It's a pnpm monorepo with three parts: the React SDK ( packages/rig ), the marketing site at dolly.dev , and a demo CRM at dollycrm.app built entirely with the rig so you can test the experience end to end. The API is deliberately small — one <RigProvider> around the app, one useWebMCPTool per tool, and a handful of imperative calls ( startWork , confirm , logTask ) dropped into code you already have. One registration touches every surface. The marketing site runs the SDK it describes — every demo button on the page drives the real provider, and the same actions are registered as WebMCP tools an agent can call. Challenges I ran into The big one: how do you tell your page is running inside ChatGPT? There's no official signal, but I found one — the bridge leaves fingerprints, a __codexWebMcpModelContext global and codex -prefixed methods on the model context. detectAgent() checks for them. The other direction was getting into the agent. ChatGPT has a deeplink ( chatgpt.com/codex/deeplink?url=... ), so I built OpenInButton around it, with a ?webmcpconnected=true handshake param that triggers onboarding on arrival. I couldn't find an equivalent for Claude or Gemini — they should ship one. Accomplishments that I am proud of The Open in ChatGPT button is the UX I keep coming back to. Land in an app you've never used and normally you have to explore, figure it out, hunt through menus. With WebMCP, the agent already knows what the site can do — you just state your goal and it starts. The learning curve shrinks to one sentence. I believe buttons like this will be common, and I think they'll move usage and conversions for the sites that add them. And the whole thing works today, end to end: click the button, land in the CRM, ask for something, and watch the page follow the action. What I learned WebMCP handles the wiring; it doesn't handle the feedback. That gap is a design problem, not a protocol problem — and it's solvable with a fairly small set of primitives. Connection, onboarding, work states, history, permission, and a tools list turned out to be enough to make an agent feel like a live partner in the work instead of dumb HTML being invisibly poked and prodded. What's next for Dolly.dev Publish @dolly/rig to npm, and add the controls that naturally live in the history log — undo, retries, error recovery. Add fingerprints and deeplinks for Claude and Gemini as they ship WebMCP support. Two bigger ideas for how WebMCP itself could evolve: agent responsive design — like a CSS media query for when an agent is present, so designers can make a site feel native beside a chat box — and suggested prompt triggers , an API to drop a ready-to-send prompt straight into the agent's chat box. Built With chatgpt claude nextjs vercel webmcp Try it out dolly.dev dollycrm.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Thanks to OpenAI, Vercel, Cloudflare, Netlify, Render, Shopify, and all the sponsors for making this possible - a lot of fun exploring the future of the web! title: Unitwatch
pitch: A public web bench for crashed systemd units. Humans paste systemctl status. Agents call the same generators via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A public web bench for crashed systemd units. Humans paste systemctl status. Agents call the same generators via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Operators already paste systemctl status dumps into chat. Unitwatch makes those generators first-class page tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The human UI and the agent share one workspace. This is not MCP-over-HTTP. 

 What it does 

 Unitwatch is a public web bench for crashed systemd units. A human pastes systemctl status or a journal snippet. An agent calls the same generators as WebMCP tools. Both see the same proposed files: a restart drop-in, a TCP watchdog timer, and a rollback. 

 Nothing SSHes. Nothing emails. Nothing is installed on a host. The page only writes files onto itself. 

 Tools: parse_systemd_status, propose_restart_dropin, propose_watchdog_timer, propose_rollback, propose_hardening_plan, get_workspace. 

 How we built it 

 Built with JavaScript on Cloudflare Workers, exposing the same generator functions to the page UI and to agents via WebMCP (document.modelContext.registerTool). Try it: open the live URL in the ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Prompt: Parse the sample unit, then propose a restart drop-in and a TCP watchdog on 8080. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Keeping one set of generators authoritative for both the human UI and the agent tools, and keeping the bench strictly read-only with respect to real hosts. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 One workspace shared by human and agent, with no host access, no SSH, and no email. 

 What we learned

title: Relief Forge — From Prompt to Printable Wall Art
pitch: Turn an exact wall-art request into an inspected, printer-packed fabrication package through four visible WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Turn an exact wall-art request into an inspected, printer-packed fabrication package through four visible WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates One prompt creates an exact 48 × 48 inch Polar Bloom: 81 deterministic parts fitted across 62 plates. Four structured WebMCP tools create, constrain, inspect, and prepare the same visible project. Inspection returns exact measurements and confirms all 81 parts fit across 62 plates. The final tool prepares a 656,651-byte fabrication package while the reviewer controls the download. Inspiration Creative manufacturing software has powerful controls, but an agent usually has to imitate mouse clicks or stop at advice. Relief Forge explores a more useful interaction: structured tools that operate the same deterministic design engine and visible editor a person uses. The motivating request is concrete: Make me a four-foot-square Polar Bloom statement piece with a reproducible design and fixed palette. Fit every part to my printer, validate the exact plan, and prepare the fabrication files. That request combines units, aesthetic intent, fabrication constraints, inspection, and a deliverable. It is a stronger use of WebMCP than adding a chat panel to a design application. What it does Relief Forge registers four focused WebMCP tools: relief_forge_create_wall_art creates supported deterministic wall art at exact finished dimensions. relief_forge_set_printer_bed applies explicit bed dimensions, edge margins, spacing, rotation, and color-packing rules. relief_forge_inspect_fabrication_plan reports the current project identity, measurements, part and plate counts, and digital geometry and packing status. relief_forge_prepare_fabrication_package prepares an export only for the current validated project snapshot, while leaving the final download as a visible reviewer action. The agent and person share one visible, editable project. A first-run Judge Quick Start card shows tool readiness, explains the workflow, and copies the exact reproducible prompt. How to run the agent demo Relief Forge is the shared workspace, not the chat. On first visit, the Judge Quick Start card shows whether all four WebMCP tools are ready. After the card reports 4 AGENT TOOLS READY , select Copy prompt for AI chat , return to the Codex or ChatGPT conversation that opened Relief Forge, paste the prompt into that conversation's message box, press Send, and keep Relief Forge open. There is intentionally no prompt box inside Relief Forge. The agent's four tool calls update the same visible project the reviewer can inspect and edit. After dismissal, the instructions can be reopened with Run agent demo . If clipboard access is blocked, the complete prompt remains visible for manual copying. Why WebMCP improves the experience Before WebMCP, an agent could recommend settings or imitate fragile UI clicks. With WebMCP, it can translate the request into explicit units and constrained parameters, update the visible project, inspect the exact result the person sees, and prepare a snapshot-consistent package. The person remains in control and can inspect or edit the artifact after every step. Reproducible result The demo creates a 48 × 48 inch Polar Bloom using seed webmcp-polar-bloom-showcase-001 and a fixed warm architectural palette. The audited result is: 1219.2 × 1219.2 mm 2.4–30 mm actual depth range 81 deterministic parts 62 print plates 256 × 256 mm full bed 5 mm margins and 4 mm spacing No part exceeds 195.808 mm in either footprint dimension 195.808 × 190.805 mm largest actual placed footprint inside a 246 × 246 mm usable area Project wall-art-g6-238bfdaa Reference Chromium ZIP: 656,651 bytes Reference SHA-256: d86d4966242fd71542fcedab83bde3071447b9239e497fea2a9f59cc587462d0 Published-video clarification (1:27): The narration describes the largest part as just under 196 mm square. The exact largest placed footprint is 195.808 × 190.805 mm; the bed-fit conclusion is unchanged. The submitted Chromium reference ZIP contains 215 entries, including 81 part STLs, 62 packed-plate STLs, 63 3MF files, three assembly PDFs, a project recipe, and matching manifests. Its byte count and hash identify that audited browser artifact; exact ZIP bytes and equivalent near-tie packing choices are not claimed to match across JavaScript runtimes. Project identity, individual part geometry, dimensions, digital fit, inventory, and the 62-plate result matched across the audited runtimes. These are software checks, not claims of physical print, strength, or installation certification. How we built it Relief Forge is a React and TypeScript browser application. Geometry and stable identifiers remain deterministic local code. Printer packing, mesh checks, project state, and exports also run locally and repeat within the audited Chromium runtime; cross-runtime ZIP byte identity is not claimed. The challenge extension adds a narrow imperative WebMCP adapter around established editor actions. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool , use explicit schemas and physical bounds, update visible state before returning serializable results, read the current computed plan, and guard export preparation against stale project or printer configurations. Existing project and challenge extension Relief Forge existed before the challenge with deterministic geometry, exact-size controls, printer-bed packing, model and assembly previews, and STL, 3MF, PDF, manifest, recipe, and ZIP exports. During the challenge period, I added the four imperative WebMCP tools, lifecycle and schema validation, deterministic named WebMCP recipes including Polar Bloom, the visible agent-action status surface, stale-export protection, automated WebMCP coverage, Judge Quick Start, challenge documentation, and a separate sign-in-gated deployment. The public repository is a sanitized copy that excludes private tester records and private repository history. The pre-webmcp-public-snapshot tag records the copied pre-WebMCP application, and the comparison to main shows the challenge work: Baseline: https://github.com/ZivBY/relief-forge-webmcp/tree/pre-webmcp-public-snapshot Challenge diff: https://github.com/ZivBY/relief-forge-webmcp/compare/pre-webmcp-public-snapshot...main Challenges The hard part was defining a small, safe manufacturing contract: explicit units, deterministic style mappings, real printer dimensions, inspection of the same revision shown onscreen, and refusal to package stale or invalid state. Accomplishments Relief Forge lets a natural-language request drive a real creative-manufacturing workflow through structured tools rather than simulated clicks. Agent and manual interaction share one source of truth. Established geometry remains deterministic, and packing is repeatable within the audited Chromium runtime. What we learned Creative-software tools work best when designed like manufacturing commands: constrained inputs, explicit measurements, visible changes, reproducible results, revision-aware exports, and honest boundaries around digital validation. What's next Add more named deterministic recipes, verified printer profiles, optional slicer-supplied material and time estimates, and coverage for additional imperative WebMCP runtimes. title: Dim Hour
pitch: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page.
about_excerpt: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Dim Hour is a city guide - the places worth your time, scored, not starred - covering more than 19,000 restaurants, bars, hotels, and venues across 24 cities. For this challenge, dimhour.com became agent-native: the page itself registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the site can search the catalog, read a venue, check what is open tonight, draft an itinerary, and hand back a booking link - without scraping a pixel. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Planning a night out is one of the most common things people already ask an agent to help with, but today the agent scrapes pages and guesses at what the site already knows. WebMCP lets dimhour.com hand the agent its real search, scoring, and booking data as structured tools, in the same tab where the person is browsing. The catalog is the product; WebMCP makes it callable. Because the tools are thin adapters over a production venue API, every agent answer is grounded in live data instead of page scraping. How it creates a better user experience One page, two users. A person browsing the Dallas guide and their agent now work on the same surface. The agent calls the site's own tools and gets back the same scored venues, hours, and booking links the UI shows - no copy-pasting between a chat window and a browser, and no agent inventing hours, addresses, or availability. The person keeps the judgment (taste, swaps, vetoes); the agent does the legwork (searching, filtering, checking, assembling). The site stays the source of truth for both of them, and saving a plan stays a human action - the tools read, they never write. What people and agents can do together Co-plan a night in one sitting, in one page. "Dinner in Deep Ellum for four on Friday, then cocktails within walking distance." The agent searches the scored catalog, filters to what is actually open tonight using the same rule the site's own tonight strip uses, pulls full venue records, and drafts an ordered itinerary with real booking links (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock) while the person watches - then interrupts: "swap the second stop for something quieter," and the agent re-plans around the constraint. Before WebMCP, the agent could read the page but not act through the site's own logic, and the person could use the site but not delegate the legwork. Now both happen at once, and the result is a plan with real reservation links attached, not a list of suggestions. How we implemented WebMCP The WebMCP layer is one feature-detected script, webmcp.js, loaded by the site's index.html. Each of the five tools is a thin adapter that POSTs JSON-RPC tools/call to Dim Hour's existing MCP server (mcp.dimhour.com) and passes the result straight through: search_venues - one strong keyword plus city, neighborhood, cuisine, score floor, and price ceiling filters get_venue - the full record: hours, score, booking path, awards find_open_tonight - venues with a happy hour or late kitchen, best score first, using the same definition the site's own "tonight" strip uses, so the agent and the page agree build_itinerary - an ordered multi-stop plan with why and how to book each stop; saving stays a human action at /trip.html get_booking_link - the reservation platform and direct booking URL for a venue, returned for the agent to present; it never opens or books anything itself The script handles the in-flight standard rename (document.modelContext first, navigator.modelContext fallback) and is a silent no-op where no WebMCP host exists. No authentication; the tools expose only public, read-only catalog data. What predates the hackathon: the venue catalog, scoring pipeline, MCP server, and site. What was built during the submission window: webmcp.js, the tool schemas, and the index.html include - the public repo's README draws that line explicitly, with dated commits. Challenges we hit Search results deliberately do not carry hours - only full venue records do - so "open tonight" meant ranking candidates first, then reading the top few individually rather than filtering a field that is not there. Booking links live in the page's own catalog rather than the API, so the booking tool merges both sources and says so honestly when a city is not loaded. The verification suite now asserts substance (tonight actually finds venues; a booking link equals the catalog's own URL), not just shape - because an early version passed every check while two tools quietly returned nothing. title: AI-Native Contract Maker with WebMCP
pitch: A bilingual contract maker where humans and AI agents safely draft, edit, validate, review changes, and undo contract updates through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A bilingual contract maker where humans and AI agents safely draft, edit, validate, review changes, and undo contract updates through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tool Activity showing a real get_contract_state call. Contract Maker interface with live preview and ChatGPT integration. Inspiration I am not confident in English, so I am using translation tools to help write this submission. I am a self-employed business owner running a food truck, and I also enjoy programming as a hobby. I already had a smartphone-friendly contract maker on my own website. When I found this WebMCP Challenge, I decided to experiment with extending that existing application with WebMCP. I wanted to see whether an AI agent could work with a real web application in a more structured way, while still keeping important actions under human control. What it does AI-Native Contract Maker with WebMCP is a browser-based contract drafting application where humans and AI agents can collaboratively create and edit contracts through structured WebMCP tools. The AI agent can: Inspect the current contract state Create a contract from natural-language instructions Update only selected fields Switch between Japanese, English, and bilingual Japanese-English output Edit individual clauses Validate missing fields, dates, and bilingual consistency Review AI change history Undo the latest AI edit For example, a user can ask the AI to change only Party B's address. The WebMCP tool updates only that field and records the before-and-after values. The user can then undo the latest AI change and restore the previous state. PDF export is intentionally kept as a human-confirmed action. How we built it The application is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebMCP, and Netlify. WebMCP tools are registered in the application using structured tool definitions. These tools provide operations for contract inspection, targeted field updates, language switching, clause editing, validation, change history, undo, and activity monitoring. I also added a WebMCP Tool Activity panel so users can see when a real WebMCP tool has been executed, including the latest tool call and execution status. Contract data is processed in the browser and is not intentionally stored in a server-side database. The original browser-based Contract Maker existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the challenge period, I extended it with WebMCP support and AI-agent collaboration features. The public GitHub repository preserves the original pre-WebMCP version as its first commit so the challenge-period development can be clearly distinguished. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was determining whether the AI was actually using WebMCP or simply interacting with the normal browser interface. To solve this, I added the WebMCP Tool Activity panel directly to the application. It makes real WebMCP tool calls visible and distinguishable from ordinary browser interaction. Another challenge was making partial edits reliable. An instruction such as "change only Party B's address" should not modify unrelated contract fields. I also wanted AI actions to remain reversible and understandable, so I added before-and-after change history and undo support. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am especially proud that the application demonstrates several human-AI collaboration patterns in one working web application: Real WebMCP tool execution Natural-language contract creation Targeted field editing Japanese-English bilingual contracts Structured validation Before-and-after change history Undo support WebMCP activity monitoring Human confirmation before PDF generation The final PDF cannot be automatically generated by the AI. The user remains in control of the final action. What we learned Before this challenge, I had no practical experience building with WebMCP. Through this project, I learned how a website can expose structured capabilities directly to an AI agent instead of requiring the agent to rely only on visual browser interaction. I also learned how important transparency, reversibility, targeted editing, and human confirmation are when an AI agent can modify real application state. What's next for AI-Native Contract Maker with WebMCP I would like to continue improving: Agent-assisted contract validation Multilingual contract support More granular human approval controls Additional contract templates Safer and more transparent human-AI collaboration The broader goal is to explore how existing web applications can become interfaces designed for both humans and AI agents without sacrificing human control. This application assists with contract drafting and does not provide legal advice. Users should review all terms before using a generated contract.
