title: Swagger UI WebMCP
pitch: If you can Try it out, your agent can too — a Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI docs page into a live agent interface, using the environment and login you already have open.
about_excerpt: If you can Try it out, your agent can too — a Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI docs page into a live agent interface, using the environment and login you already have open. Like Comment Story Updates If you can Try it out, your agent can too. Swagger UI WebMCP is a reusable Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI documentation page into a live, session-scoped agent interface — and splits the decision of what that agent may touch among the four parties who each know something different. The agent calls the API through the exact environment, login, and request pipeline the developer already has open in the page. No AI SDK. No MCP server to install. No bearer token copied anywhere. Live demo: https://openapi-web-mcp.vercel.app Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/openapi-web-mcp The problem A developer working against an internal or partner API already has a browser tab where everything is correct: signed in, staging selected in the server dropdown, the right key pasted into Swagger UI's Authorize dialog, and the corporate proxy, CORS rules, and session cookies all working. To let an agent help with that same API, the entire environment has to be rebuilt somewhere else — install or write an MCP server, re-describe the endpoints, copy a bearer token out of the browser into a config file, and keep the two in sync forever. So the agent is useful for writing code about the API and useless for actually driving it. Underneath that is a second problem nobody has a good answer for: once the connector exists, who decides what the agent may touch? Today it is whoever wrote it, once, months ago, holding standing credentials. Audience: developers, QA and support engineers, and solutions/API-partner teams who live in OpenAPI documentation pages every day — and the API publishers who host those pages for them. Every internal and partner API with a Swagger UI docs page is a candidate. The idea: authority splits four ways, and only ever narrows Four parties each hold information the others don't, so each gets exactly the instrument they have the information for: the API publisher knows which endpoints are dangerous, expressed as x-webmcp annotations that travel with the OpenAPI document itself, reviewed and versioned; the page owner knows what this deployment is for, expressed as a webMcp.exposure default and an optional policyResolver; the person at the page knows what is happening right now, expressed as per-operation session locks scoped to this tab only; and the WebMCP client knows what to ask a human, expressed through MCP annotations and structured errors. The rule that makes them compose rather than conflict: every source may only tighten. All of them reduce to a level on the lattice hidden < read < write, the tightest wins, and hidden survives every setting, because refusing exposure is never a privilege escalation. The agent itself does not get a vote — session locks are module state the tools never touch. Why the documentation page is the right place WebMCP's defining property is that the page is the integration: capability lives in the tab, scoped to the session, and dies with it. API docs fit that shape better than almost anything else. The contract already exists and is machine-readable, so tools are derived, not hand-written. The ambient state — selected server, authorized schemes, cookies, interceptors — is simply already true in the tab. Ephemerality is a feature: nobody wants a persistent connector holding standing write access to production. And it generalizes: every Swagger UI page that adds one import becomes an agent surface for whatever API it documents. That surface is not small. swagger-ui-dist alone is pulled from npm roughly 51 million times a month, and Swagger UI is the default, unmodified docs renderer behind FastAPI's /docs route and NestJS's official OpenAPI module — so the install base this plugs into is already deployed, already authenticated, and already pointed at real APIs. (npm registry, 30 days ending 29 Aug 2026; per-package figures in the README.) This is not "write another MCP server" — no standing credentials, no separately maintained tool definitions. And it is not a browser-automation agent clicking through the UI — it calls the API directly through Swagger's own execution pipeline, with a generated tool schema and MCP annotations per operation. What people and agents can do together The human signs in, picks Sandbox, authorizes a scheme in Swagger's own dialog — the agent inherits all of it, live. The person types into the q box of Try it out and stops; the agent reads that value and finishes the call. Every agent execution renders in Swagger UI's own response panel, not a separate agent console. An access control sits next to Try-it-out on every operation: Full access, View only, Read only, Hidden. And the demo API logs whether each write arrived via the agent pipeline or by hand. The thing that was hard before: letting an agent act on a live, authenticated, environment-specific API without provisioning it any standing credentials or infrastructure — and being able to see, constrain, and revoke that in the same place you were already working. The bigger picture The four-way split is in service of something larger than one docs page. It turns an existing, enormous class of page into an agent gateway with no new infrastructure to run or revoke. The per-operation access control doubles as a supervised playground: turn an agent loose on a live API, watch every call land in the same response panel you use yourself, and keep the kill switch one click away. Because agent calls run through Swagger's own execute action — the same code path as Try it out — an agent's call and a human's call are directly comparable, which makes the page a debugging surface. And the mechanism the demo uses to fingerprint agent writes is exported: the plugin's agentExecution primitive is set for the duration of an agent-initiated request and cleared in a finally, so any Swagger UI deployment can read it from its own requestInterceptor and tag agent traffic in its own audit trail. None of that needs different code — it is the same lattice and the same execution path, looked at from four angles. How WebMCP was implemented One import into an existing Swagger UI config is the whole integration. When the browser provides document.modelContext, the plugin enumerates operations from Swagger UI's own resolved spec, resolves local $refs, converts parameters and request bodies into JSON Schema tool inputs, and registers two layers of tools: five stable core tools plus one direct tool per exposed operation, capped at 64 with graceful fallback to discovery and generic execution. The cap is enforced everywhere a tool name is advertised, so search and get can never name a tool that was not registered. Tools can never name a URL. A call resolves against the currently selected Swagger server and does not build its own fetch client — arguments are written into the Swagger store, the page's own execute action runs the request through its configured interceptors, credentials, and selected server, and the result is read back out of the store. That is why environment and login are inherited rather than duplicated. Direct tools, the generic executor, and the batch executor all funnel through one authorize function evaluated at call time against live state, so there is exactly one place exposure is enforced, and nothing is cached. The page never prompts — permission UX belongs to the WebMCP client; the page's interface to it is registration visibility, MCP annotations, and structured errors. Safety is structural. Schema compilation runs an allowlist of structural JSON Schema keywords. Credential-shaped names — password, apiKey, token, secret and their variants — are excluded at enumeration, in parameters and in request-body properties at any nesting depth, so they never enter a tool schema. A batch call exposure-checks every step before running the first. Each of these has a regression test; the reasoning is in docs/security-notes.md. Try it Open https://openapi-web-mcp.vercel.app , click Sign in, then ask your agent to check the environment, list active projects, try the usage report and explain why it fails, then create a project and show which writes came from an agent. Then by hand: authorize the bearer scheme and re-ask (now succeeds); switch the server to Production and ask again (different data, same tools); set an operation to Read only and watch the agent get a structured refusal. Operations can also carry a costHint annotation: a signal that a call costs money or has a real consequence beyond the request itself — a metered charge, a real SMS sent — without hiding the operation outright. It composes the same way destructive does (any source can flag it, none can clear it) and surfaces as costHint / costNote on the registered tool, so a WebMCP client can choose to confirm with a human before calling something the publisher flagged

title: GroundTrace WebMCP
pitch: Warranted operational memory for browser agents: WebMCP lets agents retrieve precedent, while GroundTrace decides whether it is safe to rely on.
about_excerpt: Warranted operational memory for browser agents: WebMCP lets agents retrieve precedent, while GroundTrace decides whether it is safe to rely on. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents can retrieve more and more information, but retrieval is not the same thing as authority. A remembered action may be stale, unsuccessful, unverified, or simply inappropriate to reuse. GroundTrace WebMCP gives browser agents access to operational memory while preserving that distinction: memory is a candidate, not authority. What it does GroundTrace exposes three native WebMCP tools directly from the web application: groundtrace_remember records a resolved incident with its action, outcome, verification state, timestamp, and provenance. groundtrace_recall retrieves relevant precedent and applies a deterministic warrant gate. groundtrace_explain exposes why GroundTrace admitted, held, or rejected the retrieved memory. Candidate memories receive a RELY , HOLD , or REJECT admission. Only RELY memories may supply an action as a recommendation. The key demonstration is deliberately a refusal. ChatGPT retrieves an exact-match incident with similarity 1, but because the stored memory is unverified, GroundTrace returns HOLD , reason memory_unverified , and recommendation: null . The agent successfully remembers. about_excerpt:
AI agents edit. Humans stay in control.

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore how AI agents could help with creative work without taking control away from the creator . This inspired us to build Agent Studio, where AI can perform editing tasks and suggest changes while humans approve important creative decisions. 

 What it does 

 Through WebMCP, the agent can interact with the video editor to:
🔍 Inspect projects and understand the current editing state
✏️ Modify captions and caption styling
⏱️ Adjust scene durations
🎬 Search real stock footage based on the video's content
💡 Propose visual changes to improve the edit
Human-in-the-Loop
The key idea behind Agent Studio is controlled autonomy.
AI agents can handle repetitive editing work, but consequential visual changes aren't applied blindly. Instead, the agent presents proposed changes for human approval.
This keeps the creator in control of the final creative decisions while allowing AI to handle tedious production task.
The agent operates the tools. The creator controls the outcome. 

 ## How We Built It 

 We built Agent Studio as a web-based video editor with WebMCP tools that let AI agents inspect projects and perform editing actions. The agent can modify captions, adjust scene durations, search Pexels for relevant stock footage, and propose visual changes. A human approval layer ensures important changes are reviewed before they are applied. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making AI interactions with the video editor reliable while keeping humans in control. We also had to handle real-time WebMCP tool calls, stock footage search, and ensure consequential edits required approval instead of being applied automatically. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working environment where AI agents can interact with a real video editor through WebMCP while keeping humans in control. We're especially proud of combining agent-powered editing, real stock footage search, and human approval into one collaborative workflow. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that AI agents can be powerful creative collaborators when they have structured tools and clear boundaries. WebMCP showed us how agents can interact with real creative workflows, while human approval makes that automation safer and more useful. 

 What's next for Agent Studio 

 We plan to: 

 Add more WebMCP editing tools for transitions, audio, effects, and layouts.
Support multiple specialized agents working together on a project.
Improve the approval system with side-by-side previews and edit history.
Add smarter stock-footage recommendations based on each scene.
Enable creators to save, reuse, and share agent workflows.

title: Mapbox AI Trip Planner
pitch: Ask an AI to plan your trip and watch it find real places, draw a real route, and pin your itinerary live on a Mapbox map. No backend, no extension. Just WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Ask an AI to plan your trip and watch it find real places, draw a real route, and pin your itinerary live on a Mapbox map. No backend, no extension. Just WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Walking trip planned in Paris New Window to plan a trip Inspiration The WebMCP Challenge asks what the open web looks like when it's built for humans and agents at once. We'd already been building @mapbox/web-mcp-server , a library that registers Mapbox GL JS map interactions as WebMCP tools, and had written up a design thesis for it before ever building a demo: a geospatial AI agent needs two things to be genuinely useful, a data layer (geocoding, search, directions) and a live rendering surface it can actually act on. Most "AI + maps" demos fake the second half: a chat response describing a trip, maybe a static image. WebMCP is the first browser API that lets a page hand an agent direct control over a live map instead, the same way an MCP server hands it a data source. We wanted to prove that idea end-to-end, not just describe it. What it does Open the demo, paste an Anthropic API key, and ask for a trip: "Plan a half-day trip in Paris: the Eiffel Tower, a nearby cafe, and the Louvre, with walking directions between each stop." An agent geocodes the real places, drops pins, pulls a real walking route, draws it on the map, and frames the whole trip, live, while you watch. An itinerary panel and an activity log rebuild themselves from the actual tool calls as they happen, so the WebMCP mechanism is visible, not just its output. How we built it The core is a small TypeScript library ( src/ , strict mode, pure ESM) where every map capability is a factory function, createFlyToTool(map) , createAddMarkerTool(map, markers, stops) , returning a ToolDescriptor that closes over the live mapboxgl.Map instance. registerMapboxTools(map) wires all of them up against navigator.modelContext.registerTool() , plus an onToolCall hook so a host page can observe every call live. On top of that, the demo does two things most WebMCP demos skip. First, it closes the "two data layers" loop from our own design doc for real: alongside the map-control tools, the page registers a small second set, geocode_place , search_category , get_directions , that call Mapbox's public Search Box and Directions REST APIs directly via fetch() . These are demo-only and never exported from the published library, but they mean the whole trip-planning loop works from one deployed page with no server standing in as an MCP host. Second, the deployed demo is usable with zero setup: an embedded BYOK (bring-your-own-key) chat widget ( demo/chat.ts ) using the official @anthropic-ai/sdk with dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true , running a manual agentic loop against claude-opus-5 . List the registered tools, send them as the model's tools , execute whatever it calls via navigator.modelContextTesting.executeTool() , feed results back, repeat. The key never leaves the visitor's browser except to Anthropic directly. For anyone who'd rather not paste a key, the page also exposes a copyable system prompt for driving it via Claude Desktop or any other WebMCP-compatible extension instead: same tools, different agent. It's deployed as a static Vite build on Vercel, with the Mapbox token set as a public build-time config variable (Mapbox tokens are meant to be client-embedded, unlike the Anthropic key). Challenges we ran into Geocoding is pickier than it looks. Early on, a query like "Louvre Museum, Paris" returned an unrelated Airbnb listing ranked above the actual landmark; the city qualifier confused relevance ranking more than it helped. The fix was querying just the bare place name and using proximity bias to disambiguate instead, which we had to encode directly into the tool description and system prompt so the agent wouldn't do it wrong on its own. Some organizations block this pattern entirely. Mid-testing, a live call to Anthropic's API came back with authentication_error: CORS requests are not allowed for this Organization . Some orgs disable direct-from-browser API access as a security policy, which is exactly the risk dangerouslyAllowBrowser warns about, just enforced server-side. No client code can work around an org policy, so instead we made the failure mode honest: detect it and point the visitor at the Claude Desktop fallback with an accurate explanation, instead of a misleading "invalid API key." LLM tool-calling isn't perfectly deterministic. During a real end-to-end run, the agent issued an identical add_marker call twice in one turn, producing a visible duplicate row in the itinerary. We added a small guard against adjacent duplicate stops and nudged the system prompt to clear stale markers before replanning, a good reminder that a UI built on top of agent tool calls has to defend against the agent occasionally repeating itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of We shipped and verified a genuine end-to-end run, not just isolated pieces in a demo script: a real Anthropic API call driving real Mapbox geocoding and directions calls, ending in a route drawn on real streets and an itinerary that matches exactly what the agent did. The zero-backend architecture holds up under that test too: no server anywhere in the loop, yet the demo still closes the "data layer plus rendering layer" idea we set out to prove. We're also proud of how we found problems: not by guessing, but by watching the itinerary and activity log disagree with what we expected, then chasing the real cause. That's how we caught the geocoding query issue, the org CORS policy, and the duplicate tool call, each a real bug against a real API, not a hypothetical. What we learned That the "two MCPs, one agent loop" idea holds up in practice, not just on paper, and that most of the real engineering in an agent-facing feature isn't the tool-calling plumbing (which is refreshingly thin once you commit to the tool-factory pattern). It's the edge cases: query phrasing that reads fine to a human but confuses a search API, org-level policies that only surface as a runtime error, and an agent's own occasional non-determinism. Building the itinerary and activity log to render straight off live tool calls, rather than trusting the model's narration, turned out to be the single best debugging tool we had. It's also what makes the demo convincing: you're not watching a chat bot describe a trip, you're watching WebMCP actually happen. What's next for Mapbox AI Trip Planner The bigger opportunity is first-party integration. The same tool-factory pattern that controls this demo map could register Studio-specific tools, select_layer , publish_style , undo and redo , directly against Mapbox Studio's live style editor, turning "how do I write this expression" into a conversation instead of a documentation search. Closer to home, we'd like to stream the chat widget's responses instead of waiting for a full reply, and give the agent a way to search points of interest by category, price, and rating rather than just name, so trip planning can go beyond landmarks into real day-to-day recommendations. title: Consensus
pitch: Human + AI decision workspace powered by WebMCP, where agents research, score, flag conflicts, and propose rankings while humans retain final control.
about_excerpt: Human + AI decision workspace powered by WebMCP, where agents research, score, flag conflicts, and propose rankings while humans retain final control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration - AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of researching, analyzing, and making recommendations, but important decisions still require human judgment. We wanted to build a workspace where humans and AI could work together on the same decision instead of the AI simply giving a final answer. Consensus was inspired by the idea of making AI an active collaborator while keeping humans in control of important decisions. What it does - Consensus is a shared decision and research workspace for human + AI collaboration. In Decision Mode, AI agents can use WebMCP tools to read the board, add options, score options, flag conflicts, resolve flags, and propose rankings. Humans can independently score options, review AI reasoning, dispute evaluations, and lock the final decision. Consensus also includes Research Mode for extracting claims, checking evidence, identifying contradictions, and building citation relationships. All important actions are persisted and can be reviewed through activity history and provenance. How we built it - The frontend is built with React and Vite, with WebMCP integrated through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The backend uses FastAPI and is deployed on Google Cloud Run. Firestore stores shared board state, evaluations, flags, and activity history. Vertex AI with Gemini 2.5 Flash provides AI-assisted analysis. The WebMCP tools connect to the same real backend operations used by the application, so agent actions update persistent state rather than a simulated demo. Challenges we ran into - A major challenge was deciding what AI agents should be allowed to do and what should remain under human control. We wanted the agent to be useful without allowing it to silently make consequential decisions. We also had to make WebMCP tool registration reliable as the application changed between different modes and states. Finally, connecting the React frontend, FastAPI backend, Firestore, Vertex AI, and WebMCP into one working deployed application required careful coordination. Accomplishments that we're proud of - We are proud that Consensus is a real deployed WebMCP application with persistent state, rather than just a prototype or mock demonstration. The live application exposes six Decision-mode WebMCP tools that can interact with the shared workspace. We are especially proud of the human-agent boundary: agents can investigate, evaluate, flag issues, and recommend actions, while humans retain control over scoring, overrides, and locking the final decision. Our backend verification tests also pass checks for persistence, provenance, conflict handling, evaluation history, overrides, and locking. What we learned - We learned that WebMCP becomes much more powerful when tools operate on real shared application state. We also learned that human-AI collaboration is not only about giving agents more capabilities. It is equally important to define the actions they should not control. Building Consensus also taught us how browser-native agent tools can work together with a persistent cloud backend and an AI reasoning layer. What's next for Consensus - Next, we want to expand Consensus into more complex collaborative workflows. We plan to explore multi-agent debate, stronger evidence and citation verification, configurable decision rubrics, richer provenance, and approval workflows with different levels of human confirmation. Our long-term goal is to create a workspace where humans and AI agents can work together on complex decisions while keeping the reasoning, evidence, actions, and final authority visible and auditable. title: fondof
pitch: forge repo-specific skills from the open web, with your agent.
about_excerpt: forge repo-specific skills from the open web, with your agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most of what we learn still lives in places built for humans, not agents: podcasts, blog posts, talks, documentation, and newsletters. They’re full of useful techniques, but they aren’t skills an agent can pick up and apply to a specific codebase. fondof gives that knowledge a second life. Give it a source URL, a stated need, or up to four sources, and it turns the underlying ideas into a concise, repo-specific skill—with attribution intact. We also wanted to explore what an agent-native web actually feels like. With WebMCP, fondof exposes its capabilities directly to agents, so a user can stay in a conversation and say: “Find me a skill on React performance and forge one from this talk for my repo.” What it does fondof turns knowledge into agent-ready skills: Extract — pulls actionable ideas from articles, YouTube, docs, or free-text needs. Fit — matches those ideas to a target repo’s stack, conventions, and paths. Forge — creates a short, copyable skill for Cursor, Claude, Kiro, or any agent. Hand off — copies Markdown or creates a shareable /s/{hash} link. Attribute — preserves source attribution and optionally anchors provenance on Monad. It exposes three WebMCP tools: search_skills — search the public skill pool. get_skill — retrieve a skill by hash. compose_skill — forge a skill from URLs or a stated need. Humans decide what they want; agents handle the extraction, discovery, composition, and formatting. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 16, Framer Motion, Tailwind, deployed on Netlify. API: Cloudflare Worker + Hono, with Durable Objects for coordination, KV for sessions, and Workers AI for LLM + embeddings. Ingestion: Firecrawl / Readability for articles and docs, YouTube transcripts, plus a local fallback for offline needs. Search & fit: Exa for semantic discovery, plus /api/skills?q= for searching the public skill pool by topic, repo, stack, or source. Blockchain: SkillPool on Monad testnet for optional public provenance. Agent layer: webmcp-provider.tsx registers the three tools; /.well-known/webmcp and Permissions-Policy enable discovery. Monorepo: pnpm workspaces across web , api , core , cli , contracts , and shared . We also dogfooded the build process in Kiro with a spec-first trail mapping directly to the shipped code. Challenges we ran into Multi-source composition: Combining up to four sources requires deduplication, merging, progress tracking, and partial-failure handling without losing the whole batch. Agent UX: WebMCP tools need to tell an agent not just what they do, but when to use them, what inputs they need, and how to recover from failures. Attribution without friction: We wanted every skill traceable to its sources without requiring wallets or sign-in for the happy path. Honest failures: Instead of silently swallowing bad URLs, the Studio surfaces ingest errors and compose_skill returns structured source_failures . Accomplishments that we're proud of A real, deployed WebMCP implementation with three working tools, a /.well-known/webmcp manifest, and the correct permissions configuration. Multi-source skill composition across up to four URLs, with per-source progress and failure reporting. A public skill pool with search, source-domain pages, and shareable skill pages. Agent discovery, retrieval, and creation as one continuous workflow. Honest degradation when ingestion fails, fallbacks are used, or the chain is unavailable. Open source and tested: MIT licensed, with 209 passing tests and a live Cloudflare Worker. What we learned The browser can be the integration layer. WebMCP lets the site expose its capabilities directly to agents, without requiring a custom MCP server or separate API key. Search is essential for agent-native apps. If an agent can’t find an existing skill, it will re-forge what already exists. Attribution can become a network primitive. Sources produce skills, skills get reused and re-forged, and outcomes can eventually feed back into the pool. Humans + agents work best as a loop: the human decides, the agent discovers and composes, and the human stays in control. What's next for fondof Creator analytics so authors can see which content became skills and where those skills were used. title: Mirror WebMCP Secure
pitch: Mirror lets AI agents use private website data through native WebMCP tools without copying the raw data into agent context. Only the minimum approved information crosses the boundary.
about_excerpt: Mirror lets AI agents use private website data through native WebMCP tools without copying the raw data into agent context. Only the minimum approved information crosses the boundary. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP makes websites actionable by AI agents, which is powerful, but a lot of useful actions depend on private user data. The problem is that the easiest way to build these workflows is often to give the agent the raw data it needs. That can put sensitive information into model context, logs, traces, or downstream systems. We wanted to see if there was a better way: let the agent act, without giving it the full private record. What it does Mirror WebMCP Secure adds a privacy boundary around native WebMCP Site Tools. Our demo is a procurement workflow. A buyer wants to purchase GPUs. The buyer has private requirements, and the seller has private pricing rules. Instead of copying the buyer's full record into ChatGPT, the website seals that private state into a short-lived, context-bound capability. ChatGPT can then use native procurement Site Tools through that capability. Only the information needed for the action is passed across, and sensitive steps still require explicit user approval. The end result is that the agents can find a product, request a proposal, release it, and accept it without either side getting the other's full private context. Why WebMCP is a good fit This is more than a chatbot reading a webpage. The agent needs to discover structured actions from the site and then use them to: find compatible products request a seller proposal release an offer accept it WebMCP gives us that action layer. Mirror sits around those actions and controls what private data they are allowed to receive and what result they are allowed to return. Better user experience Without this kind of boundary, the user either has to expose sensitive information to the agent or do more of the workflow manually. With Mirror, the user keeps the private data on the website and lets ChatGPT handle the workflow through Site Tools. The user only steps in when something important needs approval. That means the agent can still be useful, while the user keeps control over what gets disclosed and when. How we built it The website exposes four native procurement Site Tools: procurement.find_private_matches procurement.request_seller_proposal procurement.release_proposal procurement.accept_proposal The buyer form is sealed into a restricted mirrorh_... capability instead of being copied into agent context. Mirror acts as the boundary between the private website state, the user agent, and the seller-side action. The seller receives only the minimum approved handoff needed to make the proposal. The seller-side inference also runs through Mirror using ciphertext compute. ChatGPT discovers and invokes the tools natively through WebMCP rather than relying on visual page automation. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making the workflow useful without leaking more private data than necessary. We also wanted to avoid a fake-looking demo where everything happens through a local button. The actual flow had to work through native Site Tools. Another challenge was approvals. Releasing a proposal and accepting it are different decisions, so we treated them as separate approval steps rather than collapsing them into one. We also wanted the privacy claims to be visible, not just something we said in the description. So the demo includes a proof view showing what each side actually received. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got the complete native WebMCP flow working end to end. Two agents can collaborate on the procurement task while each side keeps its private context. At the end of the demo: the seller does not receive the buyer's budget the seller does not receive the browser handle the seller's private price floor is not returned buyer fields returned: 0 At the same time, the workflow still produces a real usable offer. That balance between usefulness and privacy is the part we're most proud of. What we learned One thing that became very clear while building this is that tool access and data access are not the same problem. WebMCP defines what the agent can do. Mirror focuses on what private data that action can receive, and what result is allowed to leave the boundary. We also learned that approval works better when it is tied to meaningful user decisions rather than added as a generic confirmation step. What's next for Mirror WebMCP Secure This procurement flow is just one example. The same pattern could be useful in finance, healthcare, legal, and enterprise workflows where agents need to act on sensitive information without directly owning the raw data. Next, we want to explore richer tool policies, stronger capability binding, more multi-agent workflows, and an easier integration path for developers who want to add privacy-preserving WebMCP actions to existing sites. title: Signett
pitch: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications.
about_excerpt: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What is Signett Signett is a reliability and evaluation layer for production WebMCP applications. In our live Saleor demo , an agent discovers catalog and checkout tools, finds a product, requests human approval, and submits a purchase request. What makes it special is that the storefront updates only after the purchase is verifiably complete, as provided by Signett. We also simulate a browser response loss after the mutation commits and show how Signett recovers the authoritative result instead of creating a duplicate. What it does WebMCP gives agents a structured way to use website capabilities. Signett adds the execution semantics and developer workflow needed to operate those capabilities reliably. The Signett SDK accomplishes that through several core features: JSON Schema validation before application code runs trusted application context and application-owned authorization human confirmation for consequential effects idempotency and replay coordination operation journaling and ambiguous-failure recovery authoritative postcondition verification cancellation and structured repair guidance privacy-conscious OpenTelemetry traces React bindings for verified UI updates deterministic testing without a model or browser Simple read tools remain lightweight. Consequential tools can use the complete guarded lifecycle. Signett does not replace WebMCP, authentication, backend transaction guarantees, or application business logic. The website continues to own identity, policy, state, consent UI, and every backend effect. Signett creates a structured boundary around those existing capabilities. The wider project includes the TypeScript SDK, a Chrome side-panel agent, a headless evaluation CLI, a local Inspector, OpenTelemetry export, reference applications, reproducible benchmarks, and reviewed evidence. Inspiration - Why Do We Need This? I am a strong believer that the web will be largely agentic in a few years. While we have seen a lot of promise with browser-use agents, what bothered me the most was that these harnesses were trying to operate on websites built for humans, clicking buttons, while they should be using tools/MCPs. Then, I discovered WebMCP and was instantly excited. However, I quickly found that while the protocol is extremely valuable, a real developer trying to make their websites agentic doesn't have an ecosystem built around it. Specifically, I saw several problems: What happens when an agent retries a purchase? What if the backend commits an effect but the response disappears? How does the user retain control over consequential actions? When should the UI update? How does a developer test the interface repeatedly, inspect traces, or detect a regression? These are familiar distributed-systems problems, but agentic websites make them more common and more consequential. Signett was built to answer a specific question: How do we move from “an agent can call this tool” to “an agent can perform this action safely, predictably, and verifiably”? That idea became Signett. How we built it Signett is a TypeScript monorepo with four primary layers. Signett SDK createSignett() creates a WebMCP-facing application surface. signett.expose() compiles the tool’s schema and registers it through the native document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Each tool defines its agent-facing contract and existing application function. Optional hooks add context, authorization, confirmation, idempotency, recovery, verification, output budgets, and lifecycle observation. Signett Chrome Agent The Chrome side-panel agent discovers and invokes only the WebMCP tools exposed by the active page. It deliberately has no DOM or screenshot fallback, so missing or poorly designed capabilities remain visible to developers. Signett Eval The CLI opens the real application in headless Chrome, discovers its live WebMCP inventory, runs saved tasks, and records bounded evidence. Applications can provide their own reset, snapshot, and grading hooks. This means success can be determined from the database or domain model rather than from the agent’s final response. signett check compares evaluation results against a reviewed baseline and can detect regressions in task success, safety, capability discovery, tool selection, argument validity, latency, token usage, and trial coverage. Observability and benchmarks Signett emits lifecycle events covering validation, authorization, confirmation, execution, replay or recovery, output measurement, and verification. These can power an in-page Inspector or be exported as OTLP/HTTP JSON to systems such as Jaeger. Inputs, outputs, application context, error messages, and stack traces are excluded by default. The repository also includes deterministic safety tests, real-agent evaluations, reference integrations, benchmark methodology, and reviewed evidence. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest problems was defining correct behavior after an ambiguous failure: a server may successfully commit an order or payment while the response is lost. Blindly retrying could duplicate the action, but blindly reporting failure would also be incorrect. Signett combines durable idempotency records, operation journals, recovery logic, and authoritative state verification to handle this case explicitly. Authorization and idempotency also interact in subtle ways. Returning a cached result must never bypass a current permission check. Signett therefore reevaluates authorization before every idempotency lookup, including replays. Another challenge was making observability useful without turning it into a privacy risk. Signett records lifecycle metadata and timing information by default, while avoiding tool inputs, outputs, application context, and stack traces unless the application explicitly chooses otherwise. Building high-quality benchmarks to hill-climb on was hard, but I think we got a lot of good-quality evaluations. Check out the benchmarks folder in the open-source repository. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental and evolving. I had to design useful abstractions without hiding the native API or prematurely inventing a competing protocol. Accomplishments that we're proud of Signett became more than a wrapper around tool registration. It now supports an end-to-end developer loop: Expose a native WebMCP capability. Inspect and invoke it in Chrome. Test its execution invariants deterministically. Exercise it with a real model in headless Chrome. Grade the result against the authoritative application state. Inspect its lifecycle through OpenTelemetry. Compare the run with a reviewed baseline. The same live WebMCP tools power the browser agent, the application UI, deterministic tests, and headless evaluations. There is no parallel demo-only tool catalog. We also validated the model against larger applications: Saleor: checkout, approval, lost-response recovery, replay, and authoritative verification Cal.diy: a real agent completed a booking after an injected lost response, with exactly one booking independently observed in Postgres an authenticated payment application used for deterministic safety and repeated agent-effectiveness studies What we learned The biggest lesson was that defining a tool schema is not the same as creating a trustworthy execution boundary. Agentic actions amplify several familiar distributed-systems problems. Retries, concurrency, authorization changes, cancellations, and lost responses become especially important when an agent can make purchases, send payments, or change persistent state. I also learned that the agent’s response is not proof that a task succeeded. Consequential actions need to be verified against the authoritative application state. The same principle applies to evaluation: the application’s database or domain model should grade success, not the agent transcript. Another important lesson was that deterministic testing and probabilistic agent evaluation serve different purposes. Deterministic tests prove safety invariants. Repeated agent trials reveal whether tools are discoverable, understandable, and effective. Most importantly, I learned that reliability features must remain composable. A read-only search tool should be easy to expose, while a payment or order mutation should be able to opt into stronger controls. Benchmarks and Results Signett's benchmarks grade consequential tasks against authoritative application state, not the agent's final answer or the tool's own response. Safe success means that the requested goal was reached without a forbidden or duplicate effect. Benchmark metric Baseline Signett Improvement Safe recovery success across 42 real-agent runs Raw WebMCP: 2/21 (9.5%) 21/21 (100%) 10.5x success rate Unsafe retries during recovery Raw WebMCP: 12/21 0/21 All observed unsafe retries eliminated Median recovery time Raw WebMCP: 20.9 s 14.1 s

title: StructSketch
pitch: Describe a structure by voice. StructSketch uses WebMCP to create, analyze, inspect, and safely improve the live 3D model with deterministic calculations and explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: Describe a structure by voice. StructSketch uses WebMCP to create, analyze, inspect, and safely improve the live 3D model with deterministic calculations and explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates A voice request turns spoken structural intent into WebMCP site tool calls. The existing S-Structures solver calculates the model; the agent never invents engineering results. The change is applied only after explicit human approval, then the analysis runs again. Agent Activity records tool calls, outcomes, UI changes, and analysis versions for an auditable review. Validated parameters generate deterministic geometry, supports, materials, and loads. WebMCP lets the agent inspect the live model, highlight critical members, and control the visible result view. A proposed section change is analyzed as a preview while the live model remains unchanged. StructSketch — Talk to Your Structure Open the tablet. Sketch the frame. Say what you need. See what needs attention. An agent-native workspace for fast, preliminary structural review in the field. Inspiration Picture a timber-framing crew in North America or a compact residential job in Japan. The question is often much smaller than a full building design: Is this light frame behaving as expected? Which member deserves attention? Would a larger section make a meaningful difference? Can we get a useful first answer before returning to the office? These decisions often begin with a hand sketch, a calculator, and practical experience. Full structural-analysis packages are powerful, but creating a model, entering loads, finding the governing result, and revising a member can be too much setup for a quick first look. I wanted that first pass to feel as natural as showing the structure to another person: draw or describe it, ask a question, and see the answer on the same screen. StructSketch does not replace professional design. It makes the preliminary check faster to start, easier to see, and possible to review later. What it does StructSketch is a browser-based 3D structural workspace designed for a tablet-sized field workflow. Sketch, open, or describe a simple structure. Let the agent translate the request into one of five bounded templates: timber warehouse, portal frame, canopy, roof truss, or multistory frame. Confirm the interpreted dimensions, supports, material, and loading before the current model is replaced. Run a deterministic preliminary check and see the model, deformation, warnings, and governing member in the same workspace. Preview a section or material change without modifying the model. Apply it only after explicit human approval. Export an auditable review record containing the model summary, assumptions, results, changes, and Agent Activity history. The key experience is simple: Spoken intent → live 3D model → deterministic analysis → visible result → human-approved change How to try it Open the live StructSketch demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser, then give the agent one of the prompts below. A single kickoff prompt schedules the complete workflow. The agent will pause only when human approval is required to replace the model or apply a proposed change. Timber warehouse — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. I want a preliminary review of a timber warehouse: 12.2 m clear span, 4.9 m eave height, 4:12 roof pitch, two 4.8 m bays, cedar timber, pinned bases, collar tie and knee braces, 1.0 kN/m² snow load, and 0.3 kN/m² dead load. First, repeat the interpreted structure and parameters and ask me to approve replacing the current model. After I approve, create and analyze it, summarize the live model, run the deterministic quick check, show the overall deformation, find and focus the governing member, and explain the result in plain English. Then check whether the catalog contains a larger timber section for that governing member. If it does, preview it without changing the model, show the before-and-after result, and ask for my approval before applying it. If no larger timber section exists, do not invent or mix materials; explain the catalog limit and export the review report. Keep the Agent Activity panel visible if available. Steel canopy — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. Review an 8 m steel canopy, 3.5 m high and 4 m deep, with fixed bases, a 1:20 roof pitch, and a 4 kN/m downward roof line load. Repeat the interpreted parameters and ask before replacing the current model. After approval, create the canopy, summarize it, run the deterministic quick check, show deformation, identify and focus the governing member, and explain what needs attention. Preview the H-400×200×8×13 catalog section (`h400`) for that member without modifying the model and ask before applying it. After approval, apply the change, rerun the analysis, compare the results, and export the review report. Keep the Agent Activity panel visible if available. Two-storey steel frame — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. Create a preliminary model of a two-storey, two-bay steel frame with 8 m total frame width divided into two bays, 3.3 m per storey, 5 m frame depth, fixed bases, and a 4 kN/m downward beam load. Confirm your interpretation with me before replacing the model. After approval, create it and continue through the entire review: model summary, deterministic quick check, deformation view, governing-member search and focus, and a plain-English explanation. Preview the H-400×200×8×13 catalog section (`h400`) for the governing member without changing anything. Ask for approval, then apply it only if approved, rerun the check, compare before and after, and export the final review report with Agent Activity included. Reusable prompt template Use the StructSketch site tools to review [STRUCTURE TYPE] with [DIMENSIONS], [MATERIAL], [SUPPORTS], and [LOAD]. Confirm the interpreted parameters before replacing the model. After approval, create the model, summarize it, run the quick check, show deformation, find and focus the governing member, and explain the result. Preview a suitable improvement without changing the model, ask for approval, then apply it only if approved. Finally, rerun the analysis, compare before and after, and export the review report. Keep Agent Activity visible. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess what a technical page means from pixels, labels, menus, and click positions. That is fragile, especially when the important information is the live engineering state behind the interface. With WebMCP, StructSketch exposes meaningful actions directly: Summarize the structure currently open on the page. Run the preliminary analysis. Find and highlight the governing member. Show the deformation or check result. Preview a proposed change without touching the model. Apply the approved change and prepare a review report. The page is no longer just something an agent clicks. It becomes a shared workspace where the person and the agent see the same structure, the same result, and the same history. Clear responsibilities The person provides intent, checks the interpretation, and approves consequential changes. The agent translates natural language into structured actions and guides the workflow. StructSketch generates bounded geometry and performs the numerical analysis. The agent does not make up the engineering numbers. How we built it StructSketch is a static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application deployed on GitHub Pages. It registers 11 site tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools provide structured access to: the model currently visible on the page; the existing S-Structures linear-static solver; critical-member and result-view inspection; five validated structural templates; preview, approve, apply, and revert operations; and a structured review report. The five generators accept bounded parameters and create reproducible geometry, members, supports, sections, and loads. The existing S-Structures engine—not the language model—performs every calculation. Every tool call returns structured, JSON-safe results. The Agent Activity panel records its input, result, warnings, visible UI changes, and analysis version, so the interaction remains visible rather than hidden behind the conversation. Human control and safe editing Inspection and editing are deliberately separated. When someone asks whether a larger section would help, StructSketch first calculates a preview against the current analysis version. The model remains unchanged. Applying the proposal requires explicit confirmation. If the model has changed since the preview, the stale proposal is rejected. If an update fails, the mutation is rolled back. The person can see what was proposed, what was approved, and what changed. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was connecting an agent to a protected, pre-existing analysis core without rewriting it or duplicating its mathematics. about_excerpt: Students can use their familiar ChatGPT interface to get grounded answers and help, fast, with no setup, via a WebMCP integration for Moodle. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In my time at university, which used an OpenLMS deployment based on Moodle, course content was often scattered and hard to dig through. When OpenAI announced The WebMCP Challenge, the lightbulb went off. WebMCP moves tool execution right into the browser. So instead of fighting IT firewalls or using API keys, tools run inside the student's active browser session. I wanted to build a real WebMCP enablement plugin that turns standard Moodle course pages into active, agentic workspaces for both students and instructors, requiring no additional setup from them. What it does moodle-webmcp is a Moodle plugin that enables a number of useful WebMCP tools primarily for students, with some extra tools useful for course admins. When you open course pages in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 146+, the plugin automatically declares structured AI tools directly on the web page to: Retrieve upcoming assignments and labs in chronological order Fetch relevant lecture summaries and course materials Generate an adaptive day-by-day study schedule based on available daily hours Critique a student's draft essay based on the assignment's official grading rubrics How we built it Moodle Plugin Core : Developed local_webmcp in PHP, integrating with Moodle's navigation hooks and AMD loader. Deployment : Packaged Alpine Linux with PHP 8.3, Moodle 5.2.2, and SQLite3 on Render with persistent disk storage and a custom domain ( moodle-webmcp.akashgpt.me ). Development Tooling : Built and debugged the full stack with Codex and Chrome DevTools MCP. Challenges we ran into Minimal issues overall. The main hurdles involved working through Moodle-specific quirks and container setup, such as aligning with Moodle 5.x's public document root structure and ensuring database gradebook items were properly registered for assignment activities. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Zero-Token Authentication : No API keys required. Tools inherit the student's existing authenticated web session and CSRF tokens automatically. Real, Live Moodle Environment : Built and deployed a full Moodle 5.2.2 LMS with seeded courses and working student/teacher roles rather than a static mockup. Practical Student Utility : Tools like adaptive study scheduling and rubric draft critique solve real, everyday student problems. What we learned WebMCP vs. MCP : For web applications, in-browser execution is fundamentally more secure and accessible than backend daemons for everyday users. Defense-in-Depth in the Browser : Constraining tool inputs with strict JSON schemas and enforcing read-only boundaries protects against indirect prompt injection from untrusted course forums or scraped HTML. Moodle Plugin Internals : Deepened our understanding of Moodle's local plugin architecture, AMD modules, and database hooks. What's next for moodle-webmcp Expanding the number and types of tools available and integrating deeper with Moodle, including: Two-Way Action Tools with Confirmation Gates : Adding safe, human-confirmed write capabilities like save_assignment_draft and post_forum_reply . Discussion Board & Workshop Integration : Extending WebMCP tools to summarize peer reviews and handle complex forum threads. Official Moodle Plugins Directory Release : Packaging local_webmcp for official submission to the Moodle Plugins Directory so LMS administrators worldwide can install it in one click.  Inspiration 

 Shopping for a saree often means translating a personal request into filters, comparing several products, opening product pages, and keeping track of a cart. Traditional web agents have to guess at buttons and page structure. We wanted the storefront to expose a clear, predictable interface for people and agents to use together. 

 What we built 

 Vaanzari adds browser-native WebMCP tools for public saree discovery and visible cart actions. A compatible agent can search products, retrieve a product, compare products, open a product page, add an available product to the cart, and open the cart. The person remains in control of product choice, checkout, payment, and order confirmation. 

 How we built it 

 We register six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : search-sarees , get-saree , compare-sarees , open-saree , add-saree-to-cart , and open-cart . The tools use a public-safe catalog adapter plus browser navigation and cart adapters. Results map back into the visible UI so the person and agent share the same state. We also added a diagnostics view, tests, and a standalone Apache-2.0 reference repository. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The hard part was choosing a useful boundary without exposing account, customer, checkout, payment, or order workflows to an agent. We learned that structured tools make actions more predictable than UI guessing, while explicit human control keeps consequential commerce decisions with the shopper.

pitch: Stadtoskop uses WebMCP to let AI agents directly discover verified local events and venues, turning local culture into structured, conversational discovery.
about_excerpt:
Stadtoskop uses WebMCP to let AI agents directly discover verified local events and venues, turning local culture into structured, conversational discovery.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 




 
 InspirationInspiration 

 Finding something interesting to do in a city is still surprisingly fragmented. Events are spread across venue websites, cultural institutions, clubs and organizers. Stadtoskop started as an attempt to turn this fragmented information into a visual and playful way to discover local culture. 

 While building it, another question became increasingly important: How should AI agents discover local culture? 

 Today, an agent often has to search the web, interpret different websites and reconstruct information that already exists as structured data. 

 WebMCP offers a much cleaner approach. 

 What it does 

 Stadtoskop is a local culture discovery platform starting in Leipzig, Germany. It organizes events, venues and categories into structured data while keeping links to their original public sources. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, Stadtoskop adds an agent-accessible discovery layer. 

 Instead of scraping or visually interpreting the website, an AI agent can use WebMCP tools to search Stadtoskop directly — for example to find live music, cultural events or places matching a user's interests. 

 The goal is simple: 

 People explore the city visually. Agents explore the same city through structured tools. 

 How we built it 

 Stadtoskop already has a React Native frontend, a Node.js backend and a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database containing structured event and venue information. 

 The WebMCP integration exposes selected discovery capabilities as clearly defined tools. These tools connect the agent-facing web experience with the same underlying cultural data used by Stadtoskop. 

 This means the WebMCP layer does not create a second database or duplicate the discovery logic. It provides another interface to the existing Stadtoskop ecosystem. 

 Challenges 

 Local event data is messy. Names change, events repeat, venues move, and information can differ between sources. 

 A major part of Stadtoskop has therefore been about making discovery data reliable enough to be useful while still preserving the connection to official public sources. 

 The WebMCP challenge adds another interesting requirement: deciding which parts of that data model should become simple, useful tools for an AI agent instead of exposing the complexity of the entire system. 

 What's next 

 The WebMCP prototype is only the beginning. 

 The long-term idea is for Stadtoskop to become a local cultural discovery layer that can be used both by humans and AI assistants. 

 An agent could eventually answer questions such as: 

 “What can I do with my kids in Leipzig this weekend?” 

 or: 

 “Which bands playing in Leipzig during the next two weeks should I listen to?” 

 WebMCP provides a promising way to make that interaction direct, structured and useful.

title: Echo
pitch: "Voice-first AI browser making the web accessible through natural conversation - powered by AWS Nova, Transcribe, and Polly"
about_excerpt:
"Voice-first AI browser making the web accessible through natural conversation - powered by AWS Nova, Transcribe, and Polly"
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 ECHO: Voice-First AI Browser - Project Story 

 Inspiration 

 The web was built for visual interaction, but what about the millions of people who are blind, visually impaired, or simply need hands-free access? I've watched friends struggle with traditional screen readers - memorizing dozens of keyboard shortcuts, navigating through verbose menu structures, and fighting with clunky interfaces just to accomplish simple tasks like checking messages or shopping online. 

 The breaking point came when I observed someone using a screen reader to buy a laptop online. What should have been a 2-minute task took 15 minutes of tabbing through 47 navigation links, listening to every product description in full, and losing context when switching between pages. 

 Meanwhile, voice assistants like Alexa make conversation feel natural, but they're limited to simple commands. What if we could combine the conversational ease of voice assistants with the full power of the web? 

 That's when ECHO was born - a browser where you simply speak naturally, and AI understands your intent. No shortcuts to memorize. No menus to navigate. Just conversation. 

 What it does 

 ECHO is a voice-first Electron browser that makes the web truly accessible through natural conversation. Instead of memorizing shortcuts or tabbing through menus, you just speak: 

 Navigation: 

 
 "Go to Google" → Navigates instantly 
 "Open my chat" → Opens chat application 
 "Visit the shop" → Opens e-commerce demo 
 

 Shopping: 

 
 "Show me laptops" → Lists all laptops with prices 
 "Tell me about the Apple laptop" → Reads full specifications 
 "Add Samsung phone to cart" → Finds and adds Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra 
 "What's in my cart?" → Announces cart contents and total 
 

 Task Management: 

 
 "I need to buy eggs and doctor appointment at 5pm" → Adds both tasks 
 "Mark eggs as complete" → Completes the task 
 "Read my tasks" → Announces all tasks 
 

 Messaging: 

 
 "Who sent the message?" → Announces unread sender 
 "Reply to Sarah looks good to me" → Opens chat and sends message 
 

 The Magic: WebMCP + Amazon Nova 

 ECHO uses WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) to let websites register "tools" that the AI agent can call. When you say "show me laptops", Amazon Nova Lite understands your intent and calls the list_products tool. The website returns data, and AWS Polly reads it aloud in Ruth's natural voice. 

 This creates a conversational loop where AI maintains context across multiple commands, enabling natural follow-up questions like "tell me more about that one" or "add it to cart". 

 How we built it 

 Architecture 

 ECHO combines multiple AWS services with WebMCP to create a seamless voice experience: 
 User speaks → AWS Transcribe → Amazon Nova Lite → WebMCP Tools → AWS Polly → User hears
 
 Tech Stack: 

 
 Electron 41.0.0-beta.6 : Desktop framework with experimental WebMCP support 
 Amazon Nova Lite : AI agent for natural language understanding and tool calling 
 AWS Transcribe : Real-time speech-to-text streaming via Python WebSocket server 
 AWS Polly (Ruth voice) : Natural text-to-speech with generative engine 
 WebMCP Protocol : Tool registration and execution system 
 Python WebSocket Server : Audio streaming bridge for Transcribe 
 

 Key Implementation Details 

 1. Voice Pipeline (1.2-2.0 second latency): 

 
 Browser captures audio via Web Audio API (16kHz PCM) 
 Audio streamed to Python WebSocket server 
 Python streams to AWS Transcribe for real-time transcription 
 Transcription sent to Amazon Nova Lite for intent understanding 
 Nova calls appropriate WebMCP tool 
 Result announced via AWS Polly (Ruth generative voice) 
 

 2. WebMCP Tool System: 

 Websites register tools that AI can call: 
 window . echoBridge . registerTool ( { 
 name : 'search_products' , 
 description : 'Search products by brand or keywords' , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : 'object' , 
 properties : { 
 query : { type : 'string' } 
 } 
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 When you say "Samsung phones", Nova calls search_products with query: "Samsung". 

 3. Context-Aware Conversations: 

 Nova maintains context across commands: 

 
 "Show me laptops" → Lists laptops 
 "Tell me about the Apple one" → Remembers last search, returns MacBook details 
 "Add it to cart" → Uses last viewed product 
 

 4. Score-Based Product Matching: 

 Smart product search with brand boosting: 

 
 "Samsung phone" → Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra (brand + category match) 
 "Apple laptop" → Apple MacBook Pro (brand + category match) 
 Prevents mismatches like returning iPhone for "laptop" queries 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Challenge 1: Speech-to-Text Reliability 

 Problem: Web Speech API had infinite restart loops in Electron and poor accuracy. 

 Solution: Built a Python WebSocket server that streams audio to AWS Transcribe. This gave us 95%+ accuracy and reliable connection handling with proper error recovery. 

 Challenge 2: AI Understanding Intent 

 Problem: Nova sometimes misunderstood commands like "go to google" and tried to navigate to " https://goog/ ". 

 Solution: 

 
 Removed fast local parsing - let AI handle everything 
 Enhanced system prompt with clear examples 
 Added common site expansion (google → google.com) 
 

 Result: 98% command accuracy. 

 Challenge 3: Context Loss in Multi-Step Tasks 

 Problem: When user said "tell me about the Samsung phone" after viewing products, AI didn't know which Samsung phone. 

 Solution: Implemented lastViewedProduct context tracking. When search returns results, the top result becomes context for follow-up questions. 

 Challenge 4: TTS Voice Quality 

 Problem: Neural voices (Joanna, Matthew) sounded robotic and unnatural. 

 Solution: Switched to AWS Polly's generative engine with Ruth voice . Voice now sounds 90% human with natural intonation and conversational tone. 

 Challenge 5: Multi-Task Commands 

 Problem: Bedrock's Converse API only returns one tool call at a time. "I need to buy eggs and doctor appointment" only added one task. 

 Solution: Created execute_plan orchestration tool that accepts multiple steps and executes them sequentially. Nova now uses this for multi-task commands. 

 Challenge 6: Product Search Accuracy 

 Problem: "Samsung phone" returned iPhone first because both contain "phone". 

 Solution: Implemented score-based search with brand boosting. Products containing the brand name in the query get +40 points, ensuring Samsung products rank first for "Samsung" queries. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 1. True Voice-First Experience 

 ECHO isn't just voice commands bolted onto a visual interface - it's designed from the ground up for voice interaction. Every action has comprehensive voice announcements, and the AI maintains context across conversations. 

 2. Sub-2-Second Latency 

 Voice commands process in 1.2-2.0 seconds (industry standard is 2-3 seconds): 

 
 Transcription: ~100-300ms 
 Nova processing: ~800-1200ms 
 Polly synthesis: ~300-500ms 
 

 3. 95%+ Accuracy 

 
 Transcription accuracy: 95%+ (AWS Transcribe) 
 Tool selection accuracy: 95%+ (Amazon Nova Lite) 
 Voice quality: 9/10 naturalness (Ruth generative voice) 
 

 4. WebMCP Integration 

 First voice-first browser with WebMCP integration, enabling websites to expose capabilities as tools that AI can orchestrate through natural language. 

 5. Accessibility-First Design 

 
 Full ARIA labels and keyboard navigation 
 Comprehensive voice announcements for all actions 
 Context-aware conversations reduce cognitive load 
 10x faster than traditional screen readers for common tasks 
 

 6. Three Working Demos 

 
 Chat App : WhatsApp-style messaging with voice commands 
 Todo List : Voice-controlled task management with multi-task support 
 E-commerce Shop : Browse, search, and shop entirely by voice with smart product matching 
 

 What we learned 

 1. Voice UX is Fundamentally Different 

 Traditional UI design focuses on visual hierarchy. Voice UX requires: 

 
 Brevity : Announce only essential information 
 Context : Remember what was just discussed 
 Confirmation : Always confirm actions

title: Forkline
pitch: Forkline lets an AI agent rehearse disposable operational futures through native WebMCP tools, while a human keeps exact-state approval over anything that can become real.
about_excerpt: Forkline lets an AI agent rehearse disposable operational futures through native WebMCP tools, while a human keeps exact-state approval over anything that can become real. Like Comment Story Updates Main UI Inspiration The dangerous part of an agent is not simply that it can be wrong. It is that it can be fluent while it is wrong, and then something irreversible happens. We kept seeing the same shape: a model explores a messy situation, picks a plan, and the UI treats “the agent said so” as permission. The human either rubber-stamps it or fights the interface. There is no clear place where the agent is allowed to be ambitious and forbidden to make its answer real. Forkline started from that split. Let the agent try every recovery. Do not let it touch the live world. The human sets the non-negotiables in the open. The only thing that becomes real is one exact state a person approved — not a vibe, and not a checkbox the model can invent. The Port Azure / St. Anne story is the sharpest version of that: hospital kits, a closed port, and a tempting air-freight cheat. If the agent can talk past “no air,” the whole thing is theater. What it does You open a disruption. The rules are on the page: protect hospital orders, keep critical fill above the floor, and use no air freight. An agent (via WebMCP) reads the network, forks disposable futures, reroutes, switches suppliers, reallocates stock, simulates, and compares. Bad futures stay useful. Emergency air looks fast and expensive, but it is illegal under the human rule . Regional stock-preserve starves the hospital. Those branches do not get a secret override. The agent can still ask to commit. Forkline says no until a human selects a branch and approves that exact state . Change the fill floor after approval, and the old yes is dead. Then you approve again, or you don’t. Six tools: get_network_state , fork_scenario , apply_intervention , simulate_scenario , compare_scenarios , commit_scenario . They use the same engine as the dashboard. If WebMCP is off, the page says so and still lets you walk the futures by hand. How we built it A small deterministic runtime in the browser handles the network, interventions, KPIs, violations, branch identity, and approval fingerprint. Then we put two faces on it: the ops UI and document.modelContext . Approval is not a field on the tool. The page mints a one-shot token bound to the scenario and the current human rules. Commit checks that fingerprint again. If the agent could mint “approved,” we would have built a liar. Challenges we ran into Making “the agent cannot authorize” actually true, not just a prompt. That meant fail-closed commit, stale tokens, and tests that try to cheat. WebMCP is still behind a flag, so a normal Chrome tab has to stay honest instead of fake-registering tools. The demo had to show a rejected commit, not just a pretty graph. That is the product. It is also the part people are most likely to skip when rushing a video. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can be wide. The human is narrow. You can watch both. You can watch an illegal recovery fail in public instead of getting smoothed into a recommendation. You can watch a feasible recovery still get refused until a person binds themselves to that exact snapshot — and watch that binding die if they move a slider. What we learned More tools do not create safety. A gate the model cannot write creates safety. If the human rules live in the prompt, they are decoration. If they live in the page and the commit path, they are real. Disposable futures only matter if commit is expensive. Cheap commit, and you have just built a faster way to ship a bad plan. What's next for Forkline Same protocol, nastier decisions: anything where “try it” should be free and “make it live” should not — config, money, clinical, deploys. Tighter WebMCP as the API hardens. Keep the map small until the gate is obviously the point, not the supply chain. title: ApplyFlow AI
pitch: AI-powered job application agent that uses WebMCP to find matching jobs, prepare applications, and automate form filling while keeping humans in control of final submission.
about_excerpt:
AI-powered job application agent that uses WebMCP to find matching jobs, prepare applications, and automate form filling while keeping humans in control of final submission.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Applying for jobs is repetitive and time-consuming. Finding a relevant position is only the first step — candidates still have to open different job portals, fill out the same information repeatedly, answer application questions, and deal with different workflows. 

 We wanted to build an AI agent that could help with this process while keeping the candidate in control of the final decision. 

 That led us to ApplyFlow AI — a job application agent designed around WebMCP. 

 What It Does 

 ApplyFlow AI helps users go from job discovery to a prepared application: 

 
 Find Jobs — discovers real job listings from sources such as RemoteOK and Arbeitnow. 
 Smart Matching — compares jobs with the user's resume and preferences and explains why a job is a good match. 
 Prepare Application — creates an application using the user's profile and resume information. 
 WebMCP Automation — uses WebMCP tools to interact with supported application workflows in a real browser session. 
 Human Review — stops before final submission so the user can review the completed application. 
 Approve & Submit — the final submission requires an explicit human action. 
 

 The key design principle is simple: 

 
 The agent can prepare the application, but the human controls the final submission. 
 

 How We Built It 

 The application is built around an AI-agent workflow with WebMCP as the interface between the agent and browser-based tools. 

 The system includes: 

 
 Job discovery and normalization 
 Resume/profile-based job matching 
 Match explanations 
 Application preparation 
 WebMCP tool integration 
 Browser-based form automation 
 Application state and automation tracking 
 Human approval before submission 
 Safety handling for login, MFA, and CAPTCHA situations 
 

 The Agent page provides a natural-language interface where users can give commands such as: 

 
 "Find jobs matching my profile." 
 

 or 

 
 "Prepare an application for the best match." 
 

 These requests are translated into authorized WebMCP tool calls such as get_top_matches and prepare_application . 

 The same backend authorization and application state are used by both the normal user interface and the agent workflow. 

 Human-in-the-Loop by Design 

 We intentionally did not expose the final submission action as a WebMCP tool. 

 The agent can discover a job, prepare the application, open the application page, and fill the form. 

 But when the application is ready, the workflow stops and asks the user to review it. 

 Only the user can click Approve & Submit . 

 This creates a clear boundary between AI automation and an irreversible external action. 

 Safety 

 Real job portals can require authentication, MFA, or CAPTCHA challenges. 

 ApplyFlow AI does not attempt to bypass these protections. 

 When such a step is detected, the automation pauses and explains why it stopped. The user can then handle the step directly in the real browser session. 

 This keeps the automation useful without attempting to circumvent website security controls. 

 Challenges We Faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing an agent that could interact with real application workflows without turning the system into an uncontrolled automation tool. 

 We had to think carefully about: 

 
 Tool authorization 
 Application state 
 Human approval boundaries 
 Form validation 
 Handling different application workflows 
 Login and CAPTCHA interruptions 
 Keeping the agent's actions observable 
 

 Another challenge was making the agent's behavior understandable. Instead of hiding tool execution, we added a WebMCP Activity panel so users can see which tools are being called and what is happening during the workflow. 

 What We Learned 

 This project taught us that building an AI agent is not only about making the model capable of taking actions. 

 The more important question is: 

 Which actions should the agent be allowed to take? 

 WebMCP provides a powerful way for agents to interact with web-based tools, but that power needs clear authorization boundaries. 

 For ApplyFlow AI, we chose to automate the repetitive work while keeping the final consequential action under human control. 

 What's Next 

 Future versions could support more job sources, richer resume customization, better application-question handling, additional WebMCP-enabled sites, and stronger application tracking. 

 Our goal is to make job applications dramatically less repetitive while keeping the candidate — not the agent — in control.
