title: Polkaswap
pitch: Browser agents discover assets, quote routes, and build fresh swap plans without wallet access.
about_excerpt: Browser agents discover assets, quote routes, and build fresh swap plans without wallet access. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a swap involves identifying assets, reading precise amounts, comparing routes, and checking fees, price impact, and freshness. We wanted browser agents to obtain those facts directly from the exchange and explain them through a structured, inspectable interface. Polkaswap already connects people to SORA liquidity. WebMCP lets an agent use that same application to build a useful plan while wallet access remains a separate decision. What it does Polkaswap exposes nine public WebMCP tools for capabilities, status, readiness, asset search and resolution, common assets, quotes, unsigned swap plans, and pool information. An agent can respond to “Plan swapping 1 XOR for VAL with 0.5% slippage” by calling polkaswap_plan_swap directly. It waits for the node, resolves assets, obtains a fresh quote, and returns the route, amount bounds, fee estimate when available, warnings, expiry, network context, and unsigned SDK-call metadata. Unavailable fees produce an explicit warning. No wallet connection or prior quote-button click is required. People can inspect the same planning workflow in the agent playground. Changing the pair or amount refreshes the plan automatically; visible pages also refresh expired plans. A switch stops automatic planning. The interface prevents older responses from overwriting newer inputs. Public tools cannot expose account identity or balances, connect a wallet, create an executable intent, sign, submit, transfer funds, or change liquidity. Plans return mode: "unsigned" , canExecute: false , and requiresWallet: false . The preview is SDK-call metadata, not a SCALE-encoded transaction. This entry provides autonomous planning, with no unattended trading. How we built it The implementation uses Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, the existing SORA SDK and node connection, and FPNumber for precise token amounts. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() when WebMCP is available. The playground registers its tools at the top level and forwards calls into its same-origin application iframe. Strict schemas require decimal-string amounts and reject additional properties. Public result projection excludes wallet and provider details. Cancellation, bounded errors, network-context checks, and five-minute expiry keep planning results predictable. No executable authorization is stored by planning. Everything ships as static assets suitable for IPFS, without hosted command middleware. An optional local Node.js stdio MCP bridge shares the same public catalogue. Humans use visible controls and agents use named tools, with both reaching the application's existing planning logic. Challenges we addressed Browser agents do not discover tools registered inside the playground iframe, so discovery needed a top-level adapter. Useful market results also needed careful separation from the application's broader wallet-aware API. Planning introduced timing problems: inputs can change during a quote, results can expire, and pages can become hidden. The scheduler serializes requests, ignores superseded results, pauses while hidden, and bounds retries for transient failures. Accomplishments Native verification of the published build discovered all nine tools and directly invoked polkaswap_plan_swap . It returned an unsigned live SORA plan without wallet access. The page planner also refreshed from 1 to 2 XOR and stopped automatic refresh when disabled. The clean submission passed 306 focused tests across 21 files, 13 translation tests across four files, and nine preview-helper tests. The official Node MCP stdio check discovered all nine schemas. A separate browser registration-harness smoke verified planning and input-change replanning with zero captured console, request, or HTTP errors. Existing project and challenge contribution Polkaswap is an existing open-source exchange. Its exchange UI, SORA integration, wallet workflows, static deployment infrastructure, and earlier browser-agent foundation predate this contribution. The August 25–September 3, 2026 challenge contribution adds the public WebMCP catalogue and adapters, wallet-independent swap planning, the agent playground and automatic replanning behavior, and supporting tests and documentation. The linked public comparison identifies the changes from baseline 893783b to submission commit 4955eb0 . What's next We want clearer multi-route comparisons, more useful public market reads, and better explanations when node data is temporarily unavailable. Signing and execution remain outside the public WebMCP tools. title: AssayLens-XTT Cell Viability Assay App
pitch: A browser-based XTT plate-analysis app that delivers exploratory image-derived metabolic-activity insights with transparent QC, mapped controls, and WebMCP-assisted setup.
about_excerpt: A browser-based XTT plate-analysis app that delivers exploratory image-derived metabolic-activity insights with transparent QC, mapped controls, and WebMCP-assisted setup. Like Comment Story Updates Well anchoring Plate mapping Results analysis Inspiration Reading a 96-well XTT plate from a photograph can be useful for exploratory drug discovery work, but it is easy to overinterpret color, overlook glare, lose track of controls, or confuse a plate map with a validated biological conclusion. We built AssayLens to make the workflow more transparent: keep the image, geometry, plate map, controls, quality-control signals, and interpretation limits visible together. To the best of our knowledge, AssayLens is a first of its kind app providing streamlined workflow of image analysis for XTT cell viability assay. What it does AssayLens is a browser-based application for exploratory image analysis of XTT 96-well plates and agar endpoint spot assays. For XTT workflows, a user can load a plate image, confirm well geometry, map samples and serial dilutions, assign growth controls and reagent blanks, review well-level QC, and generate image-derived relative metabolic-activity results. The app also includes a narrow WebMCP integration that lets a browser agent inspect readiness, configure a dilution series, assign controls, run the existing analysis, and focus the highest-priority QC item. AssayLens intentionally does not present its results as calibrated plate-reader absorbance, viable-cell counts, validated MIC values, efficacy evidence, or clinical conclusions. Human review remains essential. How we built it We built AssayLens as a browser-local React and TypeScript application powered by Vite, Vitest, and browser workers. The image-analysis workflow runs in the browser, helping keep plate images, raw pixels, local paths, and API keys out of WebMCP tool outputs. The WebMCP layer exposes five bounded, page-owned tools: Inspect XTT workflow readiness and scientific limits Configure horizontal serial-dilution series Assign explicit XTT controls and normalization groups Run the existing exploratory image-analysis worker Focus the most important QC review item Tool-driven plate-map changes use the same application state as the visible editor, so the map, Selection panel, and Serial dilution panel remain synchronized. Challenges we ran into The key challenge was balancing useful automation with scientific restraint. We wanted an agent to help configure and inspect an assay workflow without allowing it to invent results, silently change scientific assumptions, or bypass human image and QC review. We also addressed an image-QC edge case involving deep-red XTT wells. A simplistic clipping rule could treat naturally low blue or green pixel values as invalid, even when the well image was usable. We refined the QC logic to preserve meaningful chromatic pixels while retaining diagnostics for genuine clipping, glare, transparent regions, and near-black pixels. Another challenge was ensuring that WebMCP mutations were not merely hidden state changes. We connected them directly to the visible plate editor so users can immediately verify what changed. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that AssayLens combines practical browser-based assay workflow support with explicit guardrails. The application makes controls, normalization groups, plate geometry, excluded wells, warnings, and review priorities visible instead of hiding them behind a single automated result. What we learned We learned that good scientific software should communicate uncertainty as clearly as it communicates results. A successful workflow is not just one that produces an output—it is one that makes the input quality, assumptions, controls, and limitations easy for a human reviewer to inspect. We also learned that agent tooling is most useful when it works alongside an existing, visible user interface. Bounded tools, strict input validation, atomic map updates, and clear state synchronization make automation more trustworthy and easier to audit. What's next for AssayLens-XTT Cell Viability Assay App Next, we plan to continue improving the image-QC and review experience, expand reproducible reporting workflows, and refine assay-specific guidance while preserving the app’s exploratory scientific scope. We will keep focusing on transparent, human-reviewed workflows rather than overstating what image-derived assay analysis can prove. More examples of WebMCP integration can be found in Lab Studio , RoboBuddy IDE , and RoboStudio Circuits . Even if I cannot submit them all, they show how human-visible, bounded agent capabilities can extend across robotics, science, and education. title: PlanOnIt
pitch: PlanOnIt gives a WebMCP agent real tools to plan your evening out — film, transport, dinner — while you keep the final approval.
about_excerpt: PlanOnIt gives a WebMCP agent real tools to plan your evening out — film, transport, dinner — while you keep the final approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a small, concrete domain to actually test what WebMCP makes possible, instead of a demo that just claims an agent did something. Planning a night out — a film, then dinner after — is a real multi-constraint problem: the showtime fixes the cinema, the cinema fixes the route, the route decides how much time is really left before the table, and every one of those choices moves the total cost. It's exactly the kind of thing an agent is good at grinding through and a person is good at approving. Most "agentic" demos I'd seen were either a chat box bolted onto a UI it couldn't see, or an agent with unchecked authority to just click "book." I wanted the version where the agent gets real capabilities and the person still holds the only button that matters. What it does PlanOnIt plans a real evening out in Dhaka — a film, the trip across the city, and dinner after — with an AI agent doing the tedious cross-referencing through 13 WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. The agent can search restaurants and showtimes, build a plan, check feasibility, calculate cost, and repair a plan a human edit just broke. It can never approve or reserve anything — that stays a real click in the UI, every time. Once approved, reservation is a genuine sandboxed transaction: a compare-and-swap against shared inventory, idempotent on retry, and it fails closed on conflict instead of quietly double-booking. How we built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite on the frontend, Zod for runtime validation, deployed as a static build to Vercel. The core decision was to build one domain layer ( src/domain.ts ) that both the human UI and the WebMCP tools call into — the same solver, the same nine feasibility checks, the same versioned mutations — so there's never a "friendly explanation for the person" that can quietly drift from "the raw check the agent gets." Every mutation carries an expectedVersion ; a stale write fails loudly with STALE_PLAN_VERSION instead of silently overwriting someone else's edit, whether that edit came from a human or another agent call. Same-origin tabs stay in sync through a Web Locks-backed compare-and-swap. Inventory sits inside a rolling two-week window computed off the real clock, so the demo never goes stale no matter when a judge opens it. Challenges we ran into The one I'm least proud of, and gladdest I caught before submitting: late in the build I found that a human could never manually pick a transport option — every click failed with "Transport option does not belong to the selected venue route." The agent's tools worked fine, and so did the auto-repair path, which made it easy to miss. It turned out the manual UI was resolving the cinema-to-restaurant route with the two location IDs swapped, and since each direction generates its own distinct set of transport-option IDs, the buttons on screen were always offering IDs from the wrong route object. It only ever broke the human path — a good reminder that "the agent's tools work" and "the manual UI works" are two separate claims, and testing one doesn't verify the other. I added a regression test that reproduces the exact failure so it can't come back silently. Building a reservation that's an actual transaction, not just a returned success string, was its own challenge: idempotency keys are bound to the reservation's content fingerprint, not just a request ID, so a retry after a dropped connection can't accidentally create a second booking, and a replayed or forged confirmation can't be pointed at a different reservation. And a last-minute one that had nothing to do with code: my original LICENSE restricted commercial use without permission, which meant it wasn't actually an open-source license, even though I'd always intended it to be. Caught and fixed to MIT before submission — "open source" has to be literally detectable, not just intended. Accomplishments that we're proud of 198 automated tests plus 21 real-browser Playwright tests, covering adversarial input, concurrency, the full reservation lifecycle, and idempotency — not just the happy path. The evaluation-symmetry property: the UI's "why isn't this plan valid yet" and the agent's validate_plan tool result are always the same function call against the same state. There's no second copy of the business logic that could quietly disagree with the first. Approval isn't gated by a permission check the agent could theoretically satisfy — it's architecturally absent from the tool surface. No WebMCP tool touches approval at all. Shipping with no login requirement, on purpose. It would have been easy to bolt on accounts to look more "complete," but this build doesn't actually need cross-device sync to do its job, so I didn't fake it. What we learned That "the agent works" has to be tested completely separately from "the human path works" — they share code, but a single reversed argument can break only one of them, silently. That documentation drifts fast: numbers like "12 tools" or "eight checks" written once during development go stale the moment the code moves on, and are worth re-deriving from the running code rather than trusting memory. And that the strongest trust story for an agentic feature isn't a more polite prompt — it's an architectural boundary the agent literally cannot cross, like approval never being expressed as a tool at all. What's next for PlanOnIt A real server-authoritative reservation boundary. The extension point already exists ( RemoteReservationAuthority in src/authority.ts ), but no concrete server ships in this build — a public browser bundle can't hold a shared bearer secret without a real per-user session, and I'd rather ship nothing than ship authentication theater. Real inventory behind the restaurants, cinemas, and routes, in place of the Dhaka sandbox data. A repair flow that explains the alternatives it considered and rejected, not just the plan it landed on.
